example: After years of quiet preparation, his novel became an overnight sensation
chineseExample: 经过多年默默准备，他的小说一夜成名
description: King Zhuang of Chu spent three years on the throne issuing no orders at all. An officer put him a riddle about a bird that for three years had neither stirred its wings nor called, and the king answered that though it had not flown, when it flew it would reach the heavens, and though it had not cried (鸣), when it cried it would startle (惊) everyone (人). Han Feizi tells that version. The Records of the Grand Historian carries a second one in its chapter on jesters, where Chunyu Kun puts the same riddle to King Wei of Qi and gets the sharper wording that became the idiom — 此鸟不飞则已，一飞冲天；不鸣则已，一鸣惊人. The first half is what supplies the years of apparent idleness that make the phrase mean more than sudden success.
description_tr: King Zhuang of Chu spent three years on the throne issuing no orders at all. Han Feizi tells that version. The Records of the Grand Historian carries a second one in its chapter on jesters, where Chunyu Kun puts the same riddle to King Wei of Qi and gets the sharper wording that became the idiom — 此鳥不飛則已，一飛沖天；不鳴則已，一鳴驚人. The first half is what supplies the years of apparent idleness that make the phrase mean more than sudden success.
chineseExample_tr: 經過多年默默準備，他的小說一夜成名

example: After years of study, she finally understood how all the concepts connected

description: Zhu Xi gave the phrase its lasting sense in the collected works, describing the point a student reaches after long effort and thorough investigation, when the separate things learned melt together (融会) and run right through (贯通) one another — raise one corner and get three back, hear one thing and know ten. The image is metal fused into a single body and a thread passed through many coins. It describes knowledge that has stopped being a collection and become a working whole.
description_tr: Zhu Xi gave the phrase its lasting sense in the collected works, describing the point a student reaches after long effort and thorough investigation, when the separate things learned melt together (融會) and run right through (貫通) one another — raise one corner and get three back, hear one thing and know ten. The image is metal fused into a single body and a thread passed through many coins. It describes knowledge that has stopped being a collection and become a working whole.
chineseExample_tr: 經過多年學習，她終於理解了所有概念之間的聯繫

meaning: Ocean of learning has no shores
example: Even at 80, she continues to learn new things every day
chineseExample: 即使八十岁了，她每天仍在学习新东西
description: This is from the second half of a well-known couplet, 书山有路勤为径，学海无涯苦作舟 — the mountain of books has a path, and diligence is that path; the sea (海) of learning (学) has no shore (无涯), and hard work is the boat. It is popularly attributed to the Tang essayist Han Yu, though the attribution is traditional rather than documented. The point is not that learning is hopeless but that it has no natural stopping place, so the only way across is to keep working. Modern usage encourages sustained study rather than the expectation of ever being finished.
description_tr: This comes from the second half of a well-known couplet, 書山有路勤為徑，學海無涯苦作舟 — the mountain of books has a path, and diligence is that path; the sea (海) of learning (學) has no shore (無涯), and hard work is the boat. The point is not that learning is hopeless but that it has no natural stopping place, so the only way across is to keep working. Modern usage encourages sustained study rather than the expectation of ever being finished.
chineseExample_tr: 即使八十歲了，她每天仍在學習新東西

example: The twins dress so similarly that their teachers can't tell them apart

description: One (一) mould (模) and one (一) appearance (样) — two castings taken from the same form, which in bronze work means they are not merely similar but the same object twice. Note the reading: 模 is mú here, not mó, and learners who know it only from 模型 tend to get it wrong. The phrase is neutral about whether identity is good. It praises precision when applied to a matched pair, and it is equally at home as a complaint about buildings, essays or opinions that could all have come from one form.

example: Despite numerous rejections, she never gave up on her dreams

description: Cai Yong wrote it on Qiao Xuan's memorial stele: his nature was grave, he disliked show and held to the plain, and he had the bearing of a man who could be broken (折) a hundred (百) times and would not (不) bend (挠), who faced a crisis and could not be moved from his ground. 折 is setbacks rather than bamboo — the image is of a person struck repeatedly, not a plant flexing. What is being praised is that the shape does not change under force, and modern usage keeps exactly that.

meaning: Knowledge and action unite as one
example: He doesn't just talk about environmental protection, he lives it

description: Wang Yangming worked the doctrine out during his exile in Guizhou and taught it from 1508: knowing (知) and acting (行) are one (合一) rather than two stages. His claim is stronger than an exhortation to put things into practice — he holds that knowledge which has not issued in action was never knowledge at all, only an opinion about it, so a man who knows what filial conduct is and does not perform it does not in fact know it. That collapses the excuse of weak will, which is exactly what it was built to do. Chinese now uses the phrase of applying principles in practice, in a considerably milder sense than Wang intended.

example: Their journey to success had many unexpected challenges

description: Wang Xizhi, writing on brush method, said that in making a single wave-stroke (一波) the brush turns three times (三折) — the long diagonal that ends a character is not one movement but three changes of direction, and a stroke drawn straight is dead. The phrase left calligraphy for narrative and now describes anything that reached its end by a route with bends in it. It gets used of negotiations, applications and journeys, and it implies arrival as well as difficulty.

example: With consistent practice, she finally mastered the difficult skill
chineseExample: 通过持续练习，她终于掌握了这项难度很大的技能
description: The Song collection Helin Yulu attaches this to the magistrate Zhang Guaiya, who had a clerk flogged for a single copper coin, was told he would not dare behead him for it, and wrote the judgment before doing exactly that: a coin a day is a thousand coins in a thousand days, and 绳锯木断，水滴石穿 — a rope used as a saw cuts through wood, and water (水) dripping (滴) bores through (穿) stone (石). The two clauses are a fixed pair. The Book of Han has the older observation that water is no drill and wears stone away by sheer continuance. Chinese uses it for study, saving, and any effort whose instalments are visibly too small to matter.

example: After understanding this principle, she could solve similar problems easily
chineseExample: 理解了这个原理后，她能轻松解决类似的问题
description: Confucius, in the Analects, said he did not go on teaching a man who, shown one corner, could not come back (反) with the other three (三) — 举一隅不以三隅反，则不复也. The image is a square: you are given one corner and expected to supply the rest. It is a statement about what a teacher owes and what a student must bring, and it is unusually blunt about the second. Chinese uses it as high praise for a learner and, in the negative, as a quiet judgement on one.
description_tr: Confucius, in the Analects, said he did not go on teaching a man who, shown one corner, could not come back (反) with the other three (三) — 舉一隅不以三隅反，則不復也. chineseExample_tr: 理解了這個原理後，她能輕鬆解決類似的問題

example: The new restaurant was so popular that it was always packed with customers
chineseExample: 这家新餐厅很受欢迎，总是顾客盈门
description: Zou Ji persuaded King Wei of Qi that everyone around him had a reason to flatter him, and the king proclaimed rewards for anyone who would name his faults. At first the gate and courtyard (门庭) were as crowded as a market (若市). After some months people still came, but only now and then; after a full year there was nothing left for anyone to submit. The phrase preserves the crowd at its height and drops the rest of the curve. Chinese applies it to a shop, an office or a household that visitors will not stop arriving at, and it is a compliment about demand rather than about the visitors.

meaning: Turn from wrong return to right
example: After the scandal, the company implemented strict ethical guidelines
chineseExample: 在丑闻之后，公司实施了严格的道德准则
description: Turning away (改) from what is wrong (邪) and returning (归) to what is right (正). The force sits in 归: rightness is treated as the place a person came from and can go back to, not somewhere new they have to be argued into. Vernacular fiction and drama supply the phrase, and there it marks a moment rather than a process — the bandit puts down the knife, the swindler shuts the shop. Chinese still uses it that way, with an expectation attached that the change is meant to be permanent, which is why it sounds far too heavy for ordinary self-improvement.

chineseExample_tr: 在醜聞之後，公司實施了嚴格的道德準則

example: The team's productivity suffered from members who avoided challenging tasks

description: To love (好) ease (逸) and hate (恶) toil (劳). The two verbs are the point: this is not laziness as a failing of will but as a preference, something the phrase presents as the ordinary human default rather than a vice peculiar to the person being described. That makes it a diagnosis more than an insult. Chinese uses it in arguments about incentives and education, where the assumption behind it is that effort has to be built against the grain rather than expected.

example: Her years of hard work finally paid off with a major breakthrough

description: Heaven's way (天道) repays (酬) diligence (勤). 酬 is the word for requiting a debt or returning a toast, so the claim is transactional: the effort is owed something, and the universe is the party that settles. That is a stronger position than simply hoping hard work pays off, and it is close to the argument of the Book of Changes that the noble person imitates heaven's unceasing motion. It is one of the most commonly written phrases in Chinese calligraphy, and it hangs in a great many classrooms and offices.

example: After the market peaked, a correction was inevitable
chineseExample: 市场达到顶峰后，调整是不可避免的
description: When a thing (物) reaches its extreme (极) it must (必) turn back (反). The formula is put most plainly in the Lüshi Chunqiu, which argues that the ruler should not occupy the complete, the extreme or the full, because what is complete will be broken, what is extreme will reverse, and what is full will drain away. It is not fatalism: it is a warning against pressing an advantage all the way to its limit, on the grounds that the limit is precisely where the advantage begins to work backwards. In practice it is used of markets, of political dominance and of personal habits, usually at the moment somebody is winning too comfortably to notice.

description: Confucius, in the Analects: 温故而知新，可以为师矣 — one who warms (温) the old (故) and thereby knows (知) the new (新) is fit to be a teacher. 温 is the word for reheating food, so the image is of returning to what you already have rather than acquiring more. The claim is specific and quite demanding: review alone is not enough, and the test is whether something new comes out of it. The final clause is why the phrase belongs to teaching, and it is usually left off in modern use.

description: In 207 BCE Xiang Yu took his army across the river to relieve Julu, and then had the boats (舟) sunk (沉) and the cooking pots (釜) smashed (破), keeping three days' rations and nothing else. The Records of the Grand Historian is explicit that this was done to show the troops they would die rather than turn back. He won. What the four characters describe is not courage but the deliberate destruction of one's own options, which is a decision taken before the fighting rather than during it. It gets used of any commitment made by removing the way back.

example: Losing his job led him to find his true calling

description: The Huainanzi tells of a man living out by the frontier, known ever since as the Old Man of the Frontier — 塞翁, from 塞, a border pass, and 翁, an old man. His horse (马) was lost (失), simply ran off. His neighbours came to console him and he asked how they knew it was not good fortune; the horse returned bringing a fine wild one. They congratulated him and he asked how they knew it was not disaster; his son was thrown from it and broke his thigh. They consoled him again — and when the frontier levies came, the lame son stayed home while nine in ten of the conscripts died. The saying is almost always given in full as 塞翁失马，焉知非福 — the old man lost his horse; how do you know it is not a blessing?

description: Su Lin, a minor officer under Fan Zhongyan, was passed over while Fan promoted others around him, and presented a couplet instead of a complaint: 近水楼台先得月，向阳花木易为春 — the tower (楼台) nearest (近) the water (水) gets the moon first, and flowers facing the sun come to spring early. Fan took the point and promoted him. The phrase names advantage that comes from position rather than merit, and it is usually said with a trace of resentment by whoever is further from the water.

example: The young researcher's innovations built upon and ultimately surpassed her mentor's original theories

description: Xunzi opens his chapter on learning with it: 青，取之于蓝，而青于蓝 — blue (青) is taken from (出于) the indigo plant (蓝), and is bluer than the plant. The point is the student's, not the teacher's: nothing is being criticised, and the dye is better precisely because the plant existed. Common speech runs it as 青出于蓝而胜于蓝, adding the surpassing explicitly. It is used of pupils outdoing masters and children outdoing parents, and it is always a compliment to both.

example: The company welcomed diverse perspectives and ideas

description: The sea (海) takes in (纳) a hundred (百) rivers (川) and is still the sea — that is the whole argument, and it is why the image is the sea and not a lake. The line is Lin Zexu's, the first half of a couplet normally quoted whole: 海纳百川，有容乃大；壁立千仞，无欲则刚 — the sea admits a hundred rivers, and capacity is what makes it great; the cliff stands a thousand fathoms, and wanting nothing is what makes it unyielding. He wrote it in 1839, in the weeks before the opium seizures at Humen. It attaches to people who can absorb difference without losing their own shape.

example: Having never left his small town, he thought his local success made him world-class
chineseExample: 从未离开过小城镇的他，以为本地的成功就意味着世界级水平
description: Yelang (夜郎) was a small state on the southwestern frontier of the Han empire. The Records of the Grand Historian relates that when a Han envoy reached it, its king asked whether Yelang or Han was the larger — a question that makes sense only to someone who has never left his own valley. The phrase fixes that moment: to be self-important (自大) in the manner of Yelang. What it targets is not arrogance in general but the particular kind produced by isolation, where the standard of comparison is simply too small. It is aimed at people, companies and institutions that mistake being the biggest thing in view for being big.

example: His kindness to others eventually came back to benefit him

description: Cause (因), effect (果), and the returning repayment (报应). The vocabulary is Buddhist and entered Chinese with the translated sutras, bringing with it a moral mechanics quite different from the older Chinese idea of heaven's mandate: consequence here is impersonal, exact, and not necessarily settled within one lifetime. That last part is what the ordinary Chinese use has dropped. Today it usually means simply that what someone did has caught up with them, and it is said with satisfaction more often than with piety.

description: Zhang Sengyou painted four dragons on a temple wall in Jinling and left them without pupils, saying that if he dotted the eyes they would fly away. Pressed, he dotted two. Dotting (点) the eyes (睛) of the dragon (画龙) therefore names the last small addition that turns a competent thing into a live one — a sentence in a report, a detail in a design.

description: A boat (舟) worked (行) against (逆) the current (水). What makes the image exact is that holding position is not a rest state: the river is doing work on the hull whether or not anyone is rowing, so standing still costs the same effort as moving and achieves less. It is standard in Chinese writing about study, training and competitive markets.

example: She broadened her perspective through extensive reading

description: This is from the couplet 读万卷书，行万里路 — read (读) ten thousand (万) scrolls (卷书), walk ten thousand li — made famous by the Ming painter and critic Dong Qichang, who used it in his writing on painting; a Yuan-dynasty verse by Fang Hui has it earlier still. It is often misattributed to Du Fu, who wrote something different: 读书破万卷，下笔如有神, on reading wearing out ten thousand scrolls until the brush moves as if inspired. Ten thousand is not literal; in Classical Chinese it stands for an exhaustive quantity. The pairing matters, since reading alone was never the whole prescription. Modern usage argues that study and direct experience each finish what the other starts.

example: The small company found itself facing competition from all sides

description: This poignant idiom originates from the final battle of Xiang Yu in 202 BCE. Surrounded by Han forces at Gaixia, Xiang Yu heard songs (歌) of his homeland Chu (楚) being sung from all four sides (四面), indicating his own people had surrendered to Liu Bang. The psychological warfare strategy proved devastating – hearing familiar Chu melodies from enemy camps broke Xiang Yu's spirit. The term evolved beyond its military origins to describe situations where someone faces complete isolation or overwhelming opposition. In modern usage, it often depicts professional or personal scenarios where former allies have become adversaries, or when someone finds themselves alone in their convictions. The idiom carries a particular resonance in corporate politics and social movements, where shifting allegiances can leave individuals suddenly isolated.

It is used almost entirely of oneself, offering a first rough idea to provoke better ones, and it is a modesty formula rather than a description of anyone else's contribution.

example: The community united to help those affected by the disaster

description: This idiom shares deep connections with China's river-centric civilization, where crossing (济) together (共) in the same boat (同舟) was often a matter of life and death. Ancient texts tell of strangers becoming allies when facing treacherous waters, especially along the mighty Yangtze. During the Three Kingdoms period, multiple accounts describe opposing armies cooperating to navigate dangerous rapids. The imagery powerfully conveys mutual dependence and collective survival. Modern applications extend to corporate partnerships, international cooperation on global challenges, and community resilience during crises. The idiom emphasizes that differences become secondary when facing shared challenges – whether environmental disasters, economic hardships, or social upheavals.

description: Sharing a boat (同舟) through wind (风) and rain (雨). The Sunzi supplies the underlying observation: the men of Wu and the men of Yue hate one another, but caught in the same boat in a gale they will help each other like the left hand and the right. That is the argument the phrase carries — not that the parties are friends, but that the boat makes the question irrelevant for as long as the weather lasts. In practice it is used of partnerships and marriages that came through something bad together, and it is warmer than 同舟共济, which stays closer to a statement of necessity.

Mencius's point is about timing, not technique: the same work done when conditions are ready yields disproportionately more. Chinese uses it of an approach that gets more out of less, and it usually loses the original point, which credited the moment rather than the method.

description: A verse of the Tang Chan master Changsha Jingcen, recorded in the Jingde Chuandenglu: a man at the top of a hundred-foot (百尺) pole (竿头) has attained something, but it is not yet real — he must step forward from there. The phrase is nearly always used in its full form 百尺竿头，更进一步, and it is what Chinese says to someone who has just done well, which makes it encouragement and a warning in the same breath.

The idiom therefore recommends something its source gently mocks — deliberation past the point of usefulness is its own failure. Modern usage advises careful thought before acting, and has entirely lost Confucius's reply.

It is what former students reach for years afterwards, about the teacher who changed them without ever appearing to try.

Modern It is said of communities in a disaster, and it is the standard phrase in appeals for that kind of help.

It is said of analysts, doctors and investigators, and it is high praise, because the phrase concedes the thing was genuinely hard to see while insisting it was nonetheless there to be seen.

description: The vivid image of ice (冰) melting (消) and tiles (瓦) breaking apart (解) originated in military texts describing the sudden collapse of seemingly solid formations. First appearing in Three Kingdoms period chronicles, it described how strong alliances could suddenly dissolve when facing internal pressures or external threats. Modern usage extends to any situation where apparently stable structures - from business empires to political systems - rapidly disintegrate under pressure.

description: Completed (成) in one (一) breath (气) — 呵 is the breath itself, the puff of warm air blown onto cold hands or onto a brush. That is why it belongs above all to writing and calligraphy, where a break in the stroke or in the argument shows afterwards. Chinese also uses it of a piece of music, a film's last act, and any job finished at one sitting because breaking off would have cost more than tiredness did.

He was not killed, and he had returned (归) it intact.

He sat the guest in the same seat, showed him the snake, and the illness lifted that day. The History of the Jin tells a close variant about Yue Guang. description: Vast (浩浩) and sweeping (荡荡) — a doubling that Chinese uses for water in volume, and the Yueyang Tower essay applies a close variant to the lake stretching past any shore. The sound is doing much of the work, four syllables of open vowels that take a long time to say. It describes mass in motion: a river in flood, a procession, an army, a crowd. Applied to human affairs it carries a suggestion of inevitability, which is why official language is fond of it.

example: Despite better offers, she honored her original commitment to the client
chineseExample: 尽管有更好的机会，她仍然信守对客户的承诺
description: Ji Bu of the early Han was reliable enough that a saying circulated in Chu: a hundred catties of gold are worth less than one promise (一诺) from Ji Bu — hence a promise worth a thousand (千) in gold (金). The Records of the Grand Historian preserves it. He is not Ji Zha of Wu, whose story about keeping faith with a dead man is a separate one. The value here is cumulative and can only be spent once: the word is worth gold because it has never yet failed. In practice it is used of somebody whose agreement makes a contract feel redundant.

example: The historian discussed ancient artifacts with intimate familiarity

description: To recite something as though counting (数) the treasures (珍) of one's own household (家) — the reading is shǔ, to enumerate, not shù. The comparison is exact about what kind of knowledge is meant: not that the person has studied the subject but that they have lived with it, so the details come without effort and in order. Chinese uses it of specialists reeling off figures and of fans on their own subject, and it always implies affection as well as command.

example: The software team continued refining their already excellent product

description: This descends from Zhu Xi's commentary on a line in the Analects about cutting and polishing: what has already been worked finely (精) should be worked finer still — 治之已精，益求其精. The phrase assumes the work is already good, which is what distinguishes it from ordinary diligence; the refinement it demands has no natural end. It is said of work that is already competent and is being pushed further, which is why it turns up in company mottoes and almost never in criticism.

example: The surgeon focused completely during the complex procedure

description: To gather (聚) the vital essence (精) and bring together (会) the spirit (神). The vocabulary is that of Daoist inner cultivation, where 精 and 神 are two of the three treasures and scattering them is what wastes a life. Applied to ordinary attention the phrase keeps that weight: it describes concentration as a gathering of something that is otherwise dissipating, not merely as looking hard at a thing. It is the standard Chinese term for full absorption in a task.

example: When the supplier failed, the manufacturer's production also suffered

description: This metaphor comes from the Zuo Zhuan, in the Spring and Autumn period. Jin sought permission to march through the small state of Yu in order to attack its neighbour Guo. Yu's advisor Gong Zhiqi objected that Yu and Guo depended on one another as lips (唇) and teeth (齿) do: once the lips are gone (亡), the teeth feel the cold (寒). The Duke of Yu, tempted by Jin's gifts, granted passage anyway. Jin destroyed Guo, and on the return march destroyed Yu as well. It gets used of two parties whose fates are joined whether or not they admit it, and usually as a warning to the one that believes itself safe.

example: His praise felt empty because it didn't match his actions

description: The Zuo Zhuan observes that where trust does not come from within — 信不由中 — pledges are worthless however elaborately they are dressed up. Words (言) that do not proceed (不由) from what is inside (衷) may be perfectly courteous and still mean nothing at all. The phrase is about the gap between what is said and what is held, not about lying: one can say something false without it, and something true with it. It is said of the polite insincerity both parties can hear, which is a commoner failure than deceit.

example: After decades of practice, the chef could create masterpieces without recipes

description: After three years of practice, Cook Ding in the Zhuangzi no longer saw the whole (全) ox (牛): his eyes (目) stopped registering the animal as a single object and took in the joints and cavities instead, so that the knife went through gaps rather than through tissue. 无 is that absence of the whole. The phrase names a particular stage of expertise rather than expertise in general — the point at which the surface of a thing stops being what you perceive — and Chinese uses it of engineers, editors and diagnosticians who look and see structure first.

Chinese applies it to appointments, to seating plans and to settlements of a dispute, and it is the standard way of saying an arrangement has worked out for everybody.

description: To boast and boast (夸夸) in one's (其) talk (谈). The doubling is what carries the judgement — a single 夸 is simply to praise or to exaggerate, and repeating it turns the exaggeration into a manner rather than an occasion. The phrase says nothing about whether the claims are false, only that the speaking is inflated and continuous. It is said of prospectuses, of conference talks and of the colleague whose contribution is entirely verbal.

example: The deadline was so close that immediate action was necessary

description: Pressing (迫) at (在) the brow (眉) and lashes (睫). The measurement is the point: the gap between eyebrow and eyelash is a few millimetres, so the phrase places the threat inside the distance at which anything can be done about it. That makes it stronger than ordinary urgency, which implies time remaining. Chinese says it of deadlines that have arrived rather than approached, and of crises already in contact — and it is the standard register of official language about emergencies.

example: The politician's public support contradicted his private actions

description: The mouth (口) says yes (是), the heart (心) says no (非). 是 and 非 are the standard classical pair for right and wrong as well as for assent and denial, so the phrase carries a moral charge that the English 'two-faced' does not quite have — the split is between what is affirmed and what is believed true. It is used of insincere agreement rather than of outright lying, and Chinese distinguishes it from ordinary politeness by the presence of an actual conviction being concealed.

example: The policy's conflicting requirements made implementation impossible

description: Han Feizi tells of a man of Chu selling weapons who said of his shields that nothing could pierce them, and of his spears that there was nothing they could not pierce. A bystander asked what would happen if one of his spears were used against one of his shields, and he had no answer. Hence spear (矛) against shield (盾) as self (自) contradiction (相) — and the two characters together, 矛盾, became the ordinary modern Chinese word for a contradiction, which is unusual for an idiom's components.

example: The exhibition's countless displays overwhelmed visitors

description: Eyes (目) with no (不) leisure (暇) to attend to (给) it all. The construction blames the abundance rather than the observer, which is what distinguishes it from distraction — the attention is working properly and there is simply more than it can be spent on. Chinese pairs it naturally with 应接不暇 from the same family. It suits markets, exhibitions, festivals and, in current use, the feed on a screen, and its tone is closer to pleasure than to complaint.

example: After years of quiet research, her breakthrough theory revolutionized the field

description: This is from Su Shi of the Song dynasty, who advised a friend to observe widely but take sparingly, to accumulate thickly and release thinly — 博观而约取，厚积而薄发. Deep (厚) accumulation (积) should issue in slight (薄) output (发). The counsel is against publishing early and often: what is put out should be a small, considered fraction of what has been gathered. It attaches to the long invisible preparation behind work that finally looks effortless, and it is offered as advice as often as it is used as description.
description_tr: This comes from Su Shi of the Song dynasty, who advised a friend to observe widely but take sparingly, to accumulate thickly and release thinly — 博觀而約取，厚積而薄發. description: Meeting (临) danger (危) without (不) fear (惧). The formulation descends from the Zhuangzi's praise of the man who faces great peril without alarm, and it hardened into a standard term of commendation in later histories and biographies. What it denotes is composure under threat rather than absence of the feeling — specifically the ability to keep acting while afraid, which is why it is awarded to people rather than claimed by them. In practice it is used of those who stayed functional in a crisis when others nearby did not.

example: Despite understanding the challenges, she accepted the complex international assignment

description: To know (知) the difficulty (难) and advance (进) anyway. It is built as the deliberate opposite of 知难而退, withdrawing in the face of difficulty, and the pair is used against each other constantly in Chinese. What both share is the first half: the knowing is not in dispute, and the phrase specifically excludes the person who pressed on because they had not understood what they were taking on. It is courage with the information already in hand.

Everything already carried counts for nothing if the last load is not. The image is deliberately cruel about proportion: the shortfall is trivial and the loss is total. Modern usage warns against abandoning something at the point where the remaining effort is smallest.

description: This one comes from the Mencius, which describes a small state as one that would measure some fifty li if you cut off the long side to supplement the short — 绝长补短. Taking (取) what is long (长) to make up (补) what is short (短) is presented as ordinary practical reckoning. Applied to people it assumes that no one has the full set, and that the sensible response is exchange rather than envy. Chinese reserves it for learning from others where you are weak, and it carries no suggestion that the borrowing costs you anything.

So the detachment is tactical rather than callous in the original. Ordinary modern use has dropped the tactics and kept the coldness, and it now describes standing by while something burns.

example: The young heirs lived in luxury, oblivious to the real world's hardships
chineseExample: 这些年轻的继承人生活在奢华中，对现实世界的艰辛毫无察觉
description: A Song collection tells of the physician Meng Fu, who fitted out a small room at home with gilded furnishings and paper so bright it dazzled; a guest who dozed there said afterwards that resting in it left a man gold-dazed and paper-drunk — 此室暂憩，令人金迷纸醉. The gold (金) and the papered walls (纸) are literal in the anecdote, and the pair of verbs — dazed (迷), drunk (醉) — became a byword for luxury that disorients. Chinese uses it of nightlife districts and of wealth arranged to be looked at, always with disapproval attached.

meaning: Metal walls, a moat of boiling water
example: The company's cybersecurity defenses were impenetrable to attackers
chineseExample: 公司的网络安全防御对攻击者来说固若金汤
description: The Book of Han has Kuai Tong warning what will follow if the magistrate who surrendered first is put to death: the other border towns will hear of it, wall themselves up, and 皆为金城汤池，不可攻也 — all become walls of metal and moats of scalding water, and cannot be attacked. The warning is conditional and about what has not happened yet, not a report of cities already impregnable. 汤 is the trap for learners: here it is boiling liquid, not soup, and the moat is heated rather than merely wet. The four characters compress it — solid (固) as (若) metal (金) and scalding water (汤) — one defence passive and one active. Chinese uses the phrase for fortifications, for alibis with no hole in them, and for systems built with several independent layers.

The warning is conditional and about what has not happened yet, not a report of cities already impregnable. 湯 is the trap for learners: here it is boiling liquid, not soup, and the moat is heated rather than merely wet. The four characters compress it — solid (固) as (若) metal (金) and scalding water (湯) — one defence passive and one active. description: Lü Meng was a Wu general dismissed as unlettered muscle until his sovereign told him to read. Pei Songzhi's commentary to the Records of the Three Kingdoms preserves it, quoting the Jiangbiao Zhuan. What it asks for is the effort of dropping an assessment that has gone stale, and it is used of people who have been underestimated.

What it describes is not fraud but decay: the institution was real once, the title was earned once, and only the label is still in service. Chinese applies it to organisations, treaties, marriages and job descriptions.

The line sits in a series about great things escaping ordinary measure, so lateness here is a property of scale rather than a delay. A later anecdote applies it to a man dismissed early and vindicated in age, which is how it is usually meant now. Modern usage reassures anyone whose ability has not yet been recognised.

It is said of interference that destroyed what it meant to help, and it is the standard phrase for pushing a child.

description: The Liezi tells of an old man of ninety whose way out was blocked by two mountains, and who began shifting (移) them (山) away a basket at a time. The Wise Old Man of Hequ laughed at him and told him to stop, and he answered that when he died his sons would remain, and their sons after them, while the mountains would not grow any higher — 子子孙孙无穷匮也，而山不加增. The names are the joke: 愚公 is the Foolish (愚) Old Man (公) and 智叟 the Wise Old Man, and the story hands the argument to the fool, whose foolishness turns out to be arithmetic the wise man had not done.

description: The Zhuangzi has a frog (蛙) at the bottom (底) of a broken well (井) boasting to a turtle of the Eastern Sea about the water reaching its armpits, the mud covering its feet, and how nothing else in the well can match it. The turtle tries to get in: its left foot is not yet inside before its right knee is wedged fast. It backs out and describes the sea instead — a thousand li does not measure its breadth, a thousand fathoms do not sound its depth. The frog is stunned. The phrase names a horizon mistaken for the world, and Chinese aims it at complacency rather than ignorance.

description: The Doctrine of the Mean has Confucius say that the noble person walks the way and gives up (废) half (半) way along the road (途) — and that he himself could not stop. As they rose, a censor said to him: the vice-councillor may be called a man who crosses (过) the river (河) and pulls down (拆) the bridge (桥). What the image supplies beyond ordinary ingratitude is the destruction. The bridge is not left behind but dismantled, so nobody follows and the crosser cannot go back — which is why it is most often said of institutions that shut the route they came in by.

What it implies is that the concealment was working until a specific slip, which makes it more pointed than simply saying someone was found out.

description: Cook Ding (庖丁) cut apart (解) an ox (牛) for Lord Wenhui with his whole body in motion and the blade whispering, never once meeting bone. At first, he said, he saw nothing but ox; after three years he no longer saw the whole animal; now he meets it with his mind rather than his eyes and guides the knife through the spaces already there. His blade was nineteen years old and had taken apart thousands of oxen, and its edge was still as new as the day it left the whetstone. The Zhuangzi tells it as a lesson in nourishing life. The phrase describes mastery that has stopped looking like effort.

The saying is nearly always given whole: 鹬蚌相争，渔翁得利 — while snipe and clam fight, the fisherman profits.

description: The superior (优) prevail (胜), the inferior (劣) are washed out (汰). This is not a classical idiom: it entered Chinese in the late Qing through Yan Fu's translation of Huxley, in the wave of thinking about survival and struggle that reached China at the moment it was losing wars to industrial powers. That history is why the phrase carries such force in Chinese and why it is applied so readily to nations and firms. 汰 is the word for panning or rinsing away, so the elimination is a sorting rather than a defeat.

It gets used of work or an argument that is orderly because something holds it together, not because it was tidied afterwards.

example: The company sought manufacturing efficiency by hiring more managers instead of upgrading equipment

description: Mencius said it to King Xuan of Qi, who wanted to extend his territory by force and expected contentment to follow. chineseExample: 创业团队以年轻的热情和无限的精力应对挑战

example: Investors rushed to purchase shares of the promising new technology company

example: Despite modest circumstances, the family found contentment in simple pleasures and each other's company

description: Mei Fu, memorialising the Han throne about how it chose officials, said that trying to find able men by the current method was like consulting Bo Le's diagram and expecting to buy a thoroughbred in the market. Centuries later the Ming scholar Yang Shen gave the story its familiar form and its wording: Bo Le's son went out with his father's manual on horses, came home with a toad, and this, Yang Shen wrote, is what is called going by the drawing (按图) in search of (索) a fine horse (骥). You will hear it of applying a rule mechanically to a case it has stopped fitting.

example: The veteran investor made consistently successful decisions throughout the volatile market
chineseExample: 这位资深投资者在波动的市场中始终做出成功的决策
description: This comes from the Strategies of the Warring States, on the archer Yang Youji of Chu, who could hit a willow leaf at a hundred paces so reliably that a hundred shots (百发) gave a hundred hits (百中). In the original a passer-by warns him that skill this great is exactly what will exhaust him, since he cannot afford a single miss. The idiom keeps the praise and drops the warning. You will hear it of unfailing accuracy, in marksmanship and in judgement alike.
description_tr: This comes from the Strategies of the Warring States, on the archer Yang Youji of Chu, who could hit a willow leaf at a hundred paces so reliably that a hundred shots (百發) gave a hundred hits (百中). example: The two competing proposals offered essentially the same features with different terminology
chineseExample: 这两个相互竞争的提案基本上提供了相同的功能，只是使用了不同的术语
description: This idiom depends on the old Chinese weight system, in which one jin was sixteen liang rather than ten. Half a jin (半斤) is therefore exactly eight liang (八两) — the same quantity, named two ways. The phrase is not about approximate similarity but about strict equality dressed up as difference, and it is nearly always disparaging: both parties are as bad as each other. Modern usage says two things or people amount to precisely the same.

example: They had only met briefly at conferences and weren't close enough for personal favors
chineseExample: 他们只在会议上简短会面过，关系还不足以请求私人帮助
description: This descends from the Book of Later Han, on Ying Feng, whose memory was such that a man glimpsed once at a half-open door was recognised by him years afterwards. A half-face (半面) acquaintance (之交) is therefore someone you have barely met — the phrase measures the thinness of the connection, not the strength of the memory. It names the slightest of acquaintanceships: somebody known by sight and hardly at all.

meaning: Fully experience seas to mulberry fields
example: The elderly shopkeeper had witnessed the neighborhood transform through war, rebuilding, and modernization
chineseExample: 年迈的店主目睹了这个社区经历战争、重建和现代化的变迁
description: 沧桑 is short for 沧海桑田, the blue sea and the mulberry fields. Ge Hong's account of the immortal Ma Gu has her mention, in passing, that since entering service she has three times seen the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields — the scale is the whole point of the remark, and it is where the phrase gets its weight. To have had one's fill (饱) of passing through (经) changes of that order (沧桑) is to have lived through more upheaval than a single life should have to contain. In practice it is used of people, cities and institutions, and it implies wear as much as experience: something has been taken out of whatever it describes.
description_tr: 滄桑 is short for 滄海桑田, the blue sea and the mulberry fields. chineseExample_tr: 年邁的店主目睹了這個社區經歷戰爭、重建和現代化的變遷

example: With bankruptcy looming, the company made a final all-or-nothing product launch
chineseExample: 在破产迫在眉睫之际，公司进行了最后的孤注一掷产品发布
description: For a single battle (一战) Han Xin drew his army up with the river (水) at their backs (背), which every officer present knew was the one formation the manuals forbid. They won, and afterwards they asked him why. Because these were levies, he said — throw them where they can run and they will run; put them where there is nowhere to go and each man fights for himself. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps the exchange. The phrase means removing your own retreat on purpose, and Han Xin's reasoning is about the troops he had rather than about courage in general.
metaphoric_meaning: Fight with total commitment having no retreat

chineseExample_tr: 在破產迫在眉睫之際，公司進行了最後的孤注一擲產品發佈

example: The company maximized short-term profits by cutting essential research funding
chineseExample: 公司通过削减必要的研究资金来实现短期利润最大化
description: Killing (杀) the hen (鸡) in order to take (取) the eggs (卵) — destroying what produces in order to have what it produced. Versions of the fable appear across many traditions, and the point is the arithmetic of impatience rather than anything about poultry. What it names is not greed alone but greed that defeats itself. Chinese says it of trading a lasting source of value for one immediate gain, and almost always about somebody else's decision.
metaphoric_meaning: Sacrifice long-term benefits for short-term gains
description_tr: Killing (殺) the hen (雞) in order to take (取) the eggs (卵) — destroying what produces in order to have what it produced. chineseExample_tr: 公司通過削減必要的研究資金來實現短期利潤最大化

example: The parents waited anxiously for their teenager to return home after midnight
chineseExample: 父母焦急地等待着午夜后他们十几岁的孩子回家
description: The heart (心) hoisted up (提) and the gall bladder (胆) left swinging (吊). Chinese physiology puts courage in the gall, so the phrase names both organs of nerve as displaced at once — it is a description of the body, not of the thoughts. That is what separates it from ordinary worry. It describes sustained dread with a physical seat: waiting for a result, sitting through a flight in weather, living beside a situation that could break at any moment.

example: The emergency room staff moved in chaotic coordination to save the accident victim
chineseExample: 急诊室的工作人员以混乱的协调配合拯救事故受害者
description: Seven (七) hands (手) and eight (八) feet (脚). Chinese pairs seven and eight to mean disordered multiplicity rather than any count, and the same device produces 乱七八糟 and 七嘴八舌. What the phrase describes is a group all helping at once — the limbs outnumber the task, everyone is doing something, and nobody is directing. Its tone is affectionate more often than critical, and it suits the scene when a table collapses and six people reach for it.
metaphoric_meaning: Many people busily working together in disorder
description_tr: Seven (七) hands (手) and eight (八) feet (腳). Chinese pairs seven and eight to mean disordered multiplicity rather than any count, and the same device produces 亂七八糟 and 七嘴八舌. example: The restoration expert handled the ancient manuscript with extreme caution
chineseExample: 修复专家极其谨慎地处理这份古代手稿
description: The Book of Songs uses it of King Wen: reverent and careful (小心翼翼) in his service. 翼翼 there means solemn and attentive rather than anything to do with wings, though the character is the one for a wing and the association is hard to shake off. In the classic it describes a religious attitude. Ordinary modern use has narrowed it to physical care — carrying something breakable, stepping on ice — and the reverence has thinned into caution.
metaphoric_meaning: Act with extreme caution and care
description_tr: The Book of Songs uses it of King Wen: reverent and careful (小心翼翼) in his service. 翼翼 there means solemn and attentive rather than anything to do with wings, though the character is the one for a wing and the association is hard to shake off. example: After the children's birthday party, the living room was completely disorganized
chineseExample: 孩子们的生日派对之后，客厅完全乱七八糟
description: Chaotic (乱) seven (七) eight (八) and a mess (糟). The seven-and-eight construction is Chinese shorthand for disorder, and a popular etymology connects the numbers to two historical catastrophes, the Rebellion of the Seven States under the Han and the War of the Eight Princes under the Jin. That derivation is almost certainly retrofitted. The phrase is thoroughly colloquial, at home describing a room, a schedule or an explanation, and it has no literary dignity at all.

example: After receiving the news, she stared out the window with a contemplative expression
chineseExample: 收到消息后，她若有所思地望着窗外
description: As if (若) there were (有) something (所) being thought about (思). The construction is careful and does the work: it describes an appearance rather than a mental state, so what is being reported is a face, not a thought. That is why it is nearly always used of somebody else. Chinese narrative uses it at the moment a character goes quiet in the middle of a conversation, and the reader is told exactly what the observer can see and no more.
metaphoric_meaning: Lost in thought with a contemplative expression

example: The once-bustling shopping mall now stood eerily deserted
chineseExample: 曾经熙熙攘攘的购物中心如今冷冷清清地矗立着
description: Li Qingzhao opens one of the most famous lyrics in the language with a run of doubled sounds — searching and searching, cold (冷冷) and clear (清清), desolate and grieving. She was writing as a refugee and a widow. The phrase keeps both halves of the sensation, temperature and silence, and Chinese uses it for places that were once full: a shop after the trade has gone, a house after a family has left, a street out of season.

example: The meteorologist predicted that rain was very likely for the weekend festival
chineseExample: 气象学家预测周末节日很可能下雨
description: Of ten (十), there are (有) eight (八) or nine (九). Its usefulness is that it names an honest degree of confidence — high but not asserted as certain. Chinese uses it constantly in speech, where English would say nine times out of ten, and it is one of the more useful things a learner can pick up because it fits almost any prediction.
metaphoric_meaning: Very high probability at about 80-90 percent

example: Both families had similar social standing, making the marriage alliance advantageous
chineseExample: 两家社会地位相当，使这门婚姻联盟有利
description: Both halves are literal architectural features. 门当 are the drum-shaped stones set in pairs at the base of a gateway; 户对 are the short carved pegs projecting above the lintel. Their number and form were regulated by rank, so a family's standing could be read off its doorway from the street. A match in which the gateposts corresponded was a match between equals. The phrase is still the standard vocabulary of Chinese discussion about marriage across a social gap.
metaphoric_meaning: Match between families of similar social status
description_tr: Both halves are literal architectural features. 門當 are the drum-shaped stones set in pairs at the base of a gateway; 戶對 are the short carved pegs projecting above the lintel. example: He was puzzled when the stranger suddenly approached him with accusations
chineseExample: 当陌生人突然带着指责接近他时，他感到困惑
description: Without (无) connection (缘) and without (无) cause (故). 缘 is the Buddhist term for the conditions that link one thing to another, and the double negation removes both the relationship and the reason, leaving an event with no attachment to anything that preceded it. That is what gives the phrase its force. It is used of unprovoked hostility above all — 无缘无故地发火, to lose your temper out of nothing — and it implies the speaker has looked for a cause and found none.

example: After retirement, the couple traveled wherever their interests led them
chineseExample: 退休后，这对夫妇随着兴趣所至四处旅行
description: A pairing of self-determination (自由) with unhindered being (自在). It belongs to Chan Buddhist recorded sayings rather than to the Zhuangzi, though the temper is close to it, and 自在 in particular is a Buddhist term for freedom from obstruction. What it names is the absence of constraint rather than the presence of choice. It names living without restriction or obligation, and Chinese applies it most readily to animals, children and the retired.

example: The investigation was based on rumors with no substantial evidence
chineseExample: 调查是基于没有实质证据的谣言
description: This descends from the Book of Han, which dismisses a fruitless pursuit as being like catching (捕) the wind (风) and seizing (捉) a shadow (影) — a thing that cannot be got hold of because there is nothing there to hold. The two objects are chosen precisely: both are real, both are visible, and neither has substance. Chinese says it of accusations and theories built on nothing anyone can take hold of.

example: His gambling addiction had reached a point where intervention seemed futile
chineseExample: 他的赌博成瘾已经到了似乎干预也无济于事的地步
description: This one comes from the Book of Songs, in a poem warning that when the burning grows fierce enough there is no (不可) saving it with medicine (救药). The image is of a fever past treatment, applied to a state whose rulers will not listen. It was a political warning before it was a medical one. It is said of a person or a situation past all remedy, usually with exasperation attached.
metaphoric_meaning: Beyond hope of redemption or reform

example: The quantum phenomenon defied all conventional understanding of physics

description: Not (不) able to be (可) thought (思) or spoken (议). The phrase is Buddhist and technical in origin, describing what lies beyond the reach of conceptual thought and language — the standard Chinese rendering of the Sanskrit acintya. That is a strong claim, and ordinary use has worn it down considerably: modern Chinese reaches for 不可思议 wherever English would say incredible, including about football results. The original sense survives only in religious writing.

example: The two championship finalists were so evenly matched that predicting a winner was impossible
chineseExample: 两位冠军决赛选手势均力敌，无法预测谁会获胜
description: Not (不) mutually (相) above and below (上下). Chinese ranks by verticality, so denying both directions denies the ranking itself — the claim is not that two things are similar but that no order can be established between them. It is used of competitors, of candidates and of rival products, and it is genuinely neutral, which makes it useful: it says the comparison failed to separate them, without implying either that both are good or that both are bad.

example: The established professor dismissed the innovative theory without serious consideration

description: Not deigning (不屑) a single (一) glance (顾). 屑 carries the sense of considering something worth the trouble, so the refusal is specifically about worth rather than interest. What makes the phrase sting is the arithmetic of 一顾: a single look is the smallest attention that could be paid, and even that is being withheld. Chinese reserves it for contempt expressed by omission, and it is stronger than any dismissal that involves actually saying something.

description: Not (不) choosing (择) among methods (手段). The moral weight sits entirely on 择. example: The once-thriving industrial city had transformed into an abandoned ghost town

The measure is deliberately inhuman: what she reports as a recurring observation is beyond any mortal lifetime. It gets used of change so complete that the earlier state is no longer recognisable.

example: The conservative members glanced disapprovingly at the newcomer's unconventional attire
chineseExample: 保守的成员们不赞成地斜眼看着新来者不寻常的着装

example: The innovative company released new product improvements in endless succession
chineseExample: 这家创新公司层出不穷地推出新产品改进

You will hear it of new technologies and new talent, and equally of new problems and new scams, and the tone comes entirely from the noun rather than from the phrase.

example: The custom-designed vacation perfectly satisfied all the family's diverse preferences
chineseExample: 这个定制设计的假期完美地满足了全家人各种不同的偏好
description: Matching (称) the heart (心) and according with (如) the intention (意). The two halves are not redundant: 心 is what a person feels and 意 is what they meant, so the phrase claims that the outcome satisfies both the wish and the plan. Note the reading — 称 is chèn here, to match or suit, not chēng. It gets used of purchases, appointments and marriages, and it is what you wish someone when the thing they wanted is about to be decided.

example: The legendary beauty attracted admiring glances wherever she appeared
chineseExample: 这位传奇美人无论在哪里出现都吸引仰慕的目光
description: The Zhuangzi is the source, and it means the opposite of what the phrase now does: Mao Qiang and Lady Li are what people call beautiful, but fish seeing them dive (沉鱼) deep and birds seeing them fly high — so who, it asks, knows what beauty actually is? The animals are fleeing. Later tradition reassigned the images to two of the Four Beauties, 沉鱼 to Xi Shi at her washing and 落雁 (落雁) to Wang Zhaojun riding out to the frontier, and turned a question about relative standards into a compliment. It now describes beauty of the highest order.
metaphoric_meaning: Beauty so stunning it affects natural world

chineseExample_tr: 這位傳奇美人無論在哪裏出現都吸引仰慕的目光

example: The startup boldly expanded during economic turbulence while competitors retreated
chineseExample: 当竞争对手退缩时，这家初创公司在经济动荡期间大胆扩张
description: The Book of Song records Zong Que's uncle asking the boy what he wanted from life, and the answer: I wish to ride the long wind (乘风) and break (破) ten thousand li of waves (浪). He was a child at the time, and he grew up to be one of the dynasty's leading generals. Li Bai later took the image up in a line quoted at least as often — 长风破浪会有时，直挂云帆济沧海, there will come a time to ride the long wind and break the waves, and I shall set my cloud-white sail straight across the sea — which is why the phrase is frequently attributed to him instead.
description_tr: The Book of Song records Zong Que's uncle asking the boy what he wanted from life, and the answer: I wish to ride the long wind (乘風) and break (破) ten thousand li of waves (浪). example: The young researcher spent hours outside the professor's office seeking mentorship
chineseExample: 这位年轻研究人员在教授办公室外花费数小时寻求指导
description: The History of Song records that Yang Shi, already an official of forty, went with a friend to put a question to the philosopher Cheng Yi and found him sitting in meditation with his eyes closed. They waited outside rather than disturb him. When Cheng Yi noticed them the snow (雪) at the door (程门) was a foot deep and they were still standing (立) in it. The phrase is the Chinese standard for respect shown to a teacher, and the detail that matters is that Yang Shi was not a boy.
metaphoric_meaning: Show profound respect and patience seeking wisdom

chineseExample_tr: 這位年輕研究人員在教授辦公室外花費數小時尋求指導

example: The competitor offered an unfairly low buyout price during the company's financial crisis
chineseExample: 竞争对手在公司财务危机期间提出了不公平的低价收购要约
description: To ride (乘) on another person's (人之) danger (危). 乘 is the verb for mounting a horse or a chariot, so the image is of using someone's difficulty as the thing you stand on to get higher. The History of the Later Han condemns it in exactly those terms. Chinese moral vocabulary treats this as distinctly worse than ordinary competition, and the phrase is a standard accusation in commerce — the buyer who appears when a seller is desperate, and names a price accordingly.

example: The rival corporation recruited top engineers from its struggling competitor
chineseExample: 这家竞争对手公司从陷入困境的竞争对手那里招募了顶尖工程师
description: The Zuo Zhuan records Sheng Zi putting it to Zimu, chief minister of Chu: Jin's ministers are not the equal of Chu's, but its officers are able men, and they are Chu's — like fine timber and leather, they went from here. Though Chu has the talent (楚材), it is Jin that actually employs it (晋用). He then listed the defectors and what each had since done to Chu. The phrase names an institutional failure rather than mere emigration, and modern Chinese applies it to companies and countries alike.

example: The judge recused herself from the case involving her former colleague
chineseExample: 法官回避了涉及她前同事的案件
description: Wholly public (大公) and without private interest (无私). The 公/私 distinction is the central axis of Chinese political ethics, and this phrase states the maximal position on it — not that private interest was outweighed but that it was absent. It is deliberately unreachable, which is how it functions: as a standard invoked in citations, in judicial ethics and in criticism, rather than as a description anyone expects to fit.

example: Upon hearing the unexpected news, the entire committee sat motionless in shock
chineseExample: 听到这个意外消息，整个委员会呆若木鸡地坐着
description: This one comes from the Zhuangzi, on a trainer who spends forty days preparing a fighting cock. At each stage the bird is still too spirited; only at the end does it stand as if (若) carved of wood (木鸡), unmoved by any challenge, and other birds turn and flee without a fight. The wooden stillness is mastery, not stupefaction — the modern sense of being dumbstruck (呆) reverses the original completely. It gets used of somebody frozen with shock, which is the exact opposite of what the trainer had achieved.

example: Securing temporary shelter became the immediate priority after the earthquake
chineseExample: 地震后，确保临时住所成为当务之急
description: Mencius says that the wise know everything, and yet treat what the present business (当务) requires as the urgent thing (之急); the benevolent love everyone, and yet make attending to the worthy their first task. The claim is about ordering, not about limits — nothing is being given up, something is being done first. Modern usage names the item that has to be dealt with before anything else can be.

example: The report was based on unverified rumors rather than documented evidence
chineseExample: 该报告基于未经证实的谣言，而非有据可查的证据
description: This one comes from the Analects, where Confucius says that to hear something on the road (道听) and repeat it on the path (途说) is to throw virtue away. The objection is not that the report is false but that the speaker has taken no trouble to find out — repeating is treated as a moral failure, not merely a careless one. It attaches to hearsay passed on by somebody who could have checked and did not.

example: Working excessive overtime earned more money but damaged his health
chineseExample: 过度加班赚取了更多钱，但损害了他的健康
description: The gain (得) does not (不) compensate (偿) the loss (失). 偿 is the word for repaying a debt, so the phrase sets the two sides of a ledger against each other and reports that the entry does not balance. What distinguishes it from simple failure is that something was in fact gained — the enterprise worked, and cost more than it returned. In practice it is used of pyrrhic victories, of litigation won at ruinous expense, and of overtime.
metaphoric_meaning: Gains not worth the cost or sacrifice

example: After the small concession was granted, he immediately demanded much more

Taken as advice it is about consolidation; used as an idiom it has soured, and now describes someone who treats each concession as a base for the next demand. Modern usage is always disapproving.

example: The coastal region's ideal climate and natural harbor created exceptional development advantages

What the phrase specifies is that the advantage was there before anyone did anything — soil, climate, position, constitution, family — so it is not a comment on merit either way. Chinese uses it of regions with natural resources and of people with an obvious gift, and it can carry a faint edge: saying someone is 得天独厚 acknowledges the advantage and quietly declines to credit them with it.

example: She frequently misplaced her keys, phone, and important documents
chineseExample: 她经常丢三落四，找不到钥匙、手机和重要文件

The numbers are deliberately non-consecutive, so the losses read as scattered rather than systematic. Vernacular fiction supplies the phrase and it has stayed colloquial. It describes a standing trait rather than an incident: the person who has left something behind again, and whose household has learned to check before the door closes.

example: After bankruptcy, the entrepreneur rebuilt his business empire from scratch
chineseExample: 破产后，这位企业家从头开始重建了他的商业帝国
description: Xie An spent his early manhood in the hills at Kuaiji, declining office and keeping company with writers, until his family's position collapsed and he took a post at forty — old for a first appointment. He ended as the minister who directed the defence at the Fei River, where a vastly larger northern army was destroyed and the south survived. Rising again (再起) from East Mountain (东山) therefore means a return after a long absence, and Chinese reserves it for comebacks with a clear implication that the person had been written off.

It attaches to restless glancing about, often with the suggestion that the person is up to something.

example: After decades of corruption, the official was finally brought to justice

example: Despite repeated financial disasters, he continued investing in high-risk ventures

example: The researcher became so absorbed in the project she barely ate or slept for days

example: The nature reserve protected various species of wildlife in their natural habitat

example: The military command analyzed every minor border incident for signs of potential conflict
chineseExample: 军事指挥部分析每一个微小的边境事件，寻找潜在冲突的迹象
description: Wind (风) blows (吹) and the grass (草) moves (动). A Dunhuang narrative of Wu Zixu in flight gives the phrase its setting, and the setting is the point: a hunted man reads the grass because it is the only instrument he has. What the phrase names is not a threat but a sign of one — the smallest observable disturbance, which may mean everything or nothing. Chinese uses it in the standard construction 一有风吹草动, at the first hint of anything.

example: The documentary explored local customs, cuisine, and social practices in the remote village
chineseExample: 这部纪录片探索了偏远村庄的当地习俗、美食和社会习惯
description: Tang Dynasty travel writers developed this comprehensive framework for documenting regional culture through climate/customs (风), geography (土), people (人), and social relationships (情). Song Dynasty ethnographers formalized it into a methodology for systematic cultural documentation. The progression from natural environment to human society creates a sophisticated tool for understanding how places shape their people.

When this reached Lian Po, he stripped to the waist, carried a bundle of thorns (负荆) on his back to Lin's gate, and asked to be punished (请罪). The two became close allies. It is Lian Po who bears the thorns, and the gesture carries because it costs him his pride.

example: The committee chair encouraged all members to share their perspectives on the proposal

What it names is a mode of discussion in which the whole range of opinion goes on the table before anyone converges, and Chinese uses it in exactly that setting: minutes of meetings, classroom instructions, and the sentence a chair says to open the floor. example: The traditional beliefs remained entrenched in the community despite modernization

Applied to habits and institutions the image is neutral in the original and unflattering now: what is hard to uproot is usually hard to reform. example: The limited production capacity couldn't satisfy the overwhelming market interest
chineseExample: 有限的生产能力无法满足市场的巨大兴趣
description: Supply (供) cannot (不) meet (应) demand (求). This is modern economic vocabulary rather than a classical idiom, and it is worth learning as such: it belongs to news reporting and business writing, and it has none of the literary texture of the phrases around it. The one thing worth noting is that Chinese uses it as unambiguous praise when the subject is a product, where English 'we cannot meet demand' is at least half a complaint about logistics.

example: The professor avoided meeting alone with students to prevent any appearance of impropriety
chineseExample: 教授避免单独与学生会面，以防止任何不当行为的出现
description: An old ballad advises the gentleman not to pull on his shoe in a melon field nor straighten his hat beneath a plum tree — 瓜田不纳履，李下不整冠 — since either motion, seen from a distance, looks exactly like theft. The counsel is not about honesty but about appearances: the man is innocent, and that is precisely why he must not be seen doing it. example: Instead of directly asking for a raise, he spoke vaguely about compensation and market rates
chineseExample: 他没有直接要求加薪，而是含糊地谈论薪酬和市场行情

Chinese uses it with mild impatience, most often in the imperative: 别拐弯抹角, stop going round the houses, which is close to the English idiom in both sense and tone.

example: Finding the specific document among millions of unorganized files seemed impossible
chineseExample: 在数百万个无组织的文件中找到特定文档似乎是不可能的
description: To dredge (捞) for a needle (针) at the bottom of the sea (海底). The commoner form is 大海捞针. What makes the image work is the mismatch of dimensions rather than mere difficulty — the search space is effectively unbounded and the target is the smallest metal object a household owns, so the task is not hard but structurally hopeless. Chinese uses it of investigations, of lost files and of looking for one person in a large city.

example: The employee's repeated violations damaged team morale and productivity

description: This one comes from the Zhuangzi, where the Yellow Emperor, lost and asking a boy herding horses how to govern the empire, is told it is no different from tending horses: simply remove whatever horse (马) harms (害) the herd (群). The answer's force is in its brevity — the boy declines the grandeur of the question. Chinese reserves it for the individual whose conduct is damaging a whole group.

example: The writer abandoned his natural style to poorly imitate a famous author
chineseExample: 这位作家放弃了自己的自然风格，拙劣地模仿一位著名作家

He never acquired their gait, and lost his own along the way, and had to crawl home. That is the whole story and it is two lines long. The phrase describes imitation that costs the imitator what they already had, and it is sharper than simply copying badly — the loss is the point.

example: The manager avoided necessary criticism and never challenged poor performance

It is used of terrain and, by extension, of any commanding strategic position.

example: She waited at the station, gazing through autumn waters for his return.

The hyperbole is about duration, and the one waiting is always the one who cannot act. In practice it is used of longing for somebody's arrival with exhausting intensity.

example: Losing that small investment was just one hair from nine oxen compared to his total wealth.

He is explaining why he accepted castration instead: a clean death would have bought nothing, because nobody would have counted it. The proportion does the work, and the nine oxen are chosen for being uncountable rather than merely many. It attaches to a quantity too small to register against the whole, very often about money.

description: Four (四) ways through (通) and eight (八) ways out (达). The construction takes the four cardinal directions and the four corners between them, so it names the compass and then claims every line of it. It is used of road networks, of junction cities and, in modern writing, of transport and communications infrastructure, and it is straightforwardly a compliment — a place described this way is one that everything passes through.

meaning: Heaven is long, earth is lasting
example: Their friendship proved to be as enduring as heaven and earth.

description: This idiom derives from Chapter 7 of the Daoist classic 'Tao Te Ching' (道德经) by Laozi: 'Heaven and earth are long-lasting.' The phrase uses the long-lasting (长) heaven (天) and enduring (久) earth (地) as metaphors for permanence and durability. It gained romantic connotations through Tang Dynasty poetry, particularly Bai Juyi's 'Song of Everlasting Sorrow' where it describes enduring love. The idiom is commonly used in wedding blessings and expressions of lasting relationships, though it can apply to any bond or commitment meant to endure through time.

description: The horse (马) arrives (到) and the thing succeeds (成功). It belongs to Yuan drama, where a general's mount reaching the field is the moment the outcome is settled, and the compression is the point: no campaign, no struggle, just arrival and result. Chinese uses it almost entirely as a wish rather than a description. It is what you write to someone before an examination, a new job or an opening, and it pairs conventionally with 旗开得胜.
description_tr: The horse (馬) arrives (到) and the thing succeeds (成功). It belongs to Yuan drama, where a general's mount reaching the field is the moment the outcome is settled, and the compression is the point: no campaign, no struggle, just arrival and result. Chinese uses it almost entirely as a wish rather than a description. It is what you write to someone before an examination, a new job or an opening, and it pairs conventionally with 旗開得勝.
chineseExample_tr: 團隊祝願她馬到成功。

meaning: Fighting for minutes and seizing seconds
example: The emergency team worked against time to save the patient.
chineseExample: 急救团队争分夺秒地抢救病人。
description: This modern idiom emerged during China's industrialization period in the 20th century, reflecting the urgency of national development. It combines 'fighting for' (争) minutes (分) and 'seizing' (夺) seconds (秒) to emphasize making the most of every moment. The phrase became particularly popular during the Great Leap Forward era and remains common in contexts requiring urgent action. It expresses the importance of efficiency and the race against time, commonly used in emergency situations, competitive environments, and deadline-driven work.
metaphoric_meaning: Race against time; make every second count
description_tr: This modern idiom emerged during China's industrialization period in the 20th century, reflecting the urgency of national development. It combines 'fighting for' (爭) minutes (分) and 'seizing' (奪) seconds (秒) to emphasize making the most of every moment. The phrase became particularly popular during the Great Leap Forward era and remains common in contexts requiring urgent action. It expresses the importance of efficiency and the race against time, commonly used in emergency situations, competitive environments, and deadline-driven work.
chineseExample_tr: 急救團隊爭分奪秒地搶救病人。

example: The market offers a bewildering variety of products.
chineseExample: 市场上的产品五花八门，令人眼花缭乱。
description: This idiom has roots in ancient Chinese military strategy, where 'five flowers' (五花) referred to five tactical formations and 'eight gates' (八门) to eight strategic positions. The phrase originally described the complexity of battlefield tactics. Over time, it evolved to describe any diverse or varied collection. Some scholars also trace it to the five-element theory and eight trigrams of Chinese philosophy. In modern usage, it describes a wide variety of things, often with a connotation of being overwhelming or confusingly diverse.
metaphoric_meaning: A bewildering variety; all kinds of

Some scholars also trace it to the five-element theory and eight trigrams of Chinese philosophy. chineseExample_tr: 市場上的產品五花八門，令人眼花繚亂。

example: A leader must always keep their promises to maintain credibility.
chineseExample: 一个领导者必须言而有信，才能保持信誉。
description: The line is Zixia's, not Confucius's: in the Analects he sets out what he would call a learned man, ending with one who, in dealings with friends, speaks (言) and is (而有) as good as his word (信). The list is deliberately made of ordinary conduct rather than of study, which is his argument. Chinese still treats the phrase as a plain statement of what makes someone worth dealing with, and it carries real weight in commercial contexts where the handshake precedes the contract.
metaphoric_meaning: To be true to one's word
description_tr: The line is Zixia's, not Confucius's: in the Analects he sets out what he would call a learned man, ending with one who, in dealings with friends, speaks (言) and is (而有) as good as his word (信). Chinese still treats the phrase as a plain statement of what makes someone worth dealing with, and it carries real weight in commercial contexts where the handshake precedes the contract.
chineseExample_tr: 一個領導者必須言而有信，才能保持信譽。

example: Learning a language requires a step-by-step approach.
chineseExample: 学习语言需要循序渐进的方法。
description: This descends from Zhu Xi of the Song dynasty, whose advice on reading insists on following (循) the order (序) and advancing (渐进) by degrees, without skipping ahead to what looks more interesting. The sequence is not arbitrary: each stage is what makes the next legible. In practice it is used of methodical progression, in study or anywhere the stages cannot be safely skipped.
description_tr: This comes from Zhu Xi of the Song dynasty, whose advice on reading insists on following (循) the order (序) and advancing (漸進) by degrees, without skipping ahead to what looks more interesting. chineseExample_tr: 學習語言需要循序漸進的方法。

example: The startup that entered the market last became the industry leader.
chineseExample: 最后进入市场的那家初创公司后来居上，成为行业领袖。
description: Ji An, passed over while men appointed after him were promoted past him, said it to Emperor Wu's face: Your Majesty uses officials the way one stacks firewood — the ones that come later (后来) go on top (居上). It was a complaint, and a pointed one. Modern usage has inverted it completely and made it a compliment, describing the late starter who overtakes those who began ahead of them, with none of Ji An's bitterness left in it.

chineseExample_tr: 最後進入市場的那家初創公司後來居上，成為行業領袖。

example: The restaurant truly lives up to its reputation as the best in town.
chineseExample: 这家餐厅名副其实，确实是城里最好的。
description: The name (名) matching (副) the reality (实). Cao Cao uses the equivalent phrase in a letter praising Wang Xiu, saying his repute and his substance corresponded and that he far surpassed ordinary men. Behind it lies the older Confucian preoccupation with 正名, the rectification of names, on the argument that disorder begins when what things are called stops matching what they are. Chinese applies it to anything that turns out to live up to its billing.
metaphoric_meaning: Living up to one's name or reputation
description_tr: The name (名) matching (副) the reality (實). Chinese applies it to anything that turns out to live up to its billing.
chineseExample_tr: 這家餐廳名副其實，確實是城裡最好的。

meaning: Heart's blood comes in a tide
example: On a whim, she decided to book a flight to Paris.
chineseExample: 她心血来潮，决定订一张去巴黎的机票。
description: The heart's blood (心血) coming in like a tide (来潮). The physiology is that of Chinese medicine, where the heart governs the blood and also the mind, so a surge in one is a surge in the other. What the phrase describes is therefore an impulse with a bodily cause and no reason behind it. Chinese uses it neutrally and often self-deprecatingly, in the construction 一时心血来潮 — on a sudden whim — usually to explain something that turned out badly.
metaphoric_meaning: Acting on a sudden impulse or whim
description_tr: The heart's blood (心血) coming in like a tide (來潮).
