Chinese uses it neutrally and often self-deprecatingly, in the construction 一時心血來潮 — on a sudden whim — usually to explain something that turned out badly.
chineseExample_tr: 她心血來潮，決定訂一張去巴黎的機票。

example: The technological revolution is an unstoppable force reshaping society.
chineseExample: 科技革命势不可挡，正在重塑社会。
description: A momentum (势) that cannot (不可) be blocked (挡). The History of the Jin has Chi Jian using it of a rebel force: their momentum cannot be met head-on, so it must be undone by calculation rather than by strength. That is the useful part — the phrase is a statement about how to respond, not just a description of force. 势 is central to Chinese strategic vocabulary, closer to positional advantage than to raw power.
description_tr: A momentum (勢) that cannot (不可) be blocked (擋). The History of the Jin has Chi Jian using it of a rebel force: their momentum cannot be met head-on, so it must be undone by calculation rather than by strength. That is the useful part — the phrase is a statement about how to respond, not just a description of force. 勢 is central to Chinese strategic vocabulary, closer to positional advantage than to raw power.
chineseExample_tr: 科技革命勢不可擋，正在重塑社會。

example: The redesigned website gave visitors a refreshing new experience.
chineseExample: 重新设计的网站让访客耳目一新。
description: Ears (耳) and eyes (目) made new (一新) all at once. The claim is about the apparatus rather than the object: what has changed is the freshness of the perception brought to a thing, which is why the phrase fits a redesign, a first visit and a change of management equally well. Chinese uses it as unambiguous praise, and it is the standard line in a review of anything that has been overhauled — the sense being that it no longer looks like the thing you had stopped noticing.
description_tr: Ears (耳) and eyes (目) made new (一新) all at once. chineseExample_tr: 重新設計的網站讓訪客耳目一新。

example: His business strategy was completely counterproductive to his stated goals.
chineseExample: 他的商业策略与既定目标南辕北辙。
description: The Strategies of the Warring States tells of a man who wanted to travel to the southern state of Chu and drove his carriage north. When asked why, he boasted of his fast horses, skilled driver, and ample provisions, failing to realize that these advantages would only take him further from his destination. The characters name the contradiction outright: the carriage shafts (辕) point south (南) while the wheel ruts (辙) run north (北). Having resources means nothing if the direction is wrong. You will hear it of effort that is carrying somebody steadily further from what they said they wanted.
description_tr: The Strategies of the Warring States tells of a man who wanted to travel to the southern state of Chu and drove his carriage north. When asked why, he boasted of his fast horses, skilled driver, and ample provisions, failing to realize that these advantages would only take him further from his destination. The characters name the contradiction outright: the carriage shafts (轅) point south (南) while the wheel ruts (轍) run north (北). Having resources means nothing if the direction is wrong. Chinese uses it of effort that is carrying somebody steadily further from what they said they wanted.
chineseExample_tr: 他的商業策略與既定目標南轅北轍。

example: Success comes from practical, grounded efforts rather than empty dreams.
chineseExample: 成功来自脚踏实地的努力，而非空想。
description: Feet (脚) planted (踏) on solid (实) ground (地). Sima Guang, who spent nineteen years compiling a history of thirteen centuries, is the man the phrase attached itself to — a contemporary is said to have used it of him, and the fit is obvious enough that it stuck. What it praises is not effort but contact with the actual: work that touches the material at every step instead of reasoning above it. It is among the most common compliments in modern Chinese, and its opposite is 好高骛远.
description_tr: Feet (腳) planted (踏) on solid (實) ground (地). Sima Guang, who spent nineteen years compiling a history of thirteen centuries, is the man the phrase attached itself to — a contemporary is said to have used it of him, and the fit is obvious enough that it stuck. What it praises is not effort but contact with the actual: work that touches the material at every step instead of reasoning above it. It is among the most common compliments in modern Chinese, and its opposite is 好高騖遠.
chineseExample_tr: 成功來自腳踏實地的努力，而非空想。

example: She dedicated herself wholeheartedly to her research.
chineseExample: 她一心一意地投入研究工作。
description: One (一) heart (心), one (一) intention (意). The repetition is doing the work: 心 and 意 are separate faculties in Chinese, feeling and purpose, and the phrase insists that both are pointed the same way, which is a stronger claim than concentration alone. Its opposites are instructive — 三心二意, three hearts and two intentions, is the standard word for being half-committed. It is used of study, of work and, very commonly, of fidelity.

chineseExample_tr: 她一心一意地投入研究工作。

example: Most smartphones today are largely similar with only minor differences.
chineseExample: 现在的智能手机大同小异，只有细微差别。
description: The Zhuangzi preserves Hui Shi's distinction: things broadly alike and slightly unlike he called the small sameness-and-difference, and the fact that all things are both wholly alike and wholly unlike he called the great one. The idiom keeps the first half — largely (大) the same (同), slightly (小) different (异) — and drops the paradox. What it asserts is that the differences are real and do not matter, which is why it tends to close an argument rather than open one. It is said of competing products, of rival proposals, and of two explanations that turn out to come to the same thing.
metaphoric_meaning: Essentially the same with minor differences
description_tr: The Zhuangzi preserves Hui Shi's distinction: things broadly alike and slightly unlike he called the small sameness-and-difference, and the fact that all things are both wholly alike and wholly unlike he called the great one. The idiom keeps the first half — largely (大) the same (同), slightly (小) different (異) — and drops the paradox. What it asserts is that the differences are real and do not matter, which is why it tends to close an argument rather than open one. Chinese uses it of competing products, of rival proposals, and of two explanations that turn out to come to the same thing.
chineseExample_tr: 現在的智能手機大同小異，只有細微差別。

example: Behind the modest entrance lies a surprisingly beautiful garden.
chineseExample: 朴素的入口后面别有洞天，是一个美丽的花园。
description: 洞天 is a Daoist term of art: the grotto-heavens, a set of worlds held to exist inside particular mountains, with their own light and seasons, reached through a cave mouth. To find another (别) such heaven (有洞天) is therefore not to find a pretty view but to find that a second world has been sitting inside the first one. Li Bai's 别有天地非人间 — there is another world here, and it is not the human one — is the ancestor of the modern phrase. Chinese uses it on stepping through a plain doorway into something unexpected, and of work whose surface gives no hint of what is underneath it.
metaphoric_meaning: A hidden paradise; unexpected inner beauty
description_tr: 洞天 is a Daoist term of art: the grotto-heavens, a set of worlds held to exist inside particular mountains, with their own light and seasons, reached through a cave mouth. To find another (別) such heaven (有洞天) is therefore not to find a pretty view but to find that a second world has been sitting inside the first one. Li Bai's 別有天地非人間 — there is another world here, and it is not the human one — is the ancestor of the modern phrase. Chinese uses it on stepping through a plain doorway into something unexpected, and of work whose surface gives no hint of what is underneath it.
chineseExample_tr: 樸素的入口後面別有洞天，是一個美麗的花園。

meaning: Without any way to deal with it
example: Faced with the natural disaster, the villagers felt helpless.
chineseExample: 面对自然灾害，村民们无可奈何。
description: Without (无) any (可) way of dealing with it (奈何). 奈何 is itself a question — how is this to be handled — so the phrase says there is no answer to the question, which is more exact than helplessness: the situation has been understood, and nothing follows from understanding it. Yan Shu's line fixed the tone: 无可奈何花落去，似曾相识燕归来, nothing to be done, the flowers are falling; and the swallows come back looking like ones I knew. It gets used of what cannot be argued with — weather, illness, time, a decision taken somewhere else — and it is resignation rather than complaint.
description_tr: Without (無) any (可) way of dealing with it (奈何). 奈何 is itself a question — how is this to be handled — so the phrase says there is no answer to the question, which is more exact than helplessness: the situation has been understood, and nothing follows from understanding it. Yan Shu's line fixed the tone: 無可奈何花落去，似曾相識燕歸來, nothing to be done, the flowers are falling; and the swallows come back looking like ones I knew. Chinese uses it of what cannot be argued with — weather, illness, time, a decision taken somewhere else — and it is resignation rather than complaint.
chineseExample_tr: 面對自然災害，村民們無可奈何。

meaning: Chicken flies away and eggs broken
example: His reckless investment left him with nothing - the chicken flew and the eggs broke.
chineseExample: 他冒险的投资让他鸡飞蛋打，一无所有。
description: The hen (鸡) gets away (飞) and the eggs (蛋) are broken (打) in the grab. The arithmetic is the whole point: the person did not merely fail to gain, they destroyed what they already had in the course of reaching for more. That separates it from ordinary loss and from ordinary greed, and it is the standard Chinese verdict on a deal that collapsed and took the existing arrangement down with it. It is said with very little sympathy, because the reaching was optional.
description_tr: The hen (雞) gets away (飛) and the eggs (蛋) are broken (打) in the grab. The arithmetic is the whole point: the person did not merely fail to gain, they destroyed what they already had in the course of reaching for more. That separates it from ordinary loss and from ordinary greed, and it is the standard Chinese verdict on a deal that collapsed and took the existing arrangement down with it. It is said with very little sympathy, because the reaching was optional.
chineseExample_tr: 他冒險的投資讓他雞飛蛋打，一無所有。

example: His carelessness caused the crucial error in the report.
chineseExample: 他的粗心大意导致报告中出现了关键错误。
description: A coarse (粗) heart (心) and a broad (大) intention (意). Both halves say the same thing about grain: the attention is set too wide a mesh, so small things pass through it. That is why the phrase describes a standing disposition rather than a single lapse, and Chinese distinguishes it from stupidity — the person is not incapable, they are simply not looking closely. It is the standard comment on careless examination mistakes.

That is why the phrase describes a standing disposition rather than a single lapse, and Chinese distinguishes it from stupidity — the person is not incapable, they are simply not looking closely. It is the standard comment on careless examination mistakes.
chineseExample_tr: 他的粗心大意導致報告中出現了關鍵錯誤。

example: His arrogance prevents him from accepting any criticism.
chineseExample: 他自以为是，无法接受任何批评。
description: This descends from the Mencius, which describes the man everyone finds agreeable and who takes his own view (自以为) to be right (是) — the type Mencius calls the thief of virtue, precisely because nothing about him invites correction. The fault is self-certainty, not error: someone who is wrong can be argued with, and this person cannot. Chinese says it of a self-assurance sealed against correction, which is exactly Mencius's complaint.
description_tr: This comes from the Mencius, which describes the man everyone finds agreeable and who takes his own view (自以為) to be right (是) — the type Mencius calls the thief of virtue, precisely because nothing about him invites correction. Chinese uses it of a self-assurance sealed against correction, which is exactly Mencius's complaint.
chineseExample_tr: 他自以為是，無法接受任何批評。

example: The championship game was his chance to showcase his skills.
chineseExample: 冠军赛是他大显身手的机会。
description: To display (大显) one's person and hands (身手) — 身手 is a compound meaning physical skill, the whole body's competence rather than a technique. The phrase belongs to martial fiction, where it names the moment a fighter who has been standing at the back finally moves. Chinese has kept the theatre in it: what it describes is not merely doing something well but doing it where it will be seen, and usually after a wait.

The phrase belongs to martial fiction, where it names the moment a fighter who has been standing at the back finally moves. Chinese has kept the theatre in it: what it describes is not merely doing something well but doing it where it will be seen, and usually after a wait.
chineseExample_tr: 冠軍賽是他大顯身手的機會。

example: The army was utterly defeated and scattered in all directions.
chineseExample: 军队被打得落花流水，四处逃散。
description: Falling (落) blossom (花) on flowing (流) water (水). It begins as a lyric image of late spring in Tang poetry, and it is worth noticing how completely the sense inverted: the same picture of petals broken off and carried away came to describe an army routed. Chinese now uses it almost exclusively for defeat, in the construction 打得落花流水, beaten to falling blossom and running water. The original melancholy survives only in deliberately literary writing.
description_tr: Falling (落) blossom (花) on flowing (流) water (水). It begins as a lyric image of late spring in Tang poetry, and it is worth noticing how completely the sense inverted: the same picture of petals broken off and carried away came to describe an army routed. Chinese now uses it almost exclusively for defeat, in the construction 打得落花流水, beaten to falling blossom and running water. The original melancholy survives only in deliberately literary writing.
chineseExample_tr: 軍隊被打得落花流水，四處逃散。

example: The children listened to the story with great enthusiasm.
chineseExample: 孩子们津津有味地听着故事。
description: 津 is saliva, or any moisture that wells up; doubled, 津津 is the mouth watering. With flavour (有味) attached, the phrase describes engagement at the level of the body rather than of the opinion — the reader who has forgotten they are reading, the listener leaning in. That physical basis is why it will not stretch to cover polite interest. It is said of somebody eating something they like and, far more often, of somebody lost in a book, a story or a piece of gossip, and it always implies the absorption is visible from outside.

With flavour (有味) attached, the phrase describes engagement at the level of the body rather than of the opinion — the reader who has forgotten they are reading, the listener leaning in. chineseExample_tr: 孩子們津津有味地聽著故事。

example: Don't limit yourself by drawing boundaries that don't exist.
chineseExample: 不要画地为牢，限制自己的发展。
description: Sima Qian, in the letter to Ren An written after his own mutilation, describes what a man of honour will do rather than face the officers: there are those for whom a circle drawn (画) on the ground (地) is a prison (为牢) they will not step out of, and a wooden figure of a jailer one they will not answer. His point is about shame, not about trust. The phrase has since inverted into a criticism, describing limits somebody has drawn for themselves and then treated as real walls.
description_tr: Sima Qian, in the letter to Ren An written after his own mutilation, describes what a man of honour will do rather than face the officers: there are those for whom a circle drawn (畫) on the ground (地) is a prison (為牢) they will not step out of, and a wooden figure of a jailer one they will not answer. chineseExample_tr: 不要畫地為牢，限制自己的發展。

example: Let's discuss this matter calmly and rationally.
chineseExample: 让我们心平气和地讨论这件事。
description: A level (平) heart (心) and settled (和) breath (气). The pairing is not decorative: 气 is the moving part of a person in Chinese medicine, and its state and the emotions are treated as one system, so steadying the breathing and steadying the temper are a single operation described twice. Su Shi uses the phrase of himself in old age. What it names is the condition under which an argument can actually be had, which is why Chinese reaches for it as an instruction — 心平气和地谈, talk about it calmly — more often than as a description.

The pairing is not decorative: 氣 is the moving part of a person in Chinese medicine, and its state and the emotions are treated as one system, so steadying the breathing and steadying the temper are a single operation described twice. Su Shi uses the phrase of himself in old age. What it names is the condition under which an argument can actually be had, which is why Chinese reaches for it as an instruction — 心平氣和地談, talk about it calmly — more often than as a description.
chineseExample_tr: 讓我們心平氣和地討論這件事。

example: Everyone was talking at once, offering different opinions.
chineseExample: 大家七嘴八舌，各抒己见。
description: Seven (七) mouths (嘴), eight (八) tongues (舌). Chinese pairs seven and eight to mean disordered multiplicity, the same device that gives 乱七八糟 and 七手八脚, and here it is applied to speech. What the phrase describes is not argument but simultaneity — everyone contributing, nobody yielding the floor, and no thread surviving. It is colloquial and mildly exasperated, and it is what you say about a family dinner or a meeting that has stopped being one conversation.
metaphoric_meaning: Everyone talking at once; lively discussion
description_tr: Seven (七) mouths (嘴), eight (八) tongues (舌). Chinese pairs seven and eight to mean disordered multiplicity, the same device that gives 亂七八糟 and 七手八腳, and here it is applied to speech. What the phrase describes is not argument but simultaneity — everyone contributing, nobody yielding the floor, and no thread surviving. It is colloquial and mildly exasperated, and it is what you say about a family dinner or a meeting that has stopped being one conversation.
chineseExample_tr: 大家七嘴八舌，各抒己見。

example: Her response was perfectly appropriate for the situation.
chineseExample: 她的回应恰如其分，非常得体。
description: Exactly (恰) as (如) its own (其) measure (分) requires. 分 is a portion allotted, what something is due, so the phrase is about matching rather than about moderation: the response is neither too much nor too little for this particular case, and what counts as right is set by the case and not by a rule. Chinese uses it of praise, of criticism, of a sentence and of a translation, and it is close to the highest thing that can be said of a judgement call, because it concedes there was a scale and grants that the speaker found the point on it.

chineseExample_tr: 她的回應恰如其分，非常得體。

example: He is known for his upright character and transparent dealings.
chineseExample: 他以光明磊落的品格和透明的处事方式著称。
description: Bright (光) and clear (明), open and unhidden (磊落). 磊 is three stones stacked out in the open, and the word keeps that sense of everything being where it can be counted. What the phrase claims is not that somebody has done no wrong but that nothing in their conduct is arranged to be hidden, which is a different and more testable virtue. Chinese uses it in references and obituaries, and it is the standard defence of somebody under suspicion — the argument being that a life run this way could not have concealed the thing alleged.

chineseExample_tr: 他以光明磊落的品格和透明的處事方式著稱。

example: Her writing was so vivid that the scenes seemed to bloom from the page.
chineseExample: 她的文笔妙笔生花，场景仿佛从纸上绽放。
description: A collection of Tang anecdotes records that Li Bai dreamed the tip of his brush had put out flowers, and that his gifts were extraordinary from then on. A marvellous (妙) brush (笔) growing (生) flowers (花) locates the talent in the instrument rather than in the labour, which is exactly what a legend about Li Bai ought to do. Chinese reserves it for writing that produces more than the words on the page appear to account for, and it is reserved for style rather than for argument — nobody's proof is ever 妙笔生花.
description_tr: A collection of Tang anecdotes records that Li Bai dreamed the tip of his brush had put out flowers, and that his gifts were extraordinary from then on. chineseExample_tr: 她的文筆妙筆生花，場景仿佛從紙上綻放。

example: Tech startups are emerging rapidly like bamboo shoots after rain.
chineseExample: 科技初创公司如雨后春笋般涌现。
description: Bamboo shoots (春笋) after (后) rain (雨). The observation is accurate rather than poetic: moso bamboo shoots can put on a great deal of height in a day once the spring rain arrives, and a grove that was bare will be full of them within a week. So the phrase claims speed and number together, and specifically the kind that appears without anyone planting anything. In practice it is used of start-ups, of coffee shops and of copycat products.

chineseExample_tr: 科技初創公司如雨後春筍般湧現。

example: She was overjoyed when she received the unexpected promotion.
chineseExample: 收到意外的晋升通知，她喜出望外。
description: Joy (喜) that comes out (出) beyond (外) what was being looked for (望). 望 is both hoping and the act of looking into the distance, so the phrase places the surprise precisely: the good thing arrived from outside the range the person had been scanning. Su Shi uses it in a letter after an unexpected reunion, and that is still its natural setting — news rather than achievement. What separates it from ordinary delight is the element of shock, and Chinese reserves it for things that had already been given up on.

example: He ignored the risks and pursued his dream regardless.
chineseExample: 他将风险置之度外，执着追求自己的梦想。
description: To place (置) something (之) outside (外) what is being reckoned (度). Emperor Guangwu, holding most of the empire with two hold-outs left, said he would put those two beyond his calculations for the time being; the phrase is his. What it describes is not forgetting a factor but deciding to stop counting it, which is a deliberate act and can be either shrewd or reckless. Chinese uses it above all of people who put their own safety outside the reckoning, and there it is unambiguous praise.

chineseExample_tr: 他將風險置之度外，執著追求自己的夢想。

example: After years of training, she can now manage the department independently.
chineseExample: 经过多年培训，她现在能够独当一面，管理整个部门。
description: Zhang Liang, advising Liu Bang on whom he could afford to rely on, said that of his generals only Han Xin could be trusted with great affairs and hold a front by himself. To take charge (当) of one side (一面) alone (独) is therefore a specific measurement of a person: not that they are talented, but that a whole sector can be handed over and not looked at again. Chinese uses it as the standard marker of professional maturity — the point at which somebody stops being supervised — and it is the compliment people most want to hear about themselves at work.

chineseExample_tr: 經過多年培訓，她現在能夠獨當一面，管理整個部門。

example: Waiting for the exam results made her extremely restless.
chineseExample: 等待考试结果让她坐立不安。
description: Unable to settle (不安) either sitting (坐) or standing (立). The phrase reports posture rather than feeling, and that is where its force comes from: the anxiety is something an observer infers from a body that keeps changing its mind. It is therefore more specific than worry, and it fits one kind of waiting in particular — for a result, a verdict, somebody who is late. Chinese says it of the person out in the corridor, with the implication that they have nothing to do and nowhere useful to put themselves.
description_tr: Unable to settle (不安) either sitting (坐) or standing (立). example: Chinese civilization has ancient roots and continues to thrive today.
chineseExample: 中华文明源远流长，延续至今。
description: A source (源) far off (远) and a current (流) that runs long (长). Both halves describe the same river from opposite ends, and what they claim together is continuity rather than mere age: the water arriving now is connected to the spring, and nothing in between has been cut. That is why it is applied to traditions, disciplines and family lines rather than to old objects. Chinese uses it in the register of official and ceremonial praise, and it is very often the opening sentence of a piece about a craft.
metaphoric_meaning: Having deep roots and long history
description_tr: A source (源) far off (遠) and a current (流) that runs long (長). example: The two friends are inseparable, always seen together.
chineseExample: 这两个朋友形影不离，总是在一起。
description: Form (形) and shadow (影) not (不) parting (离). The image is of company as unbreakable as the one thing that genuinely cannot leave you — and Chinese poetry had long used the shadow the other way about, as the only companion a solitary person has. That older and bleaker sense sits underneath the modern one and is worth knowing. Now it describes two people constantly in each other's company, best friends or a devoted couple, and it is warm, with a faint suggestion that other people have noticed.

chineseExample_tr: 這兩個朋友形影不離，總是在一起。

example: She was skeptical about his explanation but couldn't dismiss it entirely.
chineseExample: 她对他的解释半信半疑。
description: Half (半) believing (信), half (半) doubting (疑). The symmetry is exact and that is what the phrase is for: it does not describe leaning one way while entertaining the other, but a genuine deadlock in which neither acceptance nor rejection has won. Ming vernacular fiction uses it of characters who have just been told something extraordinary. You will hear it of the state one is in on hearing an unverified claim from a source that has been right before, and it is neutral — neither credulity nor cynicism, just the honest position before the evidence arrives.
description_tr: Half (半) believing (信), half (半) doubting (疑). chineseExample_tr: 她對他的解釋半信半疑。

example: It was a perfect day for the outdoor wedding ceremony.
chineseExample: 风和日丽的天气非常适合户外婚礼。
description: A gentle (和) wind (风) and a fine (丽) sun (日). Both halves are moderate on purpose — 和 is harmonious rather than strong, 丽 is lovely rather than blazing — so what is being praised is weather with nothing extreme in it, which is a whole aesthetic preference stated in four characters. It belongs at the opening of an account of a day out, and Chinese still uses it that way in travel writing and in the first line of a report on an outdoor event. It also works figuratively, of conditions that are simply not against you.
description_tr: A gentle (和) wind (風) and a fine (麗) sun (日). Both halves are moderate on purpose — 和 is harmonious rather than strong, 麗 is lovely rather than blazing — so what is being praised is weather with nothing extreme in it, which is a whole aesthetic preference stated in four characters. chineseExample_tr: 風和日麗的天氣非常適合戶外婚禮。

meaning: Worry about gain, worry about loss
example: His constant anxiety about success prevented him from enjoying the present.
chineseExample: 他患得患失的心态让他无法享受当下。
description: Confucius, in the Analects, asks whether a mean man can be served with in the government of a state: before he has got the thing he is anxious about getting (患得) it, and once he has it he is anxious about losing (患失) it — and a man anxious about losing will stop at nothing. That last clause is the sting, and it is what makes the passage a warning about colleagues rather than a comment on temperament. It gets used of a calculating anxiety that ruins both the judgement and the peace of whoever is carrying it.
metaphoric_meaning: Constantly anxious about gains and losses
description_tr: Confucius, in the Analects, asks whether a mean man can be served with in the government of a state: before he has got the thing he is anxious about getting (患得) it, and once he has it he is anxious about losing (患失) it — and a man anxious about losing will stop at nothing. Chinese uses it of a calculating anxiety that ruins both the judgement and the peace of whoever is carrying it.
chineseExample_tr: 他患得患失的心態讓他無法享受當下。

example: Her performance was incomparable, far surpassing all others.
chineseExample: 她的表演无与伦比，远超其他人。
description: Nothing (无) with which (与) to rank it (伦比). 伦 means a category or a peer group, so the claim is not that the thing is the best but that no comparison class exists for it — there is nothing of the same kind to line it up against. That is why it functions as the top of the Chinese scale of praise. It is strong enough that overuse flattens it, and careful writers keep it for cases where a comparison genuinely cannot be constructed.
description_tr: Nothing (無) with which (與) to rank it (倫比). 倫 means a category or a peer group, so the claim is not that the thing is the best but that no comparison class exists for it — there is nothing of the same kind to line it up against. That is why it functions as the top of the Chinese scale of praise. It is strong enough that overuse flattens it, and careful writers keep it for cases where a comparison genuinely cannot be constructed.
chineseExample_tr: 她的表演無與倫比，遠超其他人。

meaning: Split apart upon meeting the blade
example: Once we identified the root cause, the problem was easily solved.
chineseExample: 一旦找到根本原因，问题就迎刃而解了。
description: Du Yu, urging the Jin court to press the campaign against Wu, said the army's momentum was now like splitting bamboo: after the first few joints the rest comes apart on meeting (迎) the blade (刃) and falls open (解). The physical claim is accurate — bamboo resists the first cut and then splits its whole length along the grain. What the phrase adds to the ordinary idea of an easy solution is the condition attached: the ease is available only after the hard part, and only along the right line. Chinese uses it of problems that dissolve once the correct approach is found, never of problems that were easy to begin with.

Chinese uses it of problems that dissolve once the correct approach is found, never of problems that were easy to begin with.
chineseExample_tr: 一旦找到根本原因，問題就迎刃而解了。

example: Her indomitable spirit helped her overcome every obstacle.
chineseExample: 她不屈不挠的精神帮助她克服了每一个障碍。
description: Neither (不) bending (屈) nor (不) yielding (挠). 屈 is to bend something that ought to be straight and 挠 is to give way under a load, so the two halves cover pressure applied from outside and pressure that comes from the weight itself. Doubling the negation is the whole rhetorical move: nothing is asserted positively, and the picture is built entirely out of what does not happen. In practice it is used of people under sustained coercion rather than of ordinary persistence, and it belongs to citations, memorials and the language written about the dead.
description_tr: Neither (不) bending (屈) nor (不) yielding (撓). 屈 is to bend something that ought to be straight and 撓 is to give way under a load, so the two halves cover pressure applied from outside and pressure that comes from the weight itself. Doubling the negation is the whole rhetorical move: nothing is asserted positively, and the picture is built entirely out of what does not happen. Chinese uses it of people under sustained coercion rather than of ordinary persistence, and it belongs to citations, memorials and the language written about the dead.
chineseExample_tr: 她不屈不撓的精神幫助她克服了每一個障礙。

example: The prosecution presented overwhelming evidence against the defendant.
chineseExample: 控方提出了铁证如山的证据。
description: Proof (证) as iron (铁), immovable as a mountain (如山). The two comparisons are doing different work: iron for what cannot be bent, the mountain for what cannot be shifted or overlooked. Together they claim that the evidence is both sound and unavoidable. The phrase belongs to legal and journalistic language and is stronger than anything English uses casually — it is asserted about a case already made, not about evidence still being weighed.
description_tr: Proof (證) as iron (鐵), immovable as a mountain (如山). The two comparisons are doing different work: iron for what cannot be bent, the mountain for what cannot be shifted or overlooked. Together they claim that the evidence is both sound and unavoidable. The phrase belongs to legal and journalistic language and is stronger than anything English uses casually — it is asserted about a case already made, not about evidence still being weighed.
chineseExample_tr: 控方提出了鐵證如山的證據。

example: The sculptor's work was so realistic it seemed ready to move.
chineseExample: 雕塑家的作品栩栩如生，仿佛随时会动起来。
description: 栩栩 comes straight out of the Zhuangzi's butterfly dream — 栩栩然蝴蝶也, a butterfly vividly and contentedly itself — and the phrase adds 如生, as though alive. That origin is worth carrying: the point of the dream is that the butterfly did not know it was a man, so the vividness is complete from the inside. Applied to art, the phrase praises work that does not read as a representation of a living thing but as one.
description_tr: 栩栩 comes straight out of the Zhuangzi's butterfly dream — 栩栩然蝴蝶也, a butterfly vividly and contentedly itself — and the phrase adds 如生, as though alive. That origin is worth carrying: the point of the dream is that the butterfly did not know it was a man, so the vividness is complete from the inside. Applied to art, the phrase praises work that does not read as a representation of a living thing but as one.
chineseExample_tr: 雕塑家的作品栩栩如生，仿佛隨時會動起來。

example: He fabricated the entire story out of thin air.
chineseExample: 他无中生有，编造了整个故事。
description: This idiom has dual origins. Philosophically, it derives from the Daoist concept in 'Tao Te Ching' that all things emerge out of (中) nothingness (无) to give rise to (生) existence (有). Strategically, it appears in the 'Thirty-Six Stratagems' as a deceptive military tactic of creating threats or advantages from nothing. The phrase can describe both creative innovation and deceptive fabrication, depending on context. Modern usage often carries negative connotations of making false accusations or spreading rumors, though it can also describe genuine creativity or innovation.

example: Before making a decision, we need to understand the full context.
chineseExample: 做决定之前，我们需要了解事情的来龙去脉。
description: Both halves are technical terms from geomancy: the 来龙, the coming (来) dragon (龙), is the ridge along which a site's energy is held to travel, and the 去脉, the going (去) veins (脉), are the lines it disperses through afterwards. Reading the whole run, upstream and down, was the geomancer's job. Transferred to affairs, the phrase asks for the same thing — not what happened, but where it came from and where it went — and Chinese uses it in exactly that demanding sense: 把来龙去脉讲清楚 is a request for considerably more than a summary.
metaphoric_meaning: The whole story; causes and effects
description_tr: Both halves are technical terms from geomancy: the 來龍, the coming (來) dragon (龍), is the ridge along which a site's energy is held to travel, and the 去脈, the going (去) veins (脈), are the lines it disperses through afterwards. Reading the whole run, upstream and down, was the geomancer's job. Transferred to affairs, the phrase asks for the same thing — not what happened, but where it came from and where it went — and Chinese uses it in exactly that demanding sense: 把來龍去脈講清楚 is a request for considerably more than a summary.
chineseExample_tr: 做決定之前，我們需要了解事情的來龍去脈。

example: It's only natural that hard work leads to success.
chineseExample: 努力工作会带来成功，这是理所当然的。
description: What principle (理) makes (所) properly (当) so (然). 理 is the grain or pattern of a thing, the reason it is as it is, so the phrase claims that something follows from the nature of the case rather than from anybody's preference. That is a strong claim, and it is often made too cheaply, which is why the phrase has a second life in criticism: 觉得理所当然 is to take something for granted, and the complaint is precisely that nobody checked whether the principle was there. Chinese uses it both ways, and the tone tells you which is meant.
metaphoric_meaning: Naturally; as a matter of course
description_tr: What principle (理) makes (所) properly (當) so (然). 理 is the grain or pattern of a thing, the reason it is as it is, so the phrase claims that something follows from the nature of the case rather than from anybody's preference. That is a strong claim, and it is often made too cheaply, which is why the phrase has a second life in criticism: 覺得理所當然 is to take something for granted, and the complaint is precisely that nobody checked whether the principle was there. Chinese uses it both ways, and the tone tells you which is meant.
chineseExample_tr: 努力工作會帶來成功，這是理所當然的。

example: After losing the championship, the team left the field dejected.
chineseExample: 输掉冠军赛后，队员们垂头丧气地离开了球场。
description: Head (头) hanging (垂) and spirit (气) gone out (丧). 气 is breath and vitality at once, so the second half names something visible — a person who has deflated — rather than a mood reported from the inside. That is why the phrase works at a distance: it is what you can see across a room about somebody who has just had bad news. It gets used of a team after a defeat, a candidate after an interview and a child after a scolding, and it carries a little sympathy rather than contempt.
description_tr: Head (頭) hanging (垂) and spirit (氣) gone out (喪). 氣 is breath and vitality at once, so the second half names something visible — a person who has deflated — rather than a mood reported from the inside. That is why the phrase works at a distance: it is what you can see across a room about somebody who has just had bad news. chineseExample_tr: 輸掉冠軍賽後，隊員們垂頭喪氣地離開了球場。

example: The plot twist was completely unexpected.
chineseExample: 剧情的反转完全意想不到。
description: What thought (意想) does not (不) reach (到). The construction locates the failure in the observer rather than in the event — the thing was not improbable, it was simply outside what anyone had pictured. That is a slightly different claim from surprising, and Chinese uses it accordingly: of plot turns, of results that no forecast contained, and of consequences that nobody had thought to be afraid of.
description_tr: What thought (意想) does not (不) reach (到). The construction locates the failure in the observer rather than in the event — the thing was not improbable, it was simply outside what anyone had pictured. That is a slightly different claim from surprising, and Chinese uses it accordingly: of plot turns, of results that no forecast contained, and of consequences that nobody had thought to be afraid of.
chineseExample_tr: 劇情的反轉完全意想不到。

example: We wish you smooth sailing in your new career.
chineseExample: 祝你在新的职业生涯中一帆风顺。
description: One (一) sail (帆), the wind (风) following (顺). 顺风 is wind from astern, the condition under which a junk simply goes, and the phrase is a sailor's before it is anyone else's. It survives almost entirely as a wish rather than a description: written on cards, said at departures, and used of a career or a project that one hopes will not have to tack. Describing something that has already happened as 一帆风顺 is faintly dismissive of the effort involved.
description_tr: One (一) sail (帆), the wind (風) following (順). 順風 is wind from astern, the condition under which a junk simply goes, and the phrase is a sailor's before it is anyone else's. It survives almost entirely as a wish rather than a description: written on cards, said at departures, and used of a career or a project that one hopes will not have to tack. Describing something that has already happened as 一帆風順 is faintly dismissive of the effort involved.
chineseExample_tr: 祝你在新的職業生涯中一帆風順。

example: He was caught in a dilemma, unable to please either side.
chineseExample: 他左右为难，无法让双方都满意。
description: Difficult (为难) to the left (左) and difficult to the right (右). What it names is not indecision but a structural trap: both options are real, both have been understood, and each costs something the person is not willing to pay. That is why it describes a situation rather than a character, and why the sympathy in it is genuine. It is said of somebody caught between two loyalties — an employer and a friend, two sides of a family — and it is the standard thing to say about a position you would not want to be in yourself.
metaphoric_meaning: In a dilemma; caught between difficulties
description_tr: Difficult (為難) to the left (左) and difficult to the right (右). What it names is not indecision but a structural trap: both options are real, both have been understood, and each costs something the person is not willing to pay. That is why it describes a situation rather than a character, and why the sympathy in it is genuine. Chinese uses it of somebody caught between two loyalties — an employer and a friend, two sides of a family — and it is the standard thing to say about a position you would not want to be in yourself.
chineseExample_tr: 他左右為難，無法讓雙方都滿意。

meaning: Think a hundred times still not understand
example: No matter how much she thought about it, she couldn't understand his decision.
chineseExample: 无论她怎么想，都对他的决定百思不解。
description: To have turned it over a hundred (百) times in thought (思) and still not (不) got it undone (解). 解 is loosening a knot, which is the right image: this is not ignorance but a problem that has been worked at and has not come apart. The hundred counts attempts rather than anything real. Chinese uses it above all of other people's behaviour — a decision nobody can account for, a resignation with no reason given — and there is usually frustration in it, because the speaker has honestly tried.
metaphoric_meaning: Unable to understand despite much thought
description_tr: To have turned it over a hundred (百) times in thought (思) and still not (不) got it undone (解). 解 is loosening a knot, which is the right image: this is not ignorance but a problem that has been worked at and has not come apart. The hundred counts attempts rather than anything real. Chinese uses it above all of other people's behaviour — a decision nobody can account for, a resignation with no reason given — and there is usually frustration in it, because the speaker has honestly tried.
chineseExample_tr: 無論她怎麼想，都對他的決定百思不解。

example: She volunteered to lead the difficult project.
chineseExample: 她自告奋勇，主动承担这个困难的项目。
description: To put oneself forward (自告) with vigour (奋) and courage (勇). The construction is the point: 自告 means doing the nominating yourself, which inside a hierarchy is the difficult part, and the rest of the phrase supplies what is needed to follow through once you have. It is used where nobody has been asked and something unwelcome needs doing. Chinese treats it as straightforward praise — the volunteer, the person who put a hand up for the job with no obvious reward attached to it.
description_tr: To put oneself forward (自告) with vigour (奮) and courage (勇). The construction is the point: 自告 means doing the nominating yourself, which inside a hierarchy is the difficult part, and the rest of the phrase supplies what is needed to follow through once you have. It is used where nobody has been asked and something unwelcome needs doing. Chinese treats it as straightforward praise — the volunteer, the person who put a hand up for the job with no obvious reward attached to it.
chineseExample_tr: 她自告奮勇，主動承擔這個困難的項目。

example: The army advanced rapidly, meeting little resistance.
chineseExample: 军队势如破竹，几乎没有遇到抵抗。
description: Du Yu, urging the Jin court not to halt the campaign against Wu, said the army's momentum (势) was by now like (如) splitting bamboo (破竹): the first joints resist, and after that the whole length comes apart of its own accord. He was arguing against a pause, which is the part usually forgotten — momentum of this kind is perishable and cannot be picked up again later. Chinese uses it of winning streaks, of campaigns and of businesses in rapid expansion, and it carries that warning about stopping inside it.
description_tr: Du Yu, urging the Jin court not to halt the campaign against Wu, said the army's momentum (勢) was by now like (如) splitting bamboo (破竹): the first joints resist, and after that the whole length comes apart of its own accord. He was arguing against a pause, which is the part usually forgotten — momentum of this kind is perishable and cannot be picked up again later. Chinese uses it of winning streaks, of campaigns and of businesses in rapid expansion, and it carries that warning about stopping inside it.
chineseExample_tr: 軍隊勢如破竹，幾乎沒有遇到抵抗。

example: His elaborate excuse backfired and made things worse.
chineseExample: 他精心编造的借口弄巧成拙，让事情变得更糟。
description: Huang Tingjian used the phrase alongside the older image of drawing a snake and adding feet: working at cleverness (弄巧) and producing clumsiness (成拙) instead. What it names is a specific mechanism rather than plain failure — the harm comes from the sophistication itself, so a simpler attempt would have succeeded. It is said of over-engineered plans, of excuses that are too well constructed, and of gifts chosen with too much thought.
description_tr: Huang Tingjian used the phrase alongside the older image of drawing a snake and adding feet: working at cleverness (弄巧) and producing clumsiness (成拙) instead. What it names is a specific mechanism rather than plain failure — the harm comes from the sophistication itself, so a simpler attempt would have succeeded. Chinese uses it of over-engineered plans, of excuses that are too well constructed, and of gifts chosen with too much thought.
chineseExample_tr: 他精心編造的借口弄巧成拙，讓事情變得更糟。

example: He knowingly broke the rules despite understanding the consequences.
chineseExample: 尽管知道后果，他还是明知故犯。
description: Knowing perfectly well (明知) and committing the offence deliberately (故犯) all the same. Chinese legal thinking has always separated the wrong done in ignorance from the wrong done with the rule in view, and this phrase names the second. What it adds is not wickedness but a particular contempt: the rule was consulted and then set aside. In practice it is used of somebody who cannot claim they did not know, and it is the standard aggravating phrase — a person described this way is not being accused of carelessness.
description_tr: Knowing perfectly well (明知) and committing the offence deliberately (故犯) all the same. Chinese legal thinking has always separated the wrong done in ignorance from the wrong done with the rule in view, and this phrase names the second. What it adds is not wickedness but a particular contempt: the rule was consulted and then set aside. Chinese uses it of somebody who cannot claim they did not know, and it is the standard aggravating phrase — a person described this way is not being accused of carelessness.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管知道後果，他還是明知故犯。

example: Returning to his childhood home stirred deep emotions within him.
chineseExample: 回到儿时的家乡让他触景生情。
description: A scene (景) touched (触) upon, and feeling (情) comes up (生) out of it. The order of the characters is the argument: the outside comes first and the emotion follows, so what is described is being ambushed by a place rather than deciding to remember one. That involuntariness is what separates it from nostalgia. Chinese uses it of returning somewhere after a long absence, of coming across an object belonging to somebody dead, and it is the standard explanation offered for an unexpected reaction.
metaphoric_meaning: Moved by the sight of something familiar
description_tr: A scene (景) touched (觸) upon, and feeling (情) comes up (生) out of it. The order of the characters is the argument: the outside comes first and the emotion follows, so what is described is being ambushed by a place rather than deciding to remember one. That involuntariness is what separates it from nostalgia. Chinese uses it of returning somewhere after a long absence, of coming across an object belonging to somebody dead, and it is the standard explanation offered for an unexpected reaction.
chineseExample_tr: 回到兒時的家鄉讓他觸景生情。

meaning: Once going, nothing ahead can stop
example: With determination, they pushed forward regardless of obstacles.
chineseExample: 他们怀着坚定的决心一往无前。
description: Going forward (一往) with nothing (无) in front (前). The phrase is grammatically ambiguous in a productive way: nothing ahead can be read as no obstacle standing there, or as nothing being looked at except the objective. Both senses are in use. It belongs to military language and to exhortation, and it describes commitment made in a way that has removed the option of reconsidering, which is what separates it from ordinary courage.
description_tr: Going forward (一往) with nothing (無) in front (前). The phrase is grammatically ambiguous in a productive way: nothing ahead can be read as no obstacle standing there, or as nothing being looked at except the objective. Both senses are in use. It belongs to military language and to exhortation, and it describes commitment made in a way that has removed the option of reconsidering, which is what separates it from ordinary courage.
chineseExample_tr: 他們懷著堅定的決心一往無前。

meaning: Dimly as if separated by lifetimes
example: Returning after twenty years, the changes made him feel as if ages had passed.
chineseExample: 二十年后归来，这些变化让他恍如隔世。
description: Vaguely (恍) as if (如) a whole age (世) lay between (隔). 世 is a generation or an era, and Buddhist usage gives it the further sense of a separate lifetime, which is what the phrase borrows. What it describes is not the passing of time but a break in it: the earlier state is not merely distant, it belongs to somebody else. Chinese uses it on returning to a city after years away, on looking through old photographs, and after any change large enough that the person one was no longer joins up with the person one is.
metaphoric_meaning: Feeling as if ages have passed
description_tr: Vaguely (恍) as if (如) a whole age (世) lay between (隔). 世 is a generation or an era, and Buddhist usage gives it the further sense of a separate lifetime, which is what the phrase borrows. What it describes is not the passing of time but a break in it: the earlier state is not merely distant, it belongs to somebody else. Chinese uses it on returning to a city after years away, on looking through old photographs, and after any change large enough that the person one was no longer joins up with the person one is.
chineseExample_tr: 二十年後歸來，這些變化讓他恍如隔世。

example: Once he started talking about his hobby, he went on endlessly.
chineseExample: 一旦开始谈论他的爱好，他就滔滔不绝。
description: 滔滔 is the sound and motion of a river in flood; with 不绝, never (不) breaking off (绝), the phrase gives speech that same volume and the same refusal to stop. The water image does two things at once, praising the fluency and warning about the quantity, and which of the two is meant depends entirely on the listener. It gets used of a gifted speaker and of a colleague who has now been talking for twenty minutes, without changing a word.
metaphoric_meaning: Talk endlessly; speak at great length
description_tr: 滔滔 is the sound and motion of a river in flood; with 不絕, never (不) breaking off (絕), the phrase gives speech that same volume and the same refusal to stop. The water image does two things at once, praising the fluency and warning about the quantity, and which of the two is meant depends entirely on the listener. Chinese uses it of a gifted speaker and of a colleague who has now been talking for twenty minutes, without changing a word.
chineseExample_tr: 一旦開始談論他的愛好，他就滔滔不絕。

example: Theory and practice complement and enhance each other.
chineseExample: 理论与实践相辅相成。
description: Mutually (相) assisting (辅) and mutually (相) completing (成). 辅 is the outer brace on a cart wheel, a piece with no function of its own and without which the wheel fails — so the phrase is stronger than 'complementary'. It claims that neither element is fully itself in the other's absence. It is said of theory and practice, of policy and enforcement, of two halves of a business, and it is the standard way of saying that an apparent tension is in fact a working relationship.
description_tr: Mutually (相) assisting (輔) and mutually (相) completing (成). 輔 is the outer brace on a cart wheel, a piece with no function of its own and without which the wheel fails — so the phrase is stronger than 'complementary'. It claims that neither element is fully itself in the other's absence. Chinese uses it of theory and practice, of policy and enforcement, of two halves of a business, and it is the standard way of saying that an apparent tension is in fact a working relationship.
chineseExample_tr: 理論與實踐相輔相成。

example: Despite careful planning, things didn't turn out as hoped.
chineseExample: 尽管精心计划，结果却事与愿违。
description: Ji Kang, awaiting execution in the third century, wrote 事与愿违，遘兹淹留 — affairs (事) ran counter (违) to what I wished (愿), and so I have come to this confinement. The 与 is doing quiet work: it marks the two sides being set against each other, events on one hand and intention on the other, which is why the phrase reads as a collision rather than a disappointment. Chinese uses it where English says things did not go to plan, but with more weight, and usually where the effort was real and the outcome still went the other way.
metaphoric_meaning: Things turn out contrary to expectations
description_tr: Ji Kang, awaiting execution in the third century, wrote 事與願違，遘茲淹留 — affairs (事) ran counter (違) to what I wished (願), and so I have come to this confinement. The 與 is doing quiet work: it marks the two sides being set against each other, events on one hand and intention on the other, which is why the phrase reads as a collision rather than a disappointment. Chinese uses it where English says things did not go to plan, but with more weight, and usually where the effort was real and the outcome still went the other way.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管精心計劃，結果卻事與願違。

example: The suspicious package turned out to be harmless - just a false alarm.
chineseExample: 可疑包裹原来是无害的——虚惊一场。
description: An empty (虚) fright (惊), one (一) entire scene (场) of it. 场 is the measure word for a performance or a bout of weather, and using it here is the joke: the fear was a complete production, with a beginning, a middle and an end, and nothing behind it. That is why relief and a little embarrassment arrive together. Chinese says it of a test result that came back clear, an alarm that turned out to be a faulty sensor, and any danger that dissolved on inspection.
description_tr: An empty (虛) fright (驚), one (一) entire scene (場) of it. 場 is the measure word for a performance or a bout of weather, and using it here is the joke: the fear was a complete production, with a beginning, a middle and an end, and nothing behind it. That is why relief and a little embarrassment arrive together. Chinese uses it of a test result that came back clear, an alarm that turned out to be a faulty sensor, and any danger that dissolved on inspection.
chineseExample_tr: 可疑包裹原來是無害的——虛驚一場。

example: Environmental protection is closely linked to public health.
chineseExample: 环境保护与公众健康息息相关。
description: Breath (息) by breath (息), mutually (相) bound (关). 息 is one respiration, the smallest unit of being alive, so the phrase claims connection at that granularity — not that two things affect each other but that they do so continuously and at every moment. It is much stronger than 'related', which is where learners tend to under-translate it. Chinese uses it of a person and their surroundings, of an industry and a policy, and it is a fixture of official language about anything said to touch ordinary people's lives.
description_tr: Breath (息) by breath (息), mutually (相) bound (關). 息 is one respiration, the smallest unit of being alive, so the phrase claims connection at that granularity — not that two things affect each other but that they do so continuously and at every moment. It is much stronger than 'related', which is where learners tend to under-translate it. Chinese uses it of a person and their surroundings, of an industry and a policy, and it is a fixture of official language about anything said to touch ordinary people's lives.
chineseExample_tr: 環境保護與公眾健康息息相關。

example: The stock market's constant fluctuations are hard to predict.
chineseExample: 股市千变万化，难以预测。
description: A thousand (千) changes (变) and ten thousand (万) transformations (化). The numbers are conventional rather than counted, and the two verbs are not synonyms: 变 is change in state or appearance, 化 is change into something else entirely, so the pair covers alteration and transmutation together. That is why it reaches further than 'ever-changing'. Chinese uses it of weather, markets, tactics and faces, and it carries no anxiety of its own — any alarm comes from the context around it.
description_tr: A thousand (千) changes (變) and ten thousand (萬) transformations (化). The numbers are conventional rather than counted, and the two verbs are not synonyms: 變 is change in state or appearance, 化 is change into something else entirely, so the pair covers alteration and transmutation together. That is why it reaches further than 'ever-changing'. Chinese uses it of weather, markets, tactics and faces, and it carries no anxiety of its own — any alarm comes from the context around it.
chineseExample_tr: 股市千變萬化，難以預測。

example: For an expert, solving this problem was effortless.
chineseExample: 对于专家来说，解决这个问题轻而易举。
description: Light (轻) and therefore easy (易) to lift (举). The image is of picking something up and finding it weighs nothing, which is a particular kind of ease: the difficulty was expected and failed to materialise. That is why the phrase is as much about the lifter as the load, and why it can be quietly deflating — to describe an achievement this way concedes it was done well and denies that it cost anything. Chinese uses it admiringly and dismissively both, and the difference lies entirely in who is speaking.
description_tr: Light (輕) and therefore easy (易) to lift (舉). The image is of picking something up and finding it weighs nothing, which is a particular kind of ease: the difficulty was expected and failed to materialise. That is why the phrase is as much about the lifter as the load, and why it can be quietly deflating — to describe an achievement this way concedes it was done well and denies that it cost anything. Chinese uses it admiringly and dismissively both, and the difference lies entirely in who is speaking.
chineseExample_tr: 對於專家來說，解決這個問題輕而易舉。

meaning: Wind bending grass for a time
example: That song was hugely popular for a season.
chineseExample: 那首歌曾风靡一时。
description: Wind (风) laying the grass flat (靡), for a time (一时). The image descends from a line about the people bending before a ruler as grass bends before wind, and it is exact about how a fashion travels: not each person deciding, but a whole field going over at once. 一时 is the sting. It fixes a period and implies the end of one, so the phrase concedes the scale of the success and dates it in the same breath. You will hear it of songs, products and ideas that everybody had and nobody now mentions.
description_tr: Wind (風) laying the grass flat (靡), for a time (一時). The image descends from a line about the people bending before a ruler as grass bends before wind, and it is exact about how a fashion travels: not each person deciding, but a whole field going over at once. 一時 is the sting. It fixes a period and implies the end of one, so the phrase concedes the scale of the success and dates it in the same breath. Chinese uses it of songs, products and ideas that everybody had and nobody now mentions.
chineseExample_tr: 那首歌曾風靡一時。

example: Good management means leveraging everyone's strengths while minimizing weaknesses.
chineseExample: 好的管理意味着扬长避短，发挥每个人的优势。
description: Raising up (扬) what is long (长) and steering clear of (避) what is short (短). 长 and 短 are literally the long and the short of a thing, and Chinese uses them for strengths and weaknesses without the moral weight English puts on those words — they are measurements. That is what makes the advice practical rather than consoling: nothing is being repaired, and the deficiency is simply routed around. It is said of career choices, team composition and competitive strategy, and it is the standard argument against trying to be well-rounded.
description_tr: Raising up (揚) what is long (長) and steering clear of (避) what is short (短). 長 and 短 are literally the long and the short of a thing, and Chinese uses them for strengths and weaknesses without the moral weight English puts on those words — they are measurements. That is what makes the advice practical rather than consoling: nothing is being repaired, and the deficiency is simply routed around. Chinese uses it of career choices, team composition and competitive strategy, and it is the standard argument against trying to be well-rounded.
chineseExample_tr: 好的管理意味著揚長避短，發揮每個人的優勢。

example: A great teacher explains complex concepts in simple terms.
chineseExample: 好老师能够深入浅出地讲解复杂概念。
description: Going in (入) deep (深) and coming out (出) shallow (浅). Both halves describe the same person, and the order is the whole claim: the depth comes first and is not negotiable, and the accessibility is what gets produced afterwards. That is what separates it from simplification, which skips the first step. Chinese uses it as the highest praise available for a teacher, a textbook or a popular science writer, and the test it sets is a hard one — an expert who cannot do it is not being complimented.
metaphoric_meaning: Explain profound ideas in simple terms
description_tr: Going in (入) deep (深) and coming out (出) shallow (淺). Both halves describe the same person, and the order is the whole claim: the depth comes first and is not negotiable, and the accessibility is what gets produced afterwards. That is what separates it from simplification, which skips the first step. Chinese uses it as the highest praise available for a teacher, a textbook or a popular science writer, and the test it sets is a hard one — an expert who cannot do it is not being complimented.
chineseExample_tr: 好老師能夠深入淺出地講解複雜概念。

example: From the mountaintop, the entire valley was visible at a glance.
chineseExample: 从山顶上，整个山谷一览无余。
description: One (一) sweep of the eye (览), and nothing (无) left over (余). 余 is the remainder, what is left once everything has been accounted for, so the claim is completeness rather than mere clarity: no part of the thing escaped the single look. It began as praise for a view from a height, and Chinese still uses it that way. Applied to a situation the tone shifts — a plan that is 一览无余 is a plan with nothing held back, which is not always a compliment.
metaphoric_meaning: Take in everything at a glance
description_tr: One (一) sweep of the eye (覽), and nothing (無) left over (餘). 餘 is the remainder, what is left once everything has been accounted for, so the claim is completeness rather than mere clarity: no part of the thing escaped the single look. It began as praise for a view from a height, and Chinese still uses it that way. Applied to a situation the tone shifts — a plan that is 一覽無餘 is a plan with nothing held back, which is not always a compliment.
chineseExample_tr: 從山頂上，整個山谷一覽無餘。

example: Her criticism cut right to the heart of the problem.
chineseExample: 她的批评一针见血，直指问题核心。
description: This idiom originally described skilled acupuncturists who could draw blood (见血) with a single (一) needle (针) insertion, demonstrating perfect technique. The phrase evolved to praise any precise, direct action that achieves its goal immediately. In communication, it describes words that cut directly to the essential point without circumlocution. Modern usage commonly praises sharp analysis, direct criticism, or any statement that immediately addresses the core issue without wasting words.
metaphoric_meaning: Hit the nail on the head; incisive
description_tr: This idiom originally described skilled acupuncturists who could draw blood (見血) with a single (一) needle (針) insertion, demonstrating perfect technique. The phrase evolved to praise any precise, direct action that achieves its goal immediately. In communication, it describes words that cut directly to the essential point without circumlocution. Modern usage commonly praises sharp analysis, direct criticism, or any statement that immediately addresses the core issue without wasting words.
chineseExample_tr: 她的批評一針見血，直指問題核心。

example: He remained unmoved by all the emotional appeals.
chineseExample: 面对所有情感诉求，他无动于衷。
description: No (无) movement (动) in (于) what is innermost (衷). 衷 is specifically the inside of a person, the part not on display, so the phrase reports an absence at a depth the observer cannot actually see — which is why it is always an inference and sometimes an unjust one. Chinese uses it far more often as a criticism than as praise: the situation called for a reaction and none came. Composure is available as a reading, but it is not the one anybody reaches for first.
description_tr: No (無) movement (動) in (於) what is innermost (衷). 衷 is specifically the inside of a person, the part not on display, so the phrase reports an absence at a depth the observer cannot actually see — which is why it is always an inference and sometimes an unjust one. Chinese uses it far more often as a criticism than as praise: the situation called for a reaction and none came. Composure is available as a reading, but it is not the one anybody reaches for first.
chineseExample_tr: 面對所有情感訴求，他無動於衷。

example: For years he worked anonymously before finally gaining recognition.
chineseExample: 多年来他默默无闻地工作，最终获得认可。
description: Silent (默默) and unheard of (无闻) — 闻 is to be heard of, so the second half concerns reputation rather than noise. Doubling 默 supplies the duration: this is not one unremarked act but a working life spent below the level at which things get reported. Chinese is warm about it, and the phrase carries an argument as well as a description, that the absence of recognition says nothing about the value of the work. It is standard in tributes, and it is what people say about whoever actually kept the thing running.
description_tr: Silent (默默) and unheard of (無聞) — 聞 is to be heard of, so the second half concerns reputation rather than noise. Doubling 默 supplies the duration: this is not one unremarked act but a working life spent below the level at which things get reported. Chinese is warm about it, and the phrase carries an argument as well as a description, that the absence of recognition says nothing about the value of the work. It is standard in tributes, and it is what people say about whoever actually kept the thing running.
chineseExample_tr: 多年來他默默無聞地工作，最終獲得認可。

example: Her calligraphy has reached the highest level of mastery.
chineseExample: 她的书法已经达到了炉火纯青的境界。
description: In alchemy the furnace (炉) fire (火) shifting to a pure (纯) blue-green (青) marked the point at which the heat was finally right and the transmutation could take. What the phrase takes from that is a precise claim about mastery: its sign is a change in the quality of the thing rather than in the quantity — not a hotter fire but a different colour. It gets used of skill that has stopped being effortful and become characteristic, and it is reserved for the top of a discipline rather than for competence.
metaphoric_meaning: Highest level of mastery; consummate skill
description_tr: In alchemy the furnace (爐) fire (火) shifting to a pure (純) blue-green (青) marked the point at which the heat was finally right and the transmutation could take. What the phrase takes from that is a precise claim about mastery: its sign is a change in the quality of the thing rather than in the quantity — not a hotter fire but a different colour. Chinese uses it of skill that has stopped being effortful and become characteristic, and it is reserved for the top of a discipline rather than for competence.
chineseExample_tr: 她的書法已經達到了爐火純青的境界。

meaning: Name listed among the front reeds
example: She consistently ranked at the top of her class.
chineseExample: 她的成绩一直名列前茅。
description: An army on the march sent its forward party ahead carrying reeds (茅) as signals, and to be listed (列) among that front (前) group was to be at the very head of the column. Having one's name (名) there became the way of saying one had come out at the top. Chinese uses it for examination results, league tables and sales figures, and it is worth noticing that it does not claim first place: the front rank is a band rather than a position, so what is being asserted is membership of the leading group.
metaphoric_meaning: Rank among the best; be at the top
description_tr: An army on the march sent its forward party ahead carrying reeds (茅) as signals, and to be listed (列) among that front (前) group was to be at the very head of the column. Having one's name (名) there became the way of saying one had come out at the top. Chinese uses it for examination results, league tables and sales figures, and it is worth noticing that it does not claim first place: the front rank is a band rather than a position, so what is being asserted is membership of the leading group.
chineseExample_tr: 她的成績一直名列前茅。

example: The mountain view made her feel refreshed and at ease.
chineseExample: 山景让她心旷神怡。
description: Fan Zhongyan's Yueyang Tower essay describes a visitor who, on a clear day with the lake calm and the birds settling, finds the heart (心) opened out (旷) and the spirit (神) at ease (怡), and forgets both favour and disgrace together. 旷 is spaciousness — an uncluttered feeling rather than a happy one — which is why the phrase belongs to landscape and not to good news. It is said of what a view does to a person, with the implication that something constricting has just been let go of.
description_tr: Fan Zhongyan's Yueyang Tower essay describes a visitor who, on a clear day with the lake calm and the birds settling, finds the heart (心) opened out (曠) and the spirit (神) at ease (怡), and forgets both favour and disgrace together. 曠 is spaciousness — an uncluttered feeling rather than a happy one — which is why the phrase belongs to landscape and not to good news. Chinese uses it of what a view does to a person, with the implication that something constricting has just been let go of.
chineseExample_tr: 山景讓她心曠神怡。

meaning: Produce different from the heart's cutting
example: Her unconventional approach to the problem impressed everyone.
chineseExample: 她别出心裁的方法给大家留下了深刻印象。
description: To bring out (出) something set apart (别) by one's own (心) cutting (裁). 裁 is the tailor's cut, laying the cloth out and deciding where the shears go, so the metaphor puts originality at the planning stage rather than in the execution. What is praised is the decision to lay the pattern out differently, which is why it fits design and staging better than it fits invention. Chinese says it of an unexpected format, an unusual angle on a familiar subject, and any solution whose novelty is structural.
description_tr: To bring out (出) something set apart (別) by one's own (心) cutting (裁). 裁 is the tailor's cut, laying the cloth out and deciding where the shears go, so the metaphor puts originality at the planning stage rather than in the execution. What is praised is the decision to lay the pattern out differently, which is why it fits design and staging better than it fits invention. Chinese uses it of an unexpected format, an unusual angle on a familiar subject, and any solution whose novelty is structural.
chineseExample_tr: 她別出心裁的方法給大家留下了深刻印象。

meaning: Just arriving at the good place
example: The seasoning was just right - neither too much nor too little.
chineseExample: 调味恰到好处，不多不少。
description: Arriving (到) exactly (恰) at the right (好) spot (处). 处 is a place, and the spatial metaphor does real work: the claim is not that something was done well but that there was a point, that going past it would have been as wrong as stopping short, and that this was it. You will hear it of seasoning, of timing, of the length of a speech and of the amount of sympathy offered to somebody in trouble — and it is the one compliment that cannot be paid to anything excessive, however good.
metaphoric_meaning: Stopped at exactly the right point
description_tr: Arriving (到) exactly (恰) at the right (好) spot (處). 處 is a place, and the spatial metaphor does real work: the claim is not that something was done well but that there was a point, that going past it would have been as wrong as stopping short, and that this was it. Chinese uses it of seasoning, of timing, of the length of a speech and of the amount of sympathy offered to somebody in trouble — and it is the one compliment that cannot be paid to anything excessive, however good.
chineseExample_tr: 調味恰到好處，不多不少。

meaning: Not knowing where to put hands and feet
example: Faced with the sudden crisis, the team was at a loss.
chineseExample: 面对突如其来的危机，团队不知所措。
description: Not (不) knowing (知) where (所) to put (措) oneself. The Analects has the fuller form behind it — 无所措手足, no place to put hand or foot — and that bodily image is the right one: this is not indecision about a course of action but the more basic loss of knowing how to stand, or what to do with one's face. Chinese uses it of somebody hit by news they had no script for, and of the junior person in a room where something has just gone badly wrong. It names a state rather than a failing, and carries no blame.
metaphoric_meaning: At a loss; not knowing what to do
description_tr: Not (不) knowing (知) where (所) to put (措) oneself. The Analects has the fuller form behind it — 無所措手足, no place to put hand or foot — and that bodily image is the right one: this is not indecision about a course of action but the more basic loss of knowing how to stand, or what to do with one's face. Chinese uses it of somebody hit by news they had no script for, and of the junior person in a room where something has just gone badly wrong. It names a state rather than a failing, and carries no blame.
chineseExample_tr: 面對突如其來的危機，團隊不知所措。

example: Middle management serves as the bridge between executives and staff.
chineseExample: 中层管理人员起着承上启下的作用。
description: Taking up (承) what is above (上) and opening the way to (启) what is below (下). It began as a term in literary criticism for the transitional sentence — the one that finishes the previous argument and makes the next one possible — and is still used that way about paragraphs and scenes. The transferred sense is organisational: Chinese applies it to middle management, where the same double duty holds, carrying decisions down and information back up. It is a real compliment in both settings, because the joint is where things usually fail.
metaphoric_meaning: Serve as a link between preceding and following
description_tr: Taking up (承) what is above (上) and opening the way to (啟) what is below (下). It began as a term in literary criticism for the transitional sentence — the one that finishes the previous argument and makes the next one possible — and is still used that way about paragraphs and scenes. The transferred sense is organisational: Chinese applies it to middle management, where the same double duty holds, carrying decisions down and information back up. It is a real compliment in both settings, because the joint is where things usually fail.
chineseExample_tr: 中層管理人員起著承上啟下的作用。

example: The teacher treats all students equally regardless of background.
chineseExample: 老师对所有学生一视同仁，不论背景。
description: Han Yu wrote that the sage looks on all with a single (一) regard (视) and extends the same (同) benevolence (仁) to each, holding close those nearby and reaching out to those far off. 仁 is the central Confucian virtue and is normally graduated by relationship — more is owed to a parent than to a stranger — so applying it flat, without that gradient, is the deliberately radical part. You will hear it of teachers, employers and officials, and it is what people demand when they suspect they are being handled differently from somebody else.
description_tr: Han Yu wrote that the sage looks on all with a single (一) regard (視) and extends the same (同) benevolence (仁) to each, holding close those nearby and reaching out to those far off. 仁 is the central Confucian virtue and is normally graduated by relationship — more is owed to a parent than to a stranger — so applying it flat, without that gradient, is the deliberately radical part. Chinese uses it of teachers, employers and officials, and it is what people demand when they suspect they are being handled differently from somebody else.
chineseExample_tr: 老師對所有學生一視同仁，不論背景。

meaning: Push away clouds to see the sun
example: After months of investigation, the truth finally came to light.
chineseExample: 经过数月调查，真相终于拨云见日。
description: Parting (拨) the cloud (云) to see (见) the sun (日). 拨 is a hand movement, sweeping something aside, and that is what separates the phrase from the weather simply clearing: somebody did it. The sun was there the whole time, and the obstruction was the only thing that changed. You will hear it of an explanation that suddenly makes a confusing matter legible, and of vindication after a spell under suspicion, where the implication is that nothing about the truth needed altering.
metaphoric_meaning: Clear away confusion to see the truth
description_tr: Parting (撥) the cloud (雲) to see (見) the sun (日). 撥 is a hand movement, sweeping something aside, and that is what separates the phrase from the weather simply clearing: somebody did it. The sun was there the whole time, and the obstruction was the only thing that changed. Chinese uses it of an explanation that suddenly makes a confusing matter legible, and of vindication after a spell under suspicion, where the implication is that nothing about the truth needed altering.
chineseExample_tr: 經過數月調查，真相終於撥雲見日。

example: The damage was caused by years of neglect.
chineseExample: 这些损坏是长年累月疏忽造成的。
description: Long (长) years (年) and piled-up (累) months (月). Both halves say duration and neither adds information, which is the point: the redundancy is doing rhetorical work, making the stretch of time feel accumulated rather than merely elapsed. That is why it attaches so naturally to things that build up out of sight — a skill, a debt, a resentment, damp in a wall. Chinese uses it for processes whose result is visible and whose progress never was.
metaphoric_meaning: Over a long period of time
description_tr: Long (長) years (年) and piled-up (累) months (月). Both halves say duration and neither adds information, which is the point: the redundancy is doing rhetorical work, making the stretch of time feel accumulated rather than merely elapsed. That is why it attaches so naturally to things that build up out of sight — a skill, a debt, a resentment, damp in a wall. Chinese uses it for processes whose result is visible and whose progress never was.
chineseExample_tr: 這些損壞是長年累月疏忽造成的。

example: Her artistic style is truly one of a kind.
chineseExample: 她的艺术风格独一无二。
description: Alone (独) one (一), and without (无) a second (二). Both halves make the same claim and the doubling is the emphasis: not rare, not the best of its kind, but the only one there is. That absoluteness is why it cannot be graded — nothing is more 独一无二 than anything else. Chinese uses it of people, of experiences and, very heavily, of products, where the advertising instinct has worn it thinner than it deserves. Used sparingly it is the strongest thing available.
description_tr: Alone (獨) one (一), and without (無) a second (二). Both halves make the same claim and the doubling is the emphasis: not rare, not the best of its kind, but the only one there is. That absoluteness is why it cannot be graded — nothing is more 獨一無二 than anything else. Chinese uses it of people, of experiences and, very heavily, of products, where the advertising instinct has worn it thinner than it deserves. Used sparingly it is the strongest thing available.
chineseExample_tr: 她的藝術風格獨一無二。
