example: Good leaders can adapt their strategies to changing circumstances.
chineseExample: 好的领导者能够随机应变。
description: Following (随) the moment (机) and responding (应) to change (变). 机 is the pivot or the trigger, the point at which a situation turns, so the phrase is not about general flexibility but about acting on the particular opening as it appears. It comes out of military thinking, where a plan is understood to be a hypothesis about a battle that has not happened yet. It is said of negotiators, of teachers handling a class that has gone off the rails, and of anybody who abandoned the script correctly.
metaphoric_meaning: Adapt to circumstances; think on one's feet
description_tr: Following (隨) the moment (機) and responding (應) to change (變). 機 is the pivot or the trigger, the point at which a situation turns, so the phrase is not about general flexibility but about acting on the particular opening as it appears. It comes out of military thinking, where a plan is understood to be a hypothesis about a battle that has not happened yet. Chinese uses it of negotiators, of teachers handling a class that has gone off the rails, and of anybody who abandoned the script correctly.
chineseExample_tr: 好的領導者能夠隨機應變。

example: She willingly made sacrifices for her family's wellbeing.
chineseExample: 她心甘情愿为家人的幸福做出牺牲。
description: The heart (心) finding it sweet (甘) and the feelings (情) willing (愿). All four characters push the same way, and the insistence is deliberate: the phrase exists to rule out the readings otherwise available — duty, pressure, resignation, obligation quietly resented. What it asserts is that the person would choose it again. Chinese uses it most often of sacrifice, where the question of willingness actually arises, and it is what somebody says to shut down sympathy they do not want.
description_tr: The heart (心) finding it sweet (甘) and the feelings (情) willing (願). All four characters push the same way, and the insistence is deliberate: the phrase exists to rule out the readings otherwise available — duty, pressure, resignation, obligation quietly resented. What it asserts is that the person would choose it again. Chinese uses it most often of sacrifice, where the question of willingness actually arises, and it is what somebody says to shut down sympathy they do not want.
chineseExample_tr: 她心甘情願為家人的幸福做出犧牲。

example: Scientific research must be based on evidence rather than assumptions.
chineseExample: 科学研究必须实事求是，以证据为基础。
description: This is from the Book of Han, in its account of Liu De, Prince Xian of Hejian, praised for loving antiquity and seeking (求) what is so (是) from actual matters (实事) — that is, for checking texts against evidence rather than accepting received readings. He is not to be confused with Emperor Xian, the last Han emperor, who is a different person entirely. The phrase later became a watchword for evidential scholarship. Modern usage means grounding conclusions in the facts as they are.
description_tr: This comes from the Book of Han, in its account of Liu De, Prince Xian of Hejian, praised for loving antiquity and seeking (求) what is so (是) from actual matters (實事) — that is, for checking texts against evidence rather than accepting received readings. He is not to be confused with Emperor Xian, the last Han emperor, who is a different person entirely. The phrase later became a watchword for evidential scholarship. Modern usage means grounding conclusions in the facts as they are.
chineseExample_tr: 科學研究必須實事求是，以證據為基礎。

example: His claims about his achievements were greatly exaggerated.
chineseExample: 他对自己成就的描述言过其实。
description: Liu Bei, dying, warned Zhuge Liang about Ma Su: his words (言) run past (过) the substance (其实), and he is not to be given large responsibilities — look into it. The Records of the Three Kingdoms adds that Zhuge Liang did not agree, and made Ma Su an adviser anyway; Ma Su later lost Jieting and was executed for it. The phrase describes a reputation running ahead of the ability behind it, and the story is careful that the man who ignored the warning was the cleverest person in the room.
description_tr: Liu Bei, dying, warned Zhuge Liang about Ma Su: his words (言) run past (過) the substance (其實), and he is not to be given large responsibilities — look into it. The Records of the Three Kingdoms adds that Zhuge Liang did not agree, and made Ma Su an adviser anyway; Ma Su later lost Jieting and was executed for it. The phrase describes a reputation running ahead of the ability behind it, and the story is careful that the man who ignored the warning was the cleverest person in the room.
chineseExample_tr: 他對自己成就的描述言過其實。

example: Investing in quality now will solve the problem once and for all.
chineseExample: 现在投资高质量产品可以一劳永逸地解决问题。
description: One (一) exertion (劳) and lasting (永) ease (逸). Ban Gu uses the older form in an inscription cut on a mountain after a frontier campaign, arguing that one hard effort had bought a long peace. That is the claim the phrase always makes, and Chinese treats it with some suspicion: it appears at least as often in the negative, pointing out that no such solution exists, as it does in the positive. It is the standard vocabulary of arguments about permanent fixes.
metaphoric_meaning: Solve a problem once and for all
description_tr: One (一) exertion (勞) and lasting (永) ease (逸). Ban Gu uses the older form in an inscription cut on a mountain after a frontier campaign, arguing that one hard effort had bought a long peace. That is the claim the phrase always makes, and Chinese treats it with some suspicion: it appears at least as often in the negative, pointing out that no such solution exists, as it does in the positive. It is the standard vocabulary of arguments about permanent fixes.
chineseExample_tr: 現在投資高質量產品可以一勞永逸地解決問題。

example: The technological breakthrough was unprecedented in human history.
chineseExample: 这项技术突破在人类历史上前所未有。
description: Nothing before (前) this has (有) ever (未) been like it — 所 is the classical nominaliser holding the clause together, so the shape is that which has not previously existed. The phrase claims absolute novelty rather than rarity, and it carries the weight of a historical judgement: to say it is to say the record has been searched. Chinese officialdom and advertising both like it for exactly that reason, and constant use has worn it down, so a careful speaker saves it for things that really have no precedent.
description_tr: Nothing before (前) this has (有) ever (未) been like it — 所 is the classical nominaliser holding the clause together, so the shape is that which has not previously existed. The phrase claims absolute novelty rather than rarity, and it carries the weight of a historical judgement: to say it is to say the record has been searched. Chinese officialdom and advertising both like it for exactly that reason, and constant use has worn it down, so a careful speaker saves it for things that really have no precedent.
chineseExample_tr: 這項技術突破在人類歷史上前所未有。

example: The budget constraints left the department financially stretched.
chineseExample: 预算限制让部门捉襟见肘。
description: The Zhuangzi describes Zengzi in poverty: he had not made a coat in ten years, and when he straightened his cap the chin-strap snapped, when he pulled (捉) his lapel (襟) across, his elbow (肘) came through (见). The clothing is failing at three points at once, and the comedy is exact — every attempt to make himself presentable exposes something else. That is what the phrase carries over. In practice it is used of budgets and of staffing, where covering one gap opens another, and the sense is of a shortage that can no longer be fixed by rearrangement.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi describes Zengzi in poverty: he had not made a coat in ten years, and when he straightened his cap the chin-strap snapped, when he pulled (捉) his lapel (襟) across, his elbow (肘) came through (見). The clothing is failing at three points at once, and the comedy is exact — every attempt to make himself presentable exposes something else. That is what the phrase carries over. Chinese uses it of budgets and of staffing, where covering one gap opens another, and the sense is of a shortage that can no longer be fixed by rearrangement.
chineseExample_tr: 預算限制讓部門捉襟見肘。

example: Management deliberately ignored the obvious problems.
chineseExample: 管理层对明显的问题视而不见。
description: This comes from the Great Learning, which says that where the mind is not present, one looks (视) and does not (不) see (见), listens and does not hear, eats and does not taste. The failure is of attention rather than of the eye, and the passage treats it as a moral condition rather than a lapse. In practice it is used of deliberately not seeing what is in front of somebody, and the original charge — that this is a condition of the person and not of the eye — is still audible in it.
metaphoric_meaning: Turn a blind eye; deliberately ignore
description_tr: This comes from the Great Learning, which says that where the mind is not present, one looks (視) and does not (不) see (見), listens and does not hear, eats and does not taste. The failure is of attention rather than of the eye, and the passage treats it as a moral condition rather than a lapse. Chinese uses it of deliberately not seeing what is in front of somebody, and the original charge — that this is a condition of the person and not of the eye — is still audible in it.
chineseExample_tr: 管理層對明顯的問題視而不見。

example: After the argument, he acted as if nothing had occurred.
chineseExample: 争吵之后，他若无其事地继续工作。
description: Behaving as if (若) there were no (无) such (其) matter (事). The phrase reports a performance and declines to say what is behind it, which is exactly its usefulness: the same four characters cover admirable composure, deliberate concealment and genuine indifference, and the listener has to supply which. Chinese narrative uses it at the moment a character walks back into a room, and the tension in the sentence comes from the observer not knowing either.
description_tr: Behaving as if (若) there were no (無) such (其) matter (事). The phrase reports a performance and declines to say what is behind it, which is exactly its usefulness: the same four characters cover admirable composure, deliberate concealment and genuine indifference, and the listener has to supply which. Chinese narrative uses it at the moment a character walks back into a room, and the tension in the sentence comes from the observer not knowing either.
chineseExample_tr: 爭吵之後，他若無其事地繼續工作。

example: He built his business empire from nothing through hard work.
chineseExample: 他白手起家，通过努力建立了自己的商业帝国。
description: Starting (起) a household (家) with bare (白) hands (手). 白 is empty here rather than the colour — the same 白 as in 白跑一趟, a trip made for nothing — so what is claimed concerns what was in the hands at the beginning, which is nothing at all. 家 is a household or an estate rather than a company, and that older sense is worth keeping: what gets built is a family's standing, not a business. Chinese applies it to entrepreneurs now, and it remains the highest-status origin story available.
description_tr: Starting (起) a household (家) with bare (白) hands (手). 白 is empty here rather than the colour — the same 白 as in 白跑一趟, a trip made for nothing — so what is claimed concerns what was in the hands at the beginning, which is nothing at all. 家 is a household or an estate rather than a company, and that older sense is worth keeping: what gets built is a family's standing, not a business. Chinese applies it to entrepreneurs now, and it remains the highest-status origin story available.
chineseExample_tr: 他白手起家，通過努力建立了自己的商業帝國。

example: Instead of improving, his behavior only got worse.
chineseExample: 他的行为不但没有改善，反而变本加厉。
description: Xiao Tong, introducing his anthology, described how later writers built on their predecessors and added ornament, changing (变) the original (本) and intensifying (加厉) it. He meant it neutrally, as an account of how literature develops. The phrase has since gone entirely negative, and that reversal is worth knowing, because the modern sense is fixed: it now describes behaviour that was already bad and has been repeated harder after somebody objected. In practice it is used of an escalation that a warning failed to stop.
description_tr: Xiao Tong, introducing his anthology, described how later writers built on their predecessors and added ornament, changing (變) the original (本) and intensifying (加厲) it. He meant it neutrally, as an account of how literature develops. The phrase has since gone entirely negative, and that reversal is worth knowing, because the modern sense is fixed: it now describes behaviour that was already bad and has been repeated harder after somebody objected. Chinese uses it of an escalation that a warning failed to stop.
chineseExample_tr: 他的行為不但沒有改善，反而變本加厲。

example: He devoted his entire life to public service until his last breath.
chineseExample: 他鞠躬尽瘁，为公共服务奉献一生。
description: To bend the body (鞠躬) and spend oneself utterly (尽瘁). The line is from Zhuge Liang's second memorial before marching north: your servant will bow himself to the task and give out his whole strength, and stop only at death — and whether it ends in success or failure is not something his foresight can reach. That last clause is usually dropped and is the reason the phrase is moving: the pledge is made without any assurance it will work. It is normally quoted whole as 鞠躬尽瘁，死而后已.
metaphoric_meaning: Devote oneself completely; work until exhausted
description_tr: To bend the body (鞠躬) and spend oneself utterly (盡瘁). The line is from Zhuge Liang's second memorial before marching north: your servant will bow himself to the task and give out his whole strength, and stop only at death — and whether it ends in success or failure is not something his foresight can reach. That last clause is usually dropped and is the reason the phrase is moving: the pledge is made without any assurance it will work. It is normally quoted whole as 鞠躬盡瘁，死而後已.
chineseExample_tr: 他鞠躬盡瘁，為公共服務奉獻一生。

example: The partners shared an unspoken agreement about how to handle the situation.
chineseExample: 合伙人心照不宣地达成了共识。
description: Hearts (心) lit (照) for one another, with nothing (不) announced (宣). 照 is illumination that reveals rather than a signal that is sent, so the understanding is treated as a condition already in place and not as a message that got through. That is what separates it from tact or from hinting. You will hear it of two people who never needed to agree anything because it was never in question, and also, more coolly, of a room where everybody knows what is going on and nobody intends to be the one who says it.
description_tr: Hearts (心) lit (照) for one another, with nothing (不) announced (宣). 照 is illumination that reveals rather than a signal that is sent, so the understanding is treated as a condition already in place and not as a message that got through. That is what separates it from tact or from hinting. Chinese uses it of two people who never needed to agree anything because it was never in question, and also, more coolly, of a room where everybody knows what is going on and nobody intends to be the one who says it.
chineseExample_tr: 合夥人心照不宣地達成了共識。

example: She seems to have knowledge about every subject.
chineseExample: 她似乎无所不知。
description: There is nothing (无所) that is not (不) known (知). The construction is a double negative and is stronger for it: instead of claiming all knowledge it denies the existence of any exception, which is a harder thing to assert and an easier one to puncture. That is why the phrase is so often lightly ironic. It is said of the colleague who has an answer for everything, and its straight sense — genuine, sage-like universality — now sounds archaic outside religious contexts.
description_tr: There is nothing (無所) that is not (不) known (知). The construction is a double negative and is stronger for it: instead of claiming all knowledge it denies the existence of any exception, which is a harder thing to assert and an easier one to puncture. That is why the phrase is so often lightly ironic. Chinese uses it of the colleague who has an answer for everything, and its straight sense — genuine, sage-like universality — now sounds archaic outside religious contexts.
chineseExample_tr: 她似乎無所不知。

example: After retirement, he felt aimless with nothing to occupy his time.
chineseExample: 退休后，他无所事事，感到很迷茫。
description: There is nothing (无所) that counts as being occupied (事事). The second 事 is a verb, to be busy with something, so the phrase is not about being unoccupied by accident but about occupation itself amounting to nothing. Chinese is not kind about it: the register is critical, and the person described is understood to have the time and to be wasting it. It is distinct from resting, which is legitimate and named differently, and it is among the likeliest things a Chinese parent will say to an adult child at home.
metaphoric_meaning: Have nothing to do; be idle
description_tr: There is nothing (無所) that counts as being occupied (事事). The second 事 is a verb, to be busy with something, so the phrase is not about being unoccupied by accident but about occupation itself amounting to nothing. Chinese is not kind about it: the register is critical, and the person described is understood to have the time and to be wasting it. It is distinct from resting, which is legitimate and named differently, and it is among the likeliest things a Chinese parent will say to an adult child at home.
chineseExample_tr: 退休後，他無所事事，感到很迷茫。

meaning: Happy to hear delighted to see
example: This type of entertainment is popular with audiences of all ages.
chineseExample: 这类娱乐节目为各年龄段观众所喜闻乐见。
description: Glad (喜) to hear (闻) it and pleased (乐) to see (见) it. The two verbs cover the channels an audience receives things through, which is why the phrase attaches so readily to performance and broadcasting. What it claims is not quality but reception — that people actually want the thing — and that makes it a favourite of official and institutional language, where it is used to argue that something worthy is also popular. A learner should hear that institutional tone in it: it is not what one friend says to another about a film.
description_tr: Glad (喜) to hear (聞) it and pleased (樂) to see (見) it. The two verbs cover the channels an audience receives things through, which is why the phrase attaches so readily to performance and broadcasting. What it claims is not quality but reception — that people actually want the thing — and that makes it a favourite of official and institutional language, where it is used to argue that something worthy is also popular. A learner should hear that institutional tone in it: it is not what one friend says to another about a film.
chineseExample_tr: 這類娛樂節目為各年齡段觀眾所喜聞樂見。

meaning: Add frost on top of snow
example: Losing his job when his car broke down was adding frost to snow.
chineseExample: 车坏的时候又丢了工作，真是雪上加霜。
description: Frost (霜) added (加) on top of (上) snow (雪). Both are the same cold expressed twice, and that is the precision of it: the second misfortune is not a different kind of trouble but more of the one already there, which is what makes it feel gratuitous. It gets used of the bill that arrives during the illness, and of the second piece of bad news inside a week. English reaches for 'add insult to injury', which is close but wrong in one respect — there is no insult here, and nobody need have intended anything.
metaphoric_meaning: Add insult to injury; make things worse
description_tr: Frost (霜) added (加) on top of (上) snow (雪). Both are the same cold expressed twice, and that is the precision of it: the second misfortune is not a different kind of trouble but more of the one already there, which is what makes it feel gratuitous. Chinese uses it of the bill that arrives during the illness, and of the second piece of bad news inside a week. English reaches for 'add insult to injury', which is close but wrong in one respect — there is no insult here, and nobody need have intended anything.
chineseExample_tr: 車壞的時候又丟了工作，真是雪上加霜。

example: The sudden influx of customers left the staff overwhelmed.
chineseExample: 突然涌入的顾客让员工应接不暇。
description: Wang Xianzhi said that travelling the road through Shanyin, with the hills and rivers throwing the light back at one another, left a person 应接不暇 — no leisure (不暇) left over from meeting (应) and taking in (接) it all. The original is about abundance rather than pressure: the eye cannot keep up because there is too much worth looking at. Chinese has since carried it over to work and to visitors, where the abundance is less welcome, but the flattering sense survives — a shop can be 应接不暇 and its owner delighted.
metaphoric_meaning: Too much to cope with; overwhelmed
description_tr: Wang Xianzhi said that travelling the road through Shanyin, with the hills and rivers throwing the light back at one another, left a person 應接不暇 — no leisure (不暇) left over from meeting (應) and taking in (接) it all. The original is about abundance rather than pressure: the eye cannot keep up because there is too much worth looking at. Chinese has since carried it over to work and to visitors, where the abundance is less welcome, but the flattering sense survives — a shop can be 應接不暇 and its owner delighted.
chineseExample_tr: 突然湧入的顧客讓員工應接不暇。

meaning: Same as it has always been
example: Despite the challenges, she continued to work with the same dedication.
chineseExample: 尽管面临挑战，她一如既往地努力工作。
description: Just as (一如) it has been all along (既往). 既往 is the completed past, what has already gone by, so the phrase measures the present against the whole of the record rather than against last time. That is what makes it stronger than 'as usual': it claims an unbroken run. Chinese uses it in the register of commitment — 一如既往地支持, supporting you as we always have — and it is the standard formula for saying that a change in circumstances has changed nothing.
description_tr: Just as (一如) it has been all along (既往). 既往 is the completed past, what has already gone by, so the phrase measures the present against the whole of the record rather than against last time. That is what makes it stronger than 'as usual': it claims an unbroken run. Chinese uses it in the register of commitment — 一如既往地支持, supporting you as we always have — and it is the standard formula for saying that a change in circumstances has changed nothing.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管面臨挑戰，她一如既往地努力工作。

meaning: Minister of Works sees it habitually
example: Traffic jams have become so common that no one complains anymore.
chineseExample: 交通堵塞已经司空见惯，没人再抱怨了。
description: Liu Yuxi, dining with the retired minister Li Shen, watched the singing girls perform and wrote a poem on the spot: sights like this are ordinary to a Minister of Works (司空), and they break the heart of a mere provincial governor. The self-deprecation is the joke, and 司空见惯 — what the Minister of Works has seen (见) often enough to be used to (惯) — became the phrase. It names whatever has stopped registering because it is always there, and Chinese says it with a flatness that is usually the point.
metaphoric_meaning: So common as to attract no attention
description_tr: Liu Yuxi, dining with the retired minister Li Shen, watched the singing girls perform and wrote a poem on the spot: sights like this are ordinary to a Minister of Works (司空), and they break the heart of a mere provincial governor. The self-deprecation is the joke, and 司空見慣 — what the Minister of Works has seen (見) often enough to be used to (慣) — became the phrase. It names whatever has stopped registering because it is always there, and Chinese says it with a flatness that is usually the point.
chineseExample_tr: 交通堵塞已經司空見慣，沒人再抱怨了。

example: The family said goodbye with great reluctance at the airport.
chineseExample: 一家人在机场依依不舍地告别。
description: 依 is to lean on or cling to; doubled, 依依 is the swaying of willow branches, and it reaches Chinese from the Book of Songs line about willows at a parting. With 不舍, unwilling (不) to let go (舍), the phrase stretches the moment of separation out. What it catches is a body's reluctance rather than a decision — the pause at the door, the turning back. In practice it is used of farewells at stations and airports, and of leaving somewhere one will not be returning to.
description_tr: 依 is to lean on or cling to; doubled, 依依 is the swaying of willow branches, and it reaches Chinese from the Book of Songs line about willows at a parting. With 不捨, unwilling (不) to let go (舍), the phrase stretches the moment of separation out. What it catches is a body's reluctance rather than a decision — the pause at the door, the turning back. Chinese uses it of farewells at stations and airports, and of leaving somewhere one will not be returning to.
chineseExample_tr: 一家人在機場依依不捨地告別。

example: Instead of forcing things, she decided to let events unfold naturally.
chineseExample: 她决定顺其自然，不再强求。
description: Going along with (顺) the way things are of themselves (自然). 自然 is literally self-so, what a thing is when nothing is being done to it, and the phrase belongs to the Daoist argument that intervention usually costs more than it returns. It is not passivity and Chinese does not use it that way: it is advice offered at the specific point where effort has stopped helping. Said to somebody agonising over a decision that is no longer theirs it is a kindness; said too early it is an evasion.
description_tr: Going along with (順) the way things are of themselves (自然). 自然 is literally self-so, what a thing is when nothing is being done to it, and the phrase belongs to the Daoist argument that intervention usually costs more than it returns. It is not passivity and Chinese does not use it that way: it is advice offered at the specific point where effort has stopped helping. Said to somebody agonising over a decision that is no longer theirs it is a kindness; said too early it is an evasion.
chineseExample_tr: 她決定順其自然，不再強求。

example: Education is a long-term investment in the nation's future.
chineseExample: 教育是国家的百年大计。
description: A plan (计) of a hundred (百) years (年), on the largest (大) scale. The hundred is a real claim rather than a flourish: the phrase is used to argue that something should be judged on a horizon longer than any career or administration, which is exactly the argument hardest to win. It attaches most often to education, infrastructure and forestry. Chinese uses it to head off short-term reasoning, and the sentence it appears in is almost always making the case for spending now.
metaphoric_meaning: Long-term plan; matter of lasting importance
description_tr: A plan (計) of a hundred (百) years (年), on the largest (大) scale. The hundred is a real claim rather than a flourish: the phrase is used to argue that something should be judged on a horizon longer than any career or administration, which is exactly the argument hardest to win. It attaches most often to education, infrastructure and forestry. Chinese uses it to head off short-term reasoning, and the sentence it appears in is almost always making the case for spending now.
chineseExample_tr: 教育是國家的百年大計。

example: In the competition, each team showcased their unique strengths.
chineseExample: 比赛中，各队各显神通。
description: Each one (各) displaying (显) their divine powers (神通). 神通 is a Buddhist technical term for the supernormal faculties attributed to the enlightened, and the phrase travels attached to the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, each getting across by their own method rather than sharing a boat. That story is the whole meaning: no common approach, no coordination, and everybody arrives. Chinese reserves it for situations where people have been left to solve something their own way, and it is cheerful about it.
description_tr: Each one (各) displaying (顯) their divine powers (神通). 神通 is a Buddhist technical term for the supernormal faculties attributed to the enlightened, and the phrase travels attached to the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, each getting across by their own method rather than sharing a boat. That story is the whole meaning: no common approach, no coordination, and everybody arrives. Chinese uses it of situations where people have been left to solve something their own way, and it is cheerful about it.
chineseExample_tr: 比賽中，各隊各顯神通。

example: Don't make such a fuss over a minor mistake.
chineseExample: 不要为小错误大惊小怪。
description: Big (大) alarm (惊) at a small (小) oddity (怪). The construction sets the size of the reaction against the size of the cause in a single four-character span, which is what makes it economical as a rebuke. It is generally mild — a family word rather than a serious criticism — and it appears most often in the imperative, 别大惊小怪, don't make such a fuss, addressed to someone who has just reacted to a spider.
description_tr: Big (大) alarm (驚) at a small (小) oddity (怪). The construction sets the size of the reaction against the size of the cause in a single four-character span, which is what makes it economical as a rebuke. It is generally mild — a family word rather than a serious criticism — and it appears most often in the imperative, 別大驚小怪, don't make such a fuss, addressed to someone who has just reacted to a spider.
chineseExample_tr: 不要為小錯誤大驚小怪。

meaning: Mount Tai pressing on the head
example: The enormous pressure of the deadline weighed heavily on the team.
chineseExample: 截止日期的压力如泰山压顶。
description: Mount Tai (泰山) pressing (压) down on the crown of the head (顶). Tai is the mountain Chinese reaches for whenever weight is wanted — it is the standard against which a death is heavy or light — so the phrase takes the heaviest available object and puts it in the one position where nothing can be done about it. What it describes is pressure with no room left underneath. It gets used of deadlines, of expectations and of authority bearing down, and it is always about the sensation rather than the odds.
description_tr: Mount Tai (泰山) pressing (壓) down on the crown of the head (頂). Tai is the mountain Chinese reaches for whenever weight is wanted — it is the standard against which a death is heavy or light — so the phrase takes the heaviest available object and puts it in the one position where nothing can be done about it. What it describes is pressure with no room left underneath. Chinese uses it of deadlines, of expectations and of authority bearing down, and it is always about the sensation rather than the odds.
chineseExample_tr: 截止日期的壓力如泰山壓頂。

example: Her legal argument was flawless and impossible to challenge.
chineseExample: 她的法律论证无懈可击。
description: No (无) slackness (懈) that can (可) be struck at (击). 懈 is looseness, a lapse of tension, the place where a guard has dropped — so the phrase is defensive in origin and describes a line with no soft point anywhere along it. That is why it is stronger than 'flawless': the claim is not that a thing is fine but that an opponent hunting for the gap will not find one. Chinese reserves it for arguments, alibis and defences, and it presupposes somebody actively trying.
description_tr: No (無) slackness (懈) that can (可) be struck at (擊). 懈 is looseness, a lapse of tension, the place where a guard has dropped — so the phrase is defensive in origin and describes a line with no soft point anywhere along it. That is why it is stronger than 'flawless': the claim is not that a thing is fine but that an opponent hunting for the gap will not find one. Chinese uses it of arguments, alibis and defences, and it presupposes somebody actively trying.
chineseExample_tr: 她的法律論證無懈可擊。

example: He tends to make things up without any evidence.
chineseExample: 他经常信口开河，没有任何依据。
description: To open (开) the floodgates (河) on the strength of the mouth (信口) alone. 信 here is giving free rein rather than trusting — the same use as in 信手拈来 — so what is described is speech let loose with nothing checking it. The image is of a volume of water released, which is why it fits the person who talks confidently and at length about things they have not looked into. Chinese uses it as a real accusation: it does not mean lying, it means not caring whether it is true.
description_tr: To open (開) the floodgates (河) on the strength of the mouth (信口) alone. 信 here is giving free rein rather than trusting — the same use as in 信手拈來 — so what is described is speech let loose with nothing checking it. The image is of a volume of water released, which is why it fits the person who talks confidently and at length about things they have not looked into. Chinese uses it as a real accusation: it does not mean lying, it means not caring whether it is true.
chineseExample_tr: 他經常信口開河，沒有任何依據。

meaning: Greatly different like paths and courtyards
example: Their views on the matter are completely different.
chineseExample: 他们对这件事的看法大相径庭。
description: The Zhuangzi's wording is 大有径庭 — there is a great deal of 径庭 about it — where 径 is the footpath outside a door and 庭 the courtyard within, the gap between them standing for the distance between what was said and ordinary sense. The modern form puts 相 in, making it mutual. What the phrase asserts is a difference of kind rather than of degree, which is why Chinese will not use it for close comparisons: two things 大相径庭 are not being ranked, they are being placed apart.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi's wording is 大有徑庭 — there is a great deal of 徑庭 about it — where 徑 is the footpath outside a door and 庭 the courtyard within, the gap between them standing for the distance between what was said and ordinary sense. The modern form puts 相 in, making it mutual. What the phrase asserts is a difference of kind rather than of degree, which is why Chinese will not use it for close comparisons: two things 大相徑庭 are not being ranked, they are being placed apart.
chineseExample_tr: 他們對這件事的看法大相徑庭。

example: The nurse provided meticulous care for the patient.
chineseExample: 护士对病人的照顾无微不至。
description: There is no (无) smallness (微) that is not (不) reached (至). The construction works by exhaustion rather than by praise: nothing is said about how good the care is, only that no scale proved too fine for it to have got down to. That is why the phrase is reserved for attention sustained over time rather than for a single kindness. It gets used of nursing, of hospitality and of a parent, and it is among the warmest things available to say about somebody's conduct toward another person.
description_tr: There is no (無) smallness (微) that is not (不) reached (至). The construction works by exhaustion rather than by praise: nothing is said about how good the care is, only that no scale proved too fine for it to have got down to. That is why the phrase is reserved for attention sustained over time rather than for a single kindness. Chinese uses it of nursing, of hospitality and of a parent, and it is among the warmest things available to say about somebody's conduct toward another person.
chineseExample_tr: 護士對病人的照顧無微不至。

example: His dishonesty eventually backfired on him.
chineseExample: 他的不诚实最终让他自食其果。
description: To eat (食) the fruit (果) of one's own (自) tree (其). The metaphor is agricultural and its force lies in the ownership: the fruit is not a punishment sent from outside but the thing that grew from what was planted, so nobody has to be blamed for the outcome arriving. Chinese uses it with satisfaction rather than pity, and almost always of somebody who was warned. It is the standard phrase for a consequence that has come home, and it leaves no room for the person to be a victim of it.
metaphoric_meaning: Reap what one sows; suffer consequences
description_tr: To eat (食) the fruit (果) of one's own (自) tree (其). The metaphor is agricultural and its force lies in the ownership: the fruit is not a punishment sent from outside but the thing that grew from what was planted, so nobody has to be blamed for the outcome arriving. Chinese uses it with satisfaction rather than pity, and almost always of somebody who was warned. It is the standard phrase for a consequence that has come home, and it leaves no room for the person to be a victim of it.
chineseExample_tr: 他的不誠實最終讓他自食其果。

example: After the incident, he resolved to completely change his ways.
chineseExample: 事件之后，他决心痛改前非。
description: To change (改) one's former (前) wrongs (非) painfully (痛). 痛 is the load-bearing character: without it the phrase would describe reform, and with it the reform is required to have cost something. That is the test Chinese applies — the change is not credited unless it hurt. It belongs to formal contexts, to apologies and to accounts of somebody's return from a bad period, and it cannot be used lightly about a small correction.
description_tr: To change (改) one's former (前) wrongs (非) painfully (痛). 痛 is the load-bearing character: without it the phrase would describe reform, and with it the reform is required to have cost something. That is the test Chinese applies — the change is not credited unless it hurt. It belongs to formal contexts, to apologies and to accounts of somebody's return from a bad period, and it cannot be used lightly about a small correction.
chineseExample_tr: 事件之後，他決心痛改前非。

example: Both candidates bring different but valuable skills to the position.
chineseExample: 两位候选人各有所长，都能为职位带来价值。
description: This idiom states that each person (各) has (有) their own (所) strengths (长). It acknowledges that different individuals excel in different areas, promoting appreciation for diversity of talents. The phrase appeared in Confucian texts discussing how wise rulers recognize and employ varied talents. It counters the tendency to rank people hierarchically. Modern usage encourages recognizing everyone's unique contributions and building teams that leverage complementary strengths.
description_tr: This idiom states that each person (各) has (有) their own (所) strengths (長). It acknowledges that different individuals excel in different areas, promoting appreciation for diversity of talents. The phrase appeared in Confucian texts discussing how wise rulers recognize and employ varied talents. It counters the tendency to rank people hierarchically. Modern usage encourages recognizing everyone's unique contributions and building teams that leverage complementary strengths.
chineseExample_tr: 兩位候選人各有所長，都能為職位帶來價值。

example: Through constant practice, she became an expert.
chineseExample: 通过不断练习，她熟能生巧，成为专家。
description: Ouyang Xiu tells of an old oil seller who watched a celebrated archer at practice and nodded, only slightly impressed. Challenged, he set a gourd on the ground, laid a coin over its mouth and poured oil through the square hole without wetting the metal: 无他，但手熟尔 — nothing to it, my hand is simply practised. Familiarity (熟) is able (能) to produce (生) skill (巧), and the story has a point to make: the archer's gift is being deflated by a tradesman, and repetition turns out to be doing more of the work than anybody wants to admit.
description_tr: Ouyang Xiu tells of an old oil seller who watched a celebrated archer at practice and nodded, only slightly impressed. Challenged, he set a gourd on the ground, laid a coin over its mouth and poured oil through the square hole without wetting the metal: 無他，但手熟爾 — nothing to it, my hand is simply practised. Familiarity (熟) is able (能) to produce (生) skill (巧), and the story has a point to make: the archer's gift is being deflated by a tradesman, and repetition turns out to be doing more of the work than anybody wants to admit.
chineseExample_tr: 通過不斷練習，她熟能生巧，成為專家。

example: Her unique style sets her apart from other designers.
chineseExample: 她独特的风格使她与众不同。
description: Not (不) the same as (同) the crowd (众), with 与 marking the comparison. Chinese has long been ambivalent about the condition this names, and the ambivalence survives inside the phrase: it is a compliment when the speaker approves of the difference and a diagnosis when they do not, and nothing in the four characters settles which. That makes it more useful than English 'unique', which has worn down to mean merely good. Chinese says it of design, of a person's manner, and of children whose difference has not yet been decided about.
description_tr: Not (不) the same as (同) the crowd (眾), with 與 marking the comparison. Chinese has long been ambivalent about the condition this names, and the ambivalence survives inside the phrase: it is a compliment when the speaker approves of the difference and a diagnosis when they do not, and nothing in the four characters settles which. That makes it more useful than English 'unique', which has worn down to mean merely good. Chinese uses it of design, of a person's manner, and of children whose difference has not yet been decided about.
chineseExample_tr: 她獨特的風格使她與眾不同。

example: Despite his fame, the professor remains approachable to students.
chineseExample: 尽管名声很大，这位教授对学生仍然平易近人。
description: The Records of the Grand Historian has 平易近民 — level and easy, and close to the people — of a ruler whose administration was plain enough that people would come to him. 民 became taboo under the Tang, whose second emperor was named Li Shimin, and the phrase was rewritten with 人, which is the form still in use. Level (平易) and approachable (近人) is therefore about obstacles removed rather than about warmth. You will hear it of seniors who have not put distance between themselves and everybody else, and it is high praise precisely because rank makes it optional.
metaphoric_meaning: Approachable; easy to get along with
description_tr: The Records of the Grand Historian has 平易近民 — level and easy, and close to the people — of a ruler whose administration was plain enough that people would come to him. 民 became taboo under the Tang, whose second emperor was named Li Shimin, and the phrase was rewritten with 人, which is the form still in use. Level (平易) and approachable (近人) is therefore about obstacles removed rather than about warmth. Chinese uses it of seniors who have not put distance between themselves and everybody else, and it is high praise precisely because rank makes it optional.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管名聲很大，這位教授對學生仍然平易近人。

example: The discovery had a tremendous impact on the scientific community.
chineseExample: 这一发现在科学界引起了惊天动地的影响。
description: Startling (惊) heaven (天) and shaking (动) earth (地). The pair is the standard Chinese formula for totality — heaven and earth being everything there is — so the phrase claims that nothing was left unaffected by whatever happened. It is deliberately outsized and Chinese knows it, which is why it works both as genuine praise for something historic and as a dry exaggeration about a colleague's small crisis. The tone comes entirely from what it is attached to.
description_tr: Startling (驚) heaven (天) and shaking (動) earth (地). The pair is the standard Chinese formula for totality — heaven and earth being everything there is — so the phrase claims that nothing was left unaffected by whatever happened. It is deliberately outsized and Chinese knows it, which is why it works both as genuine praise for something historic and as a dry exaggeration about a colleague's small crisis. The tone comes entirely from what it is attached to.
chineseExample_tr: 這一發現在科學界引起了驚天動地的影響。

example: Without proper documentation, progress was impossible.
chineseExample: 没有适当的文件，工作寸步难行。
description: Unable to walk (难行) so much as an inch (寸) of a step (步). 寸步 is the smallest movement that still counts as moving, so the phrase denies not progress but motion of any kind. That is what separates it from difficulty: what is claimed is a stop rather than a struggle. Chinese uses it of paperwork that has seized up, of a project blocked at every approach, and quite literally of crowds, mud and snow.
metaphoric_meaning: Unable to move forward at all
description_tr: Unable to walk (難行) so much as an inch (寸) of a step (步). 寸步 is the smallest movement that still counts as moving, so the phrase denies not progress but motion of any kind. That is what separates it from difficulty: what is claimed is a stop rather than a struggle. Chinese uses it of paperwork that has seized up, of a project blocked at every approach, and quite literally of crowds, mud and snow.
chineseExample_tr: 沒有適當的文件，工作寸步難行。

example: She couldn't wait to share the good news with her family.
chineseExample: 她迫不及待地想和家人分享这个好消息。
description: Pressed (迫) so hard that one cannot manage (不及) to wait (待). 不及 is a failure to reach something in time, so what is described is waiting that has been overtaken rather than patience that has been lost. That is a slightly different claim, and it is why the phrase carries no criticism: nobody is being impatient, the pressure simply outran them. Chinese uses it of somebody opening a letter in the corridor, and of a child who cannot get their shoes off fast enough.
description_tr: Pressed (迫) so hard that one cannot manage (不及) to wait (待). 不及 is a failure to reach something in time, so what is described is waiting that has been overtaken rather than patience that has been lost. That is a slightly different claim, and it is why the phrase carries no criticism: nobody is being impatient, the pressure simply outran them. Chinese uses it of somebody opening a letter in the corridor, and of a child who cannot get their shoes off fast enough.
chineseExample_tr: 她迫不及待地想和家人分享這個好消息。

meaning: Orderly like a well with sequence
example: The files were arranged in perfect order.
chineseExample: 文件排列得井然有序。
description: 井然 is the orderliness of the character 井 itself — a grid of intersecting lines, the shape the classical well-field system laid over farmland — so a particular kind of order is being claimed: repeating, planned, and visible from above. 有序, having (有) sequence (序), adds that the parts also come in the right order. It gets used of warehouses, filing, evacuations and timetables, and the compliment is to the system rather than to any tidiness in the individual pieces.
description_tr: 井然 is the orderliness of the character 井 itself — a grid of intersecting lines, the shape the classical well-field system laid over farmland — so a particular kind of order is being claimed: repeating, planned, and visible from above. 有序, having (有) sequence (序), adds that the parts also come in the right order. Chinese uses it of warehouses, filing, evacuations and timetables, and the compliment is to the system rather than to any tidiness in the individual pieces.
chineseExample_tr: 文件排列得井然有序。

example: After years of struggle, success finally arrived.
chineseExample: 经过多年奋斗，终于苦尽甘来。
description: The bitter (苦) exhausted (尽) and the sweet (甘) arriving (来). Both are tastes, and the phrase treats a life as something with a flavour that changes, which is gentler than the English idea of a reward for endurance: nothing is being earned, the bitterness is simply running out. That is why it consoles rather than exhorts. Chinese says it to somebody at the end of a long bad stretch, and it is what an older relative says about a hard few years now finished.
description_tr: The bitter (苦) exhausted (盡) and the sweet (甘) arriving (來). Both are tastes, and the phrase treats a life as something with a flavour that changes, which is gentler than the English idea of a reward for endurance: nothing is being earned, the bitterness is simply running out. That is why it consoles rather than exhorts. Chinese says it to somebody at the end of a long bad stretch, and it is what an older relative says about a hard few years now finished.
chineseExample_tr: 經過多年奮鬥，終於苦盡甘來。

example: The sudden question left him completely flustered.
chineseExample: 这个突如其来的问题让他手足无措。
description: Hands (手) and feet (足) with nowhere (无) to be put (措). The Analects supplies the ancestor — 无所措手足, said of people under a government whose rules make ordinary conduct impossible — and the modern phrase keeps the bodily image while narrowing it to a moment. It reports panic from the outside, as a coordination failure anybody watching can see. In practice it is used of somebody caught completely off guard, and it is the near neighbour of 不知所措, which describes the same state from inside the person's head.
description_tr: Hands (手) and feet (足) with nowhere (無) to be put (措). The Analects supplies the ancestor — 無所措手足, said of people under a government whose rules make ordinary conduct impossible — and the modern phrase keeps the bodily image while narrowing it to a moment. It reports panic from the outside, as a coordination failure anybody watching can see. Chinese uses it of somebody caught completely off guard, and it is the near neighbour of 不知所措, which describes the same state from inside the person's head.
chineseExample_tr: 這個突如其來的問題讓他手足無措。

example: His arrogance made him treat everyone with contempt.
chineseExample: 他的傲慢让他目中无人。
description: No (无) person (人) in (中) the eye (目). The construction is precise and unkind: other people are not being looked down on, they are not registering at all, which is a stage beyond contempt. That is what makes it a strong accusation in Chinese — it denies the person any relationship with those around them rather than merely a poor one. It is used of the newly promoted, the newly rich, and anybody whose success has visibly changed the way they enter a room.
metaphoric_meaning: Extremely arrogant; look down on everyone
description_tr: No (無) person (人) in (中) the eye (目). The construction is precise and unkind: other people are not being looked down on, they are not registering at all, which is a stage beyond contempt. That is what makes it a strong accusation in Chinese — it denies the person any relationship with those around them rather than merely a poor one. It is used of the newly promoted, the newly rich, and anybody whose success has visibly changed the way they enter a room.
chineseExample_tr: 他的傲慢讓他目中無人。

example: The local economy is thriving with new businesses.
chineseExample: 当地经济欣欣向荣，新企业不断涌现。
description: Tao Yuanming, going home for good, wrote 木欣欣以向荣，泉涓涓而始流 — the trees thriving (欣欣) as they turn toward (向) flourishing (荣), the springs beginning to trickle. 欣 is gladness, so the doubling gives the growth an air of pleasure rather than mere vigour, and the phrase has kept it. You will hear it of economies, businesses and communities, where it appears constantly in official writing, and the botanical origin is worth holding on to: what it describes is growth in season, not growth that was forced.
description_tr: Tao Yuanming, going home for good, wrote 木欣欣以向榮，泉涓涓而始流 — the trees thriving (欣欣) as they turn toward (向) flourishing (榮), the springs beginning to trickle. 欣 is gladness, so the doubling gives the growth an air of pleasure rather than mere vigour, and the phrase has kept it. Chinese uses it of economies, businesses and communities, where it appears constantly in official writing, and the botanical origin is worth holding on to: what it describes is growth in season, not growth that was forced.
chineseExample_tr: 當地經濟欣欣向榮，新企業不斷湧現。

example: After repeated offenses, his patience finally ran out.
chineseExample: 在反复冒犯后，他终于忍无可忍。
description: To have borne it (忍) until there is nothing (无) further that can (可) be borne (忍). The repetition of 忍 is the whole structure, and it does something careful: it establishes that the person did endure, at length, before the sentence turned. That is why it works as a justification rather than an outburst — it is what somebody says to explain why they finally acted, and Chinese, which rates forbearance highly, accepts it as one.
metaphoric_meaning: Beyond endurance; can't take it anymore
description_tr: To have borne it (忍) until there is nothing (無) further that can (可) be borne (忍). The repetition of 忍 is the whole structure, and it does something careful: it establishes that the person did endure, at length, before the sentence turned. That is why it works as a justification rather than an outburst — it is what somebody says to explain why they finally acted, and Chinese, which rates forbearance highly, accepts it as one.
chineseExample_tr: 在反復冒犯後，他終於忍無可忍。

example: The commander made a swift decision in the crisis.
chineseExample: 指挥官在危机中当机立断。
description: To meet (当) the moment (机) and settle it (断) on the spot (立). 机 is the pivot, the point at which a situation can still be turned, and 断 is to cut, so a decision here is severed rather than arrived at. The phrase praises timing rather than judgement: the same decision an hour later would not earn it. You will hear it of commanders, of surgeons and of anybody who committed while the choice was still there, and it carries the implication that hesitating was the real risk.
description_tr: To meet (當) the moment (機) and settle it (斷) on the spot (立). 機 is the pivot, the point at which a situation can still be turned, and 斷 is to cut, so a decision here is severed rather than arrived at. The phrase praises timing rather than judgement: the same decision an hour later would not earn it. Chinese uses it of commanders, of surgeons and of anybody who committed while the choice was still there, and it carries the implication that hesitating was the real risk.
chineseExample_tr: 指揮官在危機中當機立斷。

example: The devastation from the earthquake was deeply shocking.
chineseExample: 地震造成的破坏触目惊心。
description: To strike (触) the eye (目) and startle (惊) the heart (心). The two clauses put the impact in sequence — the sight arrives and the body answers — which is why the phrase belongs to things seen rather than things learned. That precision matters: Chinese does not use it of bad news, but of the photograph, the ward, the wreckage. It has since stretched to cover statistics laid out starkly enough to work the same way, and there the metaphor is doing deliberate work.
description_tr: To strike (觸) the eye (目) and startle (驚) the heart (心). The two clauses put the impact in sequence — the sight arrives and the body answers — which is why the phrase belongs to things seen rather than things learned. That precision matters: Chinese does not use it of bad news, but of the photograph, the ward, the wreckage. It has since stretched to cover statistics laid out starkly enough to work the same way, and there the metaphor is doing deliberate work.
chineseExample_tr: 地震造成的破壞觸目驚心。

example: After his explanation, everything suddenly became clear.
chineseExample: 经过他的解释，一切豁然开朗。
description: In Tao Yuanming's account the fisherman leaves his boat and goes in through a small opening in the hillside where a little light shows. It is very narrow at first, barely wide enough for a person; a few dozen paces further and it opens out wide and bright (豁然开朗) onto level ground, ordered houses, good fields, and people living as though the last four dynasties had not happened. The phrase is used of understanding arriving the same way — after a passage narrow enough that you were not sure it went anywhere.
metaphoric_meaning: Suddenly see the light; become clear
description_tr: In Tao Yuanming's account the fisherman leaves his boat and goes in through a small opening in the hillside where a little light shows. It is very narrow at first, barely wide enough for a person; a few dozen paces further and it opens out wide and bright (豁然開朗) onto level ground, ordered houses, good fields, and people living as though the last four dynasties had not happened. The phrase is used of understanding arriving the same way — after a passage narrow enough that you were not sure it went anywhere.
chineseExample_tr: 經過他的解釋，一切豁然開朗。

example: The public exposure left him feeling deeply ashamed.
chineseExample: 公开曝光让他无地自容。
description: No (无) ground (地) in which to put (容) oneself (自). 容 is to hold or contain, so the image is of the earth declining to make room: there is nowhere to stand that is out of view. That is more specific than embarrassment — what the phrase describes is shame with an audience, the exposure being the intolerable part. You will hear it of public humiliation and of somebody caught in something they had denied, and it is strong enough to be rarely used lightly.
description_tr: No (無) ground (地) in which to put (容) oneself (自). 容 is to hold or contain, so the image is of the earth declining to make room: there is nowhere to stand that is out of view. That is more specific than embarrassment — what the phrase describes is shame with an audience, the exposure being the intolerable part. Chinese uses it of public humiliation and of somebody caught in something they had denied, and it is strong enough to be rarely used lightly.
chineseExample_tr: 公開曝光讓他無地自容。

example: The busy street sees constant traffic day and night.
chineseExample: 这条繁忙的街道车流川流不息。
description: Rivers (川) flowing (流) without (不) pause (息). The line is from the Thousand Character Classic, which generations of children learned by heart, so it reaches most Chinese speakers already familiar. 息 is to rest or to breathe, so what is denied is any interval at all. Chinese uses it above all of traffic and of crowds — the stream of people through a station, the cars on a ring road — and the figure is of volume passing continuously rather than of speed.
description_tr: Rivers (川) flowing (流) without (不) pause (息). The line is from the Thousand Character Classic, which generations of children learned by heart, so it reaches most Chinese speakers already familiar. 息 is to rest or to breathe, so what is denied is any interval at all. Chinese uses it above all of traffic and of crowds — the stream of people through a station, the cars on a ring road — and the figure is of volume passing continuously rather than of speed.
chineseExample_tr: 這條繁忙的街道車流川流不息。

meaning: Dwelling in peace think of danger
example: Even during prosperous times, wise leaders prepare for potential crises.
chineseExample: 即使在繁荣时期，明智的领导者也会居安思危。
description: The Zuo Zhuan records Wei Jiang declining half the musicians and gifts Zheng had sent, and offering advice instead, in words the Book of Documents had already supplied: 居安思危，思则有备，有备无患 — in safety think of danger, thinking brings preparation, and with preparation there is no calamity. The three clauses are a chain, and the middle one is the part usually dropped: thinking is not the point, it is what the thinking produces. It is standard in Chinese writing about risk, reserves and succession planning.
metaphoric_meaning: Be prepared for danger in times of safety
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan records Wei Jiang declining half the musicians and gifts Zheng had sent, and offering advice instead, in words the Book of Documents had already supplied: 居安思危，思則有備，有備無患 — in safety think of danger, thinking brings preparation, and with preparation there is no calamity. The three clauses are a chain, and the middle one is the part usually dropped: thinking is not the point, it is what the thinking produces. It is standard in Chinese writing about risk, reserves and succession planning.
chineseExample_tr: 即使在繁榮時期，明智的領導者也會居安思危。

example: Technology is advancing at an unprecedented pace.
chineseExample: 科技发展日新月异。
description: New (新) by the day (日), different (异) by the month (月). The phrasing echoes the basin inscription quoted in the Great Learning — 苟日新，日日新，又日新, if you can renew yourself one day then do it daily, and again — where the subject is moral cultivation and the renewal is deliberate. The idiom kept the rhythm and dropped the effort: what it describes now is change happening at that rate on its own. In practice it is used of technology and of cities, and it is admiring, with a faint undertow of not being able to keep up.
description_tr: New (新) by the day (日), different (異) by the month (月). The phrasing echoes the basin inscription quoted in the Great Learning — 苟日新，日日新，又日新, if you can renew yourself one day then do it daily, and again — where the subject is moral cultivation and the renewal is deliberate. The idiom kept the rhythm and dropped the effort: what it describes now is change happening at that rate on its own. Chinese uses it of technology and of cities, and it is admiring, with a faint undertow of not being able to keep up.
chineseExample_tr: 科技發展日新月異。

example: The virtual reality experience made users feel like they were really there.
chineseExample: 虚拟现实体验让用户身临其境。
description: The body (身) arriving (临) at that (其) very place (境). 临 is to come right to the edge of something and look at it, and 身 insists it was the person and not the imagination that got there — so the phrase claims physical presence, and is then used almost entirely for occasions when there was none. That contradiction is the whole device. Chinese uses it of a film, a book or a piece of reporting good enough that the audience stops being an audience, and it is the standard praise for immersive work.
description_tr: The body (身) arriving (臨) at that (其) very place (境). 臨 is to come right to the edge of something and look at it, and 身 insists it was the person and not the imagination that got there — so the phrase claims physical presence, and is then used almost entirely for occasions when there was none. That contradiction is the whole device. Chinese uses it of a film, a book or a piece of reporting good enough that the audience stops being an audience, and it is the standard praise for immersive work.
chineseExample_tr: 虛擬現實體驗讓用戶身臨其境。

example: The audience fell completely silent when the speaker began.
chineseExample: 演讲者开始时，观众鸦雀无声。
description: Neither crow (鸦) nor sparrow (雀) making a sound (无声). The two birds are chosen for being the commonest and least ceremonious noise in a Chinese street — always there, never quiet — so their silence measures the hush better than any statement about people could. What is being reported is a place that has stopped, and Chinese reserves it for the moment before a verdict, a hall during an announcement, and a classroom that has just worked out the teacher is angry.
metaphoric_meaning: Completely silent; so quiet you could hear a pin drop
description_tr: Neither crow (鴉) nor sparrow (雀) making a sound (無聲). The two birds are chosen for being the commonest and least ceremonious noise in a Chinese street — always there, never quiet — so their silence measures the hush better than any statement about people could. What is being reported is a place that has stopped, and Chinese uses it of the moment before a verdict, a hall during an announcement, and a classroom that has just worked out the teacher is angry.
chineseExample_tr: 演講者開始時，觀眾鴉雀無聲。

example: The project proceeded methodically through each phase.
chineseExample: 项目按部就班地进行每个阶段。
description: Lu Ji, writing on composition, describes the writer choosing meanings according to (按) their section (部) and settling words into (就) their proper rank (班) — the vocabulary is that of officials arranged by grade. The phrase therefore began as an account of good order in writing and moved outward to procedure in general. Chinese uses it both ways: approvingly of somebody working through a process properly, and impatiently of somebody doing exactly that when the situation called for improvisation.
metaphoric_meaning: Follow established procedures; step by step
description_tr: Lu Ji, writing on composition, describes the writer choosing meanings according to (按) their section (部) and settling words into (就) their proper rank (班) — the vocabulary is that of officials arranged by grade. The phrase therefore began as an account of good order in writing and moved outward to procedure in general. Chinese uses it both ways: approvingly of somebody working through a process properly, and impatiently of somebody doing exactly that when the situation called for improvisation.
chineseExample_tr: 項目按部就班地進行每個階段。

example: They were so busy they couldn't handle everything.
chineseExample: 他们忙得不可开交。
description: Unable (不可) to get free (开交). 开交 is to disentangle and separate, and the phrase survives only in the negative — nobody is ever 可开交. It began with combatants locked together and unable to break off, and the modern sense keeps that: what it describes is not having a great deal to do but being unable to put any of it down. Chinese puts 忙得 in front of it — 忙得不可开交, busy past the point of extraction — and also uses it of quarrels neither side can now leave.
description_tr: Unable (不可) to get free (開交). 開交 is to disentangle and separate, and the phrase survives only in the negative — nobody is ever 可開交. It began with combatants locked together and unable to break off, and the modern sense keeps that: what it describes is not having a great deal to do but being unable to put any of it down. Chinese puts 忙得 in front of it — 忙得不可開交, busy past the point of extraction — and also uses it of quarrels neither side can now leave.
chineseExample_tr: 他們忙得不可開交。

example: Instead of competing directly, she found an innovative alternative approach.
chineseExample: 她没有直接竞争，而是另辟蹊径。
description: To open up (辟) a separate (另) footpath (蹊径). 蹊 is a track worn by feet rather than a built road, which is exactly right: what gets made is not an alternative highway but a way through that did not exist because nobody had walked it. The phrase concedes that the main road is there and perfectly passable. Chinese uses it of research, of business strategy and of artists, and it is warm praise — the emphasis falls on having thought of it, not on having been forced to.
metaphoric_meaning: Find an alternative approach; think outside the box
description_tr: To open up (闢) a separate (另) footpath (蹊徑). 蹊 is a track worn by feet rather than a built road, which is exactly right: what gets made is not an alternative highway but a way through that did not exist because nobody had walked it. The phrase concedes that the main road is there and perfectly passable. Chinese uses it of research, of business strategy and of artists, and it is warm praise — the emphasis falls on having thought of it, not on having been forced to.
chineseExample_tr: 她沒有直接競爭，而是另闢蹊徑。

example: The couple understood each other perfectly without words.
chineseExample: 这对夫妻心心相印，无需言语。
description: Heart (心) to heart (心), mutually (相) stamped (印). 印 is a seal pressed into clay or wax, and the metaphor is exact about what Chan Buddhism meant by it: the master's understanding is not explained to the disciple but impressed, so that what appears in the second mind has the same shape as what was in the first. Words are not merely unnecessary on this account, they are the wrong instrument. Chinese now uses it of couples and close friends, and the original claim — identity rather than agreement — is still audible in it.
metaphoric_meaning: Perfect mutual understanding; hearts in harmony
description_tr: Heart (心) to heart (心), mutually (相) stamped (印). 印 is a seal pressed into clay or wax, and the metaphor is exact about what Chan Buddhism meant by it: the master's understanding is not explained to the disciple but impressed, so that what appears in the second mind has the same shape as what was in the first. Words are not merely unnecessary on this account, they are the wrong instrument. Chinese now uses it of couples and close friends, and the original claim — identity rather than agreement — is still audible in it.
chineseExample_tr: 這對夫妻心心相印，無需言語。

example: With careful budgeting, they managed to save enough for the house.
chineseExample: 通过精打细算，他们存够了买房的钱。
description: Reckoning (打) finely (精) and calculating (算) in detail (细). Both verbs are ordinary arithmetic words and the two adverbs do the work, insisting on the grain at which the counting happens. What is praised is not thrift itself but the attention that makes thrift effective — knowing where the money actually goes. Chinese reserves it for household management above all, and it is a compliment, though one that can be paid slightly drily to somebody doing it in a restaurant.
metaphoric_meaning: Calculate carefully; be frugal and precise
description_tr: Reckoning (打) finely (精) and calculating (算) in detail (細). Both verbs are ordinary arithmetic words and the two adverbs do the work, insisting on the grain at which the counting happens. What is praised is not thrift itself but the attention that makes thrift effective — knowing where the money actually goes. Chinese uses it of household management above all, and it is a compliment, though one that can be paid slightly drily to somebody doing it in a restaurant.
chineseExample_tr: 通過精打細算，他們存夠了買房的錢。

example: The research team returned with abundant findings.
chineseExample: 研究团队满载而归，收获颇丰。
description: Loaded (载) full (满) and coming home (归). The image is a boat or a cart, and the phrase covers the return leg specifically, which is where its satisfaction comes from: the risk is over, the result is aboard, and all that is left is arriving. It is said of shopping trips, conferences, fishing and negotiations, and it need not be material — coming back from a course 满载而归 means the notebook is full. It is cheerful and slightly hearty, and it belongs to the getting back rather than to the success.
description_tr: Loaded (載) full (滿) and coming home (歸). The image is a boat or a cart, and the phrase covers the return leg specifically, which is where its satisfaction comes from: the risk is over, the result is aboard, and all that is left is arriving. Chinese uses it of shopping trips, conferences, fishing and negotiations, and it need not be material — coming back from a course 滿載而歸 means the notebook is full. It is cheerful and slightly hearty, and it belongs to the getting back rather than to the success.
chineseExample_tr: 研究團隊滿載而歸，收穫頗豐。

meaning: Meeting each other regret it was late
example: The two researchers wished they had met years earlier.
chineseExample: 两位研究者相见恨晚，希望能更早相识。
description: Emperor Wu of Han, meeting three men whose memorials had impressed him, is recorded as saying 何相见之晚也 — how late our meeting has been. The idiom compresses it: to meet (相见) and to resent (恨) the lateness (晚). 恨 is stronger than English regret and closer to a grievance, which is the flavour — the time before the meeting is being counted as a loss. Chinese uses it on discovering an unexpected affinity, and it is one of the warmer things one adult can say to another on first acquaintance.
metaphoric_meaning: Regret not meeting sooner; instant rapport
description_tr: Emperor Wu of Han, meeting three men whose memorials had impressed him, is recorded as saying 何相見之晚也 — how late our meeting has been. The idiom compresses it: to meet (相見) and to resent (恨) the lateness (晚). 恨 is stronger than English regret and closer to a grievance, which is the flavour — the time before the meeting is being counted as a loss. Chinese uses it on discovering an unexpected affinity, and it is one of the warmer things one adult can say to another on first acquaintance.
chineseExample_tr: 兩位研究者相見恨晚，希望能更早相識。

example: His flimsy argument fell apart without anyone even challenging it.
chineseExample: 他站不住脚的论点不攻自破。
description: Broken (破) of itself (自), without (不) being attacked (攻). The military sense is literal, a position so unsound it fails before anybody assaults it, and the transferred sense keeps the crucial detail: nobody had to do anything. That is what makes it useful in argument. To call a claim 不攻自破 is to decline to refute it, on the grounds that stating it plainly is sufficient, and Chinese uses it exactly that way, with a certain amount of confidence behind it.
description_tr: Broken (破) of itself (自), without (不) being attacked (攻). The military sense is literal, a position so unsound it fails before anybody assaults it, and the transferred sense keeps the crucial detail: nobody had to do anything. That is what makes it useful in argument. To call a claim 不攻自破 is to decline to refute it, on the grounds that stating it plainly is sufficient, and Chinese uses it exactly that way, with a certain amount of confidence behind it.
chineseExample_tr: 他站不住腳的論點不攻自破。

example: Having experienced similar losses, they truly understood each other.
chineseExample: 经历过类似的失去，他们同病相怜。
description: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue gives it to Wu Zixu, explaining why he had taken in another exile from Chu whose family had also been destroyed: those with the same affliction (同病) pity one another (相怜), those with the same anxiety help one another. The sequel is worth knowing — the man he sheltered later helped bring about his death. Chinese still uses the phrase warmly, for the solidarity that comes from shared trouble, though the source is unusually clear-eyed about its limits.
metaphoric_meaning: Sympathize with those sharing similar troubles
description_tr: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue gives it to Wu Zixu, explaining why he had taken in another exile from Chu whose family had also been destroyed: those with the same affliction (同病) pity one another (相憐), those with the same anxiety help one another. The sequel is worth knowing — the man he sheltered later helped bring about his death. Chinese still uses the phrase warmly, for the solidarity that comes from shared trouble, though the source is unusually clear-eyed about its limits.
chineseExample_tr: 經歷過類似的失去，他們同病相憐。

example: Assigning a senior engineer to simple data entry is a waste of talent.
chineseExample: 让高级工程师做简单的数据录入是大材小用。
description: A large (大) timber (材) put to a small (小) use (用). 材 is stock or material, the same character used of a person's calibre, and the metaphor is a carpenter's: a beam cut down to make a peg is not damaged, it is wasted, and the waste becomes invisible once it is done. That is the complaint. It is said of graduates in jobs requiring none of their training and of specialists doing administration, and it is said with real irritation, usually by somebody other than the person concerned.
description_tr: A large (大) timber (材) put to a small (小) use (用). 材 is stock or material, the same character used of a person's calibre, and the metaphor is a carpenter's: a beam cut down to make a peg is not damaged, it is wasted, and the waste becomes invisible once it is done. That is the complaint. Chinese uses it of graduates in jobs requiring none of their training and of specialists doing administration, and it is said with real irritation, usually by somebody other than the person concerned.
chineseExample_tr: 讓高級工程師做簡單的數據錄入是大材小用。

example: His contribution to the project was negligible.
chineseExample: 他对项目的贡献微不足道。
description: So slight (微) that it is not (不) enough (足) to speak of (道). The construction sets a threshold — there is an amount below which a thing does not merit mention — and puts the subject under it. That gives the phrase two quite separate lives. Said of one's own contribution it is the standard modest deflection of thanks; said of somebody else's it is dismissive to the point of rudeness. Chinese speakers use the first constantly and the second with care.
metaphoric_meaning: Too slight to weigh at all
description_tr: So slight (微) that it is not (不) enough (足) to speak of (道). The construction sets a threshold — there is an amount below which a thing does not merit mention — and puts the subject under it. That gives the phrase two quite separate lives. Said of one's own contribution it is the standard modest deflection of thanks; said of somebody else's it is dismissive to the point of rudeness. Chinese speakers use the first constantly and the second with care.
chineseExample_tr: 他對項目的貢獻微不足道。

example: She always practices what she preaches.
chineseExample: 她总是言行一致。
description: Words (言) and deeds (行) at one (一致). The Analects sets the standard it assumes — 君子欲讷于言而敏于行, the gentleman wishes to be halting in speech and quick in action — and the ordering matters: the remedy for a gap between the two is taken to be saying less, not achieving more. That is a distinctly Chinese emphasis and it survives in how the phrase gets used. It is applied to institutions as readily as to people, and it is most often invoked to say the thing is missing.
description_tr: Words (言) and deeds (行) at one (一致). The Analects sets the standard it assumes — 君子欲訥於言而敏於行, the gentleman wishes to be halting in speech and quick in action — and the ordering matters: the remedy for a gap between the two is taken to be saying less, not achieving more. That is a distinctly Chinese emphasis and it survives in how the phrase gets used. It is applied to institutions as readily as to people, and it is most often invoked to say the thing is missing.
chineseExample_tr: 她總是言行一致。

example: Don't underestimate yourself - you have great potential.
chineseExample: 不要妄自菲薄，你有很大的潜力。
description: Zhuge Liang, in the memorial written before his first northern campaign, tells the young Liu Shan not to 妄自菲薄 — not to belittle (菲薄) himself (自) without cause (妄) — and not to reach for improper analogies, since either would close off the path of honest advice. The context is worth keeping: it is addressed to somebody who had real authority and was not using it. 妄 is the load-bearing character, marking the self-deprecation as unwarranted rather than modest, and Chinese still uses the phrase to tell somebody their humility has turned into a way of not trying.
description_tr: Zhuge Liang, in the memorial written before his first northern campaign, tells the young Liu Shan not to 妄自菲薄 — not to belittle (菲薄) himself (自) without cause (妄) — and not to reach for improper analogies, since either would close off the path of honest advice. The context is worth keeping: it is addressed to somebody who had real authority and was not using it. 妄 is the load-bearing character, marking the self-deprecation as unwarranted rather than modest, and Chinese still uses the phrase to tell somebody their humility has turned into a way of not trying.
chineseExample_tr: 不要妄自菲薄，你有很大的潛力。

example: Cycling to work saves money and improves health at the same time.
chineseExample: 骑车上班既省钱又健身，一举两得。
description: One (一) action (举) and two (两) gains (得). 举 is a single lifting or raising, the smallest complete unit of doing something, so the arithmetic is stated as plainly as it can be: the cost was paid once and collected on twice. Chinese uses it constantly, and it is worth distinguishing from 一石二鸟, which is a translated phrase — this one is native and carries no foreign register at all. It is what people reach for when justifying a decision that happened to solve a second problem.
metaphoric_meaning: Kill two birds with one stone
description_tr: One (一) action (舉) and two (兩) gains (得). 舉 is a single lifting or raising, the smallest complete unit of doing something, so the arithmetic is stated as plainly as it can be: the cost was paid once and collected on twice. Chinese uses it constantly, and it is worth distinguishing from 一石二鳥, which is a translated phrase — this one is native and carries no foreign register at all. It is what people reach for when justifying a decision that happened to solve a second problem.
chineseExample_tr: 騎車上班既省錢又健身，一舉兩得。

example: He couldn't help but smile when he saw her.
chineseExample: 看到她，他不由自主地笑了。
description: Not (不) proceeding from (由) one's own (自) control (主). The grammar puts the person outside the action: something happened and they were not the one directing it. That is why Chinese uses it as an exculpation as much as a description — the laugh at the wrong moment, the step back from the edge, the tears at a piece of music. It names the class of behaviour that genuinely is not chosen, and a learner should note the shape of the sentence it lives in: 不由自主地 followed by the verb.
description_tr: Not (不) proceeding from (由) one's own (自) control (主). The grammar puts the person outside the action: something happened and they were not the one directing it. That is why Chinese uses it as an exculpation as much as a description — the laugh at the wrong moment, the step back from the edge, the tears at a piece of music.
