It names the class of behaviour that genuinely is not chosen, and a learner should note the shape of the sentence it lives in: 不由自主地 followed by the verb.
chineseExample_tr: 看到她，他不由自主地笑了。

meaning: Hundred times nothing to rely on
example: With nothing to do all day, she felt utterly bored.
chineseExample: 整天无所事事，她百无聊赖。
description: A hundred (百) ways of having nothing (无) to lean on (聊赖). 聊赖 is what one depends on to get through the time, and 百 exhausts the possibilities — every direction has been looked in and none of them offers anything. That is why the phrase is heavier than boredom: what it names is closer to listlessness with a note of despondency, the state of somebody who has time and can find no use for themselves in it. Chinese uses it of convalescence, of unemployment and of long empty afternoons.
description_tr: A hundred (百) ways of having nothing (無) to lean on (聊賴). 聊賴 is what one depends on to get through the time, and 百 exhausts the possibilities — every direction has been looked in and none of them offers anything. That is why the phrase is heavier than boredom: what it names is closer to listlessness with a note of despondency, the state of somebody who has time and can find no use for themselves in it. Chinese uses it of convalescence, of unemployment and of long empty afternoons.
chineseExample_tr: 整天無所事事，她百無聊賴。

meaning: Go into boiling water step on fire
example: He would go through fire and water for his family.
chineseExample: 为了家人，他愿意赴汤蹈火。
description: To go into (赴) scalding water (汤) and tread (蹈) on fire (火). 汤 is boiling liquid rather than soup, as it is throughout classical Chinese, and the two elements are the standard pair of unsurvivable things. What is asserted is not bravery in the face of risk but willingness where the outcome is not in doubt. Chinese uses it in declarations of loyalty and in thanks — 为你赴汤蹈火, I would go through fire for you — and it is hyperbole that both parties understand as hyperbole.
metaphoric_meaning: Go through fire and water; brave any danger
description_tr: To go into (赴) scalding water (湯) and tread (蹈) on fire (火). 湯 is boiling liquid rather than soup, as it is throughout classical Chinese, and the two elements are the standard pair of unsurvivable things. What is asserted is not bravery in the face of risk but willingness where the outcome is not in doubt. Chinese uses it in declarations of loyalty and in thanks — 為你赴湯蹈火, I would go through fire for you — and it is hyperbole that both parties understand as hyperbole.
chineseExample_tr: 為了家人，他願意赴湯蹈火。

meaning: Tip of awl emerges from bag
example: Among hundreds of applicants, she stood out from the crowd.
chineseExample: 在数百名申请者中，她脱颖而出。
description: The Lord of Pingyuan used the awl to dismiss Mao Sui: a man of ability in the world is like an awl in a bag, and its point shows at once — three years, and nothing has been heard of you. Mao Sui turned it round. Had he been put in the bag earlier, he said, the whole blade would have come through (颖脱而出), not merely the tip. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps both halves, and the idiom is built from Mao Sui's reply rather than from the original jibe.
description_tr: The Lord of Pingyuan used the awl to dismiss Mao Sui: a man of ability in the world is like an awl in a bag, and its point shows at once — three years, and nothing has been heard of you. Mao Sui turned it round. Had he been put in the bag earlier, he said, the whole blade would have come through (穎脫而出), not merely the tip. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps both halves, and the idiom is built from Mao Sui's reply rather than from the original jibe.
chineseExample_tr: 在數百名申請者中，她脫穎而出。

meaning: A heart that aches for others
example: His innate sense of compassion moved him to help the stranger.
chineseExample: 他的恻隐之心促使他帮助陌生人。
description: Mencius asks what anybody would feel on suddenly seeing a child about to fall into a well, and answers that the alarm and the pity would arrive before any calculation about the parents, the neighbours or one's own reputation. That involuntary pang is the 恻隐之心 — the heart (心) that aches (恻) and is pained (隐) for another — and he takes its universality as his evidence that human nature is good. The phrase is doing philosophical work, not merely naming a feeling, and It gets used of the compassion that moves before judgement does.
description_tr: Mencius asks what anybody would feel on suddenly seeing a child about to fall into a well, and answers that the alarm and the pity would arrive before any calculation about the parents, the neighbours or one's own reputation. That involuntary pang is the 惻隱之心 — the heart (心) that aches (惻) and is pained (隱) for another — and he takes its universality as his evidence that human nature is good. The phrase is doing philosophical work, not merely naming a feeling, and Chinese uses it of the compassion that moves before judgement does.
chineseExample_tr: 他的惻隱之心促使他幫助陌生人。

example: The chart makes the data immediately understandable.
chineseExample: 这张图表让数据一目了然。
description: Wholly clear (了然) at one (一) glance (目). 了 is to finish or complete, so 了然 is the state of a thing being settled in the mind, and the claim is that the settling took no longer than the looking did. That makes it praise for the presentation rather than for the viewer. Chinese uses it of charts, signs, layouts and well-made summaries, and it is what a designer is aiming at — the standard being that no second look was required.
description_tr: Wholly clear (瞭然) at one (一) glance (目). 了 is to finish or complete, so 瞭然 is the state of a thing being settled in the mind, and the claim is that the settling took no longer than the looking did. That makes it praise for the presentation rather than for the viewer. Chinese uses it of charts, signs, layouts and well-made summaries, and it is what a designer is aiming at — the standard being that no second look was required.
chineseExample_tr: 這張圖表讓數據一目了然。

example: His belief that she would agree was just wishful thinking.
chineseExample: 他认为她会同意，不过是一厢情愿。
description: Willingness (情愿) on one (一) side (厢) only. 厢 is a wing or side chamber of a building, and the spatial figure does precise work: the feeling is real, it is simply confined to one room, and nothing corresponding to it exists in the other. That is why the phrase is not a synonym for wrong. It is used of unreciprocated affection, of assumptions about what a counterparty wants, and of plans resting on an agreement nobody ever sought, and it is gently deflating rather than cruel.
description_tr: Willingness (情願) on one (一) side (廂) only. 廂 is a wing or side chamber of a building, and the spatial figure does precise work: the feeling is real, it is simply confined to one room, and nothing corresponding to it exists in the other. That is why the phrase is not a synonym for wrong. It is used of unreciprocated affection, of assumptions about what a counterparty wants, and of plans resting on an agreement nobody ever sought, and it is gently deflating rather than cruel.
chineseExample_tr: 他認為她會同意，不過是一廂情願。

example: As the whistleblower, she became the target of everyone's criticism.
chineseExample: 作为举报人，她成了众矢之的。
description: The target (的) that many (众) arrows (矢) are aimed at. 的 is the bullseye — the same character that now does duty as the commonest particle in the language, which regularly surprises learners — and the phrase puts somebody on it. What it describes is not being criticised but being the agreed object of criticism, which is a different and lonelier position: the arrows come from people who are not otherwise coordinated. Chinese uses it of public figures and of whoever has become the convenient explanation for a shared problem.
description_tr: The target (的) that many (眾) arrows (矢) are aimed at. 的 is the bullseye — the same character that now does duty as the commonest particle in the language, which regularly surprises learners — and the phrase puts somebody on it. What it describes is not being criticised but being the agreed object of criticism, which is a different and lonelier position: the arrows come from people who are not otherwise coordinated. Chinese uses it of public figures and of whoever has become the convenient explanation for a shared problem.
chineseExample_tr: 作為舉報人，她成了眾矢之的。

example: The new funding will greatly strengthen our capabilities.
chineseExample: 新的资金将使我们如虎添翼。
description: A tiger (虎) with wings (翼) added (添). The animal was already at the top of anything it might meet, so the addition is not making it competitive but removing the last constraint on it — what changes is not the tiger's strength but the ground it can now reach. In practice it is used of capable people given resources and of strong companies given a favourable rule, and it is neutral about whether this is welcome. From the tiger's side it is delight; from anywhere else it is alarm.
metaphoric_meaning: Add to one's strength; become even more powerful
description_tr: A tiger (虎) with wings (翼) added (添). The animal was already at the top of anything it might meet, so the addition is not making it competitive but removing the last constraint on it — what changes is not the tiger's strength but the ground it can now reach. Chinese uses it of capable people given resources and of strong companies given a favourable rule, and it is neutral about whether this is welcome. From the tiger's side it is delight; from anywhere else it is alarm.
chineseExample_tr: 新的資金將使我們如虎添翼。

example: His superficial reading left him with only a shallow understanding.
chineseExample: 他浅尝辄止的阅读让他不求甚解。
description: Tao Yuanming, describing himself under an assumed name, wrote 好读书，不求甚解 — fond of reading, and not (不) pressing (求) for exhaustive (甚) explanation (解) — adding that whenever he did grasp something he would forget to eat for pleasure. In context it rejects the commentarial scholarship of his day rather than admitting to laziness, and the enjoyment is the whole point. The phrase has since gone both ways: Chinese uses it critically of shallow reading, and approvingly of somebody who reads for the sense rather than to pass an examination.
description_tr: Tao Yuanming, describing himself under an assumed name, wrote 好讀書，不求甚解 — fond of reading, and not (不) pressing (求) for exhaustive (甚) explanation (解) — adding that whenever he did grasp something he would forget to eat for pleasure. In context it rejects the commentarial scholarship of his day rather than admitting to laziness, and the enjoyment is the whole point. The phrase has since gone both ways: Chinese uses it critically of shallow reading, and approvingly of somebody who reads for the sense rather than to pass an examination.
chineseExample_tr: 他淺嘗輒止的閱讀讓他不求甚解。

example: The team is preparing intensively for the upcoming competition.
chineseExample: 球队正在厉兵秣马，为即将到来的比赛做准备。
description: Sharpening (厉) the weapons (兵) and feeding (秣) the horses (马). The Zuo Zhuan uses it flatly, as reconnaissance: a Zheng envoy looks into the guest quarters, finds the Qin troops with their baggage bound, their blades honed and their horses fed, and knows exactly what is about to happen. That is the phrase's original function and it has survived. It reports preparation observed from outside, which is why Chinese says it of a rival gearing up as readily as of one's own side.
metaphoric_meaning: Make thorough preparations; get ready for action
description_tr: Sharpening (厲) the weapons (兵) and feeding (秣) the horses (馬). The Zuo Zhuan uses it flatly, as reconnaissance: a Zheng envoy looks into the guest quarters, finds the Qin troops with their baggage bound, their blades honed and their horses fed, and knows exactly what is about to happen. That is the phrase's original function and it has survived. It reports preparation observed from outside, which is why Chinese uses it of a rival gearing up as readily as of one's own side.
chineseExample_tr: 球隊正在厲兵秣馬，為即將到來的比賽做準備。

meaning: Make noise in east, strike in west
example: The competitor's marketing campaign was just a diversion from their real strategy.
chineseExample: 竞争对手的营销活动只是声东击西的策略。
description: Making the noise (声) in the east (东) and striking (击) in the west (西). The sixth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the text states its condition: it works against an enemy whose command has already become confused, because the manoeuvre depends on the other side being unable to tell which of two signals is the real one. That detail usually gets lost. It is not simply a feint but a feint aimed at somebody already losing track, and Chinese keeps that reading in business and negotiation — the diversion has to be aimed at an opponent who cannot check.
description_tr: Making the noise (聲) in the east (東) and striking (擊) in the west (西). The sixth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the text states its condition: it works against an enemy whose command has already become confused, because the manoeuvre depends on the other side being unable to tell which of two signals is the real one. That detail usually gets lost. It is not simply a feint but a feint aimed at somebody already losing track, and Chinese keeps that reading in business and negotiation — the diversion has to be aimed at an opponent who cannot check.
chineseExample_tr: 競爭對手的營銷活動只是聲東擊西的策略。

example: Sometimes stepping back from a negotiation can lead to better results.
chineseExample: 有时在谈判中以退为进反而能取得更好的结果。
description: Taking (以) retreat (退) as (为) the way forward (进). The construction puts the two directions in a means-and-end relation instead of opposing them, and that is the whole idea: the ground given up is spent rather than lost. What separates it from an actual retreat is intention, which is invisible at the time and demonstrable only afterwards. You will hear it of negotiation, of resignations that were not defeats and of arguments conceded on purpose, and there is always a suggestion of somebody playing a longer game than they are admitting to.
description_tr: Taking (以) retreat (退) as (為) the way forward (進). The construction puts the two directions in a means-and-end relation instead of opposing them, and that is the whole idea: the ground given up is spent rather than lost. What separates it from an actual retreat is intention, which is invisible at the time and demonstrable only afterwards. Chinese uses it of negotiation, of resignations that were not defeats and of arguments conceded on purpose, and there is always a suggestion of somebody playing a longer game than they are admitting to.
chineseExample_tr: 有時在談判中以退為進反而能取得更好的結果。

example: Instead of defending directly, they attacked the competitor's main market.
chineseExample: 他们没有直接防守，而是围魏救赵，攻击对手的主要市场。
description: When Wei besieged the Zhao capital in 354 BCE, Qi sent an army under Tian Ji, and Sun Bin argued against marching to Zhao's relief at all: strike at Wei's own capital, and the Wei army will have to come home. It did, and was ambushed at Guiling on the road. Besieging (围) Wei (魏) to rescue (救) Zhao (赵) became the second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems and the standard name for relieving pressure by threatening what an opponent cannot afford to leave undefended. The insight is that a besieger is weak precisely because they are committed somewhere else.
metaphoric_meaning: Relieve pressure by attacking the source
description_tr: When Wei besieged the Zhao capital in 354 BCE, Qi sent an army under Tian Ji, and Sun Bin argued against marching to Zhao's relief at all: strike at Wei's own capital, and the Wei army will have to come home. It did, and was ambushed at Guiling on the road. Besieging (圍) Wei (魏) to rescue (救) Zhao (趙) became the second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems and the standard name for relieving pressure by threatening what an opponent cannot afford to leave undefended. The insight is that a besieger is weak precisely because they are committed somewhere else.
chineseExample_tr: 他們沒有直接防守，而是圍魏救趙，攻擊對手的主要市場。

meaning: Wishing to capture, first let go
example: The detective pretended to drop the case to make the suspect lower his guard.
chineseExample: 侦探假装放弃案件，欲擒故纵，让嫌疑人放松警惕。
description: Wanting (欲) to capture (擒) and therefore deliberately (故) letting go (纵). The sixteenth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and its argument is practical rather than psychological: an enemy pressed to the wall will fight, while one allowed to run wears himself out and loses cohesion, so the release is a way of taking the fight out before taking the prisoner. Zhuge Liang's seven captures and seven releases of Meng Huo is the standard illustration, and there the object was a surrender that would hold. Chinese says it of negotiation and of parenting.
metaphoric_meaning: Give slack before tightening; let go to catch
description_tr: Wanting (欲) to capture (擒) and therefore deliberately (故) letting go (縱). The sixteenth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and its argument is practical rather than psychological: an enemy pressed to the wall will fight, while one allowed to run wears himself out and loses cohesion, so the release is a way of taking the fight out before taking the prisoner. Zhuge Liang's seven captures and seven releases of Meng Huo is the standard illustration, and there the object was a surrender that would hold. Chinese uses it of negotiation and of parenting.
chineseExample_tr: 偵探假裝放棄案件，欲擒故縱，讓嫌疑人放鬆警惕。

meaning: Embrace the incomplete, guard the deficient
example: The company's resistance to new technology showed they were clinging to outdated methods.
chineseExample: 公司对新技术的抵制表明他们抱残守缺。
description: Liu Xin, arguing with the court scholars over which versions of the classics should be taught, accused them of clinging (抱) to what was damaged (残) and guarding (守) what was missing (缺), holding to a private fear of being proved wrong instead of a public willingness to follow what is right. The complaint was about textual scholarship and about vested interest in it. Modern usage keeps the shape and drops the philology, describing anyone defending an inadequate arrangement because it is the one they know.
metaphoric_meaning: Cling to the old and outdated; resist progress
description_tr: Liu Xin, arguing with the court scholars over which versions of the classics should be taught, accused them of clinging (抱) to what was damaged (殘) and guarding (守) what was missing (缺), holding to a private fear of being proved wrong instead of a public willingness to follow what is right. The complaint was about textual scholarship and about vested interest in it. Modern usage keeps the shape and drops the philology, describing anyone defending an inadequate arrangement because it is the one they know.
chineseExample_tr: 公司對新技術的抵制表明他們抱殘守缺。

example: The firm kept its 1990s process and watched every rival overtake it
chineseExample: 公司死守九十年代的流程，眼看着对手一个个超越
description: The standard form writes the first character 故, meaning old or former — the old (故) steps (步) one keeps taking, with oneself (自) sealed in (封). It is very often miswritten 固步自封, since 固 means fixed and seems to fit, and the error is common enough in China to be worth knowing about. The image is a person walking a route they have walked before and building a wall around it. It criticises not caution but the refusal to look at anything outside a method that once worked, and it is standard in Chinese writing about companies and institutions that stopped adapting.
metaphoric_meaning: Refuse to move beyond past methods
description_tr: The standard form writes the first character 故, meaning old or former — the old (故) steps (步) one keeps taking, with oneself (自) sealed in (封). It is very often miswritten 固步自封, since 固 means fixed and seems to fit, and the error is common enough in China to be worth knowing about. The image is a person walking a route they have walked before and building a wall around it. It criticises not caution but the refusal to look at anything outside a method that once worked, and it is standard in Chinese writing about companies and institutions that stopped adapting.
chineseExample_tr: 公司死守九十年代的流程，眼看著對手一個個超越

meaning: Fish for fame and angle for reputation
example: His charity work seemed more about publicity than genuine help.
chineseExample: 他的慈善工作似乎更多是沽名钓誉，而非真正的帮助。
description: To buy (沽) a name (名) and angle (钓) for reputation (誉). Both verbs are transactional and one of them is patient — 钓 is fishing with a line, which implies bait, waiting, and a fish that does not know it is being caught. That is what the phrase alleges: not merely wanting to be well thought of, but building the conditions under which it will happen. It gets used of conspicuous charity and of public resignations, and it is a serious accusation, because it claims to know the motive behind an act that was otherwise good.
description_tr: To buy (沽) a name (名) and angle (釣) for reputation (譽). Both verbs are transactional and one of them is patient — 釣 is fishing with a line, which implies bait, waiting, and a fish that does not know it is being caught. That is what the phrase alleges: not merely wanting to be well thought of, but building the conditions under which it will happen. Chinese uses it of conspicuous charity and of public resignations, and it is a serious accusation, because it claims to know the motive behind an act that was otherwise good.
chineseExample_tr: 他的慈善工作似乎更多是沽名釣譽，而非真正的幫助。

meaning: Command with chin gestures and breath
example: The arrogant manager treated employees like servants.
chineseExample: 傲慢的经理颐指气使地对待员工。
description: 颐 is the lower jaw and cheek; to point with it (指), and to command (使) with the breath (气), is to give orders without troubling to speak. The picture is exact and unpleasant — a lift of the chin, an audible sigh, and somebody moves. What the phrase objects to is not the authority but the withholding of words, which treats the other person as not requiring any. Chinese uses it of bosses, of officials and of the rich, and it is among the sharper things that can be said about how somebody treats subordinates.
description_tr: 頤 is the lower jaw and cheek; to point with it (指), and to command (使) with the breath (氣), is to give orders without troubling to speak. The picture is exact and unpleasant — a lift of the chin, an audible sigh, and somebody moves. What the phrase objects to is not the authority but the withholding of words, which treats the other person as not requiring any. Chinese uses it of bosses, of officials and of the rich, and it is among the sharper things that can be said about how somebody treats subordinates.
chineseExample_tr: 傲慢的經理頤指氣使地對待員工。

example: He walked through the office with an insufferably superior attitude.
chineseExample: 他趾高气扬地走过办公室。
description: The Zuo Zhuan records an officer watching the Chu commander Qu Xia set out and predicting his defeat: 举趾高，心不固矣 — he lifts his toes (趾) high (高), and his heart is not steady. The gait gave him away, and he lost. With 气扬, the spirit (气) flying up (扬), the phrase pairs the walk with the mood behind it. What it names is confidence displayed in the body before anything has been achieved, and It gets used of somebody who has just won something small and is being visible about it.
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan records an officer watching the Chu commander Qu Xia set out and predicting his defeat: 舉趾高，心不固矣 — he lifts his toes (趾) high (高), and his heart is not steady. The gait gave him away, and he lost. With 氣揚, the spirit (氣) flying up (揚), the phrase pairs the walk with the mood behind it. What it names is confidence displayed in the body before anything has been achieved, and Chinese uses it of somebody who has just won something small and is being visible about it.
chineseExample_tr: 他趾高氣揚地走過辦公室。

example: His overconfidence blinded him to his obvious weaknesses.
chineseExample: 他妄自尊大，看不到自己明显的弱点。
description: Ma Yuan, sent to take the measure of the warlord Gongsun Shu, came back and reported that the man was a frog at the bottom of a well who nonetheless made himself out to be honoured and great (尊大) without cause (妄). The judgement became the phrase, and it sits exactly opposite 妄自菲薄 — the same 妄自 construction marking a self-assessment as unwarranted, with the error running the other way. Chinese uses it of a person or an institution whose sense of its own standing is not shared by anybody outside it.
metaphoric_meaning: Be conceited; have an inflated ego
description_tr: Ma Yuan, sent to take the measure of the warlord Gongsun Shu, came back and reported that the man was a frog at the bottom of a well who nonetheless made himself out to be honoured and great (尊大) without cause (妄). The judgement became the phrase, and it sits exactly opposite 妄自菲薄 — the same 妄自 construction marking a self-assessment as unwarranted, with the error running the other way. Chinese uses it of a person or an institution whose sense of its own standing is not shared by anybody outside it.
chineseExample_tr: 他妄自尊大，看不到自己明顯的弱點。

example: She felt nervous waiting for the interview results.
chineseExample: 等待面试结果时，她忐忑不安。
description: 忐 and 忑 are 上 and 下 written over 心 — heart up, heart down — which is about as literal as Chinese characters get, and it is the best thing about the phrase. The pair describes the lurch rather than the worry, so what is reported is the physical sensation of a heart that will not settle (不安). Chinese uses it of waiting for results, of the minutes before an interview, and of the hours after sending something that cannot be recalled.
description_tr: 忐 and 忑 are 上 and 下 written over 心 — heart up, heart down — which is about as literal as Chinese characters get, and it is the best thing about the phrase. The pair describes the lurch rather than the worry, so what is reported is the physical sensation of a heart that will not settle (不安). Chinese uses it of waiting for results, of the minutes before an interview, and of the hours after sending something that cannot be recalled.
chineseExample_tr: 等待面試結果時，她忐忑不安。

example: After returning the lost wallet, he felt completely at ease.
chineseExample: 归还了丢失的钱包后，他心安理得。
description: The heart (心) at rest (安) because the reasoning (理) holds up (得). The two halves stand in a stated relation: the calm is not a temperament but a consequence, and it is available only to somebody who has actually checked. That is what makes the phrase useful, and also what makes it available for sarcasm — doing something questionable 心安理得地 describes a person who checked badly and slept well anyway. Chinese uses both senses, and the second is now at least as common as the first.
metaphoric_meaning: Feel at ease with a clear conscience
description_tr: The heart (心) at rest (安) because the reasoning (理) holds up (得). The two halves stand in a stated relation: the calm is not a temperament but a consequence, and it is available only to somebody who has actually checked. That is what makes the phrase useful, and also what makes it available for sarcasm — doing something questionable 心安理得地 describes a person who checked badly and slept well anyway. Chinese uses both senses, and the second is now at least as common as the first.
chineseExample_tr: 歸還了丟失的錢包後，他心安理得。

meaning: So pleased as to forget one's form
example: His success made him careless about his professional conduct.
chineseExample: 成功让他得意忘形，忽视了职业操守。
description: So pleased (得意) as to forget (忘) the shape one cuts (形). 形 is the body, one's outward form, so what is lost is not dignity in the abstract but awareness of how one appears — the person is still perfectly visible, they have simply stopped seeing themselves. That is a sharper observation than pride. Chinese uses it of somebody whose good news has made them briefly unbearable, and it works as a warning as much as a description, since the state passes and the memory of it does not.
description_tr: So pleased (得意) as to forget (忘) the shape one cuts (形). 形 is the body, one's outward form, so what is lost is not dignity in the abstract but awareness of how one appears — the person is still perfectly visible, they have simply stopped seeing themselves. That is a sharper observation than pride. Chinese uses it of somebody whose good news has made them briefly unbearable, and it works as a warning as much as a description, since the state passes and the memory of it does not.
chineseExample_tr: 成功讓他得意忘形，忽視了職業操守。

example: Working for someone with unpredictable moods is exhausting.
chineseExample: 为一个喜怒无常的人工作令人精疲力竭。
description: Joy (喜) and anger (怒) with no (无) regularity (常). 常 is the constant, what can be relied on to stay the same, so the complaint is not about strong feeling but about the absence of any rule connecting the feeling to its cause. That is what makes the phrase name a hazard rather than a personality: what cannot be predicted cannot be worked around. Chinese used it of rulers historically and now of bosses and of a parent, and the sympathy is always with the people nearby.
description_tr: Joy (喜) and anger (怒) with no (無) regularity (常). 常 is the constant, what can be relied on to stay the same, so the complaint is not about strong feeling but about the absence of any rule connecting the feeling to its cause. That is what makes the phrase name a hazard rather than a personality: what cannot be predicted cannot be worked around. Chinese used it of rulers historically and now of bosses and of a parent, and the sympathy is always with the people nearby.
chineseExample_tr: 為一個喜怒無常的人工作令人精疲力竭。

example: Upon discovering the betrayal, he became furious beyond control.
chineseExample: 发现背叛后，他怒不可遏。
description: Anger (怒) that cannot (不可) be dammed (遏). 遏 is to block or stop a flow, so the metaphor gives rage volume and pressure, and the phrase reports that the containing failed rather than that it was never attempted. That detail is what keeps it usable for justified fury: the person tried. Chinese reserves it for the reaction to a real outrage, and it can be approving in a way its other words for temper are not.
description_tr: Anger (怒) that cannot (不可) be dammed (遏). 遏 is to block or stop a flow, so the metaphor gives rage volume and pressure, and the phrase reports that the containing failed rather than that it was never attempted. That detail is what keeps it usable for justified fury: the person tried. Chinese uses it of the reaction to a real outrage, and it can be approving in a way its other words for temper are not.
chineseExample_tr: 發現背叛後，他怒不可遏。

example: The children's faces lit up when they saw the presents.
chineseExample: 孩子们看到礼物时喜笑颜开。
description: Pleasure (喜) breaking into a smile (笑) and the face (颜) opening (开). 开 does the work — the metaphor treats a face at rest as closed and happiness as the thing that opens it — which is why the phrase names a change rather than a state. Chinese uses it at the moment somebody hears good news, and it is warmest when the person had been worrying up until then. It belongs to older speakers and to writing more than to casual talk.
description_tr: Pleasure (喜) breaking into a smile (笑) and the face (顏) opening (開). 開 does the work — the metaphor treats a face at rest as closed and happiness as the thing that opens it — which is why the phrase names a change rather than a state. Chinese uses it at the moment somebody hears good news, and it is warmest when the person had been worrying up until then. It belongs to older speakers and to writing more than to casual talk.
chineseExample_tr: 孩子們看到禮物時喜笑顏開。

example: He described his adventure with animated enthusiasm.
chineseExample: 他眉飞色舞地描述着自己的冒险经历。
description: Eyebrows (眉) flying (飞) and the colour of the face (色) dancing (舞). Both verbs are for things that leave the ground, and the phrase is specifically about animation while talking: the features are moving faster than composure would normally allow. Chinese uses it of somebody describing their own subject — the hobby, the trip, the team — and it is affectionate. It is also the standard way of noting that a speaker has stopped reporting and started enjoying themselves.
description_tr: Eyebrows (眉) flying (飛) and the colour of the face (色) dancing (舞). Both verbs are for things that leave the ground, and the phrase is specifically about animation while talking: the features are moving faster than composure would normally allow. Chinese uses it of somebody describing their own subject — the hobby, the trip, the team — and it is affectionate. It is also the standard way of noting that a speaker has stopped reporting and started enjoying themselves.
chineseExample_tr: 他眉飛色舞地描述著自己的冒險經歷。

example: Receiving the good news, her whole face lit up with happiness.
chineseExample: 收到好消息，她眉开眼笑。
description: Brows (眉) opening (开) and eyes (眼) smiling (笑). The observation is anatomically shrewd: the brow releasing and the eyes creasing are the two things a false smile does not do, which is why the phrase reads as a claim about sincerity rather than about degree. It is said of pleasure that arrived without being managed — a grandparent handed a photograph, a customer given more than they expected — and it is the near opposite of 愁眉苦脸.
description_tr: Brows (眉) opening (開) and eyes (眼) smiling (笑). The observation is anatomically shrewd: the brow releasing and the eyes creasing are the two things a false smile does not do, which is why the phrase reads as a claim about sincerity rather than about degree. Chinese uses it of pleasure that arrived without being managed — a grandparent handed a photograph, a customer given more than they expected — and it is the near opposite of 愁眉苦臉.
chineseExample_tr: 收到好消息，她眉開眼笑。

example: He's been looking gloomy ever since he heard about the budget cuts.
chineseExample: 自从听说预算削减后，他一直愁眉苦脸。
description: Worried (愁) brows (眉) and a bitter (苦) face (脸). 苦 is the taste, and using it of an expression is exact: the mouth of an unhappy person does what the mouth of somebody eating something bitter does. The phrase reports the face and leaves the cause open, which is why it so often turns up inside a question — 愁眉苦脸的，怎么了, what's the long face about. Chinese uses it of visible low-level misery rather than of grief, and there is usually an implication that it could be cheered up.
description_tr: Worried (愁) brows (眉) and a bitter (苦) face (臉). 苦 is the taste, and using it of an expression is exact: the mouth of an unhappy person does what the mouth of somebody eating something bitter does. The phrase reports the face and leaves the cause open, which is why it so often turns up inside a question — 愁眉苦臉的，怎麼了, what's the long face about. Chinese uses it of visible low-level misery rather than of grief, and there is usually an implication that it could be cheered up.
chineseExample_tr: 自從聽說預算削減後，他一直愁眉苦臉。

example: She walked into the interview with confidence.
chineseExample: 她昂首挺胸地走进面试室。
description: Head (首) raised (昂) and chest (胸) pushed out (挺). The posture is the whole content, and the phrase stays neutral about whether the confidence behind it has been earned, which leaves context to do all the work. Marching troops and a child who has just been praised are both 昂首挺胸, and so is somebody putting a brave face on a defeat — one of its commonest uses in Chinese, since walking out with the head up is exactly what one does when the news was bad.
description_tr: Head (首) raised (昂) and chest (胸) pushed out (挺). The posture is the whole content, and the phrase stays neutral about whether the confidence behind it has been earned, which leaves context to do all the work. Marching troops and a child who has just been praised are both 昂首挺胸, and so is somebody putting a brave face on a defeat — one of its commonest uses in Chinese, since walking out with the head up is exactly what one does when the news was bad.
chineseExample_tr: 她昂首挺胸地走進面試室。

example: A good leader welcomes constructive criticism.
chineseExample: 好的领导者闻过则喜，欢迎建设性批评。
description: This descends from the Mencius, on Zilu, of whom it is said that when someone told him of a fault (过) he had heard (闻) of, he was then (则) glad (喜). Mencius sets him in a short ascending series — Zilu welcomed correction, Yu the Great bowed on hearing good words, and Shun went further still. Being pleased to be corrected is treated as an achievement rather than a temperament. You will hear it of somebody who takes criticism as information rather than as an attack, and it is rare enough to be worth remarking on.
description_tr: This comes from the Mencius, on Zilu, of whom it is said that when someone told him of a fault (過) he had heard (聞) of, he was then (則) glad (喜). Mencius sets him in a short ascending series — Zilu welcomed correction, Yu the Great bowed on hearing good words, and Shun went further still. Being pleased to be corrected is treated as an achievement rather than a temperament. Chinese uses it of somebody who takes criticism as information rather than as an attack, and it is rare enough to be worth remarking on.
chineseExample_tr: 好的領導者聞過則喜，歡迎建設性批評。

example: She readily accepts good suggestions from her team.
chineseExample: 她从善如流，乐于接受团队的好建议。
description: This one comes from the Zuo Zhuan, said of Luan Shu of Jin, who took good counsel the way water runs downhill — following (从) the good (善) as if (如) flowing (流), with no friction and no delay. What is praised is the absence of resistance: he did not have to be persuaded past his own position first. It is said of somebody who adopts the better suggestion at once, without first defending the one they walked in with.
description_tr: This comes from the Zuo Zhuan, said of Luan Shu of Jin, who took good counsel the way water runs downhill — following (從) the good (善) as if (如) flowing (流), with no friction and no delay. What is praised is the absence of resistance: he did not have to be persuaded past his own position first. Chinese uses it of somebody who adopts the better suggestion at once, without first defending the one they walked in with.
chineseExample_tr: 她從善如流，樂於接受團隊的好建議。

example: The researcher worked tirelessly on her project for years.
chineseExample: 研究人员孜孜不倦地工作了多年。
description: 孜 is diligence, and doubling it gives the unbroken kind; with 不倦, never (不) tiring (倦), the phrase adds that the effort has not decayed. The second half carries the real claim, because it is about duration rather than intensity — anybody can work hard, and what is being praised is that the rate never fell off. It attaches to scholars, teachers and long careers, and it belongs to formal citation rather than to ordinary speech.
description_tr: 孜 is diligence, and doubling it gives the unbroken kind; with 不倦, never (不) tiring (倦), the phrase adds that the effort has not decayed. The second half carries the real claim, because it is about duration rather than intensity — anybody can work hard, and what is being praised is that the rate never fell off. Chinese uses it of scholars, teachers and long careers, and it belongs to formal citation rather than to ordinary speech.
chineseExample_tr: 研究人員孜孜不倦地工作了多年。

example: The mentor skillfully guided the students through difficult concepts.
chineseExample: 导师循循善诱，带领学生理解困难的概念。
description: Yan Hui, describing what it was like to be taught by Confucius, said 夫子循循然善诱人 — the Master leads people on step after step (循循) and is good (善) at drawing them out (诱). 诱 elsewhere means to entice or to lure, which is the interesting part: the pupil is being brought along rather than instructed, and each step is arranged to make the next one attractive. Chinese uses it as the highest praise available for a teacher, and the emphasis falls entirely on the pacing.
metaphoric_meaning: Draw a learner on step by step
description_tr: Yan Hui, describing what it was like to be taught by Confucius, said 夫子循循然善誘人 — the Master leads people on step after step (循循) and is good (善) at drawing them out (誘). 誘 elsewhere means to entice or to lure, which is the interesting part: the pupil is being brought along rather than instructed, and each step is arranged to make the next one attractive. Chinese uses it as the highest praise available for a teacher, and the emphasis falls entirely on the pacing.
chineseExample_tr: 導師循循善誘，帶領學生理解困難的概念。

example: Despite explaining it many times, she remained patient with the students.
chineseExample: 尽管解释了很多遍，她仍然诲人不倦。
description: Confucius, asked about himself, claimed only 学而不厌，诲人不倦 — never tiring of learning, never wearying (不倦) of instructing (诲) people (人). He offers it as the least he can say, and the pairing is the interesting part: teaching is made the other half of study rather than a separate virtue. It attaches to the teacher who explains the same thing for the twentieth time with no change in manner, and that repetition is exactly what the phrase is measuring.
description_tr: Confucius, asked about himself, claimed only 學而不厭，誨人不倦 — never tiring of learning, never wearying (不倦) of instructing (誨) people (人). He offers it as the least he can say, and the pairing is the interesting part: teaching is made the other half of study rather than a separate virtue. Chinese uses it of the teacher who explains the same thing for the twentieth time with no change in manner, and that repetition is exactly what the phrase is measuring.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管解釋了很多遍，她仍然誨人不倦。

example: Good teachers adapt their methods to each student's learning style.
chineseExample: 好老师会因材施教，根据每个学生的学习方式调整方法。
description: Teaching (施教) according to (因) the material (材). 材 is timber or stock, what you have been given to work with, and the carpenter's metaphor does real work: the grain decides what can be made from it. The four characters are Zhu Xi's formulation, summarising how Confucius handled his students, who got different answers to the same question depending on which of them had asked. Chinese uses it as the standard argument against uniform instruction, and it is a demand as much as a compliment.
description_tr: Teaching (施教) according to (因) the material (材). 材 is timber or stock, what you have been given to work with, and the carpenter's metaphor does real work: the grain decides what can be made from it. The four characters are Zhu Xi's formulation, summarising how Confucius handled his students, who got different answers to the same question depending on which of them had asked. Chinese uses it as the standard argument against uniform instruction, and it is a demand as much as a compliment.
chineseExample_tr: 好老師會因材施教，根據每個學生的學習方式調整方法。

example: The scholarship program aims to make education accessible to all.
chineseExample: 奖学金项目旨在有教无类，让所有人都能接受教育。
description: In teaching (教) there are (有) no (无) categories (类). Confucius said it in a society where 类 meant birth and rank, so the claim was substantive rather than pious: he declined to sort applicants by where they came from, and his students included the poor and the disreputable. It remains the standard Chinese banner for educational access, and it is worth reading as the negative it is — not that everybody must be taught alike, but that nobody is to be sorted out beforehand.
description_tr: In teaching (教) there are (有) no (無) categories (類). Confucius said it in a society where 類 meant birth and rank, so the claim was substantive rather than pious: he declined to sort applicants by where they came from, and his students included the poor and the disreputable. It remains the standard Chinese banner for educational access, and it is worth reading as the negative it is — not that everybody must be taught alike, but that nobody is to be sorted out beforehand.
chineseExample_tr: 獎學金項目旨在有教無類，讓所有人都能接受教育。

meaning: Teach by words and personal example
example: The best parents teach not just through words but through their actions.
chineseExample: 最好的父母言传身教，不仅用言语更用行动教导孩子。
description: Passing it on in words (言传) and teaching by the person (身教). The two halves are not equal partners, and Chinese treats the second as the stronger: 身 is the body, one's own conduct, and the argument carried is that what is demonstrated outweighs what is stated wherever the two disagree. That is why it attaches so heavily to parents. It is used to remind somebody that the instruction they are giving is being checked against the example they are setting.
description_tr: Passing it on in words (言傳) and teaching by the person (身教). The two halves are not equal partners, and Chinese treats the second as the stronger: 身 is the body, one's own conduct, and the argument carried is that what is demonstrated outweighs what is stated wherever the two disagree. That is why it attaches so heavily to parents. It is used to remind somebody that the instruction they are giving is being checked against the example they are setting.
chineseExample_tr: 最好的父母言傳身教，不僅用言語更用行動教導孩子。

meaning: Peaches and plums fill the gate
example: The retired professor has trained hundreds of successful scholars.
chineseExample: 退休教授桃李满门，培养了数百名成功的学者。
description: Students have been called peaches (桃) and plums (李) in Chinese since antiquity — the teacher plants them and other people eat the fruit — and to have them filling (满) the gate (门) is to have taught enough of them that they turn up everywhere. 门 is the school as much as the doorway, a teacher's students being his 门下. Chinese uses it of a career rather than a year, and it is what gets said about a professor at retirement. The commoner form is 桃李满天下, filling the world instead of the gate.
description_tr: Students have been called peaches (桃) and plums (李) in Chinese since antiquity — the teacher plants them and other people eat the fruit — and to have them filling (滿) the gate (門) is to have taught enough of them that they turn up everywhere. 門 is the school as much as the doorway, a teacher's students being his 門下. Chinese uses it of a career rather than a year, and it is what gets said about a professor at retirement. The commoner form is 桃李滿天下, filling the world instead of the gate.
chineseExample_tr: 退休教授桃李滿門，培養了數百名成功的學者。

example: The army maintained strict discipline, not disturbing the civilians.
chineseExample: 军队纪律严明，对百姓秋毫无犯。
description: Not violating (无犯) so much as the autumn down (秋毫) — the fine new hair animals grow as the cold comes on, which classical Chinese uses as the standard for the smallest thing an eye can resolve. The phrase belongs to armies. It is what was said of troops that passed through a district and took nothing, rare enough to be worth recording, and the measure is deliberately absurd in order to make the claim total. Chinese uses it of discipline rather than of honesty in general, and still applies it to soldiers and to officials.
metaphoric_meaning: Show strict discipline; not take anything
description_tr: Not violating (無犯) so much as the autumn down (秋毫) — the fine new hair animals grow as the cold comes on, which classical Chinese uses as the standard for the smallest thing an eye can resolve. The phrase belongs to armies. It is what was said of troops that passed through a district and took nothing, rare enough to be worth recording, and the measure is deliberately absurd in order to make the claim total. Chinese uses it of discipline rather than of honesty in general, and still applies it to soldiers and to officials.
chineseExample_tr: 軍隊紀律嚴明，對百姓秋毫無犯。

example: He lived his life with nothing to hide or regret.
chineseExample: 他活得坦坦荡荡，无愧于心。
description: Confucius set two types against each other: 君子坦荡荡，小人长戚戚 — the gentleman is open (坦) and broad (荡), the small man is forever fretting. The doubling in both halves is the original's and does tonal work, giving the first a spaciousness and the second a nagging rhythm. What the phrase claims is a connection rather than a virtue: the openness and the absence of anxiety are one fact, because somebody with nothing hidden has nothing to keep track of. It gets used of a person who can be looked into.
description_tr: Confucius set two types against each other: 君子坦蕩蕩，小人長慼慼 — the gentleman is open (坦) and broad (蕩), the small man is forever fretting. The doubling in both halves is the original's and does tonal work, giving the first a spaciousness and the second a nagging rhythm. What the phrase claims is a connection rather than a virtue: the openness and the absence of anxiety are one fact, because somebody with nothing hidden has nothing to keep track of. Chinese uses it of a person who can be looked into.
chineseExample_tr: 他活得坦坦蕩蕩，無愧於心。

example: She is genuine - the same person in public and private.
chineseExample: 她表里如一，在公众场合和私下是同一个人。
description: The outside (表) and the inside (里) as (如) one (一). 表 and 里 are the two faces of a garment, the shown and the lining, so the metaphor is not about honesty in speech but about there being a single thing where one might have expected two. That is why it is used of a person's whole conduct rather than of any particular statement. Chinese pays it as serious praise, and describes its absence with the same pair — 表里不一 is among the more damaging things that can be said of somebody.
description_tr: The outside (表) and the inside (裡) as (如) one (一). 表 and 裡 are the two faces of a garment, the shown and the lining, so the metaphor is not about honesty in speech but about there being a single thing where one might have expected two. That is why it is used of a person's whole conduct rather than of any particular statement. Chinese pays it as serious praise, and describes its absence with the same pair — 表裡不一 is among the more damaging things that can be said of somebody.
chineseExample_tr: 她表裡如一，在公眾場合和私下是同一個人。

example: He kept his promise because he believed a man's word is his bond.
chineseExample: 他信守承诺，因为他相信一言既出，驷马难追。
description: Once (既) a word (一言) is out (出). The line is almost never left standing alone: 一言既出，驷马难追, once said, a team of four horses cannot catch it. The image is of speech travelling faster than the fastest thing available to chase it, so what the saying actually regulates is the moment before, not the moment after. Chinese uses it to close a commitment — said after agreeing to something, it means the matter is now settled — and to warn somebody who is about to say something they will then own.
metaphoric_meaning: A promise once made must be kept
description_tr: Once (既) a word (一言) is out (出). The line is almost never left standing alone: 一言既出，駟馬難追, once said, a team of four horses cannot catch it. The image is of speech travelling faster than the fastest thing available to chase it, so what the saying actually regulates is the moment before, not the moment after. Chinese uses it to close a commitment — said after agreeing to something, it means the matter is now settled — and to warn somebody who is about to say something they will then own.
chineseExample_tr: 他信守承諾，因為他相信一言既出，駟馬難追。

example: The manager handled the conflict with complete transparency.
chineseExample: 经理开诚布公地处理了冲突。
description: The Records of the Three Kingdoms assesses Zhuge Liang's administration in the words this phrase compresses: 开诚心，布公道 — he opened (开) his sincerity (诚) and spread out (布) impartial (公) dealing. Both verbs are physical and both concern display, which is the argument: the honesty and the fairness were not merely practised but made visible, so that people could see they were being treated alike. It gets used of negotiations and of management, and what it asks for is candour conducted in the open.
description_tr: The Records of the Three Kingdoms assesses Zhuge Liang's administration in the words this phrase compresses: 開誠心，布公道 — he opened (開) his sincerity (誠) and spread out (布) impartial (公) dealing. Both verbs are physical and both concern display, which is the argument: the honesty and the fairness were not merely practised but made visible, so that people could see they were being treated alike. Chinese uses it of negotiations and of management, and what it asks for is candour conducted in the open.
chineseExample_tr: 經理開誠布公地處理了衝突。

meaning: Livers and galls illuminate each other
example: The two friends shared everything with complete trust.
chineseExample: 两位朋友肝胆相照，完全信任彼此。
description: Liver (肝) and gall (胆) lighting (照) one another (相). Chinese physiology seats courage in the gall and sincerity in the liver, so the phrase does not mean two friends know each other well — it means each is showing the other the organs that hold what they are made of. The image is deliberately visceral and slightly alarming, which is the point: what gets exposed is not information but nerve. Chinese uses it of friendships formed under pressure, and it belongs to the register of loyalty rather than of affection.
description_tr: Liver (肝) and gall (膽) lighting (照) one another (相). Chinese physiology seats courage in the gall and sincerity in the liver, so the phrase does not mean two friends know each other well — it means each is showing the other the organs that hold what they are made of. The image is deliberately visceral and slightly alarming, which is the point: what gets exposed is not information but nerve. Chinese uses it of friendships formed under pressure, and it belongs to the register of loyalty rather than of affection.
chineseExample_tr: 兩位朋友肝膽相照，完全信任彼此。

example: They had a heart-to-heart talk about their concerns.
chineseExample: 他们推心置腹地谈论了彼此的担忧。
description: Emperor Guangwu, taking the surrender of troops who expected to be killed, rode among them unarmed, and they said of him that he 推赤心置人腹中, pushed his own red heart into other men's bellies. The idiom keeps the gesture: pushing out (推) the heart (心) and setting it (置) inside somebody else (腹). What it describes is trust extended first and without security, which is why it is a leader's phrase. Chinese uses it of the conversation in which one side deliberately goes first.
metaphoric_meaning: Speak from the heart; confide completely
description_tr: Emperor Guangwu, taking the surrender of troops who expected to be killed, rode among them unarmed, and they said of him that he 推赤心置人腹中, pushed his own red heart into other men's bellies. The idiom keeps the gesture: pushing out (推) the heart (心) and setting it (置) inside somebody else (腹). What it describes is trust extended first and without security, which is why it is a leader's phrase. Chinese uses it of the conversation in which one side deliberately goes first.
chineseExample_tr: 他們推心置腹地談論了彼此的擔憂。

example: They became partners because they shared the same vision.
chineseExample: 他们志同道合，因此成为合作伙伴。
description: The same (同) ambition (志) and paths that fit together (道合). 志 is what a person is aiming at and 道 is the way they mean to get there, so the phrase requires agreement on both — people who want the same thing by different means do not qualify. That is a stricter test than friendship, which is why it belongs to founding partners, political allies and collaborators rather than to companions. Chinese reserves it for the basis on which people joined, and it explains why a group holds.
metaphoric_meaning: Share the same goals and values
description_tr: The same (同) ambition (志) and paths that fit together (道合). 志 is what a person is aiming at and 道 is the way they mean to get there, so the phrase requires agreement on both — people who want the same thing by different means do not qualify. That is a stricter test than friendship, which is why it belongs to founding partners, political allies and collaborators rather than to companions. Chinese uses it of the basis on which people joined, and it explains why a group holds.
chineseExample_tr: 他們志同道合，因此成為合作夥伴。

example: From their first meeting, they knew they were kindred spirits.
chineseExample: 从第一次见面，他们就知道彼此情投意合。
description: Feelings (情) thrown toward each other (投) and intentions (意) meeting (合). 投 is to cast or hurl, which gives the first half a suddenness the second does not have, and the pairing is exact about the order in which it happens: the liking arrives first, and finding that you also think alike confirms it. Chinese reserves it for two people who took to each other immediately, covering friendship and romance both, with the emphasis on the fit rather than on the intensity.
metaphoric_meaning: Be perfectly compatible; hit it off
description_tr: Feelings (情) thrown toward each other (投) and intentions (意) meeting (合). 投 is to cast or hurl, which gives the first half a suddenness the second does not have, and the pairing is exact about the order in which it happens: the liking arrives first, and finding that you also think alike confirms it. Chinese uses it of two people who took to each other immediately, covering friendship and romance both, with the emphasis on the fit rather than on the intensity.
chineseExample_tr: 從第一次見面，他們就知道彼此情投意合。

example: Despite their different backgrounds, they became the closest of friends.
chineseExample: 尽管背景不同，他们成为了莫逆之交。
description: The Zhuangzi has four men agree that whoever can take life and death as one thread is fit company; they look at each other, laugh, and find nothing in one another's minds running against the grain — 莫逆于心. A friendship (交) with nothing (莫) counter (逆) in it is what the phrase names. The claim is not that such friends never disagree, but that no fundamental grain runs the wrong way between them. It is said of the closest sort of friendship, and the Zhuangzi's setting makes it a meeting of outlook rather than of temperament.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi has four men agree that whoever can take life and death as one thread is fit company; they look at each other, laugh, and find nothing in one another's minds running against the grain — 莫逆於心. A friendship (交) with nothing (莫) counter (逆) in it is what the phrase names. The claim is not that such friends never disagree, but that no fundamental grain runs the wrong way between them. Chinese uses it of the closest sort of friendship, and the Zhuangzi's setting makes it a meeting of outlook rather than of temperament.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管背景不同，他們成為了莫逆之交。

example: They pledged loyalty to each other through thick and thin.
chineseExample: 他们是刎颈之交，发誓同甘共苦。
description: Lian Po, a general, had been publicly slighting Lin Xiangru, a courtier promoted over him; Lin kept out of his way, explaining that Zhao survived because the two of them both existed and that a quarrel would finish it. Lian Po came to his gate carrying a rod and asked to be beaten with it. They became 刎颈之交 — friends (交) who would give the throat (刎颈) for one another. What the phrase claims is not affection but a bond in which the other's life outweighs one's own, and Chinese reserves it accordingly.
description_tr: Lian Po, a general, had been publicly slighting Lin Xiangru, a courtier promoted over him; Lin kept out of his way, explaining that Zhao survived because the two of them both existed and that a quarrel would finish it. Lian Po came to his gate carrying a rod and asked to be beaten with it. They became 刎頸之交 — friends (交) who would give the throat (刎頸) for one another. What the phrase claims is not affection but a bond in which the other's life outweighs one's own, and Chinese reserves it accordingly.
chineseExample_tr: 他們是刎頸之交，發誓同甘共苦。

example: The elderly couple supported each other through their difficult years.
chineseExample: 这对老夫妻在困难岁月里相濡以沫。
description: The Zhuangzi: when the spring dries up the fish are left together on land, blowing damp air on one another and wetting each other (相濡) with foam (以沫) — and then the sentence turns, 不如相忘于江湖, better than this would be to forget each other in the rivers and lakes. Zhuangzi is arguing against the situation, not admiring it. Chinese kept the image and dropped the argument, and it is now among the warmest things that can be said about a marriage, which is worth knowing given where it came from.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi: when the spring dries up the fish are left together on land, blowing damp air on one another and wetting each other (相濡) with foam (以沫) — and then the sentence turns, 不如相忘於江湖, better than this would be to forget each other in the rivers and lakes. Zhuangzi is arguing against the situation, not admiring it. Chinese kept the image and dropped the argument, and it is now among the warmest things that can be said about a marriage, which is worth knowing given where it came from.
chineseExample_tr: 這對老夫妻在困難歲月裡相濡以沫。

example: Their long marriage was built on mutual respect.
chineseExample: 他们的婚姻长久，建立在相敬如宾的基础上。
description: The Zuo Zhuan records an official passing a field and seeing a man's wife bring him his meal there: the two treated one another 如宾, as guests, and on the strength of that the man was recommended for office. The reasoning is that courtesy sustained where nobody is watching is evidence of character. Mutual respect (相敬) at the pitch owed to a guest (如宾) is the phrase, and In practice it is used of long marriages — admiringly, though a modern ear may catch a little coolness in it as well.
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan records an official passing a field and seeing a man's wife bring him his meal there: the two treated one another 如賓, as guests, and on the strength of that the man was recommended for office. The reasoning is that courtesy sustained where nobody is watching is evidence of character. Mutual respect (相敬) at the pitch owed to a guest (如賓) is the phrase, and Chinese uses it of long marriages — admiringly, though a modern ear may catch a little coolness in it as well.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的婚姻長久，建立在相敬如賓的基礎上。

example: Their relationship exemplifies mutual respect and devotion.
chineseExample: 他们的关系是举案齐眉的典范。
description: Meng Guang, married to the recluse Liang Hong, served his meals by lifting (举) the tray (案) level (齐) with her eyebrows (眉), so that she never looked at him over the food. The Book of Later Han records it as a marriage of unusual mutual regard, the two of them poor and hired out to other households. What the phrase preserves is a gesture rather than a feeling, which is why Chinese still uses it of couples whose respect for each other shows in small things.
metaphoric_meaning: Married couple with great mutual respect
description_tr: Meng Guang, married to the recluse Liang Hong, served his meals by lifting (舉) the tray (案) level (齊) with her eyebrows (眉), so that she never looked at him over the food. The Book of Later Han records it as a marriage of unusual mutual regard, the two of them poor and hired out to other households. What the phrase preserves is a gesture rather than a feeling, which is why Chinese still uses it of couples whose respect for each other shows in small things.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的關係是舉案齊眉的典範。

meaning: White heads together in old age
example: They wished the newlyweds a lifetime of happiness together.
chineseExample: 他们祝愿新婚夫妇白头偕老。
description: White (白) heads (头) reaching old age (老) side by side (偕). The Book of Songs supplies the wish — 及尔偕老, to grow old with you — and the white hair was added later to give it a picture. It is a blessing rather than a description: nobody says it about a marriage in progress. It is said at weddings and anniversaries and written on red envelopes, and what it asks for is duration, which is the one thing a wedding cannot promise.
description_tr: White (白) heads (頭) reaching old age (老) side by side (偕). The Book of Songs supplies the wish — 及爾偕老, to grow old with you — and the white hair was added later to give it a picture. It is a blessing rather than a description: nobody says it about a marriage in progress. It is said at weddings and anniversaries and written on red envelopes, and what it asks for is duration, which is the one thing a wedding cannot promise.
chineseExample_tr: 他們祝願新婚夫婦白頭偕老。

example: He fell in love with her the moment he saw her.
chineseExample: 他第一眼见到她就一见钟情。
description: At a single (一) sight (见), the feeling (情) gathers (钟). 钟 is the interesting character — the same one as a bell, here in its older sense of concentrating or collecting — so what is described is the whole of somebody's affection settling on one object at once. That is more specific than attraction. Chinese uses it as English uses love at first sight, and it will also stretch to objects: a person can 一见钟情 with a house or a cat, which English cannot quite manage.
description_tr: At a single (一) sight (見), the feeling (情) gathers (鍾). 鍾 is the interesting character — the same one as a bell, here in its older sense of concentrating or collecting — so what is described is the whole of somebody's affection settling on one object at once. That is more specific than attraction. Chinese uses it as English uses love at first sight, and it will also stretch to objects: a person can 一見鍾情 with a house or a cat, which English cannot quite manage.
chineseExample_tr: 他第一眼見到她就一見鍾情。

example: She promised to love him forever, no matter what happens.
chineseExample: 她承诺无论发生什么，都会爱他到海枯石烂。
description: Seas (海) drying (枯) and stones (石) crumbling (烂). Both are chosen for being the slowest imaginable changes rather than impossible ones, which is where the scale comes from — this is deep time, not never. It lives inside oaths, in the form 海枯石烂不变心, unchanged until the seas dry and the stones crumble. Chinese uses it almost entirely for promises between lovers, and it is old-fashioned enough now that saying it is usually a little self-aware.
metaphoric_meaning: Until the end of time; eternal love
description_tr: Seas (海) drying (枯) and stones (石) crumbling (爛). Both are chosen for being the slowest imaginable changes rather than impossible ones, which is where the scale comes from — this is deep time, not never. It lives inside oaths, in the form 海枯石爛不變心, unchanged until the seas dry and the stones crumble. Chinese uses it almost entirely for promises between lovers, and it is old-fashioned enough now that saying it is usually a little self-aware.
chineseExample_tr: 她承諾無論發生什麼，都會愛他到海枯石爛。

meaning: Hard to part, hard to leave
example: The farewell was emotional as neither wanted to say goodbye.
chineseExample: 告别时他们难分难舍，都不想说再见。
description: Hard (难) to divide (分) and hard (难) to let go (舍). The doubled 难 sets the two verbs in parallel and covers both halves of a parting, the separating and the releasing, so no part of the departure is left easy. It is stronger and more physical than 依依不舍, and it does not require affection: Chinese uses it of business partners breaking up, of a team disbanding, and of anything entangled long enough that the disentangling has become the difficulty.
description_tr: Hard (難) to divide (分) and hard (難) to let go (舍). The doubled 難 sets the two verbs in parallel and covers both halves of a parting, the separating and the releasing, so no part of the departure is left easy. It is stronger and more physical than 依依不捨, and it does not require affection: Chinese uses it of business partners breaking up, of a team disbanding, and of anything entangled long enough that the disentangling has become the difficulty.
chineseExample_tr: 告別時他們難分難捨，都不想說再見。

example: She kept looking back as she left her childhood home.
chineseExample: 离开童年的家时，她恋恋不舍地频频回望。
description: 恋 is love that clings, the character in 恋人 and 留恋; doubled and set against 不舍, unwilling (不) to let go (舍), the phrase gives a reluctance rooted in attachment rather than in habit. That is what separates it from 依依不舍, which reports the same scene from outside as a hesitation of the body. Here the cause is named. It attaches to leaving a house one has lived in, a job one liked, a place one was happy in — the object is as often a situation as a person.
description_tr: 戀 is love that clings, the character in 戀人 and 留戀; doubled and set against 不捨, unwilling (不) to let go (舍), the phrase gives a reluctance rooted in attachment rather than in habit. That is what separates it from 依依不捨, which reports the same scene from outside as a hesitation of the body. Here the cause is named. Chinese uses it of leaving a house one has lived in, a job one liked, a place one was happy in — the object is as often a situation as a person.
chineseExample_tr: 離開童年的家時，她戀戀不捨地頻頻回望。

example: Her homeland remained constantly in her thoughts.
chineseExample: 她魂牵梦萦地想念着故乡。
description: The soul (魂) pulled along (牵) and dreams (梦) wound about (萦). 牵 is leading an animal on a rope and 萦 is thread winding round something, so both halves make the longing an external force acting on somebody who is not choosing it. That the second half happens in sleep is the claim: the preoccupation carries on where the will cannot reach. It gets used of homesickness and of love, and it is a literary phrase — written far more often than spoken.
description_tr: The soul (魂) pulled along (牽) and dreams (夢) wound about (縈). 牽 is leading an animal on a rope and 縈 is thread winding round something, so both halves make the longing an external force acting on somebody who is not choosing it. That the second half happens in sleep is the claim: the preoccupation carries on where the will cannot reach. Chinese uses it of homesickness and of love, and it is a literary phrase — written far more often than spoken.
chineseExample_tr: 她魂牽夢縈地想念著故鄉。

meaning: Think in morning, yearn at night
example: He constantly thinks about his family back home.
chineseExample: 他朝思暮想着远方的家人。
description: Thinking (思) at dawn (朝) and thinking again (想) at dusk (暮). The two verbs are near-synonyms and the two times are the ends of the waking span, so the phrase covers a day by naming its edges. It is plainer than 魂牵梦萦 and correspondingly commoner in speech. In practice it is used of absent people, of a place somebody wants to get back to, and, quite ordinarily, of something they have been wanting to buy for months.
description_tr: Thinking (思) at dawn (朝) and thinking again (想) at dusk (暮). The two verbs are near-synonyms and the two times are the ends of the waking span, so the phrase covers a day by naming its edges. It is plainer than 魂牽夢縈 and correspondingly commoner in speech. Chinese uses it of absent people, of a place somebody wants to get back to, and, quite ordinarily, of something they have been wanting to buy for months.
chineseExample_tr: 他朝思暮想著遠方的家人。

example: After years abroad, he returned to his hometown to retire.
chineseExample: 在海外多年后，他落叶归根，回到家乡退休。
description: Fallen (落) leaves (叶) returning (归) to the root (根). The botany carries the argument: the leaf drops at the foot of the tree that made it and goes back into the soil that fed it, so the return is presented as natural process rather than as a decision anybody took. Chinese uses it above all of people who go home at the end of a life, to retire or to be buried, and it is central to how the Chinese diaspora talks about itself. It carries acceptance rather than sorrow.
metaphoric_meaning: Return to one's roots; go back home
description_tr: Fallen (落) leaves (葉) returning (歸) to the root (根). The botany carries the argument: the leaf drops at the foot of the tree that made it and goes back into the soil that fed it, so the return is presented as natural process rather than as a decision anybody took. Chinese uses it above all of people who go home at the end of a life, to retire or to be buried, and it is central to how the Chinese diaspora talks about itself. It carries acceptance rather than sorrow.
chineseExample_tr: 在海外多年後，他落葉歸根，回到家鄉退休。

example: Despite the opportunities elsewhere, he couldn't bring himself to leave.
chineseExample: 尽管别处有机会，他仍故土难离。
description: Old (故) ground (土) is hard (难) to leave (离). 故土 is the earth one comes from, and 故 is the character in 故乡 and 故人 — what is old and one's own, rather than merely former. The phrase does not argue that leaving is wrong, only that it costs, which is why it turns up in accounts of migration and resettlement as an explanation of reluctance. Chinese uses it with sympathy, and often about people who left anyway.
description_tr: Old (故) ground (土) is hard (難) to leave (離). 故土 is the earth one comes from, and 故 is the character in 故鄉 and 故人 — what is old and one's own, rather than merely former. The phrase does not argue that leaving is wrong, only that it costs, which is why it turns up in accounts of migration and resettlement as an explanation of reluctance. Chinese uses it with sympathy, and often about people who left anyway.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管別處有機會，他仍故土難離。

meaning: Content with soil, reluctant to move
example: Rural communities often maintain strong attachment to their land.
chineseExample: 农村社区往往安土重迁，对土地有强烈的依恋。
description: The Book of Han calls it the nature of the common people: 安土重迁 — settled (安) on the land (土) and treating a move (迁) as a weighty matter (重). 重 is read zhòng here, to regard as serious, not chóng, which is a standard trap. The phrase is descriptive rather than critical in origin, explaining why agricultural populations resist relocation, and Chinese still uses it in that analytical register, of communities as often as of individuals. It is the standard account of why people stay.
description_tr: The Book of Han calls it the nature of the common people: 安土重遷 — settled (安) on the land (土) and treating a move (遷) as a weighty matter (重). 重 is read zhòng here, to regard as serious, not chóng, which is a standard trap. The phrase is descriptive rather than critical in origin, explaining why agricultural populations resist relocation, and Chinese still uses it in that analytical register, of communities as often as of individuals. It is the standard account of why people stay.
chineseExample_tr: 農村社區往往安土重遷，對土地有強烈的依戀。

example: The era was characterized by unprecedented peace and prosperity.
chineseExample: 那个时代四海升平，前所未有的和平繁荣。
description: The four seas (四海) — classical Chinese for everywhere, the world being bounded by them — rising into (升) peace (平). 升平 is a set term for an era in good order, and the phrase asserts that the order holds not merely at the centre but out to the edges. That reach is the whole content. It belongs to the language of dynastic praise and of new year wishes, and Chinese uses it now in ceremonial and decorative settings rather than in political analysis.
description_tr: The four seas (四海) — classical Chinese for everywhere, the world being bounded by them — rising into (升) peace (平). 昇平 is a set term for an era in good order, and the phrase asserts that the order holds not merely at the centre but out to the edges. That reach is the whole content. It belongs to the language of dynastic praise and of new year wishes, and Chinese uses it now in ceremonial and decorative settings rather than in political analysis.
chineseExample_tr: 那個時代四海昇平，前所未有的和平繁榮。

example: The country enjoyed decades of stability and growth.
chineseExample: 国家享受了数十年的太平盛世。
description: A great (太) peace (平) and a flourishing (盛) age (世). 太平 is a term with real weight behind it — the condition of order a dynasty existed to produce, and the name a good many rebellions gave themselves. The phrase claims both halves at once, quiet and prosperous together, since either without the other was understood not to last. In practice it is used of golden ages in retrospect and, drily, of any period somebody is being told to feel grateful for.
metaphoric_meaning: Golden age of peace and prosperity
description_tr: A great (太) peace (平) and a flourishing (盛) age (世). 太平 is a term with real weight behind it — the condition of order a dynasty existed to produce, and the name a good many rebellions gave themselves. The phrase claims both halves at once, quiet and prosperous together, since either without the other was understood not to last. Chinese uses it of golden ages in retrospect and, drily, of any period somebody is being told to feel grateful for.
chineseExample_tr: 國家享受了數十年的太平盛世。

example: Good governance should prioritize national stability and citizen welfare.
chineseExample: 良好的治理应该以国泰民安为首要目标。
description: The state (国) in right order (泰) and the people (民) secure (安). 泰 is the Yijing hexagram of things standing in proper relation, heaven and earth in communication, so the first half claims order rather than mere quiet. The two halves are offered as a single outcome and not as a trade, which is the argument inside the phrase. It is the standard formula in blessings, on temple plaques and at new year, and it is what governments have always claimed to be delivering.
description_tr: The state (國) in right order (泰) and the people (民) secure (安). 泰 is the Yijing hexagram of things standing in proper relation, heaven and earth in communication, so the first half claims order rather than mere quiet. The two halves are offered as a single outcome and not as a trade, which is the argument inside the phrase. It is the standard formula in blessings, on temple plaques and at new year, and it is what governments have always claimed to be delivering.
chineseExample_tr: 良好的治理應該以國泰民安為首要目標。

example: Economic development benefits both citizens and national power.
chineseExample: 经济发展使民富国强。
description: The people (民) wealthy (富) and the state (国) strong (强). The order of the halves is the argument: prosperity in the population comes first and national strength follows from it, a position with a long history in Chinese writing on statecraft and by no means the only one ever held. Chinese uses it in the register of development policy, and putting 民富 in front still does rhetorical work whenever somebody chooses this phrase over its alternatives.
description_tr: The people (民) wealthy (富) and the state (國) strong (強). The order of the halves is the argument: prosperity in the population comes first and national strength follows from it, a position with a long history in Chinese writing on statecraft and by no means the only one ever held. Chinese uses it in the register of development policy, and putting 民富 in front still does rhetorical work whenever somebody chooses this phrase over its alternatives.
chineseExample_tr: 經濟發展使民富國強。

example: The new administration committed to reforms and better governance.
chineseExample: 新政府励精图治，致力于改革和更好的治理。
description: To rouse (励) the concentrated spirit (精) and plan for (图) good order (治). 精 is focused energy rather than cleverness, so the phrase describes effort applied at full intensity to the business of governing, and it belongs to a ruler taking hold of affairs personally after a stretch of drift. That sense of a fresh start is usually still there. Chinese uses it of new administrations and of managers brought in to turn something around, and it implies the previous period had gone slack.
description_tr: To rouse (勵) the concentrated spirit (精) and plan for (圖) good order (治). 精 is focused energy rather than cleverness, so the phrase describes effort applied at full intensity to the business of governing, and it belongs to a ruler taking hold of affairs personally after a stretch of drift. That sense of a fresh start is usually still there. Chinese uses it of new administrations and of managers brought in to turn something around, and it implies the previous period had gone slack.
chineseExample_tr: 新政府勵精圖治，致力於改革和更好的治理。

example: He dedicated himself completely to the cause.
chineseExample: 他披肝沥胆，全身心投入这项事业。
description: Laying open (披) the liver (肝) and letting the gall (胆) drip out (沥). The same two organs as in 肝胆相照, seat of sincerity and of nerve, but the verbs here are surgical rather than illuminating: this is not showing somebody your insides, it is emptying them out. That is what makes it the more extreme of the pair. You will hear it of total commitment offered to a cause or a superior, and it belongs to declarations, petitions, and the language of people staking everything on being believed.
metaphoric_meaning: Give one's all; be completely sincere
description_tr: Laying open (披) the liver (肝) and letting the gall (膽) drip out (瀝). The same two organs as in 肝膽相照, seat of sincerity and of nerve, but the verbs here are surgical rather than illuminating: this is not showing somebody your insides, it is emptying them out. That is what makes it the more extreme of the pair.
