Chinese uses it of total commitment offered to a cause or a superior, and it belongs to declarations, petitions, and the language of people staking everything on being believed.
chineseExample_tr: 他披肝瀝膽，全身心投入這項事業。

example: His commitment to justice continued until his last day.
chineseExample: 他对正义的追求死而后已。
description: Zengzi, in the Analects, says a gentleman's burden is heavy and his road long: 仁以为己任，不亦重乎？死而后已，不亦远乎？ — he takes benevolence as his own charge, and stops (已) only after (后) death (死). Zhuge Liang borrowed the four characters seven centuries later in the memorial before his northern campaigns, pairing them with 鞠躬尽瘁, bending to the task until spent, and it is that pairing most Chinese speakers know. The phrase sets no other terminating condition, which is its whole force: not until the work is done, not until it is hopeless, but until the person is gone.
description_tr: Zengzi, in the Analects, says a gentleman's burden is heavy and his road long: 仁以為己任，不亦重乎？死而後已，不亦遠乎？ — he takes benevolence as his own charge, and stops (已) only after (後) death (死). Zhuge Liang borrowed the four characters seven centuries later in the memorial before his northern campaigns, pairing them with 鞠躬盡瘁, bending to the task until spent, and it is that pairing most Chinese speakers know. The phrase sets no other terminating condition, which is its whole force: not until the work is done, not until it is hopeless, but until the person is gone.
chineseExample_tr: 他對正義的追求死而後已。

example: Achieving sustainability is a long-term challenge requiring sustained effort.
chineseExample: 实现可持续发展任重道远。
description: A heavy (重) load (任) and a long (远) road (道). The line is from the Analects, where it is Zengzi, not Confucius, who says the gentleman's burden is heavy and his road long, because benevolence is the load he carries and only death sets it down. The phrase captures the weight of important duties that require long journeys. Chinese uses it of undertakings whose difficulty is not the obstacle but the duration, and it is said at the beginning of something rather than in the middle of it.
metaphoric_meaning: Heavy burden and long journey ahead
description_tr: A heavy (重) load (任) and a long (遠) road (道). The line is from the Analects, where it is Zengzi, not Confucius, who says the gentleman's burden is heavy and his road long, because benevolence is the load he carries and only death sets it down. The phrase captures the weight of important duties that require long journeys. Chinese uses it of undertakings whose difficulty is not the obstacle but the duration, and it is said at the beginning of something rather than in the middle of it.
chineseExample_tr: 實現可持續發展任重道遠。

example: She traveled from far away to attend her friend's wedding.
chineseExample: 她千里迢迢赶来参加朋友的婚礼。
description: A thousand (千) li (里), with 迢迢 for the distance — a character meaning far which, doubled, means far in a way that is felt. The reduplication is the whole difference: 千里 alone states a measurement, and 千里迢迢 says somebody crossed it. That is why the phrase almost always travels with a person rather than a place. In practice it is used of a visitor who came a long way, and the point being made is about the effort rather than the geography.
description_tr: A thousand (千) li (裡), with 迢迢 for the distance — a character meaning far which, doubled, means far in a way that is felt. The reduplication is the whole difference: 千里 alone states a measurement, and 千里迢迢 says somebody crossed it. That is why the phrase almost always travels with a person rather than a place. Chinese uses it of a visitor who came a long way, and the point being made is about the effort rather than the geography.
chineseExample_tr: 她千里迢迢趕來參加朋友的婚禮。

meaning: Eat in wind, sleep in dew
example: The explorers endured harsh conditions during their expedition.
chineseExample: 探险队员风餐露宿，忍受着艰苦的条件。
description: Taking meals (餐) in the wind (风) and sleeping (宿) in the dew (露). The two nouns are chosen for being what you get instead of a roof, and neither is dramatic — no storms, no snow, just the ordinary outdoors happening to somebody with nowhere to be. That understatement is where the weight comes from. Chinese uses it of long journeys, of field work and of construction crews, and it is admiring rather than pitying: the person is understood to have accepted it for a reason.
metaphoric_meaning: Endure hardships of travel; rough it
description_tr: Taking meals (餐) in the wind (風) and sleeping (宿) in the dew (露). The two nouns are chosen for being what you get instead of a roof, and neither is dramatic — no storms, no snow, just the ordinary outdoors happening to somebody with nowhere to be. That understatement is where the weight comes from. Chinese uses it of long journeys, of field work and of construction crews, and it is admiring rather than pitying: the person is understood to have accepted it for a reason.
chineseExample_tr: 探險隊員風餐露宿，忍受著艱苦的條件。

example: They overcame many obstacles to reach their destination.
chineseExample: 他们跋山涉水，克服重重困难到达目的地。
description: Scrambling over (跋) mountains (山) and wading (涉) rivers (水). Both verbs are specific about effort — 跋 is a hard slog on foot, 涉 is going through water rather than over it — so what is named is travel that had to be done with the body. It covers a whole journey rather than a single obstacle, which is what separates it from its neighbours. Chinese uses it literally of remote fieldwork and figuratively of any long undertaking, and the emphasis falls on distance covered rather than on any one difficulty.
description_tr: Scrambling over (跋) mountains (山) and wading (涉) rivers (水). Both verbs are specific about effort — 跋 is a hard slog on foot, 涉 is going through water rather than over it — so what is named is travel that had to be done with the body. It covers a whole journey rather than a single obstacle, which is what separates it from its neighbours. Chinese uses it literally of remote fieldwork and figuratively of any long undertaking, and the emphasis falls on distance covered rather than on any one difficulty.
chineseExample_tr: 他們跋山涉水，克服重重困難到達目的地。

example: The postal workers delivered mail despite the mountainous terrain.
chineseExample: 邮递员翻山越岭送信。
description: Going over (翻) mountains (山) and across (越) ridges (岭). Both halves are the same kind of obstacle, unlike 跋山涉水 which pairs land with water, so what the phrase gives is a landscape that never changes — one ridge, and then another one. The repetition is the point, and it makes this the more exhausting of the two. Chinese uses it of reaching somewhere genuinely remote, and of a search or a delivery that took far longer than it should have.
metaphoric_meaning: Cross difficult terrain; overcome major obstacles
description_tr: Going over (翻) mountains (山) and across (越) ridges (嶺). Both halves are the same kind of obstacle, unlike 跋山涉水 which pairs land with water, so what the phrase gives is a landscape that never changes — one ridge, and then another one. The repetition is the point, and it makes this the more exhausting of the two. Chinese uses it of reaching somewhere genuinely remote, and of a search or a delivery that took far longer than it should have.
chineseExample_tr: 郵遞員翻山越嶺送信。

meaning: Not consider a thousand miles far
example: He traveled across the country just to see her.
chineseExample: 他不远千里，穿越全国只为见她一面。
description: Mencius opens with King Hui of Liang receiving him: 叟！不远千里而来，亦将有以利吾国乎 — venerable sir, you did not count a thousand (千) li (里) as far (远), so you must have something to profit my state. Mencius refuses the framing and answers that a king should ask about benevolence rather than profit, which is the point of the anecdote. The four characters kept the courtesy and dropped the argument. Chinese uses them of somebody who has travelled a long way on your account, usually in thanks, and the 不 negates the distance rather than the journey: the traveller did not think of it as far.
metaphoric_meaning: Willingly travel far; make great efforts
description_tr: Mencius opens with King Hui of Liang receiving him: 叟！不遠千里而來，亦將有以利吾國乎 — venerable sir, you did not count a thousand (千) li (裡) as far (遠), so you must have something to profit my state. Mencius refuses the framing and answers that a king should ask about benevolence rather than profit, which is the point of the anecdote. The four characters kept the courtesy and dropped the argument. Chinese uses them of somebody who has travelled a long way on your account, usually in thanks, and the 不 negates the distance rather than the journey: the traveller did not think of it as far.
chineseExample_tr: 他不遠千里，穿越全國只為見她一面。

example: His impatience for quick results led to poor decisions.
chineseExample: 他急于求成导致了糟糕的决定。
description: Anxious (急) about (于) obtaining (求) success (成). 急 is urgency felt as pressure rather than as speed, so the fault is located in the person's state and not in their pace: it is not that they are moving fast but that they cannot bear not to have arrived. That is why it explains bad decisions. Chinese uses it of students, of new managers and of investors, and it is usually offered as a diagnosis by somebody watching rather than as a confession.
metaphoric_meaning: Be impatient for success; rush things
description_tr: Anxious (急) about (於) obtaining (求) success (成). 急 is urgency felt as pressure rather than as speed, so the fault is located in the person's state and not in their pace: it is not that they are moving fast but that they cannot bear not to have arrived. That is why it explains bad decisions. Chinese uses it of students, of new managers and of investors, and it is usually offered as a diagnosis by somebody watching rather than as a confession.
chineseExample_tr: 他急於求成導致了糟糕的決定。

example: Rushing the project caused more delays in the end.
chineseExample: 赶工反而导致了更多延误，真是欲速不达。
description: Confucius, advising a newly appointed magistrate, told him not to want things quickly and not to be drawn by small advantages: 欲速则不达 — want (欲) speed (速) and you will not (不) arrive (达). The reasoning is administrative rather than moral, and it concerns a governor trying to show results early. The claim is causal rather than merely cautionary: the haste is the thing that prevents the arrival. In practice it is used of projects, of learning, and of anybody visibly cutting the stages short.
metaphoric_meaning: Haste makes waste; more haste less speed
description_tr: Confucius, advising a newly appointed magistrate, told him not to want things quickly and not to be drawn by small advantages: 欲速則不達 — want (欲) speed (速) and you will not (不) arrive (達). The reasoning is administrative rather than moral, and it concerns a governor trying to show results early. The claim is causal rather than merely cautionary: the haste is the thing that prevents the arrival. Chinese uses it of projects, of learning, and of anybody visibly cutting the stages short.
chineseExample_tr: 趕工反而導致了更多延誤，真是欲速不達。

example: The company grew through careful, steady expansion.
chineseExample: 公司稳扎稳打，稳步扩张。
description: Pitching camp (扎) firmly (稳) and striking (打) firmly (稳). The doubled 稳 is the whole instruction: both the halting and the advancing are to be done from a secure position, so no ground is taken that could not be held if the next move failed. It is the same thinking as 步步为营 with the emphasis on soundness rather than on pace. In practice it is used of business expansion, of study plans, and of anybody being told, usually kindly, to stop trying to skip ahead.
description_tr: Pitching camp (扎) firmly (穩) and striking (打) firmly (穩). The doubled 穩 is the whole instruction: both the halting and the advancing are to be done from a secure position, so no ground is taken that could not be held if the next move failed. It is the same thinking as 步步為營 with the emphasis on soundness rather than on pace. Chinese uses it of business expansion, of study plans, and of anybody being told, usually kindly, to stop trying to skip ahead.
chineseExample_tr: 公司穩扎穩打，穩步擴張。

example: With such a strong lead, victory seemed certain.
chineseExample: 有了这么大的领先优势，他们稳操胜券。
description: A 券 was a tally — a contract split in two so that each party held half, and holding your half was the proof of your claim. To grip (操) the winning (胜) half securely (稳) is therefore not confidence but documentation: what the phrase asserts is that the outcome has already been established and the remaining play is a formality. Chinese says it of elections, negotiations and matches, and it is a strong claim, which is why it turns up so often in accounts of somebody who turned out to be wrong.
metaphoric_meaning: Have victory in the bag; be certain to win
description_tr: A 券 was a tally — a contract split in two so that each party held half, and holding your half was the proof of your claim. To grip (操) the winning (勝) half securely (穩) is therefore not confidence but documentation: what the phrase asserts is that the outcome has already been established and the remaining play is a formality. Chinese uses it of elections, negotiations and matches, and it is a strong claim, which is why it turns up so often in accounts of somebody who turned out to be wrong.
chineseExample_tr: 有了這麼大的領先優勢，他們穩操勝券。

example: The team felt confident going into the final round.
chineseExample: 球队胜券在握地进入决赛。
description: The winning (胜) tally (券) in (在) the hand (握). Identical in sense to 稳操胜券 and different in construction: this one puts the object first and states where it is, which makes it descriptive where the other is emphatic. Chinese uses them interchangeably, with 胜券在握 slightly commoner in writing about somebody else and 稳操胜券 slightly commoner in claims made on one's own behalf. Both say the result is settled before the event has finished.
metaphoric_meaning: Have victory assured; be confident of winning
description_tr: The winning (勝) tally (券) in (在) the hand (握). Identical in sense to 穩操勝券 and different in construction: this one puts the object first and states where it is, which makes it descriptive where the other is emphatic. Chinese uses them interchangeably, with 勝券在握 slightly commoner in writing about somebody else and 穩操勝券 slightly commoner in claims made on one's own behalf. Both say the result is settled before the event has finished.
chineseExample_tr: 球隊勝券在握地進入決賽。

meaning: Circumstances demand it must be done
example: Digital transformation has become inevitable for the industry.
chineseExample: 数字化转型已势在必行。
description: The momentum (势) is such that (在) the thing must (必) go ahead (行). 势 is the force a situation has already accumulated — the same character as in 势如破竹 — so the argument being made is not that the action is wise but that conditions have removed the alternative to it. That is what makes the phrase useful, and also what makes it convenient: it presents a decision as an observation. Chinese uses it of reforms and of industry shifts, and a careful listener will notice it doing the work of an argument without making one.
description_tr: The momentum (勢) is such that (在) the thing must (必) go ahead (行). 勢 is the force a situation has already accumulated — the same character as in 勢如破竹 — so the argument being made is not that the action is wise but that conditions have removed the alternative to it. That is what makes the phrase useful, and also what makes it convenient: it presents a decision as an observation. Chinese uses it of reforms and of industry shifts, and a careful listener will notice it doing the work of an argument without making one.
chineseExample_tr: 數字化轉型已勢在必行。

example: Their championship team dominated every opponent.
chineseExample: 他们的冠军球队所向披靡。
description: Wherever (所) it is directed (向), everything goes flat (披靡). 披靡 is grass going down before wind, and the metaphor is precise about the kind of victory meant: not enemies beaten one at a time but resistance collapsing along the whole line as the thing arrives. Nothing is said about fighting at all. Chinese says it of armies, of teams on a run and of a product that has taken a market, and the emphasis falls on the absence of any check.
description_tr: Wherever (所) it is directed (向), everything goes flat (披靡). 披靡 is grass going down before wind, and the metaphor is precise about the kind of victory meant: not enemies beaten one at a time but resistance collapsing along the whole line as the thing arrives. Nothing is said about fighting at all. Chinese uses it of armies, of teams on a run and of a product that has taken a market, and the emphasis falls on the absence of any check.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的冠軍球隊所向披靡。

example: At his peak, no competitor could challenge him.
chineseExample: 在巅峰时期，他所向无敌。
description: Wherever (所) it is directed (向), there is no (无) opponent (敌). The difference from 所向披靡 is worth having: that phrase describes opposition being flattened, and this one describes there being none to flatten. The claim concerns the field rather than the fighting — nobody is in a position to make a contest of it. Chinese uses it of a dominant player during a period when the competition has simply not turned up, and it is the stronger and the rarer of the two.
description_tr: Wherever (所) it is directed (向), there is no (無) opponent (敵). The difference from 所向披靡 is worth having: that phrase describes opposition being flattened, and this one describes there being none to flatten. The claim concerns the field rather than the fighting — nobody is in a position to make a contest of it. Chinese uses it of a dominant player during a period when the competition has simply not turned up, and it is the stronger and the rarer of the two.
chineseExample_tr: 在巔峰時期，他所向無敵。

example: The army had never lost a battle.
chineseExample: 这支军队攻无不克。
description: In attacking (攻), there is nothing (无) not (不) taken (克). 克 is to overcome, and specifically to reduce a position, so the phrase concerns assaults rather than wars: every objective attempted was carried. It is normally the first half of a pair, 攻无不克，战无不胜, and using it alone is slightly unusual. Chinese applies it to sales teams and to litigators as readily as to armies, and the boast is about a record with no exceptions anywhere in it.
metaphoric_meaning: Win every battle; never fail in attacks
description_tr: In attacking (攻), there is nothing (無) not (不) taken (克). 克 is to overcome, and specifically to reduce a position, so the phrase concerns assaults rather than wars: every objective attempted was carried. It is normally the first half of a pair, 攻無不克，戰無不勝, and using it alone is slightly unusual. Chinese applies it to sales teams and to litigators as readily as to armies, and the boast is about a record with no exceptions anywhere in it.
chineseExample_tr: 這支軍隊攻無不克。

example: Their legal team has never lost a case.
chineseExample: 他们的法律团队战无不胜。
description: In battle (战), there is nothing (无) not (不) won (胜). The partner phrase to 攻无不克, and the division of labour between them is real: that one covers the taking of objectives and this one the engagements, so together they claim a record with no failure at either scale. The Strategies of the Warring States attaches a warning to the idea — 战无不胜而不知止者身且死, the man who wins every battle and does not know when to stop will die of it — which the modern phrase has dropped.
description_tr: In battle (戰), there is nothing (無) not (不) won (勝). The partner phrase to 攻無不克, and the division of labour between them is real: that one covers the taking of objectives and this one the engagements, so together they claim a record with no failure at either scale. The Strategies of the Warring States attaches a warning to the idea — 戰無不勝而不知止者身且死, the man who wins every battle and does not know when to stop will die of it — which the modern phrase has dropped.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的法律團隊戰無不勝。

example: The new product launch was immediately successful.
chineseExample: 新产品发布旗开得胜。
description: The banners (旗) unfurled (开) and the victory (胜) taken (得). The picture is of an army winning its first engagement of a campaign, on the day the flags come out, so the phrase concerns the beginning rather than the whole. That is what makes it a blessing instead of a report: it is said before something starts, never after. Chinese uses it to send somebody into an examination, a match or a first day, and it wishes for an early win specifically, on the theory that the rest then comes easier.
metaphoric_meaning: Win at the very start; immediate success
description_tr: The banners (旗) unfurled (開) and the victory (勝) taken (得). The picture is of an army winning its first engagement of a campaign, on the day the flags come out, so the phrase concerns the beginning rather than the whole. That is what makes it a blessing instead of a report: it is said before something starts, never after. Chinese uses it to send somebody into an examination, a match or a first day, and it wishes for an early win specifically, on the theory that the rest then comes easier.
chineseExample_tr: 新產品發布旗開得勝。

example: His rapid promotion took everyone by surprise.
chineseExample: 他的快速晋升让所有人惊讶，简直平步青云。
description: Walking on the level (平步) straight up into the blue (青) clouds (云). The image is of somebody climbing without the climb — the ground stays flat underfoot and the height arrives anyway — which is what makes the phrase pointed rather than simply admiring. 青云 has meant high office in Chinese since antiquity. It is used of a fast promotion, and whether it is a compliment depends entirely on the speaker, since the same four characters cover a deserved rise and one nobody can account for.
description_tr: Walking on the level (平步) straight up into the blue (青) clouds (雲). The image is of somebody climbing without the climb — the ground stays flat underfoot and the height arrives anyway — which is what makes the phrase pointed rather than simply admiring. 青雲 has meant high office in Chinese since antiquity. It is used of a fast promotion, and whether it is a compliment depends entirely on the speaker, since the same four characters cover a deserved rise and one nobody can account for.
chineseExample_tr: 他的快速晉升讓所有人驚訝，簡直平步青雲。

example: She rose from humble beginnings to great success.
chineseExample: 她从贫寒起步飞黄腾达。
description: 飞黄 is a legendary horse, and 腾达 is its rising and getting away — Han Yu uses the image in a poem urging his son to study, the fast horse going up and off while the toad on the ground is not even looked at. The comparison is the unkind part and it survives in the phrase's tone. It attaches to somebody whose career has taken off, usually said by people who have stayed where they were, and it carries a faint edge that 平步青云 does not quite have.
metaphoric_meaning: Rise to fame and fortune rapidly
description_tr: 飛黃 is a legendary horse, and 騰達 is its rising and getting away — Han Yu uses the image in a poem urging his son to study, the fast horse going up and off while the toad on the ground is not even looked at. The comparison is the unkind part and it survives in the phrase's tone. Chinese uses it of somebody whose career has taken off, usually said by people who have stayed where they were, and it carries a faint edge that 平步青雲 does not quite have.
chineseExample_tr: 她從貧寒起步飛黃騰達。

example: Stock prices soared after the announcement.
chineseExample: 公告后股价扶摇直上。
description: 扶摇 is a whirlwind that spirals upward, and the Zhuangzi has the vast Peng bird beating along it to ninety thousand li: 抟扶摇而上者九万里. To go straight (直) up (上) on it is therefore not to climb but to be carried, and the wind is doing the work. That is the picture Chinese keeps. It is used of share prices, of reputations and of careers, and the implication is of a rise too fast and too smooth to have been walked.
description_tr: 扶搖 is a whirlwind that spirals upward, and the Zhuangzi has the vast Peng bird beating along it to ninety thousand li: 摶扶搖而上者九萬里. To go straight (直) up (上) on it is therefore not to climb but to be carried, and the wind is doing the work. That is the picture Chinese keeps. It is used of share prices, of reputations and of careers, and the implication is of a rise too fast and too smooth to have been walked.
chineseExample_tr: 公告後股價扶搖直上。

example: Her talent propelled her rapidly through the ranks.
chineseExample: 她的才华让她青云直上。
description: Straight (直) up (上) into the blue (青) clouds (云). 青云 is high office, and the difference from 平步青云 lies in which part is emphasised: that phrase notes the absence of effort, and this one the absence of detours. What is claimed here is a line — no sideways moves, no waiting, nothing that had to be gone around. In practice it is used of a career that went where it was aimed, and it is more straightforwardly admiring than its neighbour.
description_tr: Straight (直) up (上) into the blue (青) clouds (雲). 青雲 is high office, and the difference from 平步青雲 lies in which part is emphasised: that phrase notes the absence of effort, and this one the absence of detours. What is claimed here is a line — no sideways moves, no waiting, nothing that had to be gone around. Chinese uses it of a career that went where it was aimed, and it is more straightforwardly admiring than its neighbour.
chineseExample_tr: 她的才華讓她青雲直上。

example: May your career continue to advance steadily.
chineseExample: 祝你事业步步高升。
description: Step (步) by step (步) rising (升) higher (高). The doubling of 步 is the whole distinction: every other phrase in this family describes a rise that skipped something, and this one insists the stages were all taken. That makes it the safe thing to say, which is why it is a blessing rather than a description. Chinese puts it on new year couplets and says it to somebody starting a job, and it wishes for advancement without any of the suggestion of luck the faster phrases carry.
description_tr: Step (步) by step (步) rising (升) higher (高). The doubling of 步 is the whole distinction: every other phrase in this family describes a rise that skipped something, and this one insists the stages were all taken. That makes it the safe thing to say, which is why it is a blessing rather than a description. Chinese puts it on new year couplets and says it to somebody starting a job, and it wishes for advancement without any of the suggestion of luck the faster phrases carry.
chineseExample_tr: 祝你事業步步高升。

example: The bestselling author achieved both recognition and wealth.
chineseExample: 畅销作家名利双收。
description: Reputation (名) and profit (利), both (双) collected (收). The two are treated in Chinese as the standard pair of worldly rewards and as ordinarily in tension — the scholar who has one is assumed to have given up the other — so the claim in 双 is that somebody got round the trade-off. That is why the phrase is used with a trace of envy. Chinese applies it to an artist whose serious work also sold, and to anybody whose success was admired and paid for at the same time.
description_tr: Reputation (名) and profit (利), both (雙) collected (收). The two are treated in Chinese as the standard pair of worldly rewards and as ordinarily in tension — the scholar who has one is assumed to have given up the other — so the claim in 雙 is that somebody got round the trade-off. That is why the phrase is used with a trace of envy. Chinese applies it to an artist whose serious work also sold, and to anybody whose success was admired and paid for at the same time.
chineseExample_tr: 暢銷作家名利雙收。

example: After decades of work, he finally achieved recognition.
chineseExample: 经过数十年的努力，他终于功成名就。
description: The work (功) completed (成) and the name (名) established (就). Both halves are achievements and the order is causal: the reputation follows the accomplishment rather than accompanying it. That is what makes the phrase retrospective. It describes a career that is finished rather than one going well, which is why Chinese uses it of people at the end of things — and why saying it of somebody still working can sound like a suggestion that they stop.
description_tr: The work (功) completed (成) and the name (名) established (就). Both halves are achievements and the order is causal: the reputation follows the accomplishment rather than accompanying it. That is what makes the phrase retrospective. It describes a career that is finished rather than one going well, which is why Chinese uses it of people at the end of things — and why saying it of somebody still working can sound like a suggestion that they stop.
chineseExample_tr: 經過數十年的努力，他終於功成名就。

example: After completing his mission, he quietly stepped aside.
chineseExample: 完成使命后，他功成身退。
description: The Dao De Jing states it as a natural law rather than as advice: 功遂身退，天之道 — the work (功) done (成), the person (身) withdraws (退), and this is the way of heaven. The argument is that staying on after the thing is finished is what destroys the people who do it, and the classic case is the general who wins the war and is then killed by the king he won it for. Chinese reserves it for graceful exits, and there is always a faint sense that the alternative was worse than obscurity.
description_tr: The Dao De Jing states it as a natural law rather than as advice: 功遂身退，天之道 — the work (功) done (成), the person (身) withdraws (退), and this is the way of heaven. The argument is that staying on after the thing is finished is what destroys the people who do it, and the classic case is the general who wins the war and is then killed by the king he won it for. Chinese uses it of graceful exits, and there is always a faint sense that the alternative was worse than obscurity.
chineseExample_tr: 完成使命後，他功成身退。

example: He wisely left the company at the height of success.
chineseExample: 他明智地在事业巅峰急流勇退。
description: To pull out (退) bravely (勇) while the current (流) is still running fast (急). The image is a boatman who turns for the bank at the point where everything is going well, and 勇 is the load-bearing character — the phrase insists that leaving takes more nerve than staying. That is the whole argument. Chinese says it of somebody who retired at the top, sold before the peak, or stood down while they were still being asked to stay, and it is unmixed admiration.
metaphoric_meaning: Retire at the peak; know when to quit
description_tr: To pull out (退) bravely (勇) while the current (流) is still running fast (急). The image is a boatman who turns for the bank at the point where everything is going well, and 勇 is the load-bearing character — the phrase insists that leaving takes more nerve than staying. That is the whole argument. Chinese uses it of somebody who retired at the top, sold before the peak, or stood down while they were still being asked to stay, and it is unmixed admiration.
chineseExample_tr: 他明智地在事業巔峰急流勇退。

example: Knowing when to take profits is key in investing.
chineseExample: 在投资中，见好就收是关键。
description: Seeing (见) that it is good (好) and then (就) taking it in (收). The advice is about stopping, and specifically about stopping while the stopping is voluntary, which is a narrower window than it sounds. 收 is to gather in, the same character used of a harvest. Chinese says it of gambling, of negotiation and of arguments that have been won, and it is what one friend says to another who is about to press an advantage one step too far.
description_tr: Seeing (見) that it is good (好) and then (就) taking it in (收). The advice is about stopping, and specifically about stopping while the stopping is voluntary, which is a narrower window than it sounds. 收 is to gather in, the same character used of a harvest. Chinese uses it of gambling, of negotiation and of arguments that have been won, and it is what one friend says to another who is about to press an advantage one step too far.
chineseExample_tr: 在投資中，見好就收是關鍵。

example: Moderation in all things is the path to balance.
chineseExample: 凡事适可而止才能保持平衡。
description: Reaching what will do (适可) and then (而) halting (止). 适可 is the point of sufficiency — enough for the purpose, not the maximum available — so the phrase names a threshold rather than a limit. What it asks for is the recognition that the point has been reached, which is the difficult part. Chinese reserves it for eating, drinking, spending, joking and criticising, and it is the standard thing said to somebody who is still going after the effect has been achieved.
metaphoric_meaning: Stop at the right point; practice moderation
description_tr: Reaching what will do (適可) and then (而) halting (止). 適可 is the point of sufficiency — enough for the purpose, not the maximum available — so the phrase names a threshold rather than a limit. What it asks for is the recognition that the point has been reached, which is the difficult part. Chinese uses it of eating, drinking, spending, joking and criticising, and it is the standard thing said to somebody who is still going after the effect has been achieved.
chineseExample_tr: 凡事適可而止才能保持平衡。

example: The police set up a dragnet to catch the fugitives.
chineseExample: 警方布下天罗地网抓捕逃犯。
description: A net (罗) over heaven (天) and a net (网) across earth (地). Two different words for a net are used, one for catching birds and one for fish, so the pair covers the air and the ground and the phrase leaves no medium unaccounted for. That completeness is the claim. It is said of manhunts and surveillance, and it belongs to the perspective of whoever set the nets — a fugitive is caught in one, never described as having laid it.
description_tr: A net (羅) over heaven (天) and a net (網) across earth (地). Two different words for a net are used, one for catching birds and one for fish, so the pair covers the air and the ground and the phrase leaves no medium unaccounted for. That completeness is the claim. Chinese uses it of manhunts and surveillance, and it belongs to the perspective of whoever set the nets — a fugitive is caught in one, never described as having laid it.
chineseExample_tr: 警方布下天羅地網抓捕逃犯。

example: Security was so tight that nothing could get through.
chineseExample: 安保密不透风。
description: So close-packed (密) that no (不) wind (风) gets through (透). Air is the test, as water is in 滴水不漏, and it is the more demanding of the two. The phrase covers physical crowding and, far more often, information: a secret 密不透风 is one that nothing has leaked from. Chinese uses it of security arrangements and of families who have kept something quiet for years, and it can carry a note of unease at how well it was done.
description_tr: So close-packed (密) that no (不) wind (風) gets through (透). Air is the test, as water is in 滴水不漏, and it is the more demanding of the two. The phrase covers physical crowding and, far more often, information: a secret 密不透風 is one that nothing has leaked from. Chinese uses it of security arrangements and of families who have kept something quiet for years, and it can carry a note of unease at how well it was done.
chineseExample_tr: 安保密不透風。

example: The plan was designed to be absolutely foolproof.
chineseExample: 计划设计得万无一失。
description: Ten thousand (万) and not (无) one (一) miss (失). 万 is the standard Chinese figure for an uncountable number rather than a literal count, so what the phrase claims is a rate rather than a record. That makes it a statement about design: the thing has been arranged so that failure has no route in. In practice it is used of preparations and of plans, and very often in the negative or under pressure — 万无一失 is what a superior demands rather than what an engineer volunteers.
description_tr: Ten thousand (萬) and not (無) one (一) miss (失). 萬 is the standard Chinese figure for an uncountable number rather than a literal count, so what the phrase claims is a rate rather than a record. That makes it a statement about design: the thing has been arranged so that failure has no route in. Chinese uses it of preparations and of plans, and very often in the negative or under pressure — 萬無一失 is what a superior demands rather than what an engineer volunteers.
chineseExample_tr: 計劃設計得萬無一失。

meaning: Moving blade with room to spare
example: The experienced chef handled the busy kitchen effortlessly.
chineseExample: 经验丰富的厨师在繁忙的厨房游刃有余。
description: Cook Ding in the Zhuangzi explains that his blade goes where the joints are already open, and that in a gap of that kind there is 恢恢乎其于游刃必有余地 — ample room for the moving (游) blade (刃) with something left over (有余). The claim is not that the work is easy but that the tool is smaller than the space it is working in. That margin is what the phrase names, and Chinese says it of somebody whose capacity clearly exceeds what the job is asking of them.
metaphoric_meaning: Handle with ease; have skill to spare
description_tr: Cook Ding in the Zhuangzi explains that his blade goes where the joints are already open, and that in a gap of that kind there is 恢恢乎其於遊刃必有餘地 — ample room for the moving (遊) blade (刃) with something left over (有餘). The claim is not that the work is easy but that the tool is smaller than the space it is working in. That margin is what the phrase names, and Chinese uses it of somebody whose capacity clearly exceeds what the job is asking of them.
chineseExample_tr: 經驗豐富的廚師在繁忙的廚房游刃有餘。

example: Having done this many times, the process was easy for him.
chineseExample: 做过很多次后，这个过程对他来说轻车熟路。
description: A light (轻) carriage (车) on a familiar (熟) road (路). Both halves reduce the same thing, effort: nothing heavy to pull and nothing about the route to work out. The pairing descends from a line of Han Yu's, and its point is that ease of this kind is not a property of the task but of the relationship between the task and the person. It gets used of work somebody has done many times, and it is usually offered as a reassurance — 轻车熟路, you have done this before.
metaphoric_meaning: Be experienced; find something easy due to familiarity
description_tr: A light (輕) carriage (車) on a familiar (熟) road (路). Both halves reduce the same thing, effort: nothing heavy to pull and nothing about the route to work out. The pairing descends from a line of Han Yu's, and its point is that ease of this kind is not a property of the task but of the relationship between the task and the person. Chinese uses it of work somebody has done many times, and it is usually offered as a reassurance — 輕車熟路, you have done this before.
chineseExample_tr: 做過很多次後，這個過程對他來說輕車熟路。

example: After years of practice, playing the piano came naturally.
chineseExample: 经过多年练习，弹钢琴已驾轻就熟。
description: Han Yu, recommending a scholar for office, wrote that he handled affairs 若驷马驾轻车就熟路 — like four horses driving (驾) a light (轻) carriage onto (就) a familiar (熟) road. Both this phrase and 轻车熟路 come out of that one line, and they differ in what they foreground: the other names the conditions, and this one names the driving. It attaches to somebody taking on a task that is squarely within what they have done before, and it is a claim about the person rather than about the road.
metaphoric_meaning: Be very familiar with; handle with expertise
description_tr: Han Yu, recommending a scholar for office, wrote that he handled affairs 若駟馬駕輕車就熟路 — like four horses driving (駕) a light (輕) carriage onto (就) a familiar (熟) road. Both this phrase and 輕車熟路 come out of that one line, and they differ in what they foreground: the other names the conditions, and this one names the driving. Chinese uses it of somebody taking on a task that is squarely within what they have done before, and it is a claim about the person rather than about the road.
chineseExample_tr: 經過多年練習，彈鋼琴已駕輕就熟。

example: The artist's brush moved exactly as she imagined.
chineseExample: 艺术家运笔得心应手。
description: The Zhuangzi's wheelwright says of his craft that he gets it in the hand and answers to it in the heart — 得之于手而应于心 — and that this is exactly what he cannot explain to his son. The idiom reverses the order, obtaining (得) in the heart (心) and answering (应) in the hand (手), which puts the intention first and makes it a claim about control. You will hear it of tools, instruments and languages, and what it describes is the point at which the thing stops being operated and starts being used.
metaphoric_meaning: Work with great ease; have complete mastery
description_tr: The Zhuangzi's wheelwright says of his craft that he gets it in the hand and answers to it in the heart — 得之於手而應於心 — and that this is exactly what he cannot explain to his son. The idiom reverses the order, obtaining (得) in the heart (心) and answering (應) in the hand (手), which puts the intention first and makes it a claim about control. Chinese uses it of tools, instruments and languages, and what it describes is the point at which the thing stops being operated and starts being used.
chineseExample_tr: 藝術家運筆得心應手。

example: His magic tricks have reached an almost supernatural level.
chineseExample: 他的魔术已经出神入化。
description: Out of (出) the spirit-like (神) and into (入) the transformative (化). Both halves name levels beyond ordinary competence, and stacking them is the device — the phrase spends its second half going past where the first half had already stopped. Chinese reserves it for performance: acting, calligraphy, martial arts, a musician's playing. It is the strongest praise in this family and it should be used as sparingly as it claims, since it asserts that the skill has left the category of skill.
description_tr: Out of (出) the spirit-like (神) and into (入) the transformative (化). Both halves name levels beyond ordinary competence, and stacking them is the device — the phrase spends its second half going past where the first half had already stopped. Chinese reserves it for performance: acting, calligraphy, martial arts, a musician's playing. It is the strongest praise in this family and it should be used as sparingly as it claims, since it asserts that the skill has left the category of skill.
chineseExample_tr: 他的魔術已經出神入化。

example: She ranked first in the national examination.
chineseExample: 她在全国考试中独占鳌头。
description: The stone steps of the palace hall were carved with a great sea-turtle (鳌), and the candidate who had come first in the examinations stood on its head (头) to receive the announcement — alone (独), by definition, occupying (占) that spot. The phrase preserves a piece of imperial ceremony that has been gone for a century. It gets used of first place in anything competitive, and it keeps a formality that plainer words for winning do not have.
description_tr: The stone steps of the palace hall were carved with a great sea-turtle (鰲), and the candidate who had come first in the examinations stood on its head (頭) to receive the announcement — alone (獨), by definition, occupying (佔) that spot. The phrase preserves a piece of imperial ceremony that has been gone for a century. Chinese uses it of first place in anything competitive, and it keeps a formality that plainer words for winning do not have.
chineseExample_tr: 她在全國考試中獨佔鰲頭。

example: His unique artistic style set him apart from all others.
chineseExample: 他独特的艺术风格独树一帜。
description: To plant (树) a banner (帜) of one's own (独一). 树 is the verb, to set up, and a banner in this context is what a faction or a school gathers under — so what is described is not merely being different but declaring a position and inviting others to it. That is a stronger claim than distinctiveness. Chinese uses it of artists and of schools of thought, and it implies the person did not merely depart from the orthodoxy but proposed something to replace it.
description_tr: To plant (樹) a banner (幟) of one's own (獨一). 樹 is the verb, to set up, and a banner in this context is what a faction or a school gathers under — so what is described is not merely being different but declaring a position and inviting others to it. That is a stronger claim than distinctiveness. Chinese uses it of artists and of schools of thought, and it implies the person did not merely depart from the orthodoxy but proposed something to replace it.
chineseExample_tr: 他獨特的藝術風格獨樹一幟。

example: The restaurant offers a distinctive dining experience.
chineseExample: 这家餐厅提供别具一格的用餐体验。
description: Possessing (具) a style (格) apart (别一). 格 is a frame or standard, the thing by which work of a kind is judged, so what is claimed is that the object does not sit inside the usual frame at all. It is milder than 独树一帜: nothing is being declared and no following is implied, only that this one is not like the others. It is said of buildings, of restaurants and of writing, and it is a compliment safe enough to pay to almost anything.
description_tr: Possessing (具) a style (格) apart (別一). 格 is a frame or standard, the thing by which work of a kind is judged, so what is claimed is that the object does not sit inside the usual frame at all. It is milder than 獨樹一幟: nothing is being declared and no following is implied, only that this one is not like the others. Chinese uses it of buildings, of restaurants and of writing, and it is a compliment safe enough to pay to almost anything.
chineseExample_tr: 這家餐廳提供別具一格的用餐體驗。

example: The architect's design showed remarkable ingenuity.
chineseExample: 建筑师的设计独具匠心。
description: To have (具) a craftsman's (匠) mind (心) that nobody else has (独). 匠心 is the artisan's conception — the design as it exists before the work is made — so the phrase locates the originality in the thinking rather than in the execution, and 独 insists nobody else arrived at it. Chinese uses it of design, of staging and of anything constructed, and it is stronger praise than it looks: it claims the idea, not merely the finish.
metaphoric_meaning: Show great ingenuity; have original design
description_tr: To have (具) a craftsman's (匠) mind (心) that nobody else has (獨). 匠心 is the artisan's conception — the design as it exists before the work is made — so the phrase locates the originality in the thinking rather than in the execution, and 獨 insists nobody else arrived at it. Chinese uses it of design, of staging and of anything constructed, and it is stronger praise than it looks: it claims the idea, not merely the finish.
chineseExample_tr: 建築師的設計獨具匠心。

example: The film director's creative vision produced a masterpiece.
chineseExample: 电影导演匠心独运，创作出一部杰作。
description: The craftsman's conception (匠心) applied (运) as nobody else would (独). The characters are those of 独具匠心 rearranged, and the difference is between having the idea and working it out — 运 is to move or operate, so this phrase covers the execution the other one stops short of. Chinese uses them almost interchangeably, with this form appearing more often in criticism of a finished thing, where the evidence of the conception is visible in what was made.
description_tr: The craftsman's conception (匠心) applied (運) as nobody else would (獨). The characters are those of 獨具匠心 rearranged, and the difference is between having the idea and working it out — 運 is to move or operate, so this phrase covers the execution the other one stops short of. Chinese uses them almost interchangeably, with this form appearing more often in criticism of a finished thing, where the evidence of the conception is visible in what was made.
chineseExample_tr: 電影導演匠心獨運，創作出一部傑作。

example: This quiet neighborhood is full of hidden talent — a true case of crouching tiger, hidden dragon.
chineseExample: 江湖里卧虎藏龙，人心里何尝不是？
description: Yu Xin of the Northern Zhou wrote 暗石疑藏虎，盘根似卧龙 — dark stones seem to hide tigers, gnarled roots resemble a reclining dragon — and the halves were later compressed into one phrase: a crouching (卧) tiger (虎), a hidden (藏) dragon (龙). It names a place where formidable people are present and unrecognised, which is how Zhuge Liang is remembered before Liu Bei found him living on Wolong Hill. Ang Lee's 2000 film took the title, and the pun is in the names: Yu Jiaolong (玉娇龙) carries the dragon and Lo Xiaohu (罗小虎) the tiger. Chinese reserves it for an organisation or a small town whose people turn out to be far more capable than the surface suggests.
metaphoric_meaning: Hidden talents or extraordinary people in an unassuming place
description_tr: Yu Xin of the Northern Zhou wrote 暗石疑藏虎，盤根似臥龍 — dark stones seem to hide tigers, gnarled roots resemble a reclining dragon — and the halves were later compressed into one phrase: a crouching (臥) tiger (虎), a hidden (藏) dragon (龍). It names a place where formidable people are present and unrecognised, which is how Zhuge Liang is remembered before Liu Bei found him living on Wolong Hill. Ang Lee's 2000 film took the title, and the pun is in the names: Yu Jiaolong (玉嬌龍) carries the dragon and Lo Xiaohu (羅小虎) the tiger. Chinese uses it of an organisation or a small town whose people turn out to be far more capable than the surface suggests.
chineseExample_tr: 江湖裡臥虎藏龍，人心裡何嘗不是？

meaning: A sincere heart achieves the divine
example: She believed that if she studied with genuine dedication, results would follow — a sincere heart achieves the divine.
chineseExample: 真心的，就会实现。我问过汉人，他们说是——心诚则灵。
description: The heart (心) being sincere (诚), the thing then (则) answers (灵). 灵 is the word used of a prayer that is heard, an oracle that proves true, a remedy that works — efficacy of the kind you cannot engineer, only deserve. That is why the phrase belongs to temples and to wishes rather than to argument: it is what is said to someone worrying whether they have performed a rite correctly, and the answer it gives is that the intention is the operative part and the procedure is not. Ang Lee put it in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, where Lo tells Jen a desert legend and adds 心诚则灵 — if the wish is truly meant, it comes true. Modern use has carried it well beyond religion, into anything where wholehearted commitment is being offered as the thing that decides the outcome.
metaphoric_meaning: Genuine sincerity brings results; a faithful heart makes wishes come true
description_tr: The heart (心) being sincere (誠), the thing then (則) answers (靈). 靈 is the word used of a prayer that is heard, an oracle that proves true, a remedy that works — efficacy of the kind you cannot engineer, only deserve. That is why the phrase belongs to temples and to wishes rather than to argument: it is what is said to someone worrying whether they have performed a rite correctly, and the answer it gives is that the intention is the operative part and the procedure is not. Ang Lee put it in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, where Lo tells Jen a desert legend and adds 心誠則靈 — if the wish is truly meant, it comes true. Modern use has carried it well beyond religion, into anything where wholehearted commitment is being offered as the thing that decides the outcome.
chineseExample_tr: 真心的，就會實現。我問過漢人，他們說是——心誠則靈。

example: With unwavering determination, she completed her marathon training despite the challenges.
chineseExample: 她在面对挑战时，持之以恒地完成了马拉松训练。
description: This is advice rather than a story: hold to it (持之) with constancy (以恒). Zeng Guofan, the Qing official whose family letters became one of the most-read Chinese manuals of self-discipline, returned to the idea continually — that character is built out of small things done without a break, and that the enemy of it is not difficulty but interruption. The phrase carries none of the drama of 悬梁刺股 or 闻鸡起舞, and that is rather the point: it names the unremarkable daily version of persistence, and it is what a Chinese teacher says about the student who is not brilliant but never stops.
description_tr: This is advice rather than a story: hold to it (持之) with constancy (以恆). Zeng Guofan, the Qing official whose family letters became one of the most-read Chinese manuals of self-discipline, returned to the idea continually — that character is built out of small things done without a break, and that the enemy of it is not difficulty but interruption. The phrase carries none of the drama of 懸樑刺股 or 聞雞起舞, and that is rather the point: it names the unremarkable daily version of persistence, and it is what a Chinese teacher says about the student who is not brilliant but never stops.
chineseExample_tr: 她在面對挑戰時，持之以恆地完成了馬拉松訓練。

example: His relentless pursuit of knowledge exemplifies the spirit of never giving up.
chineseExample: 他对知识的追求体现了坚持不懈的精神。
description: A plain compound — hold firm (坚持) without slackening (不懈) — of the kind Chinese assembles freely, and it earns its keep by being the ordinary word for the thing rather than a literary flourish. The useful contrast is with 持之以恒, which concerns continuing across long stretches of time; this one concerns not loosening your grip under pressure. One is endurance, the other resistance. It belongs to encouragement and to school reports, and nobody would call it elegant.
description_tr: A plain compound — hold firm (堅持) without slackening (不懈) — of the kind Chinese assembles freely, and it earns its keep by being the ordinary word for the thing rather than a literary flourish. The useful contrast is with 持之以恆, which concerns continuing across long stretches of time; this one concerns not loosening your grip under pressure. One is endurance, the other resistance. It belongs to encouragement and to school reports, and nobody would call it elegant.
chineseExample_tr: 他對知識的追求體現了堅持不懈的精神。

example: Her strategic planning ensured that her team won every competition they entered.
chineseExample: 她的战略规划确保了她的团队百战百胜。
description: The Guanzi has it first, but the line everyone quotes is Sun Tzu's, and there it is a warning rather than a compliment: to win a hundred victories (百胜) in a hundred battles (百战) is not the highest skill — the highest skill is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting at all. Read in context the phrase is a foil, naming the good outcome that a better strategist would not have needed in the first place. Ordinary use has lost the irony completely and takes it as straightforward praise for someone who wins everything, which is worth knowing if you ever meet it in the original.
description_tr: The Guanzi has it first, but the line everyone quotes is Sun Tzu's, and there it is a warning rather than a compliment: to win a hundred victories (百勝) in a hundred battles (百戰) is not the highest skill — the highest skill is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting at all. Read in context the phrase is a foil, naming the good outcome that a better strategist would not have needed in the first place. Ordinary use has lost the irony completely and takes it as straightforward praise for someone who wins everything, which is worth knowing if you ever meet it in the original.

example: Despite the obstacles, she bravely forged ahead with her plans for the new business.
chineseExample: 尽管有障碍，她勇往直前地推进新业务的计划。
description: Four characters doing exactly what they say: brave (勇), going (往), straight (直), forward (前). The phrase is built from the plainest available parts, and its force comes from the complete absence of sideways motion in it. What it rules out is not fear but hesitation and detour. It belongs to exhortation: coaches, commanders, graduation speeches, and the sort of encouragement offered to someone who has already decided and is casting about for a reason not to.

example: His determination to improve his skills reflects the spirit of striving for strength.
chineseExample: 他对提升技能的决心体现了奋发图强的精神。
description: This is a modern phrase in classical dress. Rouse oneself (奋发) and work toward strength (图强) reads like something out of the classics, but it belongs to the late Qing and after, when Chinese writers were arguing about how a weakened country recovers itself. That history still colours it. The phrase sits more naturally on nations, institutions and whole generations than on individuals, and it carries a note of catching up rather than simply doing well — used of a person, it tends to imply they are starting from behind.

example: He wisely chose to step back when the challenges became overwhelming
chineseExample: 当困难变得无法承受时，他明智地选择了退缩
description: The Zuo Zhuan records the Jin commanders arguing before an engagement with Chu: Chu had already made peace with Zheng, its army was in good order, and the case for withdrawing was that a fight now had nothing left to win. Those who insisted on pressing forward were beaten. In its original setting the phrase is praise for judgement — knowing (知) the difficulty (难) and pulling back (退) is what a competent commander does. Modern use has drifted, and it now often carries a sting: said of somebody else, it usually means they gave up when things got hard.

example: After years of hard work, his project achieved a perfect conclusion
chineseExample: 经过多年的努力，他的项目功德圆满
description: The expression came out of Buddhist practice, where the merit (功德) accumulated through a rite — sutras chanted, offerings made, a service carried to its proper end — is described as complete and round (圆满). 圆 is doing real work there: not merely finished but closed, with nothing left ragged. Secular Chinese borrowed the expression whole and now applies it to any undertaking brought to a clean end, a conference that ran its course, a project delivered. It keeps a faint ceremonial warmth, which is why it turns up in closing remarks far more often than in the middle of anything.

example: She worked tirelessly, never pausing in her pursuit of excellence
chineseExample: 她不知疲倦地工作，马不停蹄地追求卓越
description: A horse (马) whose hooves (蹄) never stop (不停) — the image is a mount ridden straight through without being allowed to rest, the way couriers rode. It describes a pace rather than an achievement, and unlike most perseverance idioms it carries no praise whatever: it is equally at home in a complaint. Somebody who tells you they have been 马不停蹄 all week is reporting exhaustion, not advertising their work ethic.

example: He threw himself into the project, caring little for his own safety
chineseExample: 他奋不顾身地投入到项目中，几乎不顾自己的安全
description: Sima Qian's letter to Ren An looks back on what he had said at court years before in defence of Li Ling — the general who took a small force deep into Xiongnu territory, fought until his arrows ran out, and surrendered. Li Ling, he had argued, threw himself forward (奋) with no thought (不顾) for his own body (身). Emperor Wu heard the defence as an attack on his brother-in-law's command, and Sima Qian was castrated for it; the letter is written from the far side of that, explaining why he chose to live and finish the history. The phrase carries its price inside it. It is used of firefighters, of soldiers, of anyone who moves toward danger rather than away from it, and it is unqualified praise in a way few Chinese idioms are.

example: In the face of adversity, she chose to confront the challenges head-on
chineseExample: 面对困难，她选择迎难而上
description: To meet (迎) the difficulty (难) and go up (上) into it. It belongs to the vocabulary of official encouragement — work reports, campaign slogans, school assemblies. What distinguishes it from ordinary perseverance is direction: 迎 is movement toward the thing, so the phrase describes choosing the harder route while an easier one is available. Its natural opposite is 知难而退, and Chinese sets the two against each other constantly.

example: We should learn from previous failures to avoid repeating them.
chineseExample: 前车之鉴，提醒我们在做决策时要谨慎。
description: The full image is a cart that has gone over in the road ahead: 前车覆，后车戒 — the cart in front overturns, the cart behind takes warning. The Book of Han preserves it in Jia Yi's memorial urging the young Han emperor to study why the Qin had collapsed so quickly, which gives the phrase its particular flavour. The lesson on offer is not drawn from your own failure but from watching somebody else's, early enough to steer. 鉴 is a bronze mirror, so what the wreck provides is a reflection. It is used wherever a predecessor's mistake is available and about to be repeated.

meaning: Have a beginning and an end
example: He approached the project with commitment, ensuring it was completed successfully.
chineseExample: 有始有终，才能把事情做好。
description: A plain statement of a virtue: there is (有) a beginning (始) and there is an end (终). Its weight comes instead from its opposites, which Chinese has in abundance: 有头无尾, a head with no tail; 虎头蛇尾, a tiger's head on a snake's tail; 半途而废, abandoned at the halfway point. Against that company, finishing is treated as the harder and rarer half of any undertaking. It is applied to people rather than to projects, as a judgement on character, and it is among the plainest compliments in the language.

example: He took the initiative to spearhead the project, inspiring his team.
chineseExample: 在比赛中，他一马当先，带领队伍取得胜利。
description: One horse (一马) out in front (当先) — the picture is a cavalry charge, with the leader's mount ahead of the line rather than safe inside it. It belongs to the stock of military language that Chinese fiction and drama drew on freely. What separates it from merely leading is position: the person is at the point of risk, first into whatever it is, setting the pace by taking it themselves. It suits a company entering a market before anyone else and the colleague who volunteers before the room has finished reading the request.

example: The invention of the internet opened up a whole new world of possibilities.
chineseExample: 他的研究开天辟地，改变了整个行业。
description: This is the creation itself: Pangu, the giant of Chinese myth, splitting the undifferentiated mass apart so that sky (天) opened (开) above and earth (地) was cleft (辟) below. Because it names the first event of all, the phrase sets an extremely high bar — it is not for something merely new but for something with no precedent whatever, the first of its kind rather than the best of it. Chinese speakers use it sparingly for that reason, and applying it to an ordinary product launch sounds as inflated in Chinese as the equivalent would in English.

example: With a clear vision, she set her sights on achieving greatness beyond her hometown.
chineseExample: 她志在四方，立志要在更广阔的舞台上展现自己。
description: Chong'er, the exiled prince of Jin, had settled comfortably in Qi and shown no further interest in leaving. The Zuo Zhuan gives the reproach to his wife Jiang, who told him that a man's ambition (志) lies (在) in the four directions (四方) — and then had him carried out of the state while drunk, so that he could not refuse. He went on to become one of the great hegemons. The phrase keeps that edge. It is generally said to somebody who is settling for a small life within easy reach, and it means go, not merely aspire.

example: The community came together to provide strong support for the new initiative.
chineseExample: 社区鼎力相助，支持这个新的倡议。
description: A 鼎 is a bronze ritual tripod, heavy enough that lifting one is the standard Chinese image of enormous strength; 鼎力 borrows that weight for the help being described. The important thing is who may say it. Together with 相助, mutual (相) help (助), the phrase is honorific toward the helper, so it is used of what someone else did for you, or when asking them for help — never of assistance you provided yourself. Claiming it for your own efforts applies to yourself a word reserved for praising others, and it lands badly. It belongs to formal thanks, letters and speeches rather than to casual conversation.

example: With consistent effort, he managed to achieve his goals, just like a rope saw gradually cuts through wood.
chineseExample: 他绳锯木断，经过不懈努力终于实现了目标。
description: The Song collection Helin Yulu tells of Zhang Guaiya, a magistrate who spotted a single copper coin from the treasury tucked under a clerk's headcloth and ordered him flogged. The clerk rounded on him — one coin is nothing, you may flog me but you cannot behead me — and Zhang took up his brush and wrote the judgment: a coin a day is a thousand coins in a thousand days, 绳锯木断，水滴石穿 — a rope used as a saw cuts wood through, dripping water bores stone through. He was arguing about corruption, not diligence. The phrase survived detached from the harshness of the story and now describes soft, repeated effort defeating something far harder than itself.

example: By planning ahead, she ensured that potential problems would not derail her project.
chineseExample: 有备无患的原则让她的计划顺利进行。
description: The Book of Documents states it flatly: attend to your affairs, and in preparation there is no calamity — have the preparation (有备) and you are without trouble (无患). It is the last clause of the chain quoted in the Zuo Zhuan as 居安思危，思则有备，有备无患, where Wei Jiang tells the ruler of Jin that peace is exactly when danger should be considered, since prosperity rather than crisis is what stops people looking. The phrase is not about anxiety. It is about doing the work while it is still cheap, and it is what Chinese says over insurance and fire drills.

example: His celebration turned into a tragedy when he received the bad news.
chineseExample: 他的庆祝活动在收到坏消息后变成了悲剧。
description: Chunyu Kun, who served King Wei of Qi and knew better than to lecture him directly, was asked how much he could drink. It depended, he said, and worked through the settings — under the king's eye a bottle, among close friends far more — until he arrived at the point: wine at its limit brings disorder, joy (乐) at its extreme (极) produces (生) grief (悲). The king, who was known for all-night drinking, took the hint and stopped. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps the exchange. The phrase is used at celebrations, half in warning and half in superstition, whenever things are going a little too well.

example: After years of struggle, he finally found success and happiness.
chineseExample: 经过多年的奋斗，他终于找到了成功和幸福。
description: 否 and 泰 are two hexagrams of the Book of Changes, standing opposite each other: 否 is obstruction, heaven and earth pulling apart so that nothing communicates, and 泰 is the peace that comes when they meet. The phrase runs the wheel forward — obstruction at its worst (否极) is where prosperity arrives (泰来). Note the reading: 否 is pronounced pǐ here, not fǒu, which trips up learners who know it only as the negative particle. It is offered as consolation, and the consolation is structural rather than sentimental: the bottom is not a place you stay, because it is defined as the point where the movement changes direction.

example: When it rains, it pours; his car broke down just as he lost his job.
chineseExample: 当霉运来临时，坏事总是接踵而至。
description: Disasters (祸) do not (不) travel (行) singly (单). It belongs to the fatalistic stock of everyday speech, and it is usually completed by its other half, 福无双至 — blessings do not come in pairs. Together they make a lopsided view of luck in which misfortune is gregarious and good fortune arrives alone. It is said after the second piece of bad news rather than the first, and it functions less as prediction than as a way of absorbing a run of trouble without treating it as personally aimed.

meaning: Blessings do not come in pairs
example: He realized that good luck is often fleeting and rare.
chineseExample: 他意识到好运往往是短暂而稀有的。
description: Liu Xiang's Garden of Persuasions has the older form — 福不重至，祸必重来, blessings do not come twice, misfortunes certainly come again — which settled into the pairing used today: 福无双至，祸不单行. The Water Margin puts it in characters' mouths at exactly the moment their luck turns. The asymmetry is the whole point: good fortune (福) does not arrive doubled (无双至), while trouble comes in company. It is said with resignation rather than bitterness, most often by someone who has just had one good thing happen and is declining to expect a second.

example: Sometimes, setbacks can lead to unexpected opportunities.
chineseExample: 有时候，挫折能带来意想不到的机会。
description: The thought is a commonplace of Warring States argument — that the same event is a disaster or a windfall depending on where you are standing in time, and that a skilled person converts one into the other. Chinese has a fuller story for it in 塞翁失马, the old man whose lost horse, returned horse, and injured son each reverse the previous judgement. This phrase is the compressed version: by way of (因) misfortune (祸) one obtains (得) blessing (福). It is normally said in retrospect, about a setback that turned out to have opened something, and it is the standard consolation offered to someone who has just lost a job.

example: He found happiness by adapting to his surroundings instead of fighting against them.
chineseExample: 他通过适应环境而不是与之抗争找到了快乐。
description: Meeting (随) whatever circumstance one encounters (遇) and being at ease (安) in it. It belongs to later vernacular and essay writing rather than to the early classics, and its temper is Daoist in spirit without deriving from a particular passage. The contentment it names is active rather than resigned: the person adapts to the situation instead of being defeated by it. It attaches to somebody who settles comfortably wherever they have ended up, and it is a compliment to temperament.

example: His quiet demeanor belies a strong determination to succeed.
chineseExample: 他平静的外表掩盖了他强烈的成功欲望。
description: Zhuge Liang wrote it to his son in the letter known as the Admonition to My Son, near the end of his life: without stillness and few desires there is no way to clarify (明) one's purpose (志), without quiet there is no way to reach far. The two halves became two separate idioms, this one and 宁静致远, and they are still usually hung as a pair of scrolls. 淡泊 is a taste word before it is a moral one — thin, unseasoned, unconcentrated — so what it recommends is not poverty but the deliberate lowering of appetite, on the argument that a person who wants many things cannot see clearly which one they actually want.

chineseExample_tr: 他平靜的外表掩蓋了他強烈的成功慾望。

example: In the chaos of life, he found that stillness allowed him to see further ahead.
chineseExample: 在生活的喧嚣中，他发现宁静让他看得更远。
description: This is the second half of the same sentence Zhuge Liang wrote to his son, whose first half became 淡泊明志: without quiet (宁静) there is no reaching (致) the distant (远). The distance meant is not travel but ambition and understanding — what you can see and get to from where you sit. The claim is causal rather than pleasant: stillness is presented as the precondition for range, not as a reward for having achieved it. It has become the most commonly hung piece of calligraphy in Chinese studies and offices, which has worn it smooth without making it less true.

chineseExample_tr: 在生活的喧囂中，他發現寧靜讓他看得更遠。

example: He decided to leave the corporate world behind and embrace a simpler lifestyle.
chineseExample: 他决定放弃企业生活，回归简单的生活方式。
description: This is from the Strategies of the Warring States, where the scholar Yan Chu, declining a king's patronage, says he wishes to return (返) to the uncarved jade (璞) and go back (归) to what is genuine (真). The image is of a stone before the carver reaches it, valuable precisely because it is unworked. It is a different story from the famous jade of Bian He, with which it is sometimes confused. Chinese uses it of stripping away affectation to recover an original plainness, in a person, a style or a way of living.

chineseExample_tr: 他決定放棄企業生活，回歸簡單的生活方式。

example: His seemingly naive approach often led to the most effective solutions.
chineseExample: 他看似天真的方法常常导致最有效的解决方案。
description: Su Shi wrote it in a formal note to Ouyang Xiu on his retirement: great courage looks like timidity, great wisdom (大智) looks like (若) foolishness (愚). The root is older and Daoist — the Daodejing has great skill appearing clumsy — and the observation in all versions is that genuine capacity has no need to signal itself, so it tends to be quiet and gets underestimated. Chinese uses it two ways worth keeping apart: as real praise for someone whose depth is not obvious, and as a face-saving compliment to someone who has just done something that looked slow and turned out to be right.

example: In negotiations, she proved that a gentle approach can yield better results than aggression.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，她证明了温和的方式比激进的方法更能取得好结果。
description: The root is the Daodejing, which insists repeatedly that the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, and offers water as the case in point — nothing is more yielding, and nothing is better at wearing down what is rigid. Later military writing took it up as tactics: use (以) softness (柔) to overcome (克) hardness (刚) by declining to meet force where it is strongest. It describes yielding as a technique rather than a temperament, which is the part learners tend to miss. The person applying it is not being nice; they are refusing to fight on ground that favours the other side.

chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，她證明了溫和的方式比激進的方法更能取得好結果。

example: In the world of business, like-minded individuals often come together to form successful partnerships.
chineseExample: 在商业世界中，同类的人往往聚在一起形成成功的合作关系。
description: The Book of Changes has the parent line — 方以类聚，物以群分, things gather by kind and divide by group — and the Warring States gave it an illustration in Chunyu Kun, who when asked to find talent for the king produced seven capable men at once. Challenged that talent must surely be rarer than that, he answered that birds of a kind roost together, so anyone who knows one such man knows several. The phrase is neutral in the classic and has soured in use: today 物以类聚 is most often said of bad company, with the second half 人以群分 following and the judgement implied rather than stated.

chineseExample_tr: 在商業世界中，同類的人往往聚在一起形成成功的合作關係。

example: In any community, individuals often form groups based on shared interests and beliefs.
chineseExample: 在任何社区中，个人往往根据共同的兴趣和信仰形成群体。
description: The half everyone quotes is 物以类聚，人以群分 — things gather by kind, people (人) divide (分) into groups (群). The first part descends from a line in the Book of Changes about categories sorting themselves; the second is a later proverbial addition, and it is the one that carries the sting. English reaches for birds of a feather, which matches the sense but not the tone: the Chinese is framed as a natural law rather than an observation about friends. Said of somebody's associates it is rarely a compliment, because the whole force of it is that the grouping was not accidental and tells you what you needed to know.

example: After the scandal, the truth finally came to light, revealing the real issues at hand.
chineseExample: 在丑闻之后，真相终于浮出水面，揭示了真正的问题。
description: Su Shi supplies the image in the second of his Red Cliff rhapsodies, returning to the river in winter: the mountains high, the moon small, the water fallen (水落) and the stones showing (石出). He was describing a landscape, not a principle. What made the line into an idiom is that the mechanism is so plainly right — nothing is uncovered by effort, only by the water going down, so the truth emerges through the passage of time rather than through anyone's investigation. It is used of scandals and disputes, usually by whoever is content to wait.

chineseExample_tr: 在醜聞之後，真相終於浮出水面，揭示了真正的問題。

example: In discussions, it's important to recognize that different perspectives can lead to deeper understanding.
chineseExample: 在讨论中，重要的是认识到不同的观点可以带来更深的理解。
description: The Book of Changes says of the Way that the benevolent see it and call it benevolence, the wise see it and call it wisdom — the humane (仁) see (见) one thing, the wise (智) another. The point in the original is not that all readings are equal but that each observer finds what they already are, so a description of the Way doubles as a description of the describer. Modern use has flattened it into a polite way of ending an argument: reasonable people differ, let us leave it there. It is the standard formula for declining to adjudicate a matter of taste.
description_tr: The Book of Changes says of the Way that the benevolent see it and call it benevolence, the wise see it and call it wisdom — the humane (仁) see (見) one thing, the wise (智) another. chineseExample_tr: 在討論中，重要的是認識到不同的觀點可以帶來更深的理解。

example: By the age of thirty, he finally established his career and personal identity.
chineseExample: 到三十岁时，他终于确立了自己的事业和个人身份。
description: Confucius sets out his life in stages in the Analects: 吾十有五而志于学，三十而立，四十而不惑，五十而知天命 — at fifteen bent on learning, at thirty (三十) standing (立), at forty free of doubt, at fifty knowing what heaven decreed. 立 is standing on one's own feet: a settled position, an occupation, a household. The sequence is well enough known in Chinese that naming one stage invokes the rest, and 三十而立 now carries a weight of expectation about careers and marriage that Confucius did not put there.
description_tr: Confucius sets out his life in stages in the Analects: 吾十有五而志於學，三十而立，四十而不惑，五十而知天命 — at fifteen bent on learning, at thirty (三十) standing (立), at forty free of doubt, at fifty knowing what heaven decreed. 立 is standing on one's own feet: a settled position, an occupation, a household. chineseExample_tr: 到三十歲時，他終於確立了自己的事業和個人身份。

example: He always finds joy in what he has, knowing that contentment brings peace.
chineseExample: 他总是对自己拥有的感到满足，知道知足不辱。
description: The Daodejing puts it in chapter 44, after asking whether fame or your own person is dearer: 知足不辱，知止不殆 — knowing when you have enough keeps you from disgrace, knowing when to stop keeps you from danger. The two clauses are always quoted together. The Huainanzi illustrates them with Gong Yixiu, the minister of Lu who loved fish and refused every gift of fish, reasoning that a minister who takes presents loses his post and a man without a post cannot afford fish at all. Refusing them was how he kept eating them.

example: He understands that everyone has flaws, as no one is perfect.
chineseExample: 他明白每个人都有缺点，人无完人。
description: Usually said as one half of 金无足赤，人无完人 — gold is never wholly pure, no person (人) is a complete (完) person (无). The pairing does the argument: purity is a standard that even the standard metal fails, so demanding it of a human being is a category error rather than high principle. It is used to defuse rather than to excuse, most often by a third party trying to keep a fault in proportion, and it carries an implication about the speaker's expectations more than about the person being discussed.

example: People today are less trustworthy than in the past
chineseExample: 如今的人心不古，信任变得稀少
description: Hearts (人心) are not (不) as they were in antiquity (古). The sentiment is older than any particular formulation of it, and every era has produced its own version: people were more honest once, agreements needed no paper, neighbours could be trusted. The idiom is worth learning partly as vocabulary and partly as a warning, since it is the standard opening of a certain kind of complaint. Chinese speakers use it half seriously, and a younger speaker using it about their own generation is usually being wry.

example: The harsh realities of life can be quite disheartening
chineseExample: 世态炎凉，让人感到无奈
description: 炎 is scorching and 凉 is cool, and the phrase applies both to the weather of human affairs (世态): warmth while you are useful, coolness when you are not. What it describes is specifically the temperature change around a person whose position has altered — the visitors who stop coming, the calls that go unreturned after a demotion. Chinese literature returns to it constantly, usually from the cold side and usually by someone who has just discovered how many of their friendships were attached to their office rather than to them.
description_tr: 炎 is scorching and 涼 is cool, and the phrase applies both to the weather of human affairs (世態): warmth while you are useful, coolness when you are not.
