chineseExample_tr: 世態炎涼，讓人感到無奈

example: The teacher's gentle guidance shaped her students over time
chineseExample: 老师的教导潜移默化，影响了学生们
description: Yan Zhitui, writing family instructions in the sixth century, observed that the young take their manners, speech and habits from those around them without ever deciding to, and are shaped before their characters are formed. His wording was 潜移暗化 — hidden (潜) shifting (移), unseen change. The modern form swaps in 默, making the same point with silence (默) instead of darkness: transformation (化) that announces nothing. That is the whole content of the phrase. It is not about influence in general but about the kind that leaves no memory of having been persuaded, which is why Chinese invokes it when discussing what children absorb, and what a workplace does to the people in it over years.

example: She felt a rush of emotions at her graduation ceremony
chineseExample: 在毕业典礼上，她百感交集，难以自已
description: The New Account of Tales of the World records Wei Jie, fleeing south during the collapse of the Western Jin, coming to the Yangtze and looking out at it. Seeing that vastness, he said, a hundred feelings crowd in on me at once. The original wording is 百端交集; 百感交集 is the later form. What makes it precise is 交集, an intersection — the emotions are not sequential but simultaneous and tangled, which is why no single one can be named. It belongs to reunions, funerals, and returns to places left long ago, where relief and grief arrive in the same moment.

example: Her extensive knowledge and skills made her a valuable team member
chineseExample: 她博学多才，深受大家喜爱
description: Broad learning (博学) and many talents (多才) — the Book of Jin applies it to Xi Shen, whose range across subjects was the thing contemporaries remarked on. The compliment is specifically about breadth. Chinese has separate praise for depth, and this is not it: the phrase suits the person who is genuinely competent across several unrelated fields, and would be faint praise for a specialist. It survives mainly in formal contexts — references, introductions, obituaries — and sounds slightly grand in ordinary conversation.

example: She believes in applying knowledge to solve real-world problems.
chineseExample: 她相信学以致用，解决实际问题。
description: Study (学) in order to (以) arrive at (致) use (用). The argument behind it is very old, and Chinese philosophy returns to it constantly — most sharply in Wang Yangming's insistence that knowing and doing are a single thing, and that knowledge which never issues in action was never really knowledge. The four characters are the plain modern statement of that position. They turn up in school mottoes and curriculum debates, and they are the standard rebuke to an education that produces examination results and nothing else.

example: He is not afraid to seek advice from those less experienced than him.
chineseExample: 他不耻下问，向经验不足的人请教。
description: Zigong asked Confucius why Kong Wenzi, a minister of Wei whose private conduct was not admirable, had been given the honorific 文 after his death. Confucius answered that he was quick and fond of learning, and not ashamed (不耻) to ask (问) those below him (下). The Analects preserves the exchange, and the point of it is sharper than it first appears: the quality being praised is not humility in general but the specific willingness to be seen not knowing something in front of a junior. It is still used exactly that way, of the senior person who asks the obvious question first.

example: Her extensive knowledge makes her an expert in both historical and contemporary literature.
chineseExample: 她博古通今，精通古今文学。
description: Wide in the ancient (博古) and versed in the present (通今). The Family Sayings of Confucius has Confucius say it of Laozi, though in the older wording 博古知今, knowing the present rather than being versed in it. The compliment is about span rather than depth — someone who can hold the old and the current in the same head and see how one bears on the other. Chinese keeps a suspicion of the scholar who knows only antiquity, which is what gives the second half its weight. It belongs to formal praise, and it fits the historian or the commentator rather than the specialist.

example: He often uses analogies to explain complex concepts, making them easier to grasp.
chineseExample: 他常用类比来解释复杂的概念，帮助理解。
description: The appendices to the Book of Changes describe the method: draw a thing out, extend it by category, and the whole field follows. Hence touching (触) a category (类) and connecting (通) sideways (旁) — you learn one case properly and the neighbouring cases open without being learned separately. It names a capacity rather than an effort, and it is the highest thing a Chinese teacher can say about how a student learns: not that they work hard, but that teaching them one thing has turned out to teach them four.

example: His extensive reading has filled him with knowledge equivalent to five carts of books.
chineseExample: 他的阅读量之大，学富五车。
description: The Zhuangzi says of the logician Hui Shi that his doctrines were many and his books filled five carts (五车). Worth knowing what that measured: books were bamboo slips bound with cord, so five cartloads is a great deal of cart and, by modern reckoning, not an enormous quantity of text. The phrase has floated free of the arithmetic and simply means learning (学) as abundant (富) as five cartloads. It is unambiguous praise, used of the genuinely well-read, and it is common enough in speech that nobody hears the carts any more.

example: His knowledge of literature and philosophy is unmatched, making him a true scholar.
chineseExample: 他的文学和哲学知识才高八斗，堪称真正的学者。
description: Xie Lingyun, a poet not troubled by modesty, once measured out the world's literary talent aloud: if all of it came to one 石, then Cao Zhi alone held eight 斗 of it, he himself held one, and everyone else who had ever lived divided the last. Ten 斗 make one 石, so the allocation is exact and the flattery of Cao Zhi is total. The phrase kept Cao Zhi's eight (八) 斗 and lost the rest of the arithmetic: talent (才) standing high (高) by that measure. It is used of literary or intellectual brilliance specifically, not of competence in general.
description_tr: Xie Lingyun, a poet not troubled by modesty, once measured out the world's literary talent aloud: if all of it came to one 石, then Cao Zhi alone held eight 鬥 of it, he himself held one, and everyone else who had ever lived divided the last. Ten 鬥 make one 石, so the allocation is exact and the flattery of Cao Zhi is total. The phrase kept Cao Zhi's eight (八) 鬥 and lost the rest of the arithmetic: talent (才) standing high (高) by that measure. It is used of literary or intellectual brilliance specifically, not of competence in general.
chineseExample_tr: 他的文學和哲學知識才高八斗，堪稱真正的學者。

example: Her extensive understanding of history makes her a valuable asset to the team.
chineseExample: 她对历史的满腹经纶使她成为团队的重要资产。
description: 经纶 is textile work before it is statecraft — sorting raw silk and twisting it into cord — and it became the standard metaphor for the ordering of state affairs, which is untangling of the same kind. So a belly (腹) full (满) of 经纶 is a person stocked not merely with reading but with the capacity to organise it into policy. The phrase implies usable knowledge held in reserve, which is why it so often appears in the frustrated form: 满腹经纶 and no post to apply it in.
description_tr: 經綸 is textile work before it is statecraft — sorting raw silk and twisting it into cord — and it became the standard metaphor for the ordering of state affairs, which is untangling of the same kind. The phrase implies usable knowledge held in reserve, which is why it so often appears in the frustrated form: 滿腹經綸 and no post to apply it in.
chineseExample_tr: 她對歷史的滿腹經綸使她成為團隊的重要資產。

example: His extensive travels have made him well-read and knowledgeable about different cultures.
chineseExample: 他的广泛旅行使他见多识广，了解不同的文化。
description: Having seen much (见多) and knowing widely (识广). The phrase belongs to the vernacular rather than the classics, and Ming fiction is where it becomes common, which suits it — the knowledge it praises is the kind acquired by moving about in the world rather than by reading. That distinguishes it from 博学多才 and 学富五车, both of which are about books. It is what you say about the person worth consulting because they have been somewhere and dealt with something, and it carries no implication of formal education at all.

chineseExample_tr: 他的廣泛旅行使他見多識廣，了解不同的文化。

example: Her sharp hearing and keen sight make her an excellent detective.
chineseExample: 她耳聪目明，是一位出色的侦探。
description: Ears keen (耳聪) and eyes clear (目明). The pairing is ancient and appears across the classics, generally describing a ruler or official who can actually be reached by information — the senses standing in for a mind that is not insulated. Physical acuity is the surface reading and is still available, particularly of a healthy older person. The figurative sense is the useful one: someone who notices, who is not the last to hear, and whose judgement has current facts in it rather than remembered ones.

chineseExample_tr: 她耳聰目明，是一位出色的偵探。

example: Before making a decision, he always engages in deep thought and careful consideration.
chineseExample: 在做决定之前，他总是深思熟虑。
description: Deep (深) thinking (思) and matured (熟) deliberation (虑). Both halves are pairs that appear throughout the classics, and the force is in 熟 — the same character used of cooked food and ripe fruit. What it asks for is not more thought but thought left long enough to finish. That distinguishes it from mere caution, and it is the phrase used to insist that a decision be slept on rather than merely reconsidered.

That distinguishes it from mere caution, and it is the phrase used to insist that a decision be slept on rather than merely reconsidered.
chineseExample_tr: 在做決定之前，他總是深思熟慮。

example: She mastered the piano entirely on her own, showcasing her incredible talent.
chineseExample: 她完全自学成才，展现了惊人的天赋。
description: Without (无) a teacher (师), understanding (通) by oneself (自). The phrase carries a particular weight in a culture that has traditionally organised knowledge around lineages of transmission, where the question asked of a scholar or a craftsman was whose student they had been. To arrive without that is genuinely remarkable and slightly irregular. It is used of self-taught programmers and musicians, and it praises the aptitude rather than the effort — which is why it can sound faintly like an excuse for gaps.
description_tr: Without (無) a teacher (師), understanding (通) by oneself (自). chineseExample_tr: 她完全自學成才，展現了驚人的天賦。

example: After years of living in the same neighborhood, he failed to notice the changes around him.
chineseExample: 在同一个社区生活多年后，他没有注意到周围的变化。
description: Liu Ling, the drinker among the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, wrote in praise of wine that his ideal man listens and does not hear thunder, 熟视不睹泰山之形 — looks hard (熟视) and does not see the bulk of Mount Tai. He meant it as transcendence, a mind too large to be disturbed; the modern form swaps his 不 for 无, no (无) seeing (睹) at all. The sense has entirely inverted since. It now names a failure rather than an achievement: the thing so familiar it has stopped registering, the problem walked past daily, the suffering in plain view that nobody sees any more.
description_tr: Liu Ling, the drinker among the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, wrote in praise of wine that his ideal man listens and does not hear thunder, 熟視不睹泰山之形 — looks hard (熟視) and does not see the bulk of Mount Tai. He meant it as transcendence, a mind too large to be disturbed; the modern form swaps his 不 for 無, no (無) seeing (睹) at all. The sense has entirely inverted since. It now names a failure rather than an achievement: the thing so familiar it has stopped registering, the problem walked past daily, the suffering in plain view that nobody sees any more.
chineseExample_tr: 在同一個社區生活多年後，他沒有注意到周圍的變化。

example: His ability to predict market trends shows he has a keen insight into the economy.
chineseExample: 他预测市场趋势的能力表明他对经济有敏锐的洞察力。
description: Mencius describes heaven's arrangement as one where those who understand first bring those who understand later to understanding — the first to know (先知) and the first to wake (先觉) owing something to everyone else. The obligation is the part that has been lost. In current use the phrase describes foresight and nothing more, and it is often faintly barbed, since claiming to be 先知先觉 about anything is a claim to have been right before the evidence was in. It sits most comfortably in retrospect, applied by others.
description_tr: Mencius describes heaven's arrangement as one where those who understand first bring those who understand later to understanding — the first to know (先知) and the first to wake (先覺) owing something to everyone else. It sits most comfortably in retrospect, applied by others.
chineseExample_tr: 他預測市場趨勢的能力表明他對經濟有敏銳的洞察力。

example: He believes that thorough research leads to true knowledge.
chineseExample: 他相信深入研究能获得真正的知识。
description: Four characters from the Great Learning that Chinese philosophy then argued about for eight hundred years: investigate (格) things (物) and thereby extend (致) knowledge (知). The text gives no gloss, and the gap was filled in opposite directions — Zhu Xi read 格物 as the patient examination of things in the world, one at a time, while Wang Yangming, having sat staring at bamboo for a week and fallen ill without attaining anything, concluded that the investigation must be of the mind instead. Modern Chinese leans on Zhu Xi's reading, and the phrase is now used for empirical method and, sometimes, for science itself.
description_tr: Four characters from the Great Learning that Chinese philosophy then argued about for eight hundred years: investigate (格) things (物) and thereby extend (致) knowledge (知). Modern Chinese leans on Zhu Xi's reading, and the phrase is now used for empirical method and, sometimes, for science itself.
chineseExample_tr: 他相信深入研究能獲得真正的知識。

example: In negotiations, they aimed to find shared interests while respecting each other's unique perspectives.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，他们旨在寻找共同利益，同时尊重彼此的独特观点。
description: This is a twentieth-century diplomatic phrase rather than a classical one, and it is bound up with Zhou Enlai's speech at the Bandung Conference in 1955, where a room of newly independent states with very little in common was asked to seek what was shared (求同) and set aside (存) what differed (异). 存 is the exact word: not resolve the differences, not conceal them, leave them standing. That is what makes it usable, and it has since spread well beyond diplomacy into any negotiation where agreement on everything is not available.
metaphoric_meaning: Agree on the common, shelve the rest
description_tr: This is a twentieth-century diplomatic phrase rather than a classical one, and it is bound up with Zhou Enlai's speech at the Bandung Conference in 1955, where a room of newly independent states with very little in common was asked to seek what was shared (求同) and set aside (存) what differed (異). 存 is the exact word: not resolve the differences, not conceal them, leave them standing. That is what makes it usable, and it has since spread well beyond diplomacy into any negotiation where agreement on everything is not available.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，他們旨在尋找共同利益，同時尊重彼此的獨特觀點。

example: In his lecture, he drew on a wide range of sources to support his argument.
chineseExample: 在他的讲座中，他旁征博引，引用了大量的资料来支持他的论点。
description: To seek broadly (旁征) and quote extensively (博引). It names a manner of arguing, one in which evidence is gathered from many directions and the case is built out of other people's authority. Chinese does not treat that as automatically admirable. Used warmly it praises real scholarship, and used coolly it describes the speaker who has read a great deal and is telling you about all of it, which is a distinction worth hearing before you accept the compliment.
description_tr: To seek broadly (旁徵) and quote extensively (博引). It names a manner of arguing, one in which evidence is gathered from many directions and the case is built out of other people's authority. Chinese does not treat that as automatically admirable. Used warmly it praises real scholarship, and used coolly it describes the speaker who has read a great deal and is telling you about all of it, which is a distinction worth hearing before you accept the compliment.
chineseExample_tr: 在他的講座中，他旁徵博引，引用了大量的資料來支持他的論點。

example: Her ability to recall facts and details made her an excellent historian.
chineseExample: 她博闻强记，成为了一位优秀的历史学家。
description: The Book of Rites pairs them: widely informed (博闻) and retaining strongly (强记), listed among the marks of an educated person. The older form writes the last character 识, read zhì in that sense, and both forms are current. What the phrase values is memory as a component of learning rather than an alternative to it — reading widely counts for little if nothing stays. It is the natural compliment for someone who can produce the relevant fact without looking it up, and it has survived intact into an age that has made the trick much less necessary.
description_tr: The Book of Rites pairs them: widely informed (博聞) and retaining strongly (強記), listed among the marks of an educated person. The older form writes the last character 識, read zhì in that sense, and both forms are current. What the phrase values is memory as a component of learning rather than an alternative to it — reading widely counts for little if nothing stays. It is the natural compliment for someone who can produce the relevant fact without looking it up, and it has survived intact into an age that has made the trick much less necessary.
chineseExample_tr: 她博聞強記，成為了一位優秀的歷史學家。

example: Those in charge often fail to see the bigger picture due to their close involvement.
chineseExample: 当局者迷，外人却能看得更清楚。
description: The Old Book of Tang records a dispute over which recension of a classic should stand. Yuan Xingtan, who had done the work and been overruled, made the comparison to a game of chess: the player at the board (当局者) is lost (迷) in it, while the man watching from the side sees the position. The pairing 当局者迷，旁观者清 has been inseparable ever since. What it claims is not that outsiders are cleverer but that involvement itself costs you the view, which is why the phrase is used to justify asking someone uninvolved rather than someone better qualified.
description_tr: The Old Book of Tang records a dispute over which recension of a classic should stand. Yuan Xingtan, who had done the work and been overruled, made the comparison to a game of chess: the player at the board (當局者) is lost (迷) in it, while the man watching from the side sees the position. The pairing 當局者迷，旁觀者清 has been inseparable ever since. What it claims is not that outsiders are cleverer but that involvement itself costs you the view, which is why the phrase is used to justify asking someone uninvolved rather than someone better qualified.
chineseExample_tr: 當局者迷，外人卻能看得更清楚。

example: Sometimes, those not involved can offer the best advice.
chineseExample: 旁观者清，局内人却看不明白。
description: The other half of 当局者迷，旁观者清, from the same passage of the Old Book of Tang and the same chess image: the onlooker (旁观者) sees clearly (清) precisely because nothing turns on their seeing it. English has no single expression for this, which is why it is worth learning as a unit. Used of yourself it is a modest offer of an opinion; used of someone else it can be an invitation, and it is the standard polite preface to telling a friend something about their own situation that they have not noticed.

chineseExample_tr: 旁觀者清，局內人卻看不明白。

meaning: One word worth a thousand gold
example: His advice was invaluable, proving that sometimes a single word can change everything.
chineseExample: 他的建议一字千金，改变了我们的决策。
description: Lü Buwei, merchant turned chancellor of Qin, assembled scholars to compile the encyclopaedic work that carries his name, then had it hung at the gate of the capital with a thousand pieces of gold (千金) offered to anyone who could add or delete a single character (一字). Nobody collected. The Records of the Grand Historian, reporting this, leaves open whether the text was flawless or the man too powerful to correct. The phrase is now straightforward praise for writing of great value, and the ambiguity in the original is generally forgotten.
description_tr: Lü Buwei, merchant turned chancellor of Qin, assembled scholars to compile the encyclopaedic work that carries his name, then had it hung at the gate of the capital with a thousand pieces of gold (千金) offered to anyone who could add or delete a single character (一字). Nobody collected. The Records of the Grand Historian, reporting this, leaves open whether the text was flawless or the man too powerful to correct. The phrase is now straightforward praise for writing of great value, and the ambiguity in the original is generally forgotten.
chineseExample_tr: 他的建議一字千金，改變了我們的決策。

example: Her speech was so eloquent that every word felt precious and meaningful.
chineseExample: 她的演讲字字珠玑，每一个字都显得珍贵而有意义。
description: 珠玑 is two kinds of pearl, the round and the irregular, and the phrase claims that every single character (字字) is one. It is applied to writing and to speech, and what it praises is density rather than beauty — nothing padding, nothing that could be removed. That makes it a strong compliment and a slightly awkward one, since it implies the piece could not be shortened. Chinese uses it in reviews and in praise of a well-made speech.
description_tr: 珠璣 is two kinds of pearl, the round and the irregular, and the phrase claims that every single character (字字) is one. It is applied to writing and to speech, and what it praises is density rather than beauty — nothing padding, nothing that could be removed. That makes it a strong compliment and a slightly awkward one, since it implies the piece could not be shortened. Chinese uses it in reviews and in praise of a well-made speech.
chineseExample_tr: 她的演講字字珠璣，每一個字都顯得珍貴而有意義。

example: His storytelling ability was so captivating that it flowed effortlessly like a river.
chineseExample: 他的讲故事能力口若悬河，滔滔不绝。
description: Wang Yan, asked about the philosopher Guo Xiang's talk, said that listening to him was like water pouring from a river hung overhead — pouring and never running dry. The New Account of Tales of the World keeps the remark, and the image survives in the idiom: a mouth (口) like (若) a suspended (悬) river (河). The praise is for volume and momentum rather than for precision, which leaves it usable both ways. Said of a good speaker it is admiration; said of someone at a meeting it can quietly mean they have not stopped talking.

example: His remarks were so clever and witty that they seemed to flow one after another seamlessly.
chineseExample: 他的妙语连珠让人忍俊不禁，接连不断。
description: Clever words (妙语) strung continuously (连珠) — the second half names a specific thing, pearls threaded on a cord, where the value is in each one and the effect is in the succession. The phrase describes wit arriving in a run rather than as a single remark, which is the harder feat and the reason the image is a string rather than a single stone. It suits comedians, quick speakers and good company at dinner, and it is a warmer compliment than 口若悬河.
description_tr: Clever words (妙語) strung continuously (連珠) — the second half names a specific thing, pearls threaded on a cord, where the value is in each one and the effect is in the succession. chineseExample_tr: 他的妙語連珠讓人忍俊不禁，接連不斷。

example: When they met for the first time, it felt as if they had known each other forever.
chineseExample: 他们一见如故，仿佛是老朋友。
description: Ji Zha of Wu, travelling as an envoy, met Zichan of Zheng and the Zuo Zhuan says they took to each other at once, as though they had been friends for years — meeting once (一见) and being like (如) old acquaintances (故). They exchanged gifts and talked about the fate of Zichan's state, which suggests what the phrase actually rests on: not warmth but recognition, the sense of having found someone whose judgement runs the same way as your own. It remains one of the warmest things a Chinese speaker can say about a first meeting.
description_tr: Ji Zha of Wu, travelling as an envoy, met Zichan of Zheng and the Zuo Zhuan says they took to each other at once, as though they had been friends for years — meeting once (一見) and being like (如) old acquaintances (故). They exchanged gifts and talked about the fate of Zichan's state, which suggests what the phrase actually rests on: not warmth but recognition, the sense of having found someone whose judgement runs the same way as your own. It remains one of the warmest things a Chinese speaker can say about a first meeting.
chineseExample_tr: 他們一見如故，彷彿是老朋友。

example: He showed his loyalty by standing by his friend even in difficult times.
chineseExample: 在困难时刻，他两肋插刀，支持了他的朋友。
description: The phrase belongs to the world of Sui and Tang storytelling, and attaches above all to Qin Shubao, the sworn-brotherhood hero who takes the risk himself so that his friends are not taken. Knives (刀) driven into (插) both ribs (两肋) is the image, and it is deliberately physical — the register is martial fiction and street loyalty rather than anything classical. That register still governs it. Chinese uses it warmly and slightly theatrically, most often in the promise 为朋友两肋插刀, and hearing it in a business meeting would be as odd as swearing a blood oath over a contract.

Knives (刀) driven into (插) both ribs (兩肋) is the image, and it is deliberately physical — the register is martial fiction and street loyalty rather than anything classical. That register still governs it. chineseExample_tr: 在困難時刻，他兩肋插刀，支持了他的朋友。

example: Despite not being related by blood, they treated each other like family.
chineseExample: 尽管没有血缘关系，他们却情同手足。
description: Feeling (情) the same as (同) between hands (手) and feet (足). It is the active twin of 手足之情: that phrase names the bond between actual brothers, while this one claims it for people who are not related. That is the whole point of the construction — 同 is doing the comparing. It is what Chinese says about sworn brothers, old army units and friendships of thirty years, and it is a considerable claim rather than a pleasantry.
description_tr: Feeling (情) the same as (同) between hands (手) and feet (足). It is the active twin of 手足之情: that phrase names the bond between actual brothers, while this one claims it for people who are not related. That is the whole point of the construction — 同 is doing the comparing. It is what Chinese says about sworn brothers, old army units and friendships of thirty years, and it is a considerable claim rather than a pleasantry.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管沒有血緣關係，他們卻情同手足。

example: He was willing to sacrifice everything for his friends, showing his true loyalty.
chineseExample: 为了朋友，他甘愿肝脑涂地，表现出真正的忠诚。
description: Lou Jing, arguing that Liu Bang should site his capital in the defensible Guanzhong rather than the exhausted central plain, described what the wars of the previous decade had actually left behind: fathers and sons with their livers (肝) and brains (脑) smeared (涂) on the ground (地). The phrase began as a description of massacre. It has since inverted into a pledge — I would give my liver and brains for this — and is now used to swear total commitment, usually to a ruler, a country or a cause. The original horror has drained out of it almost completely.

It has since inverted into a pledge — I would give my liver and brains for this — and is now used to swear total commitment, usually to a ruler, a country or a cause. example: Her innocence and kindness reflect the heart of a child, untouched by the world's harshness.
chineseExample: 她的纯真和善良体现了赤子之心，未曾被世俗的残酷所污染。
description: 赤子 is a newborn, called red for the colour it is born. Mencius wrote that the great person is the one who has not lost the heart (心) of the newborn (赤子之), and he meant something specific by it: not innocence in the sense of ignorance, but an unmanaged directness of response that most people trade away in exchange for competence. The phrase is high praise and is usually reserved for artists, scientists and the very old. It sits oddly on the young, since the point of it is that the quality survived something.

Mencius wrote that the great person is the one who has not lost the heart (心) of the newborn (赤子之), and he meant something specific by it: not innocence in the sense of ignorance, but an unmanaged directness of response that most people trade away in exchange for competence. The phrase is high praise and is usually reserved for artists, scientists and the very old. It sits oddly on the young, since the point of it is that the quality survived something.
chineseExample_tr: 她的純真和善良體現了赤子之心，未曾被世俗的殘酷所污染。

example: The holiday season is a time for the joy of family reunion, where laughter and love fill the air.
chineseExample: 节假日是天伦之乐的时刻，欢声笑语充满了每个角落。
description: Li Bai wrote it in the preface to a spring night's drinking with his cousins in a garden of peach and plum blossom: the joys (乐) of natural relation (天伦), set out among the flowers, with the wine going round and the poems being made. 天伦 is the bond you did not choose — parents, siblings, children — as against relations built by agreement. That is what gives the phrase its warmth and also its limit. It describes the pleasure of family gathered and doing nothing in particular, and it is what Chinese reaches for at New Year.
description_tr: Li Bai wrote it in the preface to a spring night's drinking with his cousins in a garden of peach and plum blossom: the joys (樂) of natural relation (天倫), set out among the flowers, with the wine going round and the poems being made. 天倫 is the bond you did not choose — parents, siblings, children — as against relations built by agreement. That is what gives the phrase its warmth and also its limit. It describes the pleasure of family gathered and doing nothing in particular, and it is what Chinese reaches for at New Year.
chineseExample_tr: 節假日是天倫之樂的時刻，歡聲笑語充滿了每個角落。

example: Even after years apart, their bond remained strong, proving that flesh and blood are connected.
chineseExample: 即使多年未见，他们的纽带依然牢固，证明了骨肉相连。
description: Bone (骨) and flesh (肉) joined (相连). 骨肉 is the ordinary Chinese word for close blood kin, so the phrase is not really a metaphor: it states that parents and children, brothers and sisters, are one body distributed across several people. Its force is that the connection is involuntary and cannot be dissolved by falling out. It appears constantly in writing about separated families, and in political language about territories claimed as inseparable.
description_tr: Bone (骨) and flesh (肉) joined (相連). 骨肉 is the ordinary Chinese word for close blood kin, so the phrase is not really a metaphor: it states that parents and children, brothers and sisters, are one body distributed across several people. Its force is that the connection is involuntary and cannot be dissolved by falling out. It appears constantly in writing about separated families, and in political language about territories claimed as inseparable.
chineseExample_tr: 即使多年未見，他們的紐帶依然牢固，證明了骨肉相連。

example: Their bond was evident in the way they supported each other through thick and thin.
chineseExample: 他们之间的手足之情在于无论何时都互相支持。
description: Hands (手) and feet (足) have named brothers in Chinese since antiquity, and the metaphor is exact in a way that most kinship metaphors are not: they are separate limbs of one body, they cannot be exchanged for others, and losing one is not the sort of loss that is repaired. The affection (情) named here rests on that. Modern usage has widened it to friends close enough to count as family, and it appears constantly in appeals for solidarity, where the claim being made is that the parties are not really separate parties at all.
description_tr: Hands (手) and feet (足) have named brothers in Chinese since antiquity, and the metaphor is exact in a way that most kinship metaphors are not: they are separate limbs of one body, they cannot be exchanged for others, and losing one is not the sort of loss that is repaired. The affection (情) named here rests on that. Modern usage has widened it to friends close enough to count as family, and it appears constantly in appeals for solidarity, where the claim being made is that the parties are not really separate parties at all.
chineseExample_tr: 他們之間的手足之情在於無論何時都互相支持。

example: His actions reflected a high moral standard that inspired those around him.
chineseExample: 他的行为展现了高风亮节，激励着周围的人。
description: High bearing (高风) and bright integrity (亮节). 节 is a bamboo joint before it is a moral term, and the metaphor is structural — the joints are what let the stem bend a long way and spring back without breaking. Chinese moral vocabulary leans on that image constantly. The phrase is reserved for character tested under pressure rather than merely admirable in comfort, which is why it attaches to figures like Su Wu, who kept his loyalty through nineteen years of detention among the Xiongnu.
description_tr: High bearing (高風) and bright integrity (亮節). 節 is a bamboo joint before it is a moral term, and the metaphor is structural — the joints are what let the stem bend a long way and spring back without breaking. Chinese moral vocabulary leans on that image constantly. The phrase is reserved for character tested under pressure rather than merely admirable in comfort, which is why it attaches to figures like Su Wu, who kept his loyalty through nineteen years of detention among the Xiongnu.
chineseExample_tr: 他的行為展現了高風亮節，激勵著周圍的人。

example: He is regarded as a virtuous gentleman who always acts with honor and respect.
chineseExample: 他被视为正人君子，总是以荣誉和尊重行事。
description: An upright person (正人), a gentleman (君子) — the compound is old and was straightforwardly complimentary, describing the scholar-official who behaved as the training was supposed to make him behave. Its modern life is almost entirely sarcastic. Said today, 正人君子 usually means someone conspicuously performing rectitude, and the more solemn the delivery the more certain the irony. Learners should treat it as unusable as praise: to compliment integrity, Chinese has 德高望重 or simply 正直, and this phrase will be heard as an accusation.
description_tr: An upright person (正人), a gentleman (君子) — the compound is old and was straightforwardly complimentary, describing the scholar-official who behaved as the training was supposed to make him behave. Its modern life is almost entirely sarcastic. Said today, 正人君子 usually means someone conspicuously performing rectitude, and the more solemn the delivery the more certain the irony. Learners should treat it as unusable as praise: to compliment integrity, Chinese has 德高望重 or simply 正直, and this phrase will be heard as an accusation.
chineseExample_tr: 他被視為正人君子，總是以榮譽和尊重行事。

example: Her contributions to the community earned her a reputation for high virtue and respect.
chineseExample: 她对社区的贡献使她赢得了德高望重的声誉。
description: Virtue (德) high (高) and standing (望) weighty (重). 望 is the key character — not what a person is but how they are regarded, the reputation that has accumulated around them — so the phrase claims both the substance and the recognition, and it is not usable of someone admirable whom nobody has heard of. It is reserved for the old. Applied to a person in mid-career it sounds absurd, and it belongs to introductions, memorials and the naming of the person asked to speak first.
description_tr: Virtue (德) high (高) and standing (望) weighty (重). 望 is the key character — not what a person is but how they are regarded, the reputation that has accumulated around them — so the phrase claims both the substance and the recognition, and it is not usable of someone admirable whom nobody has heard of. It is reserved for the old. Applied to a person in mid-career it sounds absurd, and it belongs to introductions, memorials and the naming of the person asked to speak first.
chineseExample_tr: 她對社區的貢獻使她贏得了德高望重的聲譽。

meaning: Throw stones at someone in a well
example: He took advantage of her misfortune to criticize her, showing his true character.
chineseExample: 他在她落难时对她指责，真是落井下石。
description: Han Yu, writing the tomb inscription for his friend Liu Zongyuan, turned aside to describe how people behave when a man's fortunes collapse: he falls into the pit, and rather than putting out a hand they shove him further and drop stones (下石) in after him. The four-character form keeps the pit as a well (落井). It is among the strongest condemnations available in ordinary Chinese, because what it names is not merely failing to help but choosing the moment of someone's weakness as the moment to strike.
description_tr: Han Yu, writing the tomb inscription for his friend Liu Zongyuan, turned aside to describe how people behave when a man's fortunes collapse: he falls into the pit, and rather than putting out a hand they shove him further and drop stones (下石) in after him. The four-character form keeps the pit as a well (落井). It is among the strongest condemnations available in ordinary Chinese, because what it names is not merely failing to help but choosing the moment of someone's weakness as the moment to strike.
chineseExample_tr: 他在她落難時對她指責，真是落井下石。

example: Instead of being grateful, he turned against those who helped him, embodying the worst of human nature.
chineseExample: 他本该感恩，却恩将仇报，真让人失望。
description: Kindness (恩) taken (将) and repaid (报) with enmity (仇). It is the standard vernacular charge of ingratitude, and Ming fiction is full of it — Journey to the West returns to the pattern repeatedly, with Sun Wukong rescuing someone who then turns on him. The phrase is stronger than the English 'ungrateful', because it does not describe an absence of thanks but an active reversal, help answered with harm. It is an accusation rather than a complaint.
description_tr: Kindness (恩) taken (將) and repaid (報) with enmity (仇). It is the standard vernacular charge of ingratitude, and Ming fiction is full of it — Journey to the West returns to the pattern repeatedly, with Sun Wukong rescuing someone who then turns on him. The phrase is stronger than the English 'ungrateful', because it does not describe an absence of thanks but an active reversal, help answered with harm. It is an accusation rather than a complaint.
chineseExample_tr: 他本該感恩，卻恩將仇報，真讓人失望。

example: He forgot all the help he received and acted selfishly, showing his true colors.
chineseExample: 他忘恩负义，完全不记得曾经的帮助。
description: Forget (忘) the kindness (恩) and turn your back on (负) what is owed (义). 义 is the load-bearing character: not loyalty as sentiment but obligation as a moral fact, the thing a person owes whether or not they feel like it. That is why the phrase bites. It charges someone not with coldness but with breaking a real debt, and Chinese treats it as among the more serious things you can say about a person's character, well beyond ordinary rudeness or neglect.
description_tr: Forget (忘) the kindness (恩) and turn your back on (負) what is owed (義). 義 is the load-bearing character: not loyalty as sentiment but obligation as a moral fact, the thing a person owes whether or not they feel like it. That is why the phrase bites. It charges someone not with coldness but with breaking a real debt, and Chinese treats it as among the more serious things you can say about a person's character, well beyond ordinary rudeness or neglect.
chineseExample_tr: 他忘恩負義，完全不記得曾經的幫助。

example: He sabotaged his colleague's project to advance his own career, demonstrating a lack of integrity.
chineseExample: 他损人利己，完全不顾同事的努力。
description: Harm (损) others (人), benefit (利) yourself (己). Its interest is that Chinese moral vocabulary has a graded scale of which this is only one point. 损人利己 is condemned; 利己 alone is not, and self-interest that costs nobody anything passes without comment. There is even 损人不利己, harming others without benefiting yourself, which is treated as worse because it is stupid as well as bad. The phrase names the ordinary, comprehensible version of selfishness.
description_tr: Harm (損) others (人), benefit (利) yourself (己). Its interest is that Chinese moral vocabulary has a graded scale of which this is only one point. 損人利己 is condemned; 利己 alone is not, and self-interest that costs nobody anything passes without comment. There is even 損人不利己, harming others without benefiting yourself, which is treated as worse because it is stupid as well as bad. The phrase names the ordinary, comprehensible version of selfishness.
chineseExample_tr: 他損人利己，完全不顧同事的努力。

example: She was dismissed for her looks, showing how superficial judgments can be misleading.
chineseExample: 他以貌取人，错过了很多优秀的人才。
description: Confucius, according to the Records of the Grand Historian, admitted two misjudgements. He had expected much of Zai Yu, who spoke well, and was disappointed; and he had thought little of Ziyu, whose appearance was against him, and who became a teacher with three hundred followers. Judging (取) people (人) by (以) appearance (貌), he concluded, was how he had lost Ziyu. The phrase carries that confession in it, which is why it lands harder than a general warning about superficiality: the person who got it wrong was Confucius.
description_tr: Confucius, according to the Records of the Grand Historian, admitted two misjudgements. He had expected much of Zai Yu, who spoke well, and was disappointed; and he had thought little of Ziyu, whose appearance was against him, and who became a teacher with three hundred followers. Judging (取) people (人) by (以) appearance (貌), he concluded, was how he had lost Ziyu. The phrase carries that confession in it, which is why it lands harder than a general warning about superficiality: the person who got it wrong was Confucius.
chineseExample_tr: 他以貌取人，錯過了很多優秀的人才。

example: He always acts pious, but his true nature is quite different.
chineseExample: 他总是道貌岸然，但他的真实本性却大相径庭。
description: 岸 is a river bank, and 岸然 means towering, standing up sheer — so the phrase describes a bearing (道貌) that is imposing and morally elevated. It was once neutral, even admiring. It is now almost purely sarcastic, and the sarcasm is aimed precisely at the visibility of the virtue: the person is not merely a hypocrite but a conspicuous one, wearing the manner so plainly that it invites doubt. Chinese has no ordinary use for it as praise any more, and learners should treat it as a hostile word.
description_tr: 岸 is a river bank, and 岸然 means towering, standing up sheer — so the phrase describes a bearing (道貌) that is imposing and morally elevated. It was once neutral, even admiring. It is now almost purely sarcastic, and the sarcasm is aimed precisely at the visibility of the virtue: the person is not merely a hypocrite but a conspicuous one, wearing the manner so plainly that it invites doubt. Chinese has no ordinary use for it as praise any more, and learners should treat it as a hostile word.
chineseExample_tr: 他總是道貌岸然，但他的真實本性卻大相徑庭。

example: Even in his seventies, he runs marathons and stays active.
chineseExample: 他虽然年过七十，但老当益壮，依然参加马拉松。
description: Ma Yuan, the Han general who kept taking commands into his sixties, was reported in the History of the Later Han to have said that a man of purpose should be firmer for being poor and stronger (壮) for being old (老) — 穷当益坚，老当益壮. He died on campaign in his sixties, which the phrase's users generally know. 益 does the work: not still strong despite age but more so because of it. It is said to and about the old, and it is a genuine compliment rather than a consolation.
description_tr: Ma Yuan, the Han general who kept taking commands into his sixties, was reported in the History of the Later Han to have said that a man of purpose should be firmer for being poor and stronger (壯) for being old (老) — 窮當益堅，老當益壯. He died on campaign in his sixties, which the phrase's users generally know. 益 does the work: not still strong despite age but more so because of it. It is said to and about the old, and it is a genuine compliment rather than a consolation.
chineseExample_tr: 他雖然年過七十，但老當益壯，依然參加馬拉松。

meaning: No deception of young or old
example: The shop is known for its honesty, treating everyone fairly.
chineseExample: 这家店童叟无欺，所有顾客都能得到公正的对待。
description: A shop sign before it was an idiom, and still most at home painted on one: neither children (童) nor the old (叟) are cheated (无欺). The pairing names the two customers easiest to short-change, one too inexperienced to check and one assumed unable to, so honesty toward them is offered as proof of honesty toward everyone. It is a merchant's claim about himself, which gives it a faint period flavour in modern use, and Chinese speakers deploy it half-ironically about anyone insisting a little too firmly on their own fairness.
description_tr: A shop sign before it was an idiom, and still most at home painted on one: neither children (童) nor the old (叟) are cheated (無欺). The pairing names the two customers easiest to short-change, one too inexperienced to check and one assumed unable to, so honesty toward them is offered as proof of honesty toward everyone. It is a merchant's claim about himself, which gives it a faint period flavour in modern use, and Chinese speakers deploy it half-ironically about anyone insisting a little too firmly on their own fairness.
chineseExample_tr: 這家店童叟無欺，所有顧客都能得到公正的對待。

meaning: Respect the old, love the young
example: In our community, we practice respect for the elderly and kindness to children.
chineseExample: 在我们的社区，尊老爱幼是大家共同遵守的原则。
description: Respect (尊) the old (老), cherish (爱) the young (幼). The four characters are a modern compression, but the thought is Mencius at his most quoted — treat your own elders as elders and extend it to the elders of others, treat your own young as young and extend it to the young of others — which makes the phrase a summary of Confucian social ethics in the space of a slogan. It functions as one. It appears on public notices, in civics education, and above priority seating on buses.
description_tr: Respect (尊) the old (老), cherish (愛) the young (幼). The four characters are a modern compression, but the thought is Mencius at his most quoted — treat your own elders as elders and extend it to the elders of others, treat your own young as young and extend it to the young of others — which makes the phrase a summary of Confucian social ethics in the space of a slogan. It functions as one. It appears on public notices, in civics education, and above priority seating on buses.
chineseExample_tr: 在我們的社區，尊老愛幼是大家共同遵守的原則。

example: In our team, everyone is encouraged to contribute their unique skills.
chineseExample: 在我们的团队中，人尽其才，充分发挥每个人的特长。
description: The Huainanzi argues that a ruler's skill lies in placing people where their particular capacity is worth something, and illustrates it with the philosopher Gongsun Long, who took on a disciple whose only distinction was an enormously loud voice. The other students thought it absurd until the party reached a river with the ferryman on the far bank. Let each person (人) exhaust (尽) their (其) talent (才) — the claim is not that everyone is talented but that talent is specific, and that the failure is usually in the placing rather than the person.
description_tr: The Huainanzi argues that a ruler's skill lies in placing people where their particular capacity is worth something, and illustrates it with the philosopher Gongsun Long, who took on a disciple whose only distinction was an enormously loud voice. The other students thought it absurd until the party reached a river with the ferryman on the far bank. Let each person (人) exhaust (盡) their (其) talent (才) — the claim is not that everyone is talented but that talent is specific, and that the failure is usually in the placing rather than the person.
chineseExample_tr: 在我們的團隊中，人盡其才，充分發揮每個人的特長。

example: In a successful team, everyone should contribute their strengths to maximize results.
chineseExample: 在一个成功的团队中，每个人都应该发挥自己的优势，物尽其用。
description: Let each thing (物) exhaust (尽) its (其) usefulness (用). It is the companion of 人尽其才 and comes from the same modern formulation of them, Sun Yat-sen's programme that people should fulfil their talents, land its yield, things their use, and goods their circulation. The four clauses were a description of a functioning economy. On its own the phrase has narrowed considerably and now belongs to thrift and recycling — the argument for repairing rather than replacing, and for finding the leftover a job.
description_tr: Let each thing (物) exhaust (盡) its (其) usefulness (用). It is the companion of 人盡其才 and comes from the same modern formulation of them, Sun Yat-sen's programme that people should fulfil their talents, land its yield, things their use, and goods their circulation. The four clauses were a description of a functioning economy. On its own the phrase has narrowed considerably and now belongs to thrift and recycling — the argument for repairing rather than replacing, and for finding the leftover a job.
chineseExample_tr: 在一個成功的團隊中，每個人都應該發揮自己的優勢，物盡其用。

example: The new leader was chosen based on the collective hopes of the community.
chineseExample: 新领导的产生是众望所归。
description: What the many (众) hope for (望) is where it comes to rest (所归). The Book of Jin has it, and the metaphor in 归 is of water finding its way to the sea — the expectations of a great many people converging on one person without anyone organising it. That is what distinguishes the phrase from mere popularity. It describes the appointment that surprises nobody, and Chinese uses it of the candidate everyone had already assumed would be chosen.
description_tr: What the many (眾) hope for (望) is where it comes to rest (所歸). The Book of Jin has it, and the metaphor in 歸 is of water finding its way to the sea — the expectations of a great many people converging on one person without anyone organising it. That is what distinguishes the phrase from mere popularity. It describes the appointment that surprises nobody, and Chinese uses it of the candidate everyone had already assumed would be chosen.
chineseExample_tr: 新領導的產生是眾望所歸。

example: His contributions to the community were recognized by all, earning him widespread acclaim.
chineseExample: 他对社区的贡献得到了大家的认可，有口皆碑。
description: The Song Buddhist compilation Wudeng Huiyuan has the line: do not trouble to carve the stubborn stone, for the mouths of travellers on the road are the tablet. Chinese practice was to record a good official's deeds on an inscribed stele; the argument here is that what people say about you unprompted does the same work and cannot be commissioned. Hence every mouth (有口皆) a monument (碑). It is used of reputation that has clearly not been bought, which is precisely the kind that is worth having.
description_tr: The Song Buddhist compilation Wudeng Huiyuan has the line: do not trouble to carve the stubborn stone, for the mouths of travellers on the road are the tablet. Chinese practice was to record a good official's deeds on an inscribed stele; the argument here is that what people say about you unprompted does the same work and cannot be commissioned. Hence every mouth (有口皆) a monument (碑). It is used of reputation that has clearly not been bought, which is precisely the kind that is worth having.
chineseExample_tr: 他對社區的貢獻得到了大家的認可，有口皆碑。

example: In negotiations, it's crucial to take the initiative to set the terms.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，先发制人是至关重要的。
description: As the risings against Qin spread in 209 BCE, the Kuaiji governor Yin Tong proposed rebelling and put the maxim to Xiang Liang: 先即制人，后则为人所制 — strike first (先发) and you control (制) other men (人); strike late and other men control you. He offered Xiang Liang a command in the rising. Xiang Liang took the advice and not the partnership: he gave his nephew Xiang Yu a look, Xiang Yu drew and beheaded the governor where he sat, and they held the commandery by evening. The man who spoke the line was killed for not acting on it fast enough. The phrase is neutral about whether the aggression is justified — it is about tempo, not about right — and it is used in business and litigation as readily as in war.
description_tr: As the risings against Qin spread in 209 BCE, the Kuaiji governor Yin Tong proposed rebelling and put the maxim to Xiang Liang: 先即制人，後則為人所制 — strike first (先發) and you control (制) other men (人); strike late and other men control you. He offered Xiang Liang a command in the rising. Xiang Liang took the advice and not the partnership: he gave his nephew Xiang Yu a look, Xiang Yu drew and beheaded the governor where he sat, and they held the commandery by evening. The man who spoke the line was killed for not acting on it fast enough. The phrase is neutral about whether the aggression is justified — it is about tempo, not about right — and it is used in business and litigation as readily as in war.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，先發制人是至關重要的。

example: After facing criticism, she adapted her strategy and turned the situation around.
chineseExample: 在遭遇批评后，她后发制人，调整了策略。
description: Xunzi's chapter on warfare contains the counter-doctrine: move later (后发) and arrive before. Where 先发制人 claims the advantage of tempo, this claims the advantage of information — let the other side commit, spend itself, and reveal its shape, then move once against a target that has stopped moving. It is not passivity, and translating it as patience undersells it. The waiting is instrumental, and the phrase implies that the moment to act has been identified rather than merely awaited.
description_tr: Xunzi's chapter on warfare contains the counter-doctrine: move later (後發) and arrive before. Where 先發制人 claims the advantage of tempo, this claims the advantage of information — let the other side commit, spend itself, and reveal its shape, then move once against a target that has stopped moving. It is not passivity, and translating it as patience undersells it. The waiting is instrumental, and the phrase implies that the moment to act has been identified rather than merely awaited.
chineseExample_tr: 在遭遇批評後，她後發制人，調整了策略。

example: In negotiations, he often uses clever tactics to outsmart his opponents.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，他常常使用巧妙的策略来智胜对手。
description: Before the battle of Chengpu, Duke Wen of Jin asked how to fight an enemy with more men. His uncle Fan answered that in matters of ritual one cannot have too much good faith, but between armies one cannot have too much deception — soldiers (兵) are not sated by (不厌) trickery (诈). Han Feizi preserves the exchange, and the two halves matter together: the licence is explicitly bounded to war, not extended to life. It is now used well outside that boundary, in negotiation and competition, and usually as a pre-emptive excuse rather than an observation.
description_tr: Before the battle of Chengpu, Duke Wen of Jin asked how to fight an enemy with more men. His uncle Fan answered that in matters of ritual one cannot have too much good faith, but between armies one cannot have too much deception — soldiers (兵) are not sated by (不厭) trickery (詐). Han Feizi preserves the exchange, and the two halves matter together: the licence is explicitly bounded to war, not extended to life. It is now used well outside that boundary, in negotiation and competition, and usually as a pre-emptive excuse rather than an observation.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，他常常使用巧妙的策略來智勝對手。

example: To succeed in business, it's essential to understand both your strengths and your competitors' weaknesses.
chineseExample: 在商业中，了解自己和竞争对手的优劣势至关重要。
description: Sun Tzu's line in the chapter on attack by stratagem runs 知彼知己，百战不殆 — know the other and know yourself, and a hundred engagements will not endanger you. Two things get lost in the popular version. The order is reversed, the enemy coming first; and the promise is not a hundred victories but a hundred fights without peril, which is a colder and more accurate claim. Sun Tzu grades the rest: knowing yourself alone gives even odds, and knowing neither loses every time.
description_tr: Sun Tzu's line in the chapter on attack by stratagem runs 知彼知己，百戰不殆 — know the other and know yourself, and a hundred engagements will not endanger you. Two things get lost in the popular version. The order is reversed, the enemy coming first; and the promise is not a hundred victories but a hundred fights without peril, which is a colder and more accurate claim. Sun Tzu grades the rest: knowing yourself alone gives even odds, and knowing neither loses every time.
chineseExample_tr: 在商業中，了解自己和競爭對手的優劣勢至關重要。

example: The team's unexpected strategy caught their rivals off guard, leading to a decisive win.
chineseExample: 球队出奇制胜，出乎对手的意料，取得了决定性的胜利。
description: Sun Tzu's formulation is that engagement is made with the orthodox and victory is secured (制胜) by putting out (出) the unorthodox (奇) — 奇 being the force held aside, committed where it is not expected. Tian Dan supplied the illustration a few centuries later at Jimo, tying blades to a thousand oxen, setting their tails alight and driving them into the Yan camp at night. It is worth keeping 奇 distinct from mere surprise: the character means odd in the sense of the leftover, the piece not accounted for in the enemy's arithmetic.
description_tr: Sun Tzu's formulation is that engagement is made with the orthodox and victory is secured (制勝) by putting out (出) the unorthodox (奇) — 奇 being the force held aside, committed where it is not expected. Tian Dan supplied the illustration a few centuries later at Jimo, tying blades to a thousand oxen, setting their tails alight and driving them into the Yan camp at night. It is worth keeping 奇 distinct from mere surprise: the character means odd in the sense of the leftover, the piece not accounted for in the enemy's arithmetic.
chineseExample_tr: 球隊出奇制勝，出乎對手的意料，取得了決定性的勝利。

meaning: Avoid the strong, attack the weak
example: In negotiations, he skillfully sidesteps direct confrontation to find a more advantageous position.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，他巧妙地避实就虚，寻找更有利的位置。
description: Sun Tzu, in the chapter on the full and the empty, compares an army to water — it avoids heights and runs to low ground, and so should force avoid (避) what is solid (实) and go to (就) what is hollow (虚). The military sense is straightforward. What learners should watch for is the second life the phrase has developed: applied to speech rather than war, 避实就虚 means dodging the substantive question and answering an easy one instead, and there the tone is entirely disapproving.
description_tr: Sun Tzu, in the chapter on the full and the empty, compares an army to water — it avoids heights and runs to low ground, and so should force avoid (避) what is solid (實) and go to (就) what is hollow (虛). The military sense is straightforward. What learners should watch for is the second life the phrase has developed: applied to speech rather than war, 避實就虛 means dodging the substantive question and answering an easy one instead, and there the tone is entirely disapproving.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，他巧妙地避實就虛，尋找更有利的位置。

example: To distract the competitor, she created a diversion that allowed her team to gain the upper hand.
chineseExample: 为了分散竞争对手的注意力，她制造了一个转移，帮助团队占据了上风。
description: The fifteenth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the illustration usually given is Sun Ce against Liu Xun, whose position was too strong to attack directly. Sun Ce sent gifts and flattery, urging Liu Xun to go and take a rich neighbouring prize; Liu Xun marched out, and Sun Ce took the base he had left behind. Luring (调) the tiger (虎) away from (离) its mountain (山) is the whole idea — an opponent formidable in position and ordinary out of it, so the work is done by the invitation rather than by the fight.
description_tr: The fifteenth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the illustration usually given is Sun Ce against Liu Xun, whose position was too strong to attack directly. chineseExample_tr: 為了分散競爭對手的注意力，她製造了一個轉移，幫助團隊佔據了上風。

example: By making a sudden move, he revealed his opponent's hidden plans.
chineseExample: 通过突然的举动，他揭示了对手隐藏的计划。
description: A magistrate named Wang Lu, whose own hands were far from clean, was handed a petition accusing his clerk of taking bribes. He wrote on it: you may only have struck the grass (打草), but I am the snake already startled (蛇惊). The confession was accidental and the phrase has outlived him. It names the clumsy move that alerts the person you were hoping to catch unprepared, and it is used most often as a warning before acting — the reason for not asking the obvious question too early.
description_tr: A magistrate named Wang Lu, whose own hands were far from clean, was handed a petition accusing his clerk of taking bribes. He wrote on it: you may only have struck the grass (打草), but I am the snake already startled (蛇驚). The confession was accidental and the phrase has outlived him. chineseExample_tr: 透過突然的舉動，他揭示了對手隱藏的計劃。

example: He manipulated the situation to eliminate his rival without getting his hands dirty.
chineseExample: 他操控局势，借刀杀人，轻松消灭了对手。
description: The third of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: when the enemy is clear but an ally is uncommitted, induce the ally to do the work. Kill a man (杀人) with a borrowed (借) knife (刀). What the phrase specifically supplies is the borrowing — the hand that acts is not yours, so neither is the blame, and the instrument may not understand it is being used. Chinese applies it to office politics as readily as to war, and it is always an accusation, never a description of one's own conduct.
description_tr: The third of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: when the enemy is clear but an ally is uncommitted, induce the ally to do the work. Kill a man (殺人) with a borrowed (借) knife (刀). What the phrase specifically supplies is the borrowing — the hand that acts is not yours, so neither is the blame, and the instrument may not understand it is being used. Chinese applies it to office politics as readily as to war, and it is always an accusation, never a description of one's own conduct.
chineseExample_tr: 他操控局勢，借刀殺人，輕鬆消滅了對手。

meaning: Take advantage of fire to rob
example: Taking advantage of the chaos, he seized the opportunity to profit.
chineseExample: 趁火打劫，他在混乱中获利。
description: The fifth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and among the bluntest: when the enemy is in serious trouble, that is the moment to take from him. Take advantage of (趁) the fire (火) to loot (打劫). Unlike most of the stratagems it has not stayed inside its military frame at all, and in ordinary Chinese it is a straightforward moral condemnation — the supplier who raises prices during a shortage, the rival who briefs against a colleague during their illness. Nobody uses it approvingly.
description_tr: The fifth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and among the bluntest: when the enemy is in serious trouble, that is the moment to take from him. Take advantage of (趁) the fire (火) to loot (打劫). Unlike most of the stratagems it has not stayed inside its military frame at all, and in ordinary Chinese it is a straightforward moral condemnation — the supplier who raises prices during a shortage, the rival who briefs against a colleague during their illness. chineseExample_tr: 趁火打劫，他在混亂中獲利。

example: He managed to escape the scrutiny by cleverly disguising his intentions.
chineseExample: 他巧妙地伪装自己的意图，金蝉脱壳，逃过了审查。
description: The twenty-first of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, though the image is older than the list and appears freely in drama and fiction. A cicada leaves behind a complete, convincing shell, still gripping the bark in the shape of the insect: the golden cicada (金蝉) sheds (脱) its case (壳) and what the pursuer keeps watching is an empty replica. The essential part is the decoy, not the escape. It describes a withdrawal arranged so that the position appears still to be held long after it has been abandoned.
description_tr: The twenty-first of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, though the image is older than the list and appears freely in drama and fiction. A cicada leaves behind a complete, convincing shell, still gripping the bark in the shape of the insect: the golden cicada (金蟬) sheds (脫) its case (殼) and what the pursuer keeps watching is an empty replica. The essential part is the decoy, not the escape. It describes a withdrawal arranged so that the position appears still to be held long after it has been abandoned.
chineseExample_tr: 他巧妙地偽裝自己的意圖，金蟬脫殼，逃過了審查。

example: He took advantage of the situation, easily guiding his team to victory.
chineseExample: 他顺手牵羊，轻松带领团队取得胜利。
description: The twelfth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the mildest in the list: exploit the smallest gap, take the smallest advantage. To lead away (牵) a sheep (羊) in passing (顺手) is deliberately petty — not a campaign but a hand reaching out because the opportunity happened to be there. In modern Chinese it has drifted almost entirely into the sense of casual pilfering, and it is what you say about the guest who leaves with the towels rather than about a strategist.
description_tr: The twelfth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the mildest in the list: exploit the smallest gap, take the smallest advantage. To lead away (牽) a sheep (羊) in passing (順手) is deliberately petty — not a campaign but a hand reaching out because the opportunity happened to be there. In modern Chinese it has drifted almost entirely into the sense of casual pilfering, and it is what you say about the guest who leaves with the towels rather than about a strategist.
chineseExample_tr: 他順手牽羊，輕鬆帶領團隊取得勝利。

example: The general used a clever ruse to mislead the enemy while executing his plan.
chineseExample: 将军用巧妙的计谋来误导敌人，同时执行他的计划。
description: The first of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, illustrated by a tale of Tang Taizong, who had to cross the sea and could not bear the sight of it. His officers built a great enclosed structure hung with curtains, walked him into what appeared to be a house, and set him at a banquet; when the wind rose he pulled back a curtain and found himself well out to sea. Deceiving (瞒) heaven (天) to cross (过) the sea (海) works by the ordinary rather than the exotic — the most complete cover is a familiar thing nobody thinks to inspect.
description_tr: The first of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, illustrated by a tale of Tang Taizong, who had to cross the sea and could not bear the sight of it. Deceiving (瞞) heaven (天) to cross (過) the sea (海) works by the ordinary rather than the exotic — the most complete cover is a familiar thing nobody thinks to inspect.
chineseExample_tr: 將軍用巧妙的計謀來誤導敵人，同時執行他的計劃。

example: In negotiations, he sacrificed one deal to secure a more advantageous one.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，他牺牲了一个交易以确保一个更有利的交易。
description: A Han ballad in the Yuefu collection supplies the image: a peach tree grows by the well, a plum tree beside it, and when insects come to gnaw the peach's roots the plum stands in its place and dies (僵) instead. The poem draws the moral about brothers who fail to do the same for each other. So the plum (李) substitutes for (代) the peach (桃), and the phrase names a sacrifice of one part to preserve another — used both for the scapegoat who takes a punishment and, coldly, for the piece a strategist decides to give up.
description_tr: A Han ballad in the Yuefu collection supplies the image: a peach tree grows by the well, a plum tree beside it, and when insects come to gnaw the peach's roots the plum stands in its place and dies (僵) instead.
