So the plum (李) substitutes for (代) the peach (桃), and the phrase names a sacrifice of one part to preserve another — used both for the scapegoat who takes a punishment and, coldly, for the piece a strategist decides to give up.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，他犧牲了一個交易以確保一個更有利的交易。

example: In the meeting, she took charge and redirected the discussion to her agenda.
chineseExample: 在会议上，她掌控了局面，将讨论引导到她的议程上。
description: The thirtieth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the textbook illustration is Liu Bei in Yi Province: Liu Zhang invited him in as a guest to deal with Zhang Lu, quartered his troops and supplied them, and found by 214 that the guest held the province. The stratagem text describes the method as gradual — get a foot in the gap, take hold of the controls, advance by degrees. In Chinese social terms guest (客) and host (主) are strictly ranked, the host setting the terms and the guest accepting them, so reversing (反) them is a status inversion as much as a tactical one. It describes the consultant who ends up running the department, and the junior partner who ends up setting the agenda.
description_tr: The thirtieth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, and the textbook illustration is Liu Bei in Yi Province: Liu Zhang invited him in as a guest to deal with Zhang Lu, quartered his troops and supplied them, and found by 214 that the guest held the province. The stratagem text describes the method as gradual — get a foot in the gap, take hold of the controls, advance by degrees. In Chinese social terms guest (客) and host (主) are strictly ranked, the host setting the terms and the guest accepting them, so reversing (反) them is a status inversion as much as a tactical one. It describes the consultant who ends up running the department, and the junior partner who ends up setting the agenda.
chineseExample_tr: 在會議上，她掌控了局面，將討論引導到她的議程上。

example: To resolve the conflict, they targeted the leader rather than the followers.
chineseExample: 为了解决冲突，他们的目标是领导者而不是追随者。
description: Du Fu wrote it in a frontier poem, in a couplet that is quoted more often than the poem: to shoot a man first shoot his horse, to catch the bandits (擒贼) first catch (擒) their king (王). The eighteenth stratagem takes it up. What makes it more than obvious advice is the second half of Du Fu's argument, that killing has limits and states have borders — the point of going for the head is to end the thing quickly rather than to fight everyone. It is used of root causes as often as of people.
description_tr: Du Fu wrote it in a frontier poem, in a couplet that is quoted more often than the poem: to shoot a man first shoot his horse, to catch the bandits (擒賊) first catch (擒) their king (王). The eighteenth stratagem takes it up. What makes it more than obvious advice is the second half of Du Fu's argument, that killing has limits and states have borders — the point of going for the head is to end the thing quickly rather than to fight everyone. It is used of root causes as often as of people.
chineseExample_tr: 為了解決衝突，他們的目標是領導者而不是追隨者。

example: By limiting options, they effectively trapped their competitor in a corner.
chineseExample: 通过限制选择，他们有效地将竞争对手逼入了绝境。
description: The twenty-second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: against a small and mobile enemy, close the escape first and fight second, because a force you cannot catch will simply return. Shut (关) the door (门) and take (捉) the thief (贼). The stratagem is careful to limit itself to a weak opponent — cornering a strong one produces the desperate resistance the tactic is meant to avoid — and that qualification is generally lost when the phrase is used outside its source.
description_tr: The twenty-second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: against a small and mobile enemy, close the escape first and fight second, because a force you cannot catch will simply return. Shut (關) the door (門) and take (捉) the thief (賊). The stratagem is careful to limit itself to a weak opponent — cornering a strong one produces the desperate resistance the tactic is meant to avoid — and that qualification is generally lost when the phrase is used outside its source.
chineseExample_tr: 通過限制選擇，他們有效地將競爭對手逼入了絕境。

example: In the game of politics, forming alliances with distant nations while undermining local rivals can be a winning strategy.
chineseExample: 在政治博弈中，远交近攻的策略常常能取得胜利。
description: Fan Ju arrived in Qin and told King Zhaoxiang that his campaigns made no sense: Qin was attacking distant states and leaving neighbours intact, so every victory produced land it could not hold. Ally with the far (远交) and attack the near (近攻), he argued, and each conquest is contiguous and keepable. The Strategies of the Warring States records it, and Qin's unification of China followed the policy for decades. It remains a genuinely useful principle about the order of operations, in business as much as in war.
description_tr: Fan Ju arrived in Qin and told King Zhaoxiang that his campaigns made no sense: Qin was attacking distant states and leaving neighbours intact, so every victory produced land it could not hold. Ally with the far (遠交) and attack the near (近攻), he argued, and each conquest is contiguous and keepable. The Strategies of the Warring States records it, and Qin's unification of China followed the policy for decades. It remains a genuinely useful principle about the order of operations, in business as much as in war.
chineseExample_tr: 在政治博弈中，遠交近攻的策略常常能取得勝利。

meaning: Borrow the way to attack Guo
example: He cleverly used a false pretext to undermine his competitor's position in the market.
chineseExample: 他巧妙地假道伐虢，削弱了竞争对手的市场地位。
description: This strategic idiom originates from the historical account in the 'Zuo Zhuan' (左传), a classical Chinese text. During the Spring and Autumn period, the state of Jin (晋国) sought to conquer the neighboring state of Guo (虢国). To achieve this, Jin needed to pass through the state of Yu (虞国). The Jin minister, Xun Xi (荀息), advised offering Yu valuable gifts to borrow their territory as a pathway. Despite warnings from his advisor Gong Zhiqi (宫之奇), the ruler of Yu accepted the gifts and allowed Jin's army to pass. Jin subsequently attacked and conquered Guo, and later turned on Yu, annexing it as well. The idiom '假道伐虢' (jiǎ dào fá guó) literally means 'borrow the way to attack Guo' and highlights the danger of short-sighted decisions. In modern usage, it warns against allowing others to exploit one's resources for their own gain.
description_tr: This strategic idiom originates from the historical account in the 'Zuo Zhuan' (左傳), a classical Chinese text. During the Spring and Autumn period, the state of Jin (晉國) sought to conquer the neighboring state of Guo (虢國). To achieve this, Jin needed to pass through the state of Yu (虞國). The Jin minister, Xun Xi (荀息), advised offering Yu valuable gifts to borrow their territory as a pathway. Despite warnings from his advisor Gong Zhiqi (宮之奇), the ruler of Yu accepted the gifts and allowed Jin's army to pass. Jin subsequently attacked and conquered Guo, and later turned on Yu, annexing it as well. The idiom '假道伐虢' (jiǎ dào fá guó) literally means 'borrow the way to attack Guo' and highlights the danger of short-sighted decisions. In modern usage, it warns against allowing others to exploit one's resources for their own gain.
chineseExample_tr: 他巧妙地假道伐虢，削弱了競爭對手的市場地位。

example: His unexpected promotion was like flowers blooming on a tree, surprising everyone around him.
chineseExample: 他的意外晋升就像树上开花，让周围的人都感到惊讶。
description: The twenty-ninth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: where a tree (树) has no blossom, tie silk flowers (花) onto (上) it, and at a distance it appears to bloom (开). Applied to war, it means borrowing an appearance of strength you do not possess. The example usually given is Zhang Fei alone at the bridge on the Changban road, with his few horsemen dragging branches in the woods behind him to raise dust like an army in reserve. The whole force of the stratagem is that the deception must not be inspected, so it buys time rather than victory.
description_tr: The twenty-ninth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: where a tree (樹) has no blossom, tie silk flowers (花) onto (上) it, and at a distance it appears to bloom (開). Applied to war, it means borrowing an appearance of strength you do not possess. The example usually given is Zhang Fei alone at the bridge on the Changban road, with his few horsemen dragging branches in the woods behind him to raise dust like an army in reserve. The whole force of the stratagem is that the deception must not be inspected, so it buys time rather than victory.
chineseExample_tr: 他的意外晉升就像樹上開花，讓周圍的人都感到驚訝。

example: When faced with overwhelming odds, sometimes the best strategy is to retreat and regroup.
chineseExample: 面对压倒性的敌人，有时候走为上计是最好的策略。
description: Wang Jingze, in rebellion during the Southern Qi, heard that his opponent was preparing to flee the capital and remarked that of Duke Tan's thirty-six stratagems, running was the best one — the earliest surviving reference to any such list, and the origin of its name. He meant it as mockery. The phrase kept the number and lost the sneer, and running (走) as the best (上) plan (计) is now offered seriously: when a position cannot be held, leaving it intact is a better outcome than being destroyed in it.
description_tr: Wang Jingze, in rebellion during the Southern Qi, heard that his opponent was preparing to flee the capital and remarked that of Duke Tan's thirty-six stratagems, running was the best one — the earliest surviving reference to any such list, and the origin of its name. He meant it as mockery. The phrase kept the number and lost the sneer, and running (走) as the best (上) plan (計) is now offered seriously: when a position cannot be held, leaving it intact is a better outcome than being destroyed in it.
chineseExample_tr: 面對壓倒性的敵人，有時候走為上計是最好的策略。

example: The detective set a trap to catch all the suspects in one go.
chineseExample: 侦探设下圈套，一网打尽所有嫌疑犯。
description: One (一) net (网) taking (打) the lot (尽). A Song anecdote has an official using it after arresting an entire faction at a single banquet, and the phrase has kept that flavour of a coordinated sweep. Chinese uses it most naturally of police operations and anti-corruption drives, where the point is that nobody was left to warn the others. Applied to opportunities or customers it sounds ambitious and slightly predatory, which is often exactly the intention.
description_tr: One (一) net (網) taking (打) the lot (盡). A Song anecdote has an official using it after arresting an entire faction at a single banquet, and the phrase has kept that flavour of a coordinated sweep. Chinese uses it most naturally of police operations and anti-corruption drives, where the point is that nobody was left to warn the others. Applied to opportunities or customers it sounds ambitious and slightly predatory, which is often exactly the intention.
chineseExample_tr: 偵探設下圈套，一網打盡所有嫌疑犯。

example: In a heated debate, it's sometimes better to avoid the sharp points and focus on common ground.
chineseExample: 在激烈的辩论中，有时候避其锐气更能达成共识。
description: This strategic idiom originates from the ancient military text 'The Art of War' by Sun Tzu (孙子兵法). It advises military leaders to avoid (避, bì) confronting the enemy's initial vigor (锐气, ruì qì) when their morale is high. Instead, it suggests waiting until the enemy becomes fatigued and complacent before launching an attack. This tactic was famously applied during the Battle of Changshao (长勺之战) in the Spring and Autumn period, where the strategist Cao Gui (曹刿) led the state of Lu to victory by exploiting the enemy's diminishing morale. In modern contexts, this idiom is used to describe strategies in competitive fields, emphasizing the importance of timing and patience in overcoming opponents.
description_tr: This strategic idiom originates from the ancient military text 'The Art of War' by Sun Tzu (孫子兵法). It advises military leaders to avoid (避, bì) confronting the enemy's initial vigor (銳氣, ruì qì) when their morale is high. Instead, it suggests waiting until the enemy becomes fatigued and complacent before launching an attack. This tactic was famously applied during the Battle of Changshao (長勺之戰) in the Spring and Autumn period, where the strategist Cao Gui (曹刿) led the state of Lu to victory by exploiting the enemy's diminishing morale. In modern contexts, this idiom is used to describe strategies in competitive fields, emphasizing the importance of timing and patience in overcoming opponents.
chineseExample_tr: 在激烈的辯論中，有時候避其銳氣更能達成共識。

meaning: Three in the morning, four at night
example: His indecisiveness led to constant changes in plans, leaving everyone confused.
chineseExample: 他的优柔寡断导致计划不断变化，让大家感到困惑。
description: The Zhuangzi tells of a monkey keeper who, running short, told his monkeys they would have three acorns in the morning (朝三) and four at night (暮四). The monkeys were furious. He offered four in the morning and three at night, and they were delighted. Zhuangzi's point is about the sage, who wearies neither himself nor others by disputing over what is in substance identical. The modern meaning has drifted well away from that: today 朝三暮四 nearly always means fickle and changeable, and the arithmetic in the story has been forgotten.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi tells of a monkey keeper who, running short, told his monkeys they would have three acorns in the morning (朝三) and four at night (暮四). The monkeys were furious. He offered four in the morning and three at night, and they were delighted. Zhuangzi's point is about the sage, who wearies neither himself nor others by disputing over what is in substance identical. The modern meaning has drifted well away from that: today 朝三暮四 nearly always means fickle and changeable, and the arithmetic in the story has been forgotten.
chineseExample_tr: 他的優柔寡斷導致計劃不斷變化，讓大家感到困惑。

example: In a close friendship, their support for each other is essential for their well-being.
chineseExample: 在亲密的友谊中，他们彼此的支持对彼此的幸福至关重要。
description: Two states that cannot survive each other's loss lean (相依) on one another as lips (唇) and teeth (齿) do. The image comes from the Zuo Zhuan, where Gong Zhiqi of Yu opposed letting Jin march through to attack Guo and quoted the proverb 辅车相依，唇亡齿寒 — cheekbone and jaw depend on each other, and when the lips are gone the teeth are cold. He was overruled; Jin destroyed Guo and took Yu on the way home. This exact four-character form is later, from a Wei official in the Records of the Three Kingdoms describing Wu and Shu as 唇齿相依. 唇亡齿寒 states the consequence, and this one states the relation.
description_tr: Two states that cannot survive each other's loss lean (相依) on one another as lips (唇) and teeth (齒) do. The image comes from the Zuo Zhuan, where Gong Zhiqi of Yu opposed letting Jin march through to attack Guo and quoted the proverb 輔車相依，唇亡齒寒 — cheekbone and jaw depend on each other, and when the lips are gone the teeth are cold. He was overruled; Jin destroyed Guo and took Yu on the way home. This exact four-character form is later, from a Wei official in the Records of the Three Kingdoms describing Wu and Shu as 唇齒相依. 唇亡齒寒 states the consequence, and this one states the relation.
chineseExample_tr: 在親密的友誼中，他們彼此的支持對彼此的幸福至關重要。

example: His quiet demeanor often led others to underestimate his intelligence.
chineseExample: 他的沉默寡言常常让人低估他的智慧。
description: Silent (沉默) and sparing of words (寡言). What makes it worth learning is that it is neutral to positive in Chinese where its English equivalents tend not to be. Calling someone taciturn or uncommunicative implies a deficiency; 沉默寡言 more often implies weight, a person who does not speak until there is something to say. It is a normal thing to write in a reference, which 'says very little' would not be.
description_tr: Silent (沉默) and sparing of words (寡言). What makes it worth learning is that it is neutral to positive in Chinese where its English equivalents tend not to be. Calling someone taciturn or uncommunicative implies a deficiency; 沉默寡言 more often implies weight, a person who does not speak until there is something to say. It is a normal thing to write in a reference, which 'says very little' would not be.
chineseExample_tr: 他的沉默寡言常常讓人低估他的智慧。

example: He chose to report his corrupt brother to the authorities, prioritizing justice over family loyalty.
chineseExample: 他选择向当局举报腐败的兄弟，把正义置于家庭忠诚之上。
description: Shi Que's son Shi Hou had helped Zhou Xu murder the ruler of Wei and take his place. Shi Que, retired and consulted as an elder, arranged for both men to travel to Chen, and sent word ahead that they should be seized. Both were executed, his son among them. The Zuo Zhuan's compiler calls this great duty (大义) destroying (灭) kin (亲), and means it as praise. The phrase is still used approvingly, and it retains the weight of the original case — it is not for reporting a relative's parking offence.

chineseExample_tr: 他選擇向當局舉報腐敗的兄弟，把正義置於家庭忠誠之上。

example: He focused on self-improvement and personal growth, choosing to prioritize his own development over social distractions.
chineseExample: 他专注于自我提升和个人成长，选择将自己的发展置于社交干扰之上。
description: Mencius states it as a pair: 穷则独善其身，达则兼善天下 — in obscurity, perfect yourself alone; in success, extend that good to the world. The first half was never meant to stand by itself, and lifting it out is what changed its meaning. On its own it now describes someone who tends their own patch and declines to be involved in anything else, and Chinese speakers use it with a distinct coolness. The full sentence makes solitary self-cultivation a holding position; the idiom as used makes it a settled policy.

example: The new skincare treatment promises to turn back the clock on aging.
chineseExample: 这种新的护肤疗法承诺能让人返老还童。
description: The phrase belongs to Daoist longevity literature, where reversing (返) age (老) and returning (还) to childhood (童) was not a figure of speech but the stated aim of a practice — breath work, diet, alchemy, the whole apparatus of internal cultivation. Nobody uses it literally now. What survives is the observation of unexpected vitality in someone old, and it is a warm thing to say: the retired colleague who has taken up cycling, the grandmother who is suddenly the loudest person at the table.

chineseExample_tr: 這種新的護膚療法承諾能讓人返老還童。

example: By planning ahead, the company avoided potential crises.
chineseExample: 通过提前规划，公司防患未然。
description: The Book of Changes gives the underlying instruction — the superior person thinks about trouble and guards against it beforehand — and this is its compressed form: guard against (防) the calamity (患) that has not yet (未) happened (然). What distinguishes it from ordinary caution is the tense. It concerns the problem that does not exist, which is the hardest kind to spend money or attention on, and Chinese uses it in exactly the arguments where that is the difficulty: maintenance budgets, safety procedure, seeing a doctor while still well.

example: His contributions to science have left a lasting legacy.
chineseExample: 他的科学贡献丰功伟绩，流传后世。
description: Abundant (丰) merit (功) and great (伟) achievement (绩). 绩 is a weaving word underneath — the twisting of hemp fibres into thread — so what the phrase measures is accumulation rather than a single stroke, work laid down over a long time until it amounts to something. That suits its use. It is applied to careers and reigns rather than to individual feats, it belongs to eulogies and official histories, and using it about a colleague's quarter would be heavy irony.

example: The harvest this year was abundant, thanks to the perfect weather.
chineseExample: 今年的收成丰收，风调雨顺。
description: Winds (风) in measure (调) and rains (雨) in season (顺). It is agricultural before it is anything else, and precise about what farming actually needs — not good weather but timely weather, arriving in the right order and quantity. The phrase is ancient and appears in early statecraft texts as the mark of a well-governed reign, on the theory that heaven answered good government with regular seasons. It survives mainly in New Year greetings and on temple offerings, usually paired with 国泰民安, the country at peace and its people secure.
description_tr: Winds (風) in measure (調) and rains (雨) in season (順). It is agricultural before it is anything else, and precise about what farming actually needs — not good weather but timely weather, arriving in the right order and quantity. chineseExample_tr: 今年的收成豐收，風調雨順。

example: After realizing his errors, he decided to change his ways and improve.
chineseExample: 意识到错误后，他决定改过自新。
description: The Records of the Grand Historian tells of Chunyu Yi, sentenced to mutilation, whose youngest daughter Tiying travelled to the capital and petitioned the emperor: a punishment that removes a limb cannot be undone, so a man who later wishes to correct (改) his faults (过) and renew (新) himself (自) has no road back. Emperor Wen abolished the mutilating punishments. The phrase carries that argument inside it — the case for reform rests on the claim that the door must be left open.
description_tr: The Records of the Grand Historian tells of Chunyu Yi, sentenced to mutilation, whose youngest daughter Tiying travelled to the capital and petitioned the emperor: a punishment that removes a limb cannot be undone, so a man who later wishes to correct (改) his faults (過) and renew (新) himself (自) has no road back. chineseExample_tr: 意識到錯誤後，他決定改過自新。

meaning: Look far from a high place
example: The leader's vision for the future was clear and inspiring, guiding the team toward long-term success.
chineseExample: 这位领导的远见卓识为团队指明了长期成功的方向。
description: High (高) looking (瞻), far (远) gazing (瞩) — a person on high ground, seeing distance rather than detail. The compliment is specifically about scale of view, and Chinese distinguishes it from cleverness: someone can be 高瞻远瞩 and quite wrong about particulars, which is often exactly what is meant. It suits founders, planners and statesmen, and it appears constantly in official writing. In ordinary conversation it is grand enough that it can tip into irony if the plan in question has not worked.
description_tr: High (高) looking (瞻), far (遠) gazing (矚) — a person on high ground, seeing distance rather than detail. chineseExample_tr: 這位領導的遠見卓識為團隊指明了長期成功的方向。

example: In a diverse team, everyone contributes their unique skills, leading to a well-rounded project.
chineseExample: 在这个多元化的团队中，各行其是，大家各自发挥特长，最终完成了一个全面的项目。
description: Each (各) does (行) what they (其) think right (是). The final character is the trap for learners: 是 here means right or correct, not the copula, so the phrase describes people acting on their own judgement rather than merely acting separately. That is what makes it a criticism. The problem it names is not laziness or conflict but the absence of a settled common line, with everyone conscientiously pursuing their own version, and it is the standard Chinese diagnosis of a committee that has stopped functioning.

chineseExample_tr: 在這個多元化的團隊中，各行其是，大家各自發揮特長，最終完成了一個全面的項目。

example: She always puts the team's needs above her own, earning the respect of her colleagues.
chineseExample: 她总是把团队的需求放在自己之上，赢得了同事们的尊重。
description: For the public good (公) and thereby forgetting (忘) the private (私). The Book of Han attaches the sentiment to Jia Yi, the young scholar-official whose memorials to Emperor Wen argued for reforms that cost him his position at court. The construction matters: not sacrificing self-interest, which implies a struggle, but forgetting it, which claims the interest never came up. That is a very high bar and the phrase knows it. It belongs to citations and memorials, and it is said about people more often than by them.
metaphoric_meaning: Public duty crowds out private interest

chineseExample_tr: 她總是把團隊的需求放在自己之上，贏得了同事們的尊重。

example: He decided to invest all his savings in the startup, believing it was his best chance for success.
chineseExample: 他决定孤注一掷，把所有的积蓄都投资在这个初创公司上，认为这是他成功的最佳机会。
description: The History of Song records the slander that Wang Qinruo laid before Emperor Zhenzong about Kou Zhun, who had pushed the emperor to the front at the Chanyuan campaign: a gambler down to his last stake (孤注) throws (掷) everything on one cast, and Your Majesty was that stake. The accusation worked and Kou Zhun fell. The phrase keeps the gambling table exactly. It describes the move made because no further moves remain, and it is neutral about courage — the same act reads as decisive or desperate depending only on the result.

example: By focusing too much on minor details, he overlooked the bigger picture and missed the deadline.
chineseExample: 他过于关注细节，顾此失彼，最终错过了截止日期。
description: Attend to (顾) this one (此) and lose (失) that one (彼). The phrase names a specific failure mode rather than general carelessness: not neglect, but the impossibility of covering two things with resources sufficient for one, so that every correction opens a gap somewhere else. It is what you say about a defence stretched along too long a line, a team of three running four projects, or a budget being moved from one shortfall to another. The implication is always that the underlying allocation is wrong.

chineseExample_tr: 他過於關注細節，顧此失彼，最終錯過了截止日期。

example: She worked tirelessly through difficult times to achieve her dreams.
chineseExample: 她在艰难的时刻努力工作，实现了自己的梦想。
description: 茹 is to swallow, and 辛 is pungent rather than bitter — the sharpness of ginger and pepper. So the phrase is about holding (含) something acrid in the mouth and swallowing (茹) something bitter (苦), which is a more physical image than English 'endure hardship'. Its usage is strongly gendered by custom: it attaches above all to mothers, and specifically to years of unremarked domestic effort on someone else's behalf. It is a phrase of gratitude, most often said too late.

meaning: Fond of high and distant goals
example: His lofty ambitions often lead to disappointment when reality sets in.
chineseExample: 他的雄心壮志常常在现实面前让他失望。
description: To be fond of (好) the high (高) and chase (骛) the distant (远). Song neo-Confucian writing uses it as a complaint about students who find the near and low beneath them and reach straight for the profound. 骛 is a horse galloping, and it carries the flavour of the whole phrase — not ambition but ambition that will not stay still long enough to do the groundwork. It is one of the most common criticisms in Chinese education, aimed at the person who wants the result without the sequence that produces it.

Song neo-Confucian writing uses it as a complaint about students who find the near and low beneath them and reach straight for the profound. 騖 is a horse galloping, and it carries the flavour of the whole phrase — not ambition but ambition that will not stay still long enough to do the groundwork. It is one of the most common criticisms in Chinese education, aimed at the person who wants the result without the sequence that produces it.
chineseExample_tr: 他的雄心壯志常常在現實面前讓他失望。

example: His ambitions are as lofty as those of a swan soaring in the sky.
chineseExample: 他的志向像天上的鸿鹄一样高远。
description: Chen Sheng, hired out as a farm labourer, told the others in the field that if any of them grew rich they should not forget the rest. They laughed at a hired hand talking about wealth. He answered: how should the sparrow and the swallow know the ambition (志) of the great swan (鸿鹄)? Within a few years he had raised the first rebellion against Qin. He was also dead within months of raising it, which the Records of the Grand Historian records without comment. The phrase means ambition that the people around you are not equipped to recognise.

The phrase means ambition that the people around you are not equipped to recognise.
chineseExample_tr: 他的志向像天上的鴻鹄一樣高遠。

example: Their wedding was a perfect celebration of love and harmony.
chineseExample: 他们的婚礼是对爱情与和谐的完美庆祝。
description: Flowers (花) at their best (好), the moon (月) full (圆). Both halves name a peak that is by definition brief — blossom and full moon each last a few days — so the phrase carries its own transience inside it, which is very Chinese and largely invisible in translation. In practice it has become a wedding formula, painted on gifts and said in toasts, and the wistfulness has been worn away by use. It is the standard wish for a couple, and nobody hears the clock in it any more.

chineseExample_tr: 他們的婚禮是對愛情與和諧的完美慶祝。

example: True friends stand by each other in both good times and bad.
chineseExample: 真正的朋友在患难与共时相互支持。
description: The Book of Rites, describing the conduct of the scholar, includes standing together with others through trouble. Hence sharing (与共) hardship (患难). The phrase claims something narrower than friendship: it is specifically about the behaviour of the relationship under load, and the implicit contrast is with the companions who are present for the good part. Chinese pairs it naturally with 同甘共苦, and it appears in wedding vows, in political rhetoric about allies, and in the retrospective assessment of who actually turned up.

example: He spends money so freely that it seems he doesn't value it at all.
chineseExample: 他花钱挥金如土，完全不在乎。
description: Scattering (挥) gold (金) like (如) dirt (土). The Song writer Mao Pang used it in a funeral piece for a friend whose openhandedness was the point of the praise, and traces of that warmth occasionally survive. Modern use is almost entirely disapproving. What the phrase condemns is not the quantity spent but the attitude in 挥, a hand thrown out carelessly — money treated as if it were the one thing there is no need to count, generally by someone who did not earn it.

example: Realizing his mistakes, he decided to turn back and seek redemption.
chineseExample: 意识到自己的错误后，他决定回头是岸。
description: Buddhist teaching supplies the picture: the sea of suffering is boundless, and the shore is behind you — 苦海无边，回头是岸. To turn the head (回头) is (是) the shore (岸). What makes the phrase forceful is that no journey is required. The shore is not reached by swimming further but by turning, so the distance to safety is zero at every point, however far out the swimmer has gone. It is said to people who believe they have gone too far to stop, and it is the standard Chinese appeal to someone in the middle of ruining their life.
description_tr: Buddhist teaching supplies the picture: the sea of suffering is boundless, and the shore is behind you — 苦海無邊，回頭是岸. To turn the head (回頭) is (是) the shore (岸). example: He is known for his courage in defending those who are wronged.
chineseExample: 他以见义勇为而闻名，常常为受害者辩护。
description: Confucius put it as a negative — to see what is right (见义) and not do it is to lack courage (无勇) — and the idiom is his sentence turned the right way up: seeing what is right and acting (为) bravely (勇) on it. The specific condition is that nothing obliges you. In modern China the phrase has a concrete legal and civic life, attached to awards and compensation schemes for bystanders injured while intervening, which is an unusually direct survival of a line from the Analects.
description_tr: Confucius put it as a negative — to see what is right (見義) and not do it is to lack courage (無勇) — and the idiom is his sentence turned the right way up: seeing what is right and acting (為) bravely (勇) on it. chineseExample_tr: 他以見義勇為而聞名，常常為受害者辯護。

example: He is trying to maintain relationships with both sides, which is causing confusion.
chineseExample: 他脚踏两船，导致了许多误会。
description: A foot (脚) planted (踏) in two (两) boats (船) — usually said in full as 脚踏两只船. The image does its own arguing: the position is possible only while the boats stay together, and boats do not. Chinese uses it in two settled contexts, the person hedging between two employers or factions, and the person conducting two romances at once, where it is the ordinary way of putting the accusation. In both, the prediction is the same, and it is about physics rather than morality.

example: Unexpected complications arose, making the project more difficult than anticipated.
chineseExample: 项目中节外生枝，导致了许多额外的工作。
description: Zhu Xi used it complaining about how people read: a branch (枝) sprouting (生) outside (外) the joint (节), growth in the wrong place that draws strength from the plant. He meant the reader who cannot take a text as it stands without spinning off questions it did not raise. Modern use has widened to any unnecessary complication arriving mid-task — the new objection at the end of a negotiation, the extra requirement added after sign-off — and it is nearly always said with irritation.

example: The new features in the app are just the icing on the cake.
chineseExample: 这个应用程序的新功能简直是锦上添花。
description: Adding flowers (添花) onto brocade (锦上), which is already patterned with them. Song poets used the image, and its whole force comes from the phrase Chinese sets against it: 雪中送炭, carrying charcoal to someone in the snow. One is help that arrives when it changes nothing, the other help that arrives when it changes everything. Because the pairing is so well established, 锦上添花 is rarely neutral — describing a gesture that way quietly notes that the giver waited until the recipient no longer needed them.

One is help that arrives when it changes nothing, the other help that arrives when it changes everything. Because the pairing is so well established, 錦上添花 is rarely neutral — describing a gesture that way quietly notes that the giver waited until the recipient no longer needed them.
chineseExample_tr: 這個應用程式的新功能簡直是錦上添花。

example: After the incident, he became very jumpy and anxious.
chineseExample: 事件发生后，他变得像惊弓之鸟一样，十分紧张。
description: Geng Lei told the King of Wei he could bring down a bird without an arrow. A goose came over, he plucked the empty bowstring, and it dropped. Asked how, he said he had read the bird: 飞徐者，故疮痛也；鸣悲者，久失群也 — it flew slowly because an old wound still hurt, and cried sadly because it had long been separated from its flock. At the sound of the string it climbed, tore the wound open and fell. The Strategies of the Warring States tells it as a lesson about a defeated army. The bird (鸟) startled (惊) by the bow (弓) alone is the image, and it describes anyone whose past injury does the enemy's work for them.
description_tr: Geng Lei told the King of Wei he could bring down a bird without an arrow. A goose came over, he plucked the empty bowstring, and it dropped. Asked how, he said he had read the bird: 飛徐者，故瘡痛也；鳴悲者，久失群也 — it flew slowly because an old wound still hurt, and cried sadly because it had long been separated from its flock. At the sound of the string it climbed, tore the wound open and fell. The Strategies of the Warring States tells it as a lesson about a defeated army. The bird (鳥) startled (驚) by the bow (弓) alone is the image, and it describes anyone whose past injury does the enemy's work for them.
chineseExample_tr: 事件發生後，他變得像驚弓之鳥一樣，十分緊張。

example: Her attention to detail in the project was nothing short of exquisite.
chineseExample: 她在这个项目中的细致入微，真是精雕细刻。
description: Fine (精) carving (雕) and detailed (细) cutting (刻) — the vocabulary of the workshop, jade and wood and seal-stone, where the material permits no correction and the whole quality of the piece is in the patience. Applied to other work it keeps that implication: not merely careful but slow by necessity, with the finish inseparable from the time taken. It is genuine praise for craft, and it turns faintly critical only when the object plainly did not deserve the hours.
description_tr: Fine (精) carving (雕) and detailed (細) cutting (刻) — the vocabulary of the workshop, jade and wood and seal-stone, where the material permits no correction and the whole quality of the piece is in the patience. Applied to other work it keeps that implication: not merely careful but slow by necessity, with the finish inseparable from the time taken. It is genuine praise for craft, and it turns faintly critical only when the object plainly did not deserve the hours.
chineseExample_tr: 她在這個項目中的細緻入微，真是精雕細刻。

example: His arrogance about his success made him unpopular among his peers.
chineseExample: 他对自己的成就居功自傲，导致同事们都不喜欢他。
description: To sit on (居) one's merit (功) and be arrogant (自傲) about it. Chinese history supplies a standing example in Xu You, who crossed over to Cao Cao in the tenth month of 200, at the crisis of the Guandu campaign, and brought with him the intelligence that won it, and afterwards would not stop reminding everyone — including Cao Cao — that they owed him the victory. He was killed for it. The phrase names a specific sequence rather than ordinary vanity: the achievement is real, the claim is just, and the insistence on it destroys the credit anyway.
description_tr: To sit on (居) one's merit (功) and be arrogant (自傲) about it. Chinese history supplies a standing example in Xu You, who crossed over to Cao Cao in the tenth month of 200, at the crisis of the Guandu campaign, and brought with him the intelligence that won it, and afterwards would not stop reminding everyone — including Cao Cao — that they owed him the victory. He was killed for it. The phrase names a specific sequence rather than ordinary vanity: the achievement is real, the claim is just, and the insistence on it destroys the credit anyway.
chineseExample_tr: 他對自己的成就居功自傲，導致同事們都不喜歡他。

example: The artist is globally recognized for her unique style.
chineseExample: 这位艺术家在全球举世闻名。
description: Lifted up (举) before the world (世), heard of (闻) by name (名). It differs from its near-neighbour 举世瞩目 in tense: 瞩目 is the world watching now, while 闻名 is the world already knowing. So this one describes established reputation and that one describes current attention. It suits monuments, dishes and long-dead scientists, and it is the ordinary way to say world-famous.
description_tr: Lifted up (舉) before the world (世), heard of (聞) by name (名). It differs from its near-neighbour 舉世矚目 in tense: 矚目 is the world watching now, while 聞名 is the world already knowing. So this one describes established reputation and that one describes current attention. It suits monuments, dishes and long-dead scientists, and it is the ordinary way to say world-famous.
chineseExample_tr: 這位藝術家在全球舉世聞名。

example: The athlete's record-breaking performance drew global attention.
chineseExample: 这位运动员的破纪录表现举世瞩目。
description: The whole world (举世) fixes its gaze (瞩目). The construction is old — early texts speak of being under the eyes of the people of a state — and the modern phrase simply enlarges the audience. It is neutral about the verdict, which is worth knowing: it describes the volume of attention and not its warmth, so an achievement and a scandal can both be 举世瞩目. In practice Chinese official writing uses it almost entirely for the favourable case, and the neutrality only shows when someone is being careful.
description_tr: The whole world (舉世) fixes its gaze (矚目). The construction is old — early texts speak of being under the eyes of the people of a state — and the modern phrase simply enlarges the audience. It is neutral about the verdict, which is worth knowing: it describes the volume of attention and not its warmth, so an achievement and a scandal can both be 舉世矚目. In practice Chinese official writing uses it almost entirely for the favourable case, and the neutrality only shows when someone is being careful.
chineseExample_tr: 這位運動員的破紀錄表現舉世矚目。

example: Every time I read a new book, I learn something valuable.
chineseExample: 每当我读一本新书，开卷有益。
description: Emperor Taizong of Song commissioned a vast encyclopaedia and then undertook to read the whole of it, three scrolls a day, finishing in a year. Told he was damaging his health, he answered that opening (开) a scroll (卷) is always of benefit (有益), and that he did not find it tiring. The book was renamed in honour of the imperial reading and is known by that title still. The phrase is now what Chinese adults say to children about reading anything at all, which is a fair extension of an emperor's argument for not skipping a day.
description_tr: Emperor Taizong of Song commissioned a vast encyclopaedia and then undertook to read the whole of it, three scrolls a day, finishing in a year. Told he was damaging his health, he answered that opening (開) a scroll (卷) is always of benefit (有益), and that he did not find it tiring. The book was renamed in honour of the imperial reading and is known by that title still. The phrase is now what Chinese adults say to children about reading anything at all, which is a fair extension of an emperor's argument for not skipping a day.
chineseExample_tr: 每當我讀一本新書，開卷有益。

example: Her tough love advice was meant to help him improve.
chineseExample: 她的苦口婆心是为了帮助他进步。
description: Two halves that pull against each other. 苦口 is the bitter mouth of the proverb 良药苦口利于病，忠言逆耳利于行 — good medicine tastes bitter but cures, honest words grate on the ear but help the conduct. 婆心 is a grandmother's heart, patient well past the point where patience is deserved. Together they describe someone saying a hard thing repeatedly and gently to a person who does not want to hear it. The phrase is warm about the speaker and faintly exasperated on their behalf, and it usually appears as 苦口婆心地劝.
description_tr: Two halves that pull against each other. 苦口 is the bitter mouth of the proverb 良藥苦口利於病，忠言逆耳利於行 — good medicine tastes bitter but cures, honest words grate on the ear but help the conduct. 婆心 is a grandmother's heart, patient well past the point where patience is deserved. Together they describe someone saying a hard thing repeatedly and gently to a person who does not want to hear it. The phrase is warm about the speaker and faintly exasperated on their behalf, and it usually appears as 苦口婆心地勸.
chineseExample_tr: 她的苦口婆心是為了幫助他進步。

meaning: Spur the horse to full speed
example: With his new strategy, the team is pushing forward even faster.
chineseExample: 有了新策略，团队快马加鞭，向前推进。
description: Whip (加鞭) applied to a horse (马) that is already fast (快). Song poets used it, and the sense has never shifted: not starting to hurry but hurrying something already at speed. That is what distinguishes it from ordinary haste, and it carries a mild suggestion of strain, since the horse in the image has nothing held back. It suits deadlines that have moved, projects being accelerated after a good start, and it is very common in official language about construction and reform.
description_tr: Whip (加鞭) applied to a horse (馬) that is already fast (快). Song poets used it, and the sense has never shifted: not starting to hurry but hurrying something already at speed. That is what distinguishes it from ordinary haste, and it carries a mild suggestion of strain, since the horse in the image has nothing held back. It suits deadlines that have moved, projects being accelerated after a good start, and it is very common in official language about construction and reform.
chineseExample_tr: 有了新策略，團隊快馬加鞭，向前推進。

example: The project has been ongoing for years without resolution.
chineseExample: 这个项目旷日持久，始终没有解决。
description: The Strategies of the Warring States records the argument against Zhao's plan to buy Qi's military help with a gift of territory: the campaign would drag, the land would be gone, and the aid would arrive too late to matter. Days (日) left empty (旷) and a thing dragged out (持久). The phrase always carries the criticism — it is not a neutral word for a long undertaking but specifically one that has consumed time without producing a result, and it attaches naturally to litigation, negotiations and wars nobody can end.
description_tr: The Strategies of the Warring States records the argument against Zhao's plan to buy Qi's military help with a gift of territory: the campaign would drag, the land would be gone, and the aid would arrive too late to matter. Days (日) left empty (曠) and a thing dragged out (持久). The phrase always carries the criticism — it is not a neutral word for a long undertaking but specifically one that has consumed time without producing a result, and it attaches naturally to litigation, negotiations and wars nobody can end.
chineseExample_tr: 這個項目曠日持久，始終沒有解決。

example: Through years of dedication and effort, she finally reached her career goals.
chineseExample: 经过多年的努力，她终于达到了职业目标。
description: At the banquet at Hongmen, with Xiang Yu's men waiting for a signal to kill Liu Bang, Fan Kuai forced his way in and made the case aloud: this is a man whose toil (劳苦) and achievement (功高) are of this order, and he has had no reward, while you plan to murder him. The interruption saved Liu Bang's life. The phrase kept the shape of the argument and is used to say that a person's contribution has been large and their recognition has not, generally as a preface to asking for something on their behalf.
description_tr: At the banquet at Hongmen, with Xiang Yu's men waiting for a signal to kill Liu Bang, Fan Kuai forced his way in and made the case aloud: this is a man whose toil (勞苦) and achievement (功高) are of this order, and he has had no reward, while you plan to murder him. The interruption saved Liu Bang's life. The phrase kept the shape of the argument and is used to say that a person's contribution has been large and their recognition has not, generally as a preface to asking for something on their behalf.
chineseExample_tr: 經過多年的努力，她終於達到了職業目標。

example: His advice was just the same old story that everyone has heard before.
chineseExample: 他的建议只是大家听过的老生常谈。
description: He Yan and Deng Yang, powerful and uneasy, summoned the diviner Guan Lu and asked what their prospects were. He told them to be humble and generous, and to fear what their positions invited. Deng Yang dismissed it as the stale talk (常谈) of an old student (老生). Both men were executed within the year. The phrase now means a platitude, and the story sits behind it as a standing joke: the advice was indeed unoriginal, and it was also correct, and dismissing it on the first ground cost them the benefit of the second.
description_tr: He Yan and Deng Yang, powerful and uneasy, summoned the diviner Guan Lu and asked what their prospects were. He told them to be humble and generous, and to fear what their positions invited. Deng Yang dismissed it as the stale talk (常談) of an old student (老生). Both men were executed within the year. The phrase now means a platitude, and the story sits behind it as a standing joke: the advice was indeed unoriginal, and it was also correct, and dismissing it on the first ground cost them the benefit of the second.
chineseExample_tr: 他的建議只是大家聽過的老生常談。

example: He immerses himself in his work and never seems to tire of it.
chineseExample: 他全心投入工作，乐此不疲。
description: Emperor Guangwu of Han held court every morning and did not break off until past noon, then called in his ministers to discuss the classics and the business of governing until the middle of the night. His son urged him to rest, saying he had none of the appetite for ease a ruler was allowed. The emperor answered 我自乐此，不为疲也 — I enjoy (乐) this (此), and so I am not (不) worn out (疲). The History of the Later Han keeps the line. The phrase describes work that returns more energy than it costs, and Chinese uses it with a touch of affectionate mockery for anyone whose hobby has become indistinguishable from labour.
description_tr: Emperor Guangwu of Han held court every morning and did not break off until past noon, then called in his ministers to discuss the classics and the business of governing until the middle of the night. His son urged him to rest, saying he had none of the appetite for ease a ruler was allowed. The emperor answered 我自樂此，不為疲也 — I enjoy (樂) this (此), and so I am not (不) worn out (疲). The History of the Later Han keeps the line. The phrase describes work that returns more energy than it costs, and Chinese uses it with a touch of affectionate mockery for anyone whose hobby has become indistinguishable from labour.
chineseExample_tr: 他全心投入工作，樂此不疲。

example: The plan was successful because the team coordinated perfectly with external partners.
chineseExample: 这个计划之所以成功，是因为团队里应外合。
description: Those inside (里) answer (应) and those outside (外) join them (合) — the pincer in which a siege is broken by a gate opened from within. It appears in Yuan drama and belongs to the vocabulary of military plotting. Modern use has kept the structure and lost the walls: it now describes any operation requiring a person on the inside, and it is as likely to describe fraud or a leak as a legitimate coordination. Whether it is praise or accusation depends entirely on who is speaking.
description_tr: Those inside (裡) answer (應) and those outside (外) join them (合) — the pincer in which a siege is broken by a gate opened from within. It appears in Yuan drama and belongs to the vocabulary of military plotting. Modern use has kept the structure and lost the walls: it now describes any operation requiring a person on the inside, and it is as likely to describe fraud or a leak as a legitimate coordination. Whether it is praise or accusation depends entirely on who is speaking.
chineseExample_tr: 這個計劃之所以成功，是因為團隊裡應外合。

example: The wedding was held on a perfect day, surrounded by stunning landscapes.
chineseExample: 婚礼在良辰美景中举行，令人难忘。
description: Xie Lingyun wrote that fine hours, beautiful scenery, a heart at ease and joy in the doing are four things rarely granted together. The idiom keeps the first two: a good time (良辰) and a fine view (美景). Because the original insists that the four seldom coincide, the phrase carries a note of conditional luck rather than simple pleasure — the setting is right, which is only part of what is needed. It is used of occasions worth not wasting, and often with mild regret that something is spoiling it.
description_tr: Xie Lingyun wrote that fine hours, beautiful scenery, a heart at ease and joy in the doing are four things rarely granted together. The idiom keeps the first two: a good time (良辰) and a fine view (美景). Because the original insists that the four seldom coincide, the phrase carries a note of conditional luck rather than simple pleasure — the setting is right, which is only part of what is needed. It is used of occasions worth not wasting, and often with mild regret that something is spoiling it.
chineseExample_tr: 婚禮在良辰美景中舉行，令人難忘。

example: The compromise allowed both parties to feel satisfied with the outcome.
chineseExample: 这个妥协让双方都能两全其美。
description: In the Yuan play about the chain of stratagems the line is spoken to Wang Yun, by a man pressing him to hand Diaochan over: give her to me and it is complete (全) beauty (美) on both (两) sides. Wang Yun's own plan was the opposite of an accommodation — promise her to both Dong Zhuo and his adopted son Lü Bu, and let the two tear each other apart, which is what happened. The phrase has since been entirely domesticated. It now simply means an arrangement that satisfies everyone, with none of the original irony surviving.
description_tr: In the Yuan play about the chain of stratagems the line is spoken to Wang Yun, by a man pressing him to hand Diaochan over: give her to me and it is complete (全) beauty (美) on both (兩) sides. Wang Yun's own plan was the opposite of an accommodation — promise her to both Dong Zhuo and his adopted son Lü Bu, and let the two tear each other apart, which is what happened. The phrase has since been entirely domesticated. It now simply means an arrangement that satisfies everyone, with none of the original irony surviving.
chineseExample_tr: 這個妥協讓雙方都能兩全其美。

example: He often admires the success of others but never takes action to pursue his own dreams.
chineseExample: 他常常临渊羡鱼，却从不付诸行动。
description: Standing over (临) the pool (渊) envying (羡) the fish (鱼) — better, the Huainanzi says, to go home and knit a net. The Book of Han repeats it as advice to an emperor about reform. Two things make the phrase sharper than a general injunction to act. The fish are real and reachable, so the wanting is not foolish; and the net is unglamorous, slow, and the entire content of the recommendation. It is aimed at people who have correctly identified what they want and are still standing at the water.
description_tr: Standing over (臨) the pool (淵) envying (羨) the fish (魚) — better, the Huainanzi says, to go home and knit a net. The Book of Han repeats it as advice to an emperor about reform. Two things make the phrase sharper than a general injunction to act. The fish are real and reachable, so the wanting is not foolish; and the net is unglamorous, slow, and the entire content of the recommendation. It is aimed at people who have correctly identified what they want and are still standing at the water.
chineseExample_tr: 他常常臨淵羨魚，卻從不付諸行動。

meaning: Fragrance flows for a hundred generations
example: Her contributions to education will leave a lasting legacy for future generations.
chineseExample: 她对教育的贡献将流芳百世。
description: Huan Wen, who commanded the armies of Eastern Jin and considered taking the throne, is recorded speaking as he lay, then sitting abruptly up: a man unable to let his fragrance (芳) flow (流) down a hundred (百) generations (世) should at least leave a stench for ten thousand years. The pairing 流芳百世 and 遗臭万年 has been fixed ever since, and its logic is bleak: the thing he could not tolerate was neither honour nor infamy but being forgotten. Only the first half is in ordinary use, in eulogies, entirely without the ambition that produced it.
description_tr: Huan Wen, who commanded the armies of Eastern Jin and considered taking the throne, is recorded speaking as he lay, then sitting abruptly up: a man unable to let his fragrance (芳) flow (流) down a hundred (百) generations (世) should at least leave a stench for ten thousand years. The pairing 流芳百世 and 遺臭萬年 has been fixed ever since, and its logic is bleak: the thing he could not tolerate was neither honour nor infamy but being forgotten. Only the first half is in ordinary use, in eulogies, entirely without the ambition that produced it.
chineseExample_tr: 她對教育的貢獻將流芳百世。

example: The calligraphy exhibition showcased works that were vibrant and full of life.
chineseExample: 这次书法展览的作品龙飞凤舞，生动活泼。
description: Dragon (龙) in flight (飞), phoenix (凤) in dance (舞). The phrase belongs above all to calligraphy, describing the running and cursive scripts where the brush does not lift and the characters move. It has a second life worth knowing about, because the same qualities describe handwriting that cannot be read: said of a doctor's prescription or a student's notes, 龙飞凤舞 is a polite way of saying the writing is illegible, and the compliment and the complaint are the same four characters.
description_tr: Dragon (龍) in flight (飛), phoenix (鳳) in dance (舞). The phrase belongs above all to calligraphy, describing the running and cursive scripts where the brush does not lift and the characters move. It has a second life worth knowing about, because the same qualities describe handwriting that cannot be read: said of a doctor's prescription or a student's notes, 龍飛鳳舞 is a polite way of saying the writing is illegible, and the compliment and the complaint are the same four characters.
chineseExample_tr: 這次書法展覽的作品龍飛鳳舞，生動活潑。

example: The athletes' performance at the championship was nothing short of spectacular.
chineseExample: 运动员们在比赛中的表现龙腾虎跃，令人惊叹。
description: Dragons (龙) rising (腾) and tigers (虎) leaping (跃) — the two most powerful animals in the Chinese repertoire, both shown mid-movement. What the phrase describes is collective energy rather than individual achievement: a workshop in full production, a sports ground, a construction site. It is very common in official and journalistic writing about national effort, and it describes the look of vigorous activity, which is not always the same thing as its results.
description_tr: Dragons (龍) rising (騰) and tigers (虎) leaping (躍) — the two most powerful animals in the Chinese repertoire, both shown mid-movement. What the phrase describes is collective energy rather than individual achievement: a workshop in full production, a sports ground, a construction site. It is very common in official and journalistic writing about national effort, and it describes the look of vigorous activity, which is not always the same thing as its results.
chineseExample_tr: 運動員們在比賽中的表現龍騰虎躍，令人驚嘆。

example: Her confident presence made everyone feel at ease during the meeting.
chineseExample: 她在会议上的落落大方让每个人都感到轻松。
description: 落落 suggests standing apart without stiffness; 大方 is the opposite of small, cramped or fussy. Together they describe bearing rather than beauty — someone at ease in a room, neither shrinking nor performing. Chinese values this specifically in social exposure, and the phrase is standard praise for how a person carries themselves on a stage, at a formal dinner or meeting strangers. Its opposite, 扭捏, is awkward self-consciousness, and the pair is worth learning together.
description_tr: 落落 suggests standing apart without stiffness; 大方 is the opposite of small, cramped or fussy. Together they describe bearing rather than beauty — someone at ease in a room, neither shrinking nor performing. Chinese values this specifically in social exposure, and the phrase is standard praise for how a person carries themselves on a stage, at a formal dinner or meeting strangers. Its opposite, 扭捏, is awkward self-consciousness, and the pair is worth learning together.
chineseExample_tr: 她在會議上的落落大方讓每個人都感到輕鬆。

example: After receiving the good news, she walked into the room with a beaming smile.
chineseExample: 听到好消息后，她满面春风地走进房间。
description: A face (面) filled (满) with spring breeze (春风) — the look of someone whose good humour is visible before they speak. The comparison is to weather rather than to expression: the warmth is taken to be radiating outward rather than performed. It is also written 春风满面, with the halves reversed. It is said of somebody visibly pleased and at ease, and often of a host.
description_tr: A face (面) filled (滿) with spring breeze (春風) — the look of someone whose good humour is visible before they speak. The comparison is to weather rather than to expression: the warmth is taken to be radiating outward rather than performed. It is also written 春風滿面, with the halves reversed. Chinese uses it of somebody visibly pleased and at ease, and often of a host.
chineseExample_tr: 聽到好消息後，她滿面春風地走進房間。

example: Navigating life without a plan is like a blind man on a blind horse, leading to uncertainty.
chineseExample: 没有计划地生活就像盲人瞎马，充满了不确定性。
description: The New Account of Tales of the World records a party game in which the guests competed to name the most dangerous thing. One offered a blind man (盲人) on a blind horse (瞎马) at midnight, at the edge of a deep pool. Yin Zhongkan, who was present and blind in one eye, said that this one cut rather close. The image is the most economical statement of compounded risk in the language: neither rider nor mount can see, so there is no redundancy anywhere in the system, and the phrase is used of exactly that situation.
description_tr: The New Account of Tales of the World records a party game in which the guests competed to name the most dangerous thing. One offered a blind man (盲人) on a blind horse (瞎馬) at midnight, at the edge of a deep pool. Yin Zhongkan, who was present and blind in one eye, said that this one cut rather close. The image is the most economical statement of compounded risk in the language: neither rider nor mount can see, so there is no redundancy anywhere in the system, and the phrase is used of exactly that situation.
chineseExample_tr: 沒有計劃地生活就像盲人瞎馬，充滿了不確定性。

example: Their glances across the room spoke volumes about their unspoken affection.
chineseExample: 他们的眼神交流中眉目传情。
description: Eyebrows (眉) and eyes (目) carrying (传) feeling (情). The phrase is fixed in Chinese literature by The Romance of the Western Chamber, where the lovers conduct much of their courtship in a household where speaking is not possible. That is the setting it implies. It describes affection communicated under constraint, which is why it belongs to romance rather than to ordinary friendliness, and why it can carry a whiff of impropriety — the looks are being exchanged because the words would be noticed.
description_tr: Eyebrows (眉) and eyes (目) carrying (傳) feeling (情). The phrase is fixed in Chinese literature by The Romance of the Western Chamber, where the lovers conduct much of their courtship in a household where speaking is not possible. That is the setting it implies. It describes affection communicated under constraint, which is why it belongs to romance rather than to ordinary friendliness, and why it can carry a whiff of impropriety — the looks are being exchanged because the words would be noticed.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的眼神交流中眉目傳情。

example: After his departure, the once-bustling shop became deserted and quiet.
chineseExample: 他离开后，这家曾经热闹的商店门可罗雀。
description: Zhai Gong, when he held high office, had a doorway crowded with visitors. Dismissed, he found the gateway (门) so empty that one could (可) have strung a net (罗) across it for sparrows (雀). Restored to office, he saw the visitors coming back, and wrote on his gate that only in death and life is friendship known, only in poverty and wealth is its quality seen. The Records of the Grand Historian preserves the sign. The phrase describes deserted premises, and it never entirely loses Zhai Gong's bitterness about what emptied them.

chineseExample_tr: 他離開後，這家曾經熱鬧的商店門可羅雀。

example: Her presentation was thorough, addressing every point with clarity and detail.
chineseExample: 她的演讲面面俱到，清晰而详细地涵盖了每一个要点。
description: Every face (面面) reached (俱到). The phrase is genuinely double-edged and learners should hear both sides. Used warmly it praises thoroughness, the plan with no gap in it, the host who has thought of everything. Used coolly it describes work that has covered every requirement and committed to nothing — the report that mentions all considerations and recommends none, the speech that offends no one because it says nothing. Which meaning is active is usually clear from what is being described.

example: His contributions to science ensured that his name would be remembered for generations.
chineseExample: 他的科学贡献使得名垂青史，世世代代都有人铭记。
description: 青史 is green history, and the colour is not decorative: records were written on bamboo, and fresh green bamboo had to be roasted over fire to sweat out its moisture before it would take ink and resist insects. So the phrase means a name (名) hanging down (垂) into the treated bamboo of the record. What it claims is permanence of a specific kind — not being remembered but being written where memory is no longer required. It is reserved for the historically significant and is heavy praise.

example: When he heard the news, he was left utterly speechless, unable to respond.
chineseExample: 听到这个消息后，他目瞪口呆，无法反应。
description: Eyes (目) staring (瞪) and mouth (口) slack (呆). It is straightforwardly descriptive and belongs to vernacular fiction and everyday speech. The pairing of the two features is what makes it work: Chinese has separate words for astonishment, and this one insists on the face, so it is used when the reaction was visible to others. It is common in narrative and in retelling — the standard way to report how a room looked when the news landed.

example: Despite the challenges, she chose to accept her fate rather than fight against it.
chineseExample: 尽管面临挑战，她选择逆来顺受，而不是反抗。
description: What comes against you (逆来), receive compliantly (顺受). The Yuan drama The Story of the Lute puts it in the mouth of a woman enduring what she cannot alter, and that is roughly its range. The phrase is not neutral. Chinese uses it with a distinct undertone of criticism or pity, describing someone who absorbs unfair treatment without protest, and it is the standard diagnosis of a person who has been imposed on for years and never once objected.

example: He chose to stand by his principles, even if it meant losing everything.
chineseExample: 他宁愿为自己的原则而玉碎，也不愿意妥协。
description: The History of Northern Qi has Yuan Jinghao refuse to save himself by taking the ruling house's surname: 大丈夫宁可玉碎，不能瓦全 — a real man would rather (宁) be jade (玉) shattered (碎) than a roof tile kept whole. He was killed for it. The form quoted today smooths 可 and 能 into a matched pair, but the comparison is unchanged, and it does all the work: jade broken is still jade, tile intact is still roofing, so the choice offered is not between destruction and survival but between two kinds of remaining. It is quoted in Chinese for principled refusal, and it is a heavy phrase, not used lightly.

example: Through hard work and dedication, his dreams transformed from mere fantasies into reality.
chineseExample: 通过努力和奉献，他的梦想从假象变成了现实。
description: To handle (弄) the false (假) until it becomes (成) the true (真). The phrase is vernacular and belongs to drama and fiction, where the plot device is standard: the sham betrothal that ends in a marriage, the fabricated pretext that turns out to describe the facts. Chinese uses it about both happy and disastrous versions, and the constant element is loss of control — the pretence acquires consequences that its author did not plan and cannot now withdraw.

chineseExample_tr: 通過努力和奉獻，他的夢想從假象變成了現實。

example: After years of working behind the scenes, she finally decided to step into the spotlight.
chineseExample: 经过多年的幕后工作，她终于决定抛头露面。
description: To throw out (抛) the head (头) and show (露) the face (面). It began as a reproach aimed specifically at women appearing in public, in a society where seclusion was the expectation, and the disapproval is built into 抛 — the head is not merely shown but flung out. That original charge has faded, though not entirely. Modern usage is broader and much milder, describing anyone who appears publicly and often carrying only a light suggestion that they would rather not.

example: After years apart, they finally reconciled and repaired their broken relationship.
chineseExample: 经过多年的分离，他们终于破镜重圆，修复了关系。
description: Xu Deyan, married to the princess of Lechang as the Chen dynasty collapsed, broke (破) a bronze mirror (镜) in two and gave her half, telling her to have it sold in the capital market on the fifteenth day of the first month. The dynasty fell, she was taken into the household of the Sui minister Yang Su, and a servant offered the half-mirror for sale at an impossible price. He matched it to his own and wrote a poem on it. Yang Su, told the story, returned her to him. The halves made round (圆) again (重) give the phrase, which is used of any reunion after long separation, and most often of a marriage repaired.
description_tr: Xu Deyan, married to the princess of Lechang as the Chen dynasty collapsed, broke (破) a bronze mirror (鏡) in two and gave her half, telling her to have it sold in the capital market on the fifteenth day of the first month. example: The festival brought together people from all walks of life to celebrate in unity.
chineseExample: 这个节日让来自各行各业的人们普天同庆。
description: All under heaven (普天) celebrating (庆) together (同). The scale is imperial: the occasions that warranted it were amnesties, accessions, victories, the announcement of an heir — events proclaimed to the whole realm and marked everywhere at once. That grandeur is still attached. Chinese uses it for national celebration and for genuinely large news, and applying it to a private success is a joke, in the way that declaring a public holiday for one's own birthday would be.

example: His writing style is so repetitive that it feels like reading the same thing over and over again.
chineseExample: 他的写作风格千篇一律，让人觉得读的都是同样的内容。
description: A thousand (千) pieces (篇) to one (一) pattern (律). 律 is the load-bearing character — a rule, a fixed measure, the pitch standard in music — so what is being described is not similarity but conformity to a template. The phrase began as literary criticism, aimed at writers whose considerable output turned out to be one poem written many times, and it has spread to buildings, curricula and product design. It is always hostile, and the accusation is specifically that the sameness was a choice.

meaning: A thousand jun on one hair
example: The project is hanging by a thread, and any mistake could lead to disaster.
chineseExample: 这个项目千钧一发，任何错误都可能导致灾难。
description: A weight of a thousand (千) 钧 hung from a single hair (一发). The 钧 was thirty catties, so the figure is not merely heavy but absurd, which is the point. The Book of Han gives it to Mei Cheng, writing to warn the King of Wu against rebellion: what you are doing is a thread carrying that weight above an unmeasured drop, and it cannot be re-tied once it goes. Liu Bi rebelled anyway and was destroyed. The phrase describes the moment before a break, not the break itself.

example: After traveling through countless obstacles, she finally reached her destination.
chineseExample: 她经历了千山万水，终于到达了目的地。
description: A thousand (千) mountains (山), ten thousand (万) rivers (水). Chinese uses paired large numbers as an intensifier rather than a count, and the pairing here is geographic in a specific way: mountains and rivers are what actually stopped pre-modern travel, so the phrase measures distance in obstacles rather than in miles. It survives mainly in the language of separation — the distance between people who cannot easily reach each other — and it appears constantly in songs, letters and the standard phrase for having come a long way to be present.
description_tr: A thousand (千) mountains (山), ten thousand (萬) rivers (水). example: After all the hard work, losing the final match felt like throwing everything away.
chineseExample: 经过所有的努力，最后一场比赛的失利让人觉得前功尽弃。
description: Su Li went to the ruler of Zhou with an argument to be put to the Qin general Bai Qi, then at the height of a run of victories. Chu had an archer, Yang Youji, who could split a willow leaf at a hundred paces a hundred times over — but let him miss once at the end and 前功尽矣, the whole record counts for nothing. Press this campaign, the argument ran, and your earlier merit (前功) is entirely (尽) discarded (弃); better to plead illness and stay in. The Strategies of the Warring States records this as advice spoken at the Zhou court, not as a letter. The phrase describes not ordinary failure but the specific case where stopping short, or one late error, cancels everything already banked.

example: Her beauty was so captivating that it could bring nations to their knees.
chineseExample: 她的美貌倾国倾城，令人心醉神迷。
description: Li Yannian sang to Emperor Wu of a beauty in the north, standing alone and without equal: one glance and she topples (倾) a city (城), a second glance and she topples a kingdom (国). The emperor asked whether such a woman existed; she was the singer's sister, and she entered the palace. 倾 is the crucial character and the translation usually loses it — not captivating a city but overturning one, the way a state falls. The compliment therefore contains a warning, and classical Chinese was entirely aware of it.

example: After exhausting all options, he felt trapped with no way out.
chineseExample: 在穷途末路的情况下，他感到无路可退。
description: A road exhausted (穷途) and the end of the way (末路). The phrase is inseparable in Chinese memory from Ruan Ji, the Wei poet who would drive his cart out with no destination and, when the track finally gave out, sit and weep before turning back. He was living under a regime in which saying anything was fatal, and the weeping was understood as being about more than the road. The idiom describes the point where options are genuinely gone, and it carries that weight — it is not used of ordinary difficulty.

The idiom describes the point where options are genuinely gone, and it carries that weight — it is not used of ordinary difficulty.
chineseExample_tr: 在窮途末路的情況下，他感到無路可退。

example: On a clear autumn day, the sky was bright and the air crisp, making it perfect for a picnic.
chineseExample: 在秋高气爽的日子里，我们去野餐。
description: Autumn (秋) high (高), air (气) crisp (爽). 秋高 describes something specific to the season in northern China: the summer haze clears, the cloud base lifts, and the sky reads as much further away than it did in July. The phrase is a weather report and a mood in one, and Chinese treats this particular combination as the best weather of the year. It appears in forecasts, tourism copy and the standard opening of a letter written in September.

It appears in forecasts, tourism copy and the standard opening of a letter written in September.
chineseExample_tr: 在秋高氣爽的日子裡，我們去野餐。

example: She gave her all in the competition, leaving no effort spared.
chineseExample: 在比赛中，她全力以赴，毫不留力。
description: Whole (全) strength (力) with which to (以) go (赴). 赴 is a verb of committed motion — going toward something, as in going to a post or answering a summons — so the phrase is about direction as well as effort. It belongs to ordinary modern speech. What it claims is that nothing is being held in reserve, which is why it appears in undertakings and promises far more often than in descriptions after the fact.

example: With sheer determination, he overcame all obstacles that stood in his way.
chineseExample: 凭借坚定的意志，人定胜天，他克服了所有的困难。
description: The classical sources have something narrower than the modern reading — that people (人) in sufficient numbers can prevail (胜) over heaven (天), meaning that human circumstances are not simply dictated by fate. The received modern sense reads 定 as determination and makes the phrase a general claim that human will defeats nature. That version had an enormous political career in twentieth-century China, as the slogan of campaigns to remake landscapes, some of which went very badly. Chinese speakers today use it both sincerely and with considerable irony, and the context decides which.

example: In this vibrant city, new talents are constantly emerging in various fields.
chineseExample: 在这个充满活力的城市里，人才辈出。
description: Talented people (人才) emerging (出) generation after generation (辈). 辈 is the operative character: not a crowd at one moment but a succession, cohort following cohort. That makes it a claim about an institution rather than about individuals — a school, a region, a discipline that keeps producing rather than one that produced once. It appears constantly in institutional self-description and in writing about periods of cultural flourishing, and it is what a university says about itself.

example: In that small town, many great artists emerged, proving it to be a place of talent and inspiration.
chineseExample: 在那个小镇上，许多杰出的人才涌现，证明了这是一个人杰地灵的地方。
description: Wang Bo wrote it in his preface on the Pavilion of Prince Teng, matching it with a line about the region's produce and treasures: the people are outstanding (人杰) and the land is numinous (地灵). The relation runs both ways and the phrase is deliberately ambiguous about the direction — whether remarkable people arise because the place has power in it, or whether the place acquires its power from them. Chinese local pride has been using it either way ever since, and it appears on the gates of a great many towns.
description_tr: Wang Bo wrote it in his preface on the Pavilion of Prince Teng, matching it with a line about the region's produce and treasures: the people are outstanding (人傑) and the land is numinous (地靈). Chinese local pride has been using it either way ever since, and it appears on the gates of a great many towns.

example: To achieve his goals, he had to endure many hardships and keep pushing forward despite the challenges.
chineseExample: 为了实现他的目标，他不得不忍辱负重，继续前行。
description: Liu Bei invaded Wu in 221 and Lu Xun was given the command against him the following year, over veteran officers who did not disguise what they thought of a young scholar being put above them. Lu Xun's answer to them is the phrase: the state has bent them to his authority because he can endure humiliation (忍辱) and carry the weight (负重). He then refused battle for months while Liu Bei's army wore itself out, and burned it at Yiling. What the phrase claims is that the two things are one capacity — the insult absorbed is the price of the responsibility held.
metaphoric_meaning: Bear disgrace to discharge a duty

example: As a manager, she handles countless responsibilities every day, ensuring everything runs smoothly.
chineseExample: 作为经理，她每天都要处理日理万机的事务，确保一切顺利进行。
description: Governing measured in volume: ten thousand (万) matters (机) handled (理) in a day (日). The construction is ancient, from the language of early statecraft about a ruler's daily burden, and it has stayed at that altitude. It is applied to heads of state and very senior officials, and its most common use in ordinary life is apologetic and slightly flattering — a preface to asking a busy person for something, acknowledging that they have ten thousand things and this is one more.

example: The debate was intense and passionate, with each side presenting their arguments fervently.
chineseExample: 这场辩论如火如荼，双方都热情洋溢地表达观点。
description: Before an assembly of the states, the king of Wu drew up his army in three enormous blocks and marched them out at dawn: one all in white with white banners and armour, so that from a distance the field looked like (如) reed-flowers (荼) in bloom, and one all in red, which looked like fire (火). The Discourses of the States records that the Jin delegation conceded precedence without a fight. The phrase now describes an activity at full pitch and full visibility, and it has kept the sense of spectacle as well as intensity.
description_tr: Before an assembly of the states, the king of Wu drew up his army in three enormous blocks and marched them out at dawn: one all in white with white banners and armour, so that from a distance the field looked like (如) reed-flowers (荼) in bloom, and one all in red, which looked like fire (火). The Discourses of the States records that the Jin delegation conceded precedence without a fight. The phrase now describes an activity at full pitch and full visibility, and it has kept the sense of spectacle as well as intensity.
chineseExample_tr: 這場辯論如火如荼，雙方都熱情洋溢地表達觀點。

meaning: As if facing a great enemy
example: Approaching the final exam, she prepared as if she were facing a formidable opponent.
chineseExample: 面对期末考试，她如临大敌般做好准备。
description: As if (如) facing (临) a great (大) enemy (敌). The phrase describes a posture rather than a situation, and that is what makes it double-edged. Used approvingly it praises proper seriousness in the face of something genuinely dangerous. Used dryly — which is at least as common — it observes that the precautions are wildly out of proportion to the threat, and it is the standard Chinese comment on an organisation mobilising its entire apparatus against a minor inconvenience.

chineseExample_tr: 面對期末考試，她如臨大敵般做好準備。

meaning: As if releasing a heavy burden
example: After finally finishing her thesis, she felt as if a weight had been lifted off her shoulders.
chineseExample: 她终于完成了论文，感觉如释重负。
description: The Guliang commentary describes the state of Lu after Duke Zhao, whose misgovernment had cost him everything, finally fled: 民如释重负 — the people felt as though (如) a heavy (重) load (负) had been set down (释). The phrase is precise about the physiology of relief: the sensation is in the shoulders, and it arrives at the moment the weight leaves rather than afterwards. It is used at the end of examinations, of long illnesses and of projects, and the original context is worth remembering, since the burden that lifted was a person.
