chineseExample_tr: 她終於完成了論文，感覺如釋重負。

example: During the tense negotiation, he felt like he was sitting on needles, unable to relax.
chineseExample: 在紧张的谈判中，他感觉如坐针毡，无法放松。
description: Du Xi served as tutor to a crown prince who did not want advice and grew to resent receiving it. The History of the Jin records that the prince had needles (针) put into the felt (毡) of the mat where Du Xi sat. Sitting (坐) as if (如) on needles is what the phrase describes, and its modern use is entirely figurative: the meeting one cannot leave, the dinner where the subject keeps approaching, the wait for a result. The discomfort it names is specifically the kind that must be endured while appearing composed.
description_tr: Du Xi served as tutor to a crown prince who did not want advice and grew to resent receiving it. chineseExample_tr: 在緊張的談判中，他感覺如坐針氈，無法放鬆。

meaning: Three visits to the thatched cottage
example: His persistence in seeking the expert's advice was reminiscent of the three visits to the thatched cottage.
chineseExample: 他坚持不懈地寻求专家的建议，令人想起三顾茅庐。
description: Zhuge Liang's own memorial to the throne is the source, and it is worth reading for the tone: the late emperor, he wrote, did not think me contemptible, and three times (三顾) came to see me in my thatched hut (茅庐) among the fields. Liu Bei was a warlord and Zhuge Liang was twenty-six and unemployed. The phrase describes the courting of talent by someone who does not need to be doing the travelling, and Chinese uses it of recruitment, of persistence, and of the flattery of being pursued.

chineseExample_tr: 他堅持不懈地尋求專家的建議，令人想起三顧茅廬。

example: The company decided to fire one employee as a warning to others about the importance of compliance.
chineseExample: 公司决定杀一儆百，以警示其他员工遵守规定。
description: Yin Wengui, taking up a difficult post, opened by prosecuting the single most protected criminal in the district rather than the easiest, and executed him. The Book of Han reports that the rest gave no further trouble. Killing (杀) one (一) to caution (儆) a hundred (百) is a statement about audience: the punishment is not aimed at the person receiving it. That is also its problem, which Chinese discussions of the phrase have always recognised, since the one selected is being used as a message.

chineseExample_tr: 公司決定殺一儆百，以警示其他員工遵守規定。

example: He always believes that a good plan leads to a successful outcome, embodying the principle of starting and finishing well.
chineseExample: 他总是相信善始善终，好的计划会带来成功的结果。
description: To begin (始) well (善) and end (终) well. The Zhuangzi has the thought and the Records of the Grand Historian applies it to Chen Ping, who survived the entire savage transition from Liu Bang to the Empress Lü to Emperor Wen with his position and his reputation intact — which in that generation of politics was the achievement. The phrase is not about excellence throughout so much as about landing: many people begin well, and the Chinese observation is that the ending is the part that is usually botched.

example: When the leader demonstrates integrity, it inspires the entire team to follow suit.
chineseExample: 当领导展现诚信时，整个团队都受到鼓舞。
description: Duke Huan of Qi liked purple, so the court wore purple, so the whole state wanted purple and the price of the dye went to five times that of plain cloth. Guan Zhong told him to say at court that he disliked the smell of it and to turn away anyone wearing it. Within three days, Han Feizi reports, nobody in the capital was in purple. Those above act (上行) and those below copy (下效) — the phrase is usually a warning, and the story is unusual in showing the mechanism used deliberately to undo itself.

chineseExample_tr: 當領導展現誠信時，整個團隊都受到鼓舞。

example: He always puts his friends' needs before his own, embodying the spirit of selflessness.
chineseExample: 他总是把朋友的需求放在自己之前，体现了无私的精神。
description: To set aside (舍) oneself (己) for (为) others (人). The sentiment is thoroughly Confucian, and the construction appears in the classics in related forms. What is worth noticing is how strong 舍 is: not subordinating one's interests but relinquishing them, which is why the phrase is reserved for real cost. Chinese uses it in commendations and citations, and it would be excessive praise for ordinary generosity.

chineseExample_tr: 他總是把朋友的需求放在自己之前，體現了無私的精神。

example: The general always leads from the front, inspiring his troops to follow his bravery.
chineseExample: 这位将军总是身先士卒，激励他的士兵们跟随他的勇气。
description: Self (身) ahead of (先) the soldiers (士卒). The phrase belongs to the historical literature of command and describes a specific and verifiable thing: the officer physically in front of the line, taking the first risk rather than directing from behind it. Chinese has kept it almost intact for modern management, where it is the standard praise for a manager who does the unpleasant part of the work personally, and the standard implied criticism of one who does not.

example: The festival was filled with energetic performances, making the atmosphere vibrant and lively.
chineseExample: 节日的表演充满了生龙活虎的气氛。
description: A living (生) dragon (龙) and an active (活) tiger (虎). The two characters doing the work are 生 and 活, which both mean alive — the phrase is not simply comparing someone to powerful animals but insisting the animals are in motion. It describes physical vitality rather than character, and it belongs particularly to the young and to recovery: it is what Chinese says about children in a courtyard, and about someone up and about a week after everyone expected them to be in bed.

example: His actions led to an infamous reputation that overshadowed any of his previous achievements.
chineseExample: 他的行为导致了声名狼藉，掩盖了他之前的成就。
description: 狼藉 describes the state a wolf leaves its bedding grass in — trampled flat and scattered in every direction — and Chinese has used it for wreckage and disorder since the Han. Attach it to a name (声名) and you have a reputation not merely damaged but strewn about. The phrase is severe. It is not the word for having made a mistake; it describes someone whose name has become a byword, and Chinese newspapers use it of the disgraced rather than the merely criticised.

example: He studied diligently for a decade, only to achieve great success in his exams.
chineseExample: 他在寒窗十年后终于考上了大学。
description: Ten years (十年) at a cold (寒) window (窗) — unheated, because warming a study through a northern winter cost money, and the window because that was where the light was. The phrase belongs to the examination system, and its companion line states the bargain exactly: 十年窗下无人问，一举成名天下知 — ten years beneath the window with nobody asking after you, then one success and the whole world knows your name. It is still what Chinese reaches for about the years before a result.

chineseExample_tr: 他在寒窗十年後終於考上了大學。

example: After sending out his application, he felt like his hopes had vanished without a trace.
chineseExample: 他的申请就像石沉大海，再也没有消息。
description: A stone (石) sinking (沉) into the open sea (大海). What the image supplies that 'no reply' does not is the total absence of evidence — no splash worth noting, no floating remnant, no way to establish that anything was thrown at all. That is the specific frustration it names. It is used of job applications, submitted manuscripts, petitions and messages, and the complaint is less about refusal than about the silence, which leaves nothing to respond to.

chineseExample_tr: 他的申請就像石沉大海，再也沒有消息。

example: She was so engrossed in her studies that she hardly noticed the time passing.
chineseExample: 他手不释卷，沉浸在书本中。
description: The hand (手) that does not put down (不释) the scroll (卷). Cao Pi used it of his father Cao Cao, who went on reading through the campaigns — 虽在军旅，手不释卷 — and who liked to say that of men still able to study hard once grown there were only himself and Yuan Yi. The story usually told alongside it is Lü Meng's: a Wu general dismissed as illiterate muscle, told by his sovereign to read, who did, and startled a visiting colleague so thoroughly that the man said he was no longer the Lü Meng of the old days. The phrase praises reading fitted into a life that does not obviously allow for it.

chineseExample_tr: 他手不釋卷，沉浸在書本中。

example: In the world of technology, she is truly a leader, standing out above all others.
chineseExample: 在科技界，她首屈一指，无人能及。
description: Chinese counts by folding fingers down rather than raising them, and the thumb (首指) goes first. So to be the one bent (屈) first is to be counted first — position one in the enumeration. The metaphor is about ranking rather than praise, which gives the phrase its slightly official flavour: it belongs to league tables, industry standing and formal introductions. It claims a place at the top of a list, and it implies the list exists and someone has drawn it up.

example: The security at the event was so tight that no one could get in without proper clearance.
chineseExample: 这个地方的安保水泄不通，任何人都无法进入。
description: So tight that water (水) cannot leak (泄) through (不通). The phrase comes out of Chan Buddhist writing, where such formulations describe a completeness with no gap in it, and the everyday use has kept the geometry and dropped the metaphysics. Chinese applies it to two situations in particular: a crowd so dense that nobody can move, and a cordon so complete that nobody can slip out. Holiday train stations and police operations are its natural homes.

Holiday train stations and police operations are its natural homes.
chineseExample_tr: 這個地方的安保水泄不通，任何人都無法進入。

example: The festival attracted visitors from all corners of the country.
chineseExample: 这个节日吸引了四面八方的游客。
description: Four faces (四面) and eight directions (八方). The eight are the cardinal points and the corners between them, so the phrase enumerates the compass and then claims all of it. It is used for convergence far more often than for dispersal — help arriving from everywhere, people gathering from everywhere — and that gives it a warmth that a simple statement of direction would not have. It appears constantly in accounts of disaster relief and of crowds drawn to an event.

example: The battle was costly, resulting in significant losses on both sides.
chineseExample: 这场战斗损兵折将，损失惨重。
description: Losing (损) the rank and file (兵) and breaking (折) the officers (将). 折 is snapping rather than merely losing, and the phrase's force is in naming both levels: an army can absorb casualties among its soldiers, but the loss of commanders is what makes a defeat structural. It comes from Yuan drama and is standard in vernacular fiction. Modern Chinese applies it freely to companies losing staff and executives together, and to sports teams losing players to injury.

chineseExample_tr: 這場戰鬥損兵折將，損失慘重。

example: Their friendship has lasted through thick and thin over the years.
chineseExample: 他们的友谊天长日久，历久弥新。
description: Heaven (天) is long (长) and the days (日) many (久). It is worth keeping apart from its near-twin 天长地久, which is about eternal love and belongs to weddings; this one is unromantic and simply means over a long enough period. The Dream of the Red Chamber uses it that way. Its characteristic use is faintly ominous, introducing the consequence that accumulates unnoticed: do this for long enough, and the phrase supplies what follows.

example: The political landscape changed dramatically after the revolution.
chineseExample: 革命后，天翻地覆的变化让人震惊。
description: Heaven (天) overturned (翻), earth (地) upended (覆). The pairing is total by construction — there is nothing left that is not one of the two — so the phrase describes change with no fixed point remaining, not merely a large change. It is neutral about direction and Chinese uses it for revolutions, for a city redeveloped past recognition, and for a household after a baby arrives. It also has an idiomatic use for uproar: 闹得天翻地覆 is to turn the place upside down.

example: Her speech was so beautiful that it captivated everyone in the audience.
chineseExample: 她的演讲天花乱坠，令人陶醉。
description: A Buddhist sutra describes heavenly flowers (天花) falling in confusion (乱坠) as a sermon is preached, and the tale attached to it has a monk expounding so movingly before Emperor Wu of Liang that blossoms came down out of the sky. The idiom has kept the image and reversed the verdict entirely. It now describes talk that is beautiful, fluent and not to be believed — sales patter, prospectuses, promises — and it is the standard Chinese warning that a description has outrun the thing described.

example: In his speech, he emphasized the importance of justice and morality in society.
chineseExample: 在他的演讲中，他强调了社会中正义和道德的重要性。
description: The Zuo Zhuan records a discussion of ritual propriety during a Zhou succession crisis, defining it as the constant thread (经) of heaven (天) and the right order (义) of earth (地). 经 is the warp of a fabric, the fixed threads that everything else is woven across. The phrase therefore claims that something is not a rule but a structural fact. It is used for what is taken to need no argument — and, quite often, in an argument about exactly that, by whichever side would rather not supply one.

The phrase therefore claims that something is not a rule but a structural fact. example: His imagination knows no bounds, creating worlds that captivate everyone.
chineseExample: 他的想象力无穷无尽，创造出迷住每一个人的世界。
description: Han China imported horses from the far west and wrote about them extravagantly, as celestial creatures that sweated blood and could cover impossible distances; a heavenly horse (天马) moving through empty sky (行空) is that reputation taken to its limit. Later critics borrowed the image for writing that goes where it likes without harness. The phrase carries both readings still. Applied to imagination it is admiring, and applied to an argument or a plan it usually means that nothing in it is attached to the ground.

example: They traveled to the farthest reaches of the world in search of adventure.
chineseExample: 他们走遍天涯海角，寻找冒险。
description: The edge (涯) of the sky and the corner (角) of the sea. Han Yu's lament for his dead nephew has the source of the sentiment — one of us at heaven's edge, one at earth's corner — and the phrase names the farthest place there is. Two uses dominate: separation, where it measures how far apart people are, and commitment, in promises to follow someone anywhere. There is also a real cape on Hainan called 天涯海角, which is where Chinese tourists go to stand at the end of the world.

chineseExample_tr: 他們走遍天涯海角，尋找冒險。

example: Their defenses were so strong that no enemy could breach them.
chineseExample: 他们的防御如铜墙铁壁，敌人无法攻破。
description: Walls (墙) of bronze (铜) and ramparts (壁) of iron (铁). The phrase belongs to vernacular fiction and describes fortification that cannot be breached. What is worth noticing is how readily Chinese moves it off physical defences: it is used of an alibi with no hole in it, of a bureaucracy that cannot be got past, and — most commonly in modern political language — of a population described as an unbreachable wall, where the metal is people rather than masonry.
description_tr: Walls (牆) of bronze (銅) and ramparts (壁) of iron (鐵). The phrase belongs to vernacular fiction and describes fortification that cannot be breached. What is worth noticing is how readily Chinese moves it off physical defences: it is used of an alibi with no hole in it, of a bureaucracy that cannot be got past, and — most commonly in modern political language — of a population described as an unbreachable wall, where the metal is people rather than masonry.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的防禦如銅牆鐵壁，敵人無法攻破。

example: His arguments were so logical that everyone agreed with him.
chineseExample: 他的论点头头是道，大家都赞同。
description: A Chan expression before it was anything else, meaning that the Way (道) is present at every point (头头) — wherever you put your hand down, that is it. Secularised, it describes speech in which every part connects to every other and the whole thing hangs together. The compliment is about structure rather than truth, and that is the catch: Chinese quite often uses 说得头头是道 of someone whose reasoning is beautifully organised and whose conclusion is wrong.
description_tr: A Chan expression before it was anything else, meaning that the Way (道) is present at every point (頭頭) — wherever you put your hand down, that is it. Secularised, it describes speech in which every part connects to every other and the whole thing hangs together. The compliment is about structure rather than truth, and that is the catch: Chinese quite often uses 說得頭頭是道 of someone whose reasoning is beautifully organised and whose conclusion is wrong.
chineseExample_tr: 他的論點頭頭是道，大家都贊同。

example: In negotiations, he was cautious, knowing that aggressive tactics could backfire.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，他小心翼翼，因为知道激进的策略可能会适得其反。
description: Jia Yi, arguing that senior officials should not be punished like common criminals, quoted a village proverb: you want to throw something at the rat (投鼠) but you think of the vessel (忌器) it is sitting beside. The Book of Han preserves the argument. The phrase names the specific paralysis of having a clear target that cannot be struck without breaking something valuable next to it, and it is used of hostage situations, of dismissing an executive with client relationships, and of any strike whose collateral is the real constraint.
description_tr: Jia Yi, arguing that senior officials should not be punished like common criminals, quoted a village proverb: you want to throw something at the rat (投鼠) but you think of the vessel (忌器) it is sitting beside. The Book of Han preserves the argument. The phrase names the specific paralysis of having a clear target that cannot be struck without breaking something valuable next to it, and it is used of hostage situations, of dismissing an executive with client relationships, and of any strike whose collateral is the real constraint.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，他小心翼翼，因為知道激進的策略可能會適得其反。

example: The garden in spring is a riot of colors, showcasing nature's beauty.
chineseExample: 春天的花园里万紫千红，展示了大自然的美丽。
description: Zhu Xi's poem on a spring day ends with the line: once you know the face of the east wind, the ten thousand purples (万紫) and thousand reds (千红) are all of them spring. The image is a hillside in flower, and the argument is that the variety is one thing underneath. That double sense survives in use. The phrase describes profusion and diversity together, and Chinese applies it to gardens, to festivals and, in official language, to a cultural scene doing well.
description_tr: Zhu Xi's poem on a spring day ends with the line: once you know the face of the east wind, the ten thousand purples (萬紫) and thousand reds (千紅) are all of them spring. The image is a hillside in flower, and the argument is that the variety is one thing underneath. That double sense survives in use. The phrase describes profusion and diversity together, and Chinese applies it to gardens, to festivals and, in official language, to a cultural scene doing well.
chineseExample_tr: 春天的花園裡萬紫千紅，展示了大自然的美麗。

example: He was so engrossed in the concert that he lost track of time.
chineseExample: 他陶醉于音乐会中，忘乎所以，完全忘记了时间。
description: To forget (忘) about (乎) the wherefore (所以) of oneself — the grammar is deliberately vague and the sense is losing track of who and where you are. It belongs to vernacular fiction and describes a specific failure: not arrogance in general but the temporary kind produced by a success, elation or flattery, in which someone's sense of proportion goes missing for an evening. Chinese reserves it for people who have just been promoted, praised in public, or allowed to talk for too long.
description_tr: To forget (忘) about (乎) the wherefore (所以) of oneself — the grammar is deliberately vague and the sense is losing track of who and where you are. It belongs to vernacular fiction and describes a specific failure: not arrogance in general but the temporary kind produced by a success, elation or flattery, in which someone's sense of proportion goes missing for an evening. Chinese uses it of people who have just been promoted, praised in public, or allowed to talk for too long.
chineseExample_tr: 他陶醉於音樂會中，忘乎所以，完全忘記了時間。

example: In business, he is known for his ruthless pursuit of profit above all else.
chineseExample: 在商业上，他以唯利是图而闻名，毫不顾及道德。
description: The Zuo Zhuan has the phrase as 唯利是视, only profit is looked to, and it is Qin's own oath quoted back at it: Chu reported to Jin that Qin had sworn that whatever it did with Jin it would look only to advantage, and Jin's envoy Lü Xiang read the oath out in the formal denunciation that broke the alliance. The grammar repays attention: 唯…是… is a classical construction that pulls the object in front of the verb for emphasis, so the literal shape is only (唯) profit (利) is what is sought (图), with 是 a grammatical marker rather than the verb to be. It is a hard-edged accusation in modern Chinese, standard in criticism of companies and of people who have priced a friendship.
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan has the phrase as 唯利是視, only profit is looked to, and it is Qin's own oath quoted back at it: Chu reported to Jin that Qin had sworn that whatever it did with Jin it would look only to advantage, and Jin's envoy Lü Xiang read the oath out in the formal denunciation that broke the alliance. The grammar repays attention: 唯…是… is a classical construction that pulls the object in front of the verb for emphasis, so the literal shape is only (唯) profit (利) is what is sought (圖), with 是 a grammatical marker rather than the verb to be. It is a hard-edged accusation in modern Chinese, standard in criticism of companies and of people who have priced a friendship.
chineseExample_tr: 在商業上，他以唯利是圖而聞名，毫不顧及道德。

example: His ability to predict market trends seems almost supernatural.
chineseExample: 他的市场趋势预测能力未卜先知，令人惊叹。
description: 卜 is divination by heat-cracked bone and shell, the oldest recorded Chinese writing system's original purpose. To know (知) first (先) without having divined (未卜) is therefore to reach the answer without the apparatus. The phrase comes from Yuan drama and is usually light in tone — it is what you say to someone who guessed correctly, or, in the negative, to disclaim any special insight: 我又不是未卜先知, I'm not a fortune-teller.
description_tr: 卜 is divination by heat-cracked bone and shell, the oldest recorded Chinese writing system's original purpose. To know (知) first (先) without having divined (未卜) is therefore to reach the answer without the apparatus. The phrase comes from Yuan drama and is usually light in tone — it is what you say to someone who guessed correctly, or, in the negative, to disclaim any special insight: 我又不是未卜先知, I'm not a fortune-teller.
chineseExample_tr: 他的市場趨勢預測能力未卜先知，令人驚嘆。

example: His eloquent speech and polished demeanor impressed everyone at the gala.
chineseExample: 他在晚会上文质彬彬的演讲给大家留下了深刻的印象。
description: Confucius set two things against each other in the Analects: 质, raw substance, and 文, cultivation and polish. Substance overrunning polish gives you a boor; polish overrunning substance gives you a clerk. Only when the two are 彬彬 — evenly matched, neither showing through the other — is there a gentleman. The phrase has drifted somewhat in modern use, where it tends to describe a scholarly, mild-mannered appearance, and the balance Confucius insisted on is often reduced to just the polished half.
description_tr: Confucius set two things against each other in the Analects: 質, raw substance, and 文, cultivation and polish. Substance overrunning polish gives you a boor; polish overrunning substance gives you a clerk. Only when the two are 彬彬 — evenly matched, neither showing through the other — is there a gentleman. The phrase has drifted somewhat in modern use, where it tends to describe a scholarly, mild-mannered appearance, and the balance Confucius insisted on is often reduced to just the polished half.
chineseExample_tr: 他在晚會上文質彬彬的演講給大家留下了深刻的印象。

example: She felt a sense of peace knowing she had acted with integrity in the situation.
chineseExample: 她心里问心无愧，知道自己在这个问题上做得很对。
description: To ask (问) the heart (心) and find nothing to be ashamed of (无愧). The construction places the tribunal inside the person, which is the whole point: the phrase is used precisely when external judgement has gone against you, and it asserts a standard that the verdict did not reach. Chinese uses it after a loss, an accusation or a decision that cost something, and it is closer to a defence than a boast.
description_tr: To ask (問) the heart (心) and find nothing to be ashamed of (無愧). The construction places the tribunal inside the person, which is the whole point: the phrase is used precisely when external judgement has gone against you, and it asserts a standard that the verdict did not reach. Chinese uses it after a loss, an accusation or a decision that cost something, and it is closer to a defence than a boast.
chineseExample_tr: 她心裡問心無愧，知道自己在這個問題上做得很對。

example: The ocean stretched out before us, vast and limitless, inviting exploration.
chineseExample: 大海无边无际，令人感到渺小而敬畏。
description: Without (无) edge (边), without (无) boundary (际). Chinese doubles the negation for scale, and the two nouns are not synonyms — 边 is the rim of a thing and 际 is where two things meet — so between them they deny both the object's own limit and any point at which something else begins. It is used of oceans, deserts and night skies, and figuratively of anything unmeasurable, from grief to possibility.
description_tr: Without (無) edge (邊), without (無) boundary (際). Chinese doubles the negation for scale, and the two nouns are not synonyms — 邊 is the rim of a thing and 際 is where two things meet — so between them they deny both the object's own limit and any point at which something else begins. It is used of oceans, deserts and night skies, and figuratively of anything unmeasurable, from grief to possibility.
chineseExample_tr: 大海無邊無際，令人感到渺小而敬畏。

example: Many people share similar experiences, proving that we are not alone in our struggles.
chineseExample: 在这个问题上，无独有偶，很多人都有相似的经历。
description: Not (无) single (独) but having (有) a counterpart (偶). What makes it worth learning is the tone, which learners consistently get wrong. It is not a neutral word for coincidence: Chinese uses it when the second instance makes the first one worse, revealing that what looked like a one-off is a pattern. A second embezzlement, a second identical complaint, a second company doing the same thing. It introduces the second item and implies there may be more.
description_tr: Not (無) single (獨) but having (有) a counterpart (偶). What makes it worth learning is the tone, which learners consistently get wrong. It is not a neutral word for coincidence: Chinese uses it when the second instance makes the first one worse, revealing that what looked like a one-off is a pattern. A second embezzlement, a second identical complaint, a second company doing the same thing. It introduces the second item and implies there may be more.
chineseExample_tr: 在這個問題上，無獨有偶，很多人都有相似的經歷。

example: Her friendship is a priceless treasure that I cherish deeply.
chineseExample: 她的友谊是我无价之宝，我非常珍惜。
description: A treasure (宝) without (无) a price (价). The claim is not that something is expensive but that the pricing operation does not apply to it, which is a different and stronger statement. Chinese uses it both ways. Of objects it means an irreplaceable artefact; of everything else — health, a teacher, years with someone — it means the thing that people notice the value of only when the question of replacing it comes up.
description_tr: A treasure (寶) without (無) a price (價). The claim is not that something is expensive but that the pricing operation does not apply to it, which is a different and stronger statement. Chinese uses it both ways. Of objects it means an irreplaceable artefact; of everything else — health, a teacher, years with someone — it means the thing that people notice the value of only when the question of replacing it comes up.
chineseExample_tr: 她的友誼是我無價之寶，我非常珍惜。

example: She lived a carefree life, enjoying every moment without stress.
chineseExample: 她过着无忧无虑的生活，享受每一个没有压力的时刻。
description: Without (无) sorrow (忧), without (无) anxiety (虑). The pairing separates two things English tends to run together: 忧 is grief over what has happened and 虑 is calculation about what might. Being free of both is therefore a fuller claim than 'carefree'. Yuan drama supplies the phrase, and Chinese uses it above all of childhood and of animals, with an unmistakable note of retrospect — it is generally said by someone describing a state they no longer occupy.
description_tr: Without (無) sorrow (憂), without (無) anxiety (慮). The pairing separates two things English tends to run together: 憂 is grief over what has happened and 慮 is calculation about what might. Being free of both is therefore a fuller claim than 'carefree'. Yuan drama supplies the phrase, and Chinese uses it above all of childhood and of animals, with an unmistakable note of retrospect — it is generally said by someone describing a state they no longer occupy.
chineseExample_tr: 她過著無憂無慮的生活，享受每一個沒有壓力的時刻。

example: He was so impressed by her talent that he felt utterly humbled.
chineseExample: 他对她的才华感到五体投地，完全被震撼了。
description: The five (五) parts of the body (体) thrown (投) to the ground (地): both knees, both elbows and the forehead, which is the full Buddhist prostration. Xuanzang describes it among the Indian forms of reverence in his account of the western regions, ranking it the highest of them. Chinese has secularised it completely and now uses it as hyperbole for admiration — 佩服得五体投地, so impressed as to be flat on the floor — and it is often faintly comic.
description_tr: The five (五) parts of the body (體) thrown (投) to the ground (地): both knees, both elbows and the forehead, which is the full Buddhist prostration. Xuanzang describes it among the Indian forms of reverence in his account of the western regions, ranking it the highest of them. Chinese has secularised it completely and now uses it as hyperbole for admiration — 佩服得五體投地, so impressed as to be flat on the floor — and it is often faintly comic.
chineseExample_tr: 他對她的才華感到五體投地，完全被震撼了。

example: His ability to predict market trends showed his remarkable foresight.
chineseExample: 他的市场趋势预测能力展现了先见之明。
description: Cao Cao asked Yang Biao why he had grown so thin. Yang Biao answered that he lacked Jin Midi's clarity (明) of seeing (见) in advance (先) and still carried the old cow's love of licking her calf. Jin Midi, generations earlier, had killed his own son on discovering his misconduct, before it could destroy the family. Yang Biao's son was Yang Xiu, whom Cao Cao had just executed. The whole reproach is in the phrase, delivered to the man responsible, and it is used now for foresight that others lacked.
description_tr: Cao Cao asked Yang Biao why he had grown so thin. Yang Biao answered that he lacked Jin Midi's clarity (明) of seeing (見) in advance (先) and still carried the old cow's love of licking her calf. Jin Midi, generations earlier, had killed his own son on discovering his misconduct, before it could destroy the family. Yang Biao's son was Yang Xiu, whom Cao Cao had just executed. The whole reproach is in the phrase, delivered to the man responsible, and it is used now for foresight that others lacked.
chineseExample_tr: 他的市場趨勢預測能力展現了先見之明。

example: In negotiations, establishing a strong initial position is crucial.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，先入为主的立场至关重要。
description: What enters (入) first (先) becomes (为) the master (主). The Book of Han uses it in warning an emperor whose favourites had established themselves in his judgement before any competing account could be heard. The metaphor is territorial — the first occupant holds the ground — and the phrase is always a criticism. It names the specific error of assessing later evidence by whether it fits the first version, rather than assessing the first version at all.
description_tr: What enters (入) first (先) becomes (為) the master (主). The Book of Han uses it in warning an emperor whose favourites had established themselves in his judgement before any competing account could be heard. The metaphor is territorial — the first occupant holds the ground — and the phrase is always a criticism. It names the specific error of assessing later evidence by whether it fits the first version, rather than assessing the first version at all.
chineseExample_tr: 在談判中，先入為主的立場至關重要。

example: It's unfair to compare such different artists in the same discussion.
chineseExample: 把这两位艺术家相提并论是不公平的。
description: Dou Ying, having failed to protect the deposed crown prince, was advised that his conspicuous retirement into private pleasures would be read as a rebuke to the emperor — that the two matters would be raised together (相提) and discussed as one (并论). The Records of the Grand Historian keeps the warning. The phrase is now used almost entirely in the negative: 不能相提并论, these cannot be mentioned in the same breath, and it is the standard Chinese objection to a false equivalence.
description_tr: Dou Ying, having failed to protect the deposed crown prince, was advised that his conspicuous retirement into private pleasures would be read as a rebuke to the emperor — that the two matters would be raised together (相提) and discussed as one (並論). The Records of the Grand Historian keeps the warning. The phrase is now used almost entirely in the negative: 不能相提並論, these cannot be mentioned in the same breath, and it is the standard Chinese objection to a false equivalence.
chineseExample_tr: 把這兩位藝術家相提並論是不公平的。

example: After receiving the good news, she felt an overwhelming joy that she couldn't contain.
chineseExample: 收到好消息后，她感到一种无法抑制的喜悦。
description: Flowers (花) of the heart (心) bursting (放) open. The character that misleads learners is 怒, which here does not mean angry but describes growth at full force — the same usage as in 怒放 for flowers in full bloom and 怒吼 for a roar. So the image is a heart flowering violently rather than a heart in a temper. It describes sudden delight, and Chinese uses it for the news that arrives unexpectedly rather than for settled contentment.
description_tr: Flowers (花) of the heart (心) bursting (放) open. The character that misleads learners is 怒, which here does not mean angry but describes growth at full force — the same usage as in 怒放 for flowers in full bloom and 怒吼 for a roar. So the image is a heart flowering violently rather than a heart in a temper. It describes sudden delight, and Chinese uses it for the news that arrives unexpectedly rather than for settled contentment.
chineseExample_tr: 收到好消息後，她感到一種無法抑制的喜悅。

example: After the disappointing news, he felt utterly defeated and lost all motivation.
chineseExample: 在失望的消息后，他感到完全沮丧，失去了所有的动力。
description: Heart (心) turned to ash (灰), will (意) gone cold (冷). Both halves are about heat leaving rather than pain arriving, and that is the state being described: not grief, which is active, but the flatness after it, when the thing that used to motivate you no longer produces any response. You will hear it of people who have stopped trying — after a business failure, a relationship, or one rejection too many — and it implies the giving up is settled rather than momentary.
description_tr: Heart (心) turned to ash (灰), will (意) gone cold (冷). Both halves are about heat leaving rather than pain arriving, and that is the state being described: not grief, which is active, but the flatness after it, when the thing that used to motivate you no longer produces any response. Chinese uses it of people who have stopped trying — after a business failure, a relationship, or one rejection too many — and it implies the giving up is settled rather than momentary.
chineseExample_tr: 在失望的消息後，他感到完全沮喪，失去了所有的動力。

example: He is known for his blunt honesty, often saying exactly what he thinks without hesitation.
chineseExample: 他以直言不讳而闻名，常常毫不犹豫地说出自己的想法。
description: A straight (直) heart (心) and a quick (快) mouth (口). The phrase is genuinely double-edged and Chinese uses both edges freely. As praise it describes someone who will tell you the truth and can be relied on not to be managing you. As criticism, or as a pre-emptive excuse, it describes someone who says the damaging thing before considering it — and 我这人心直口快 is very often an apology issued in advance for what is about to be said.
description_tr: A straight (直) heart (心) and a quick (快) mouth (口). The phrase is genuinely double-edged and Chinese uses both edges freely. As praise it describes someone who will tell you the truth and can be relied on not to be managing you. As criticism, or as a pre-emptive excuse, it describes someone who says the damaging thing before considering it — and 我這人心直口快 is very often an apology issued in advance for what is about to be said.
chineseExample_tr: 他以直言不諱而聞名，常常毫不猶豫地說出自己的想法。

example: The children were in high spirits, celebrating their victory with laughter and cheer.
chineseExample: 孩子们兴高采烈地庆祝他们的胜利，笑声不断。
description: Liu Xie, writing on style and temperament, characterised the poet Ji Kang as lofty in inspiration (兴高) and vivid in expression (采烈). 采 there means literary colouring, not picking or gathering. The phrase has left criticism for ordinary speech and now simply means in high spirits, applied to children at a festival and to teams that have just won. Nothing of Ji Kang survives in it, which is a pity, since he was executed at forty for exactly the temperament being praised.
description_tr: Liu Xie, writing on style and temperament, characterised the poet Ji Kang as lofty in inspiration (興高) and vivid in expression (采烈). 採 there means literary colouring, not picking or gathering. The phrase has left criticism for ordinary speech and now simply means in high spirits, applied to children at a festival and to teams that have just won. Nothing of Ji Kang survives in it, which is a pity, since he was executed at forty for exactly the temperament being praised.
chineseExample_tr: 孩子們興高采烈地慶祝他們的勝利，笑聲不斷。

example: With his dreams of becoming an entrepreneur, he has always had big aspirations for his future.
chineseExample: 他一直怀有成为企业家的梦想，对未来有着伟大的抱负。
description: To carry (怀) great (大) ambition (志) in the chest (胸). Chinese consistently locates aspiration in the chest cavity rather than the head, which is why the same 胸 appears in 心胸开阔 for tolerance and 胸有成竹 for a plan already formed. The phrase describes ambition that is held rather than announced, and its natural setting is biography — it is the standard thing to say about someone's early years, once the later years have justified it.
description_tr: To carry (懷) great (大) ambition (志) in the chest (胸). Chinese consistently locates aspiration in the chest cavity rather than the head, which is why the same 胸 appears in 心胸開闊 for tolerance and 胸有成竹 for a plan already formed. The phrase describes ambition that is held rather than announced, and its natural setting is biography — it is the standard thing to say about someone's early years, once the later years have justified it.
chineseExample_tr: 他一直懷有成為企業家的夢想，對未來有著偉大的抱負。

example: He faced challenges that seemed insurmountable, like climbing a sheer cliff.
chineseExample: 他面临的挑战似乎无法克服，就像攀登悬崖峭壁一样。
description: A cliff that hangs (悬崖) and a wall of rock that is sheer (峭壁). The two halves are the same geography twice, and the doubling is the point: what is described is not one drop but a whole face of country that offers nothing to hold. Chinese uses it literally, in accounts of mountain roads and of climbing, far more often than it uses it as a metaphor — which is worth knowing, because the English instinct is to reach straight for the figurative reading.
description_tr: A cliff that hangs (懸崖) and a wall of rock that is sheer (峭壁). The two halves are the same geography twice, and the doubling is the point: what is described is not one drop but a whole face of country that offers nothing to hold. Chinese uses it literally, in accounts of mountain roads and of climbing, far more often than it uses it as a metaphor — which is worth knowing, because the English instinct is to reach straight for the figurative reading.
chineseExample_tr: 他面臨的挑戰似乎無法克服，就像攀登懸崖峭壁一樣。

example: The exhibition was a perfect blend of high art and popular appeal, attracting a diverse audience.
chineseExample: 这个展览完美地结合了雅俗共赏，吸引了不同的观众。
description: Worth admiring (赏) to the refined (雅) and the common (俗) alike (共). 雅 and 俗 are a standing pair in Chinese criticism, the polished against the popular, and they are normally opposed — work that pleases one is assumed to have lost the other. The phrase claims both at once, which is why it is a serious compliment rather than a bland one. Chinese says it of performances, of films and of writing, and what it praises is reach without dilution.
description_tr: Worth admiring (賞) to the refined (雅) and the common (俗) alike (共). 雅 and 俗 are a standing pair in Chinese criticism, the polished against the popular, and they are normally opposed — work that pleases one is assumed to have lost the other. The phrase claims both at once, which is why it is a serious compliment rather than a bland one. Chinese uses it of performances, of films and of writing, and what it praises is reach without dilution.
chineseExample_tr: 這個展覽完美地結合了雅俗共賞，吸引了不同的觀眾。

example: After a long digression, he finally returned to the main topic of the discussion.
chineseExample: 经过长时间的偏离，他终于言归正传，回到了讨论的主题。
description: The last character is read zhuàn and means a narrative or a formal account, not 'to transmit'. That is because the phrase is a storyteller's formula: professional tellers used it to close a digression and pick up the thread, and vernacular fiction preserved the convention in print. Bringing the words (言) back (归) to the proper (正) narrative (传) has kept exactly that job. It is what a Chinese speaker says to end their own tangent, and it is mildly self-deprecating.
description_tr: The last character is read zhuàn and means a narrative or a formal account, not 'to transmit'. That is because the phrase is a storyteller's formula: professional tellers used it to close a digression and pick up the thread, and vernacular fiction preserved the convention in print. Bringing the words (言) back (歸) to the proper (正) narrative (傳) has kept exactly that job. It is what a Chinese speaker says to end their own tangent, and it is mildly self-deprecating.
chineseExample_tr: 經過長時間的偏離，他終於言歸正傳，回到了討論的主題。

meaning: Untouched by a single speck of dust
example: Her integrity remained unblemished, untouched by the corruption around her.
chineseExample: 她的品德一尘不染，未受周围腐败的影响。
description: In Buddhist analysis the 六尘, the six dusts, are the objects of the senses — what settles on a mind and clouds it. So a single (一) speck of dust (尘) not (不) staining (染) anything is a technical claim about a mind untouched by sense objects, and the phrase reaches Chinese through Tang Buddhist compilations. Two uses survive. Of a person it means incorruptible, typically an official; of a room, it means spotless, and the sacred sense is entirely gone.
description_tr: In Buddhist analysis the 六塵, the six dusts, are the objects of the senses — what settles on a mind and clouds it. So a single (一) speck of dust (塵) not (不) staining (染) anything is a technical claim about a mind untouched by sense objects, and the phrase reaches Chinese through Tang Buddhist compilations. Two uses survive. Of a person it means incorruptible, typically an official; of a room, it means spotless, and the sacred sense is entirely gone.
chineseExample_tr: 她的品德一塵不染，未受周圍腐敗的影響。

example: His leadership style was so effective that every time he called for help, everyone rushed to assist.
chineseExample: 他的领导风格非常有效，每当他一呼百应，大家都会迅速前来帮助。
description: One (一) call (呼) and a hundred (百) answer (应). The phrase describes a specific kind of standing: not authority, which compels, but the sort of following that responds without needing to be persuaded first. Chinese distinguishes them carefully, and this one is about voluntary response. It is used of union organisers, of popular figures within an institution, and now routinely of people with large followings online, where the arithmetic is considerably more than a hundred.
description_tr: One (一) call (呼) and a hundred (百) answer (應). The phrase describes a specific kind of standing: not authority, which compels, but the sort of following that responds without needing to be persuaded first. Chinese distinguishes them carefully, and this one is about voluntary response. It is used of union organisers, of popular figures within an institution, and now routinely of people with large followings online, where the arithmetic is considerably more than a hundred.
chineseExample_tr: 他的領導風格非常有效，每當他一呼百應，大家都會迅速前來幫助。

example: After the scandal, his reputation fell dramatically.
chineseExample: 在丑闻之后，他的名声一落千丈。
description: Han Yu's poem on hearing the monk Ying play the zither tracks the music climbing, inch by inch, until it can go no higher — and then losing its footing and dropping (落) a thousand (千) 丈 (zhàng) and more. It is a description of pitch. The 丈 is about three metres, so the figure is a fall of some kilometres, which is the point. Chinese now applies it to share prices, grades, reputations and form, and it always implies the fall was both sudden and from a height.
description_tr: Han Yu's poem on hearing the monk Ying play the zither tracks the music climbing, inch by inch, until it can go no higher — and then losing its footing and dropping (落) a thousand (千) 丈 (zhàng) and more.
