Chinese now applies it to share prices, grades, reputations and form, and it always implies the fall was both sudden and from a height.
chineseExample_tr: 在醜聞之後，他的名聲一落千丈。

example: Their family values have been passed down through generations.
chineseExample: 他们的家族价值观一脉相承。
description: One (一) vein (脉) inherited (承) down the line (相). 脉 is a blood vessel and also the seam of ore in rock or the ridge line of a mountain range — in every sense, a continuous thing running underground. That is the claim: not resemblance between two things but a single strand connecting them. It is used of schools of thought, of craft lineages and of institutional culture, and it can be either a compliment or, of an inherited bad habit, a diagnosis.
description_tr: One (一) vein (脈) inherited (承) down the line (相). 脈 is a blood vessel and also the seam of ore in rock or the ridge line of a mountain range — in every sense, a continuous thing running underground. That is the claim: not resemblance between two things but a single strand connecting them. It is used of schools of thought, of craft lineages and of institutional culture, and it can be either a compliment or, of an inherited bad habit, a diagnosis.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的家族價值觀一脈相承。

example: He is so stingy that he won't even lend a penny.
chineseExample: 他一毛不拔，连一分钱都不肯借。
description: Mencius describes the philosopher Yang Zhu's position as pure egoism: he would not pluck (拔) a single (一) hair (毛) from his body even if it would benefit the whole world. The doctrine was more serious than the caricature — Yang Zhu argued against sacrificing the self to public causes — but the phrase kept the caricature. It is now the ordinary Chinese word for a miser, and it is blunt rather than literary, closer to English 'tight-fisted' than to anything philosophical.
description_tr: Mencius describes the philosopher Yang Zhu's position as pure egoism: he would not pluck (拔) a single (一) hair (毛) from his body even if it would benefit the whole world. The doctrine was more serious than the caricature — Yang Zhu argued against sacrificing the self to public causes — but the phrase kept the caricature. It is now the ordinary Chinese word for a miser, and it is blunt rather than literary, closer to English 'tight-fisted' than to anything philosophical.
chineseExample_tr: 他一毛不拔，連一分錢都不肯借。

example: He knows nothing about the subject; he can't even understand the basics.
chineseExample: 他对这个话题一窍不通。
description: Ancient Chinese anatomy credited the heart with apertures (窍) through which understanding was thought to pass. The Lüshi Chunqiu reports that when the last Shang king had his uncle Bi Gan cut open, Confucius said 其窍通则比干不死矣 — had the king's apertures been open, Bi Gan would not have died. The king's stated motive, that he wanted to see whether a sage's heart really had seven apertures, comes from the Records of the Grand Historian rather than from this passage. Not (不) one (一) aperture (窍) open (通) is therefore total obtuseness. Modern use is much lighter, and Chinese speakers most often apply it to themselves about some subject they cannot follow.
description_tr: Ancient Chinese anatomy credited the heart with apertures (竅) through which understanding was thought to pass. The Lüshi Chunqiu reports that when the last Shang king had his uncle Bi Gan cut open, Confucius said 其竅通則比干不死矣 — had the king's apertures been open, Bi Gan would not have died. The king's stated motive, that he wanted to see whether a sage's heart really had seven apertures, comes from the Records of the Grand Historian rather than from this passage. Not (不) one (一) aperture (竅) open (通) is therefore total obtuseness. Modern use is much lighter, and Chinese speakers most often apply it to themselves about some subject they cannot follow.
chineseExample_tr: 他對這個話題一竅不通。

meaning: Hide the sky with one hand
example: He tried to control everything, but his efforts were futile.
chineseExample: 他一手遮天，结果却是徒劳无功。
description: One (一) hand (手) covering (遮) the sky (天). The image contains its own refutation, and classical uses of it say so — no hand is large enough, and the attempt is visible to everyone not standing directly behind it. That is what makes the phrase an accusation rather than a description of success. It is used of officials who control the local information supply, and of anyone whose position lets them decide what the people above them get to hear.
description_tr: One (一) hand (手) covering (遮) the sky (天). The image contains its own refutation, and classical uses of it say so — no hand is large enough, and the attempt is visible to everyone not standing directly behind it. That is what makes the phrase an accusation rather than a description of success. It is used of officials who control the local information supply, and of anyone whose position lets them decide what the people above them get to hear.
chineseExample_tr: 他一手遮天，結果卻是徒勞無功。

example: He came out of the water with nothing on at all
chineseExample: 他一丝不挂地从水里走出来
description: This one begins in Chan Buddhist writing, where 丝 is a fishing line and the point is a fish with no thread attached to it — nothing hooked, nothing tying it to anything. That is the state of non-attachment. Learners must know that modern Chinese has taken it somewhere else entirely: in ordinary use today 一丝不挂 means stark naked, with 丝 read as a thread of clothing. The spiritual sense survives only in Buddhist contexts, and using the phrase for freedom from cares will be badly misunderstood.
description_tr: This one begins in Chan Buddhist writing, where 絲 is a fishing line and the point is a fish with no thread attached to it — nothing hooked, nothing tying it to anything. That is the state of non-attachment. Learners must know that modern Chinese has taken it somewhere else entirely: in ordinary use today 一絲不掛 means stark naked, with 絲 read as a thread of clothing. The spiritual sense survives only in Buddhist contexts, and using the phrase for freedom from cares will be badly misunderstood.
chineseExample_tr: 他一絲不掛地從水裡走出來

example: He recounted the events with precise details, making it easy to understand.
chineseExample: 他把事情一五一十地讲述清楚，让人容易理解。
description: Chinese counts large quantities in fives and tens, so 一五一十 is the sound of someone tallying aloud — five, ten, fifteen — without skipping. Applied to speech it means an account given in that manner: everything in order, nothing rounded off, nothing left out. It is used above all of testimony and confession, where the point is completeness rather than eloquence, and it commonly appears as 一五一十地说出来, to tell the whole thing.
description_tr: Chinese counts large quantities in fives and tens, so 一五一十 is the sound of someone tallying aloud — five, ten, fifteen — without skipping. Applied to speech it means an account given in that manner: everything in order, nothing rounded off, nothing left out. It is used above all of testimony and confession, where the point is completeness rather than eloquence, and it commonly appears as 一五一十地說出來, to tell the whole thing.
chineseExample_tr: 他把事情一五一十地講述清楚，讓人容易理解。

example: The situation was so complex that it was hard to summarize in a single statement.
chineseExample: 这个情况复杂，一言难尽。
description: One (一) word (言) cannot exhaust (难尽) it. The phrase is doing social work as much as descriptive work: in practice it is the standard Chinese way of declining to answer a question about how things have been, without refusing outright. It signals that the true answer is long and probably unhappy, and that the speaker would rather not begin. Asked how the last few years have gone, 一言难尽 is both an honest answer and a request to change the subject.
description_tr: One (一) word (言) cannot exhaust (難盡) it. The phrase is doing social work as much as descriptive work: in practice it is the standard Chinese way of declining to answer a question about how things have been, without refusing outright. It signals that the true answer is long and probably unhappy, and that the speaker would rather not begin. Asked how the last few years have gone, 一言難盡 is both an honest answer and a request to change the subject.
chineseExample_tr: 這個情況複雜，一言難盡。

example: As a manager, she always leads by personal example, inspiring her team to follow suit.
chineseExample: 作为经理，她以身作则，激励团队效仿。
description: To take (以) one's own person (身) and make (作) it the standard (则). 则 is a rule or a model in the strict sense — the thing others are measured against — so the claim is precise: not setting a good example in general but being the reference copy. Chinese applies it to parents, teachers and officials, and it carries the corresponding implication that failing to do it invalidates whatever you say. It is the standard requirement laid on anyone in charge.
description_tr: To take (以) one's own person (身) and make (作) it the standard (則). 則 is a rule or a model in the strict sense — the thing others are measured against — so the claim is precise: not setting a good example in general but being the reference copy. Chinese applies it to parents, teachers and officials, and it carries the corresponding implication that failing to do it invalidates whatever you say. It is the standard requirement laid on anyone in charge.
chineseExample_tr: 作為經理，她以身作則，激勵團隊效仿。

example: By preparing thoroughly, he was able to wait for the right moment to act without stress.
chineseExample: 他充分准备，以逸待劳，轻松应对挑战。
description: Sun Tzu's chapter on manoeuvre lists the pairings: meet the distant with the near, the tired with the rested, the hungry with the fed. This is the second of them — using (以) ease (逸) to await (待) exhaustion (劳) — and it is the fourth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. The essential point is that the advantage is manufactured rather than found. The waiting side is expected to have chosen the ground and forced the other to do the marching, which distinguishes it from simply being patient.
description_tr: Sun Tzu's chapter on manoeuvre lists the pairings: meet the distant with the near, the tired with the rested, the hungry with the fed. This is the second of them — using (以) ease (逸) to await (待) exhaustion (勞) — and it is the fourth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. The essential point is that the advantage is manufactured rather than found. The waiting side is expected to have chosen the ground and forced the other to do the marching, which distinguishes it from simply being patient.
chineseExample_tr: 他充分準備，以逸待勞，輕鬆應對挑戰。

example: In project management, it's crucial to adapt strategies based on the specific context of each location.
chineseExample: 在项目管理中，根据每个地方的具体情况调整策略至关重要。
description: Wu Zixu, advising the king of Wu on building a state, is recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue as arguing that walls, fields and defences should follow the ground rather than a template. According to (因) the land (地), determine (制) what suits (宜). The phrase is now central to Chinese policy language, where it functions as the standard argument against uniform national prescriptions, and it is equally at home in agriculture, architecture and teaching.
description_tr: Wu Zixu, advising the king of Wu on building a state, is recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue as arguing that walls, fields and defences should follow the ground rather than a template. According to (因) the land (地), determine (制) what suits (宜). The phrase is now central to Chinese policy language, where it functions as the standard argument against uniform national prescriptions, and it is equally at home in agriculture, architecture and teaching.
chineseExample_tr: 在項目管理中，根據每個地方的具體情況調整策略至關重要。

example: Choosing to ignore the problem may provide temporary relief, but it ultimately leads to greater consequences.
chineseExample: 选择忽视问题可能会带来暂时的缓解，但最终会导致更大的后果。
description: The 鸩 is a poisonous bird of legend whose feathers, steeped in wine, made a reliable and untraceable method of murder. Huo Xu, defending his uncle against a capital charge, argued to the authorities that no man would do what was alleged, since it would be like drinking (饮) that wine to stop (止) thirst (渴) — relief for a moment, death immediately after. The History of the Later Han preserves the plea. The phrase describes a remedy whose cost is larger than the problem, and it is standard in Chinese discussion of debt.
description_tr: The 鴆 is a poisonous bird of legend whose feathers, steeped in wine, made a reliable and untraceable method of murder. Huo Xu, defending his uncle against a capital charge, argued to the authorities that no man would do what was alleged, since it would be like drinking (飲) that wine to stop (止) thirst (渴) — relief for a moment, death immediately after. The History of the Later Han preserves the plea. The phrase describes a remedy whose cost is larger than the problem, and it is standard in Chinese discussion of debt.
chineseExample_tr: 選擇忽視問題可能會帶來暫時的緩解，但最終會導致更大的後果。

example: His courage in the face of adversity made him a leader among his peers.
chineseExample: 他在逆境中的勇气使他成为同龄人中的领袖。
description: 三军 is the full establishment of an ancient army, its three divisions, so to crown (冠) all three with one's courage (勇) is to be the bravest man in the entire force. The phrase comes from the letter attributed to Li Ling writing to Su Wu, praising the general Li Guang. It has stayed close to its origins and remains distinctly martial. Chinese uses it for genuine physical courage, and applying it to a boardroom would sound like deliberate hyperbole.
description_tr: 三軍 is the full establishment of an ancient army, its three divisions, so to crown (冠) all three with one's courage (勇) is to be the bravest man in the entire force. The phrase comes from the letter attributed to Li Ling writing to Su Wu, praising the general Li Guang. It has stayed close to its origins and remains distinctly martial. Chinese uses it for genuine physical courage, and applying it to a boardroom would sound like deliberate hyperbole.
chineseExample_tr: 他在逆境中的勇氣使他成為同齡人中的領袖。

example: The evidence of his hard work is clear for everyone to see.
chineseExample: 他努力工作的证据有目共睹。
description: Having (有) eyes (目), all together (共) see it (睹). The construction is worth noticing: the claim is not that everyone agrees, but that possessing eyes is the only qualification required, which forecloses the argument rather than winning it. That is exactly how it is used. It appears in Chinese official and commercial language about achievements, and its rhetorical function is to treat a contested claim as though it were a matter of plain observation. A learner who meets it in a sales pitch should read it as a signal that no evidence is going to follow.
description_tr: Having (有) eyes (目), all together (共) see it (睹). The construction is worth noticing: the claim is not that everyone agrees, but that possessing eyes is the only qualification required, which forecloses the argument rather than winning it. That is exactly how it is used. It appears in Chinese official and commercial language about achievements, and its rhetorical function is to treat a contested claim as though it were a matter of plain observation. A learner who meets it in a sales pitch should read it as a signal that no evidence is going to follow.
chineseExample_tr: 他努力工作的證據有目共睹。

example: The performance was vibrant and full of life, captivating the audience completely.
chineseExample: 这场表演有声有色，完全吸引了观众。
description: Having (有) sound (声) and having (有) colour (色). The phrase began in literary criticism, praising writing that engaged more than one sense at once, and it has widened to any performance or undertaking carried off with energy and visible effect. What it praises is presentation rather than substance, which leaves a small opening for irony — a project described as running 有声有色 is definitely making an impression, and the phrase does not by itself say whether it is working.
description_tr: Having (有) sound (聲) and having (有) colour (色). The phrase began in literary criticism, praising writing that engaged more than one sense at once, and it has widened to any performance or undertaking carried off with energy and visible effect. What it praises is presentation rather than substance, which leaves a small opening for irony — a project described as running 有聲有色 is definitely making an impression, and the phrase does not by itself say whether it is working.
chineseExample_tr: 這場表演有聲有色，完全吸引了觀眾。

example: In the chaotic market, it's hard to distinguish the genuine from the counterfeit.
chineseExample: 在这个混乱的市场中，很难分辨真伪。
description: Fish (鱼) and dragons (龙) mixed (混杂) together. The pairing depends on a Chinese belief that a carp which passes the Dragon Gate becomes a dragon, so the two are not simply different creatures but different stages — which is why they can be in the same water and hard to tell apart. The phrase describes a group whose members are of very unequal quality, and it is mildly disapproving. It suits open markets, unvetted crowds and any profession with no barrier to entry.
description_tr: Fish (魚) and dragons (龍) mixed (混雜) together. The pairing depends on a Chinese belief that a carp which passes the Dragon Gate becomes a dragon, so the two are not simply different creatures but different stages — which is why they can be in the same water and hard to tell apart. The phrase describes a group whose members are of very unequal quality, and it is mildly disapproving. It suits open markets, unvetted crowds and any profession with no barrier to entry.
chineseExample_tr: 在這個混亂的市場中，很難分辨真偽。

example: Her heartfelt advice carried a weight that resonated deeply with him.
chineseExample: 她的真诚建议让他深受感动。
description: Words (语) that are weighty (重) and a heart (心) that reaches far (长). The two halves describe different things: the speech is serious, and the concern behind it extends beyond the present moment. That combination is what makes the phrase specific. It is used of advice from someone older who has thought about your life for longer than you have, and it is nearly always said in retrospect, about a conversation whose point arrived years later.
description_tr: Words (語) that are weighty (重) and a heart (心) that reaches far (長). The two halves describe different things: the speech is serious, and the concern behind it extends beyond the present moment. That combination is what makes the phrase specific. It is used of advice from someone older who has thought about your life for longer than you have, and it is nearly always said in retrospect, about a conversation whose point arrived years later.
chineseExample_tr: 她的真誠建議讓他深受感動。

example: He stubbornly adhered to his principles, even when faced with practical challenges.
chineseExample: 他固执地坚持自己的原则，即使面临实际挑战。
description: A man (人) of Zheng (郑), wanting to buy (买) shoes (履), measured his foot with a cord and left the cord at home. Reaching the market he found he had forgotten it and went back for it, and by the time he returned the market had closed. Asked why he had not simply tried the shoes on his feet, he said: I trust the measurement, I do not trust myself. Han Feizi tells it against rulers who prefer the precedent to the case in front of them, and the punchline is the whole idiom — the foot was available the entire time.
description_tr: A man (人) of Zheng (鄭), wanting to buy (買) shoes (履), measured his foot with a cord and left the cord at home. Reaching the market he found he had forgotten it and went back for it, and by the time he returned the market had closed. Asked why he had not simply tried the shoes on his feet, he said: I trust the measurement, I do not trust myself. Han Feizi tells it against rulers who prefer the precedent to the case in front of them, and the punchline is the whole idiom — the foot was available the entire time.
chineseExample_tr: 他固執地堅持自己的原則，即使面臨實際挑戰。

example: In the debate, there were so many conflicting opinions that it was hard to reach a consensus.
chineseExample: 在辩论中，众多相互矛盾的意见让人难以达成共识。
description: Many (众) accounts (说), tangled and numerous (纷纭). 纷纭 is a reduplicative describing things scattered and interwoven, the same word used of falling blossom and drifting snow. So the phrase is not about disagreement between two sides but about a field of opinion with no shape to it. It is used when the facts are not yet settled — an unexplained event, an unattributed decision — and it implies that none of the accounts has yet earned precedence.
description_tr: Many (眾) accounts (說), tangled and numerous (紛紜). 紛紜 is a reduplicative describing things scattered and interwoven, the same word used of falling blossom and drifting snow. So the phrase is not about disagreement between two sides but about a field of opinion with no shape to it. It is used when the facts are not yet settled — an unexplained event, an unattributed decision — and it implies that none of the accounts has yet earned precedence.
chineseExample_tr: 在辯論中，眾多相互矛盾的意見讓人難以達成共識。

example: The seasons change, reminding us that life is a continuous cycle of beginnings and endings.
chineseExample: 四季更替，让我们意识到生活是一个不断循环的过程。
description: To go round (周) and then (而) begin again (复始). Chinese thought organises time cyclically by default — the sixty-year calendar, the五行 sequence, the seasons — and this phrase is the plain statement of the pattern. It carries no verdict. Used of nature it is calm, and used of human affairs it is generally weary, describing the meeting that produces the decision that produces the same meeting, and the historical pattern that keeps arriving as though for the first time.
description_tr: To go round (周) and then (而) begin again (復始). Chinese thought organises time cyclically by default — the sixty-year calendar, the五行 sequence, the seasons — and this phrase is the plain statement of the pattern. It carries no verdict. Used of nature it is calm, and used of human affairs it is generally weary, describing the meeting that produces the decision that produces the same meeting, and the historical pattern that keeps arriving as though for the first time.
chineseExample_tr: 四季更替，讓我們意識到生活是一個不斷循環的過程。

example: After losing his job, he fell into despair and gave up on life.
chineseExample: 失去工作后，他自暴自弃，放弃了生活。
description: Mencius distinguishes two failures and the phrase joins them. The man who does violence to himself (自暴) cannot be talked with, because he has decided that right and propriety are not worth discussing; the man who throws himself away (自弃) cannot be worked with, because he has decided he is incapable of them. One is contempt for the standard, the other is despair of meeting it. Chinese uses the compound for the settled version of giving up, and it is a serious thing to say about someone.
description_tr: Mencius distinguishes two failures and the phrase joins them. The man who does violence to himself (自暴) cannot be talked with, because he has decided that right and propriety are not worth discussing; the man who throws himself away (自棄) cannot be worked with, because he has decided he is incapable of them. One is contempt for the standard, the other is despair of meeting it. Chinese uses the compound for the settled version of giving up, and it is a serious thing to say about someone.
chineseExample_tr: 失去工作後，他自暴自棄，放棄了生活。

example: He thought he could easily complete the project, but he underestimated the challenges ahead.
chineseExample: 他以为自己能轻松完成这个项目，却自不量力。
description: The Zuo Zhuan lists five faults in the small state of Xi, which attacked its stronger neighbour Zheng: it did not weigh its virtue, did not measure (量) its own (自) strength (力), was not kind to its kin, did not examine the wording of the quarrel, and did not establish who was at fault. Xi's army was routed, and the chronicler adds that this was how one knew the state would eventually fall. Failing to measure one's own force is therefore a specific administrative error rather than mere arrogance. Modern Chinese uses the phrase bluntly, often as a contemptuous dismissal — 自不量力 said of a challenger means they have not done the arithmetic.
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan lists five faults in the small state of Xi, which attacked its stronger neighbour Zheng: it did not weigh its virtue, did not measure (量) its own (自) strength (力), was not kind to its kin, did not examine the wording of the quarrel, and did not establish who was at fault. Xi's army was routed, and the chronicler adds that this was how one knew the state would eventually fall. Failing to measure one's own force is therefore a specific administrative error rather than mere arrogance. Modern Chinese uses the phrase bluntly, often as a contemptuous dismissal — 自不量力 said of a challenger means they have not done the arithmetic.
chineseExample_tr: 他以為自己能輕鬆完成這個項目，卻自不量力。

example: She felt self-conscious and ashamed when she compared herself to her more accomplished peers.
chineseExample: 她看到更优秀的同龄人时，自惭形秽。
description: Wang Ji was a handsome man and knew it. The New Account of Tales of the World says that whenever he saw his nephew Wei Jie he would sigh 珠玉在侧，觉我形秽 — with pearl and jade beside me, I am aware of how coarse I look. The idiom supplies the word he left out: shame (惭) at one's own (自) form (形) being coarse (秽) next to another's. Wei Jie's looks were famous enough that crowds gathered to see him, and he died young — the wits said of being stared to death. The phrase describes being diminished by proximity rather than by any criticism, which is what makes it so recognisable.
description_tr: Wang Ji was a handsome man and knew it. The New Account of Tales of the World says that whenever he saw his nephew Wei Jie he would sigh 珠玉在側，覺我形穢 — with pearl and jade beside me, I am aware of how coarse I look. The idiom supplies the word he left out: shame (慚) at one's own (自) form (形) being coarse (穢) next to another's. Wei Jie's looks were famous enough that crowds gathered to see him, and he died young — the wits said of being stared to death. The phrase describes being diminished by proximity rather than by any criticism, which is what makes it so recognisable.
chineseExample_tr: 她看到更優秀的同齡人時，自慚形穢。

example: In business, he skillfully navigated the negotiations to secure a favorable deal.
chineseExample: 在商业中，他纵横捭阖，成功达成了有利的交易。
description: 纵 and 横 are the vertical and horizontal alliances of the Warring States — the north-south coalition against Qin and the east-west accommodation with it — and the men who built and broke them were professional persuaders. 捭 and 阖 mean to open and to close, from the manual attributed to Guiguzi, their legendary teacher. The phrase names the whole craft: opening a party up, closing it off, working a system of states by talk alone. It is used of diplomacy and high politics, with a distinct edge of manipulation.
description_tr: 縱 and 橫 are the vertical and horizontal alliances of the Warring States — the north-south coalition against Qin and the east-west accommodation with it — and the men who built and broke them were professional persuaders. 捭 and 闔 mean to open and to close, from the manual attributed to Guiguzi, their legendary teacher. The phrase names the whole craft: opening a party up, closing it off, working a system of states by talk alone. It is used of diplomacy and high politics, with a distinct edge of manipulation.
chineseExample_tr: 在商業中，他縱橫捭闔，成功達成了有利的交易。

example: She pondered over the decision from every angle before making a choice.
chineseExample: 她在做决定之前，左思右想了很久。
description: Thinking (思) to the left (左) and considering (想) to the right (右). Its value is in the picture of the head physically turning. What it describes is not depth of thought but its restless, unresolved quality — turning a matter over repeatedly without arriving. That is how Chinese uses it: usually of a sleepless night, and usually followed by whatever the person finally decided, or by the admission that they did not.
description_tr: Thinking (思) to the left (左) and considering (想) to the right (右). Its value is in the picture of the head physically turning. What it describes is not depth of thought but its restless, unresolved quality — turning a matter over repeatedly without arriving. That is how Chinese uses it: usually of a sleepless night, and usually followed by whatever the person finally decided, or by the admission that they did not.
chineseExample_tr: 她在做決定之前，左思右想了很久。

example: By strategically positioning himself, he was able to benefit from the hard work of others.
chineseExample: 通过巧妙的布局，他坐收渔利。
description: Su Dai, dissuading Zhao from attacking Yan, told the king a story. A clam lay open on the bank; a snipe stabbed at its flesh and the shell closed on its beak. Each told the other it would die first, and while they held on a fisherman came along and took the pair. Qin, said Su Dai, is the fisherman. The full saying is 鹬蚌相争，渔翁得利, and this phrase names the same figure from the other side: the third party who sits still (坐) and collects (收) while two others exhaust each other.
description_tr: Su Dai, dissuading Zhao from attacking Yan, told the king a story. A clam lay open on the bank; a snipe stabbed at its flesh and the shell closed on its beak. Each told the other it would die first, and while they held on a fisherman came along and took the pair. Qin, said Su Dai, is the fisherman. The full saying is 鷸蚌相爭，漁翁得利, and this phrase names the same figure from the other side: the third party who sits still (坐) and collects (收) while two others exhaust each other.
chineseExample_tr: 通過巧妙的佈局，他坐收漁利。

example: He always knows to stay within his limits and not overreach.
chineseExample: 他总是安分守己，不会过分追求。
description: Content with (安) one's allotted station (分) and keeping to (守) oneself (己). The phrase has two lives in Chinese and they are not easy to reconcile. As praise it describes an honest person who does their job and causes nobody trouble. As something colder it describes the citizen who does not ask questions, and it has been used approvingly by authorities in exactly that sense for a very long time. Whether it is a compliment depends heavily on who is applying it to whom.
description_tr: Content with (安) one's allotted station (分) and keeping to (守) oneself (己). The phrase has two lives in Chinese and they are not easy to reconcile. As praise it describes an honest person who does their job and causes nobody trouble. As something colder it describes the citizen who does not ask questions, and it has been used approvingly by authorities in exactly that sense for a very long time. Whether it is a compliment depends heavily on who is applying it to whom.
chineseExample_tr: 他總是安分守己，不會過分追求。

example: Time flies, and before we know it, years have passed like a white horse through a narrow gap.
chineseExample: 时光荏苒，白驹过隙。
description: The Zhuangzi asks what a human life is between heaven and earth and answers: a white colt (白驹) glimpsed through (过) a gap in the wall (隙), and then it is over. Everything in the image is doing work — the horse is at a gallop, the crack is narrow, and the observer's view is fixed. Chinese uses it for the retrospective sense that a long period went past without being noticed, which is why it belongs to memorials, reunions and the end of the year.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi asks what a human life is between heaven and earth and answers: a white colt (白駒) glimpsed through (過) a gap in the wall (隙), and then it is over. Everything in the image is doing work — the horse is at a gallop, the crack is narrow, and the observer's view is fixed. Chinese uses it for the retrospective sense that a long period went past without being noticed, which is why it belongs to memorials, reunions and the end of the year.
chineseExample_tr: 時光荏苒，白駒過隙。

example: Her talent is truly exceptional, standing out as one in a hundred in her field.
chineseExample: 她的才华真是百里挑一。
description: One (一) picked (挑) out of a hundred (百里). 里 here reads as a measure of the pool rather than a distance. The phrase is a claim about ratio and, unlike most Chinese superlatives, it names a number that is high but not absurd — one in a hundred, not one in ten thousand. That keeps it usable. The Dream of the Red Chamber applies it to people, and it remains most natural about a person rather than a thing, particularly a prospective spouse or a hire.
description_tr: One (一) picked (挑) out of a hundred (百里). 裡 here reads as a measure of the pool rather than a distance. The phrase is a claim about ratio and, unlike most Chinese superlatives, it names a number that is high but not absurd — one in a hundred, not one in ten thousand. That keeps it usable. The Dream of the Red Chamber applies it to people, and it remains most natural about a person rather than a thing, particularly a prospective spouse or a hire.
chineseExample_tr: 她的才華真是百里挑一。

example: After the merger, the company now controls half the market share.
chineseExample: 合并后，公司占据了半壁江山。
description: 半壁 is half a wall and 江山, rivers and mountains, is the standard Chinese word for a realm — territory as the thing a dynasty holds. The phrase is inseparable from the memory of the Song court driven south of the Yangtze, ruling half of what it had, and it carries that specific grief: not defeat but partial survival, with the lost half still in view. Modern use has softened it to any large fraction of a whole, though in writing about history it keeps all of its original weight.
description_tr: 半壁 is half a wall and 江山, rivers and mountains, is the standard Chinese word for a realm — territory as the thing a dynasty holds. The phrase is inseparable from the memory of the Song court driven south of the Yangtze, ruling half of what it had, and it carries that specific grief: not defeat but partial survival, with the lost half still in view. Modern use has softened it to any large fraction of a whole, though in writing about history it keeps all of its original weight.
chineseExample_tr: 合併後，公司佔據了半壁江山。

example: His philosophy embraces all aspects of life, making him a well-rounded individual.
chineseExample: 他的哲学包罗万象，使他成为一个全面发展的人。
description: To wrap up (包) and net (罗) the ten thousand (万) phenomena (象). 万象 is a set expression for the totality of appearances in the world, and 罗 is a fine-meshed net, so the claim is not merely of breadth but of catching everything, including the small things. It is used of encyclopaedias, museums, sprawling novels and very long meetings. Applied to something that ought to have been selective it becomes a criticism, since containing everything and having a point are different achievements.
description_tr: To wrap up (包) and net (羅) the ten thousand (萬) phenomena (象). 萬象 is a set expression for the totality of appearances in the world, and 羅 is a fine-meshed net, so the claim is not merely of breadth but of catching everything, including the small things. It is used of encyclopaedias, museums, sprawling novels and very long meetings. Applied to something that ought to have been selective it becomes a criticism, since containing everything and having a point are different achievements.
chineseExample_tr: 他的哲學包羅萬象，使他成為一個全面發展的人。

example: He spends his days indulging in food without any thought for the future.
chineseExample: 他整天饱食终日，毫无未来的考虑。
description: Confucius, in the Analects: to eat one's fill (饱食) the whole day (终日) with the mind put to no use at all — this is a hard case. He then says, with some asperity, that there are games of chess, and that playing them would at least be something. The phrase carries that impatience. It describes not idleness in the sense of rest but the unused mind, and Chinese applies it to comfortable, occupied lives in which nothing is actually being thought about.
description_tr: Confucius, in the Analects: to eat one's fill (飽食) the whole day (終日) with the mind put to no use at all — this is a hard case. He then says, with some asperity, that there are games of chess, and that playing them would at least be something. The phrase carries that impatience. It describes not idleness in the sense of rest but the unused mind, and Chinese applies it to comfortable, occupied lives in which nothing is actually being thought about.
chineseExample_tr: 他整天飽食終日，毫無未來的考慮。

example: Their opinions on the matter are so different that they seem to be running in opposite directions.
chineseExample: 他们在这个问题上的看法背道而驰。
description: Turning one's back (背) on the road (道) and galloping (驰) the other way. It belongs to Tang prose rather than to a single early parable, and it is often told with the story of the man driving north to reach Chu — but that story belongs to 南辕北辙, which is a separate idiom with its own source in the Strategies of the Warring States. The force here is in 背: the direction is not merely wrong, it is the exact opposite. Chinese reserves it for effort working directly against the goal it claims to serve.
metaphoric_meaning: Run directly counter to the aim
description_tr: Turning one's back (背) on the road (道) and galloping (馳) the other way. It belongs to Tang prose rather than to a single early parable, and it is often told with the story of the man driving north to reach Chu — but that story belongs to 南轅北轍, which is a separate idiom with its own source in the Strategies of the Warring States. The force here is in 背: the direction is not merely wrong, it is the exact opposite. Chinese uses it of effort working directly against the goal it claims to serve.
chineseExample_tr: 他們在這個問題上的看法背道而馳。

example: He felt he had no choice but to rebel against the system, much like those who were forced onto Liangshan.
chineseExample: 他觉得自己别无选择，只能像被逼上梁山的人一样反抗体制。
description: Liangshan is the marsh stronghold of the outlaws in the Water Margin, and the novel's structure is the phrase's meaning: its heroes are not born rebels but officers, instructors and clerks driven there one by one by officials they could not appeal against. Lin Chong, framed and hunted, is the type. Being forced (逼) up (上) to Liangshan (梁山) therefore describes rebellion entered as the last remaining option, and modern Chinese uses it for any drastic step someone was manoeuvred into rather than chose.
description_tr: Liangshan is the marsh stronghold of the outlaws in the Water Margin, and the novel's structure is the phrase's meaning: its heroes are not born rebels but officers, instructors and clerks driven there one by one by officials they could not appeal against. Lin Chong, framed and hunted, is the type. Being forced (逼) up (上) to Liangshan (梁山) therefore describes rebellion entered as the last remaining option, and modern Chinese uses it for any drastic step someone was manoeuvred into rather than chose.
chineseExample_tr: 他覺得自己別無選擇，只能像被逼上梁山的人一樣反抗體制。

example: In today's fast-paced world, trends seem to change without constancy, making it hard to keep up.
chineseExample: 在当今快节奏的世界里，趋势变化无常，让人难以跟上。
description: Change (变化) without (无) constancy (常). The Zhuangzi supplies it, and 无常 is worth knowing separately: it is also the standard Chinese rendering of the Buddhist impermanence, and personified as 无常 it is the spirit that comes to collect the dying. The phrase therefore sits on a serious foundation, though ordinary use is much lighter — weather, moods, markets, and anything whose next state cannot be predicted from its last one.
description_tr: Change (變化) without (無) constancy (常). The Zhuangzi supplies it, and 無常 is worth knowing separately: it is also the standard Chinese rendering of the Buddhist impermanence, and personified as 無常 it is the spirit that comes to collect the dying. The phrase therefore sits on a serious foundation, though ordinary use is much lighter — weather, moods, markets, and anything whose next state cannot be predicted from its last one.
chineseExample_tr: 在當今快節奏的世界裡，趨勢變化無常，讓人難以跟上。

example: The harsh winter landscape made it difficult for anyone to venture outside.
chineseExample: 严寒的冬季景象让任何人都难以外出。
description: Ice (冰) for a sky (天) and snow (雪) for ground (地). The construction assigns the two elements to the two halves of the world, leaving nothing outside the cold, which is what distinguishes it from simply saying it is freezing. The phrase belongs to the Chinese northeast and to accounts of hardship — Qing poetry uses it of the destitute in winter. It is used both literally, of genuinely severe weather, and figuratively of conditions in which something has to be done anyway.
description_tr: Ice (冰) for a sky (天) and snow (雪) for ground (地). The construction assigns the two elements to the two halves of the world, leaving nothing outside the cold, which is what distinguishes it from simply saying it is freezing. The phrase belongs to the Chinese northeast and to accounts of hardship — Qing poetry uses it of the destitute in winter. It is used both literally, of genuinely severe weather, and figuratively of conditions in which something has to be done anyway.
chineseExample_tr: 嚴寒的冬季景象讓任何人都難以外出。

example: She tirelessly pursued her goals, never once complaining about the effort required.
chineseExample: 她不辞辛劳地追求自己的目标，从不抱怨所需的努力。
description: Not (不) declining (辞) the bitter (辛) labour (劳). The key character is 辞, to refuse or excuse oneself — the phrase is about what someone did not do, namely find a reason to be elsewhere. That makes it quieter praise than it first appears, and appropriately so: it is used of the person who was reliably there for the tedious and unrewarded parts, and it appears constantly in citations, thanks and eulogies for exactly that sort of contribution.
description_tr: Not (不) declining (辭) the bitter (辛) labour (勞). The key character is 辭, to refuse or excuse oneself — the phrase is about what someone did not do, namely find a reason to be elsewhere. That makes it quieter praise than it first appears, and appropriately so: it is used of the person who was reliably there for the tedious and unrewarded parts, and it appears constantly in citations, thanks and eulogies for exactly that sort of contribution.
chineseExample_tr: 她不辭辛勞地追求自己的目標，從不抱怨所需的努力。

example: The eerie silence of the abandoned house made everyone feel a chill of fear.
chineseExample: 废弃房屋的诡异寂静让每个人都感到一阵恐惧的寒意。
description: The Records of the Grand Historian describes Yi Zong, an official of Emperor Wu's who executed more than four hundred people in a single day, and reports that afterwards the people of the district shivered (栗) though the weather was not (不) cold (寒). The phrase keeps the physiology exactly: the body producing a cold response with no cold present. It is used of news, discoveries and prospects that are frightening rather than merely bad, and it is stronger than the English 'chilling'.
description_tr: The Records of the Grand Historian describes Yi Zong, an official of Emperor Wu's who executed more than four hundred people in a single day, and reports that afterwards the people of the district shivered (慄) though the weather was not (不) cold (寒). The phrase keeps the physiology exactly: the body producing a cold response with no cold present. It is used of news, discoveries and prospects that are frightening rather than merely bad, and it is stronger than the English 'chilling'.
chineseExample_tr: 廢棄房屋的詭異寂靜讓每個人都感到一陣恐懼的寒意。

example: There are countless stars in the night sky, each one a distant sun.
chineseExample: 夜空中有不计其数的星星，每一颗都是遥远的太阳。
description: Not (不) counting (计) their (其) number (数). The construction is precise about what is being claimed — not that the things are infinite but that nobody has counted them and nobody is going to. That makes it a statement about the counter as much as the counted. It is one of the most common Chinese superlatives for quantity, entirely neutral in tone, and it is at home in casualty figures, catalogue sizes and the number of times someone has been asked something.
description_tr: Not (不) counting (計) their (其) number (數). The construction is precise about what is being claimed — not that the things are infinite but that nobody has counted them and nobody is going to. That makes it a statement about the counter as much as the counted. It is one of the most common Chinese superlatives for quantity, entirely neutral in tone, and it is at home in casualty figures, catalogue sizes and the number of times someone has been asked something.
chineseExample_tr: 夜空中有不計其數的星星，每一顆都是遙遠的太陽。

example: Her innovative approach to solving problems showed that creativity knows no bounds.
chineseExample: 她创新的解决问题的方法表明，创造力不拘一格。
description: Gong Zizhen, in the year 1839, wrote a poem asking heaven to rouse itself and send down talent 不拘一格 — not confined (不拘) to a single (一) mould (格). China was on the edge of the Opium War, and the poem opens on a country where ten thousand horses stand mute — 万马齐喑 — which is the silence the talent is wanted to break. 格 is a frame or a set form. The line became one of the most quoted in modern Chinese, and the phrase is now standard in arguments about hiring, admissions and the recognition of unconventional ability.
metaphoric_meaning: Not confined to a single mould
description_tr: Gong Zizhen, in the year 1839, wrote a poem asking heaven to rouse itself and send down talent 不拘一格 — not confined (不拘) to a single (一) mould (格). China was on the edge of the Opium War, and the poem opens on a country where ten thousand horses stand mute — 萬馬齊喑 — which is the silence the talent is wanted to break. 格 is a frame or a set form. The line became one of the most quoted in modern Chinese, and the phrase is now standard in arguments about hiring, admissions and the recognition of unconventional ability.
chineseExample_tr: 她創新的解決問題的方法表明，創造力不拘一格。

example: He expected to receive a promotion without putting in any hard work.
chineseExample: 他期望不劳而获，得到晋升。
description: To obtain (获) without (不) labouring (劳). Chinese has a strong and consistent moral vocabulary around this, and the phrase is its plainest statement. It is worth distinguishing from luck, which Chinese does not condemn: what 不劳而获 names is a structural arrangement in which someone else's work produces your return. It is applied to landlords, to middlemen, to inherited position, and by parents to children, in a tone that is usually more disappointed than angry.
description_tr: To obtain (獲) without (不) labouring (勞). Chinese has a strong and consistent moral vocabulary around this, and the phrase is its plainest statement. It is worth distinguishing from luck, which Chinese does not condemn: what 不勞而獲 names is a structural arrangement in which someone else's work produces your return. It is applied to landlords, to middlemen, to inherited position, and by parents to children, in a tone that is usually more disappointed than angry.
chineseExample_tr: 他期望不勞而獲，得到晉升。

example: His style of writing is so unique that it doesn't fit into any specific genre.
chineseExample: 他的写作风格不伦不类，无法归入任何特定的类型。
description: Neither in the proper relation (不伦) nor of the proper kind (不类). 伦 is the word used for the cardinal human relationships, so both halves are about category — the thing has no place in any recognised order. English reaches for neither fish nor fowl, which matches the sense but understates the disapproval. Chinese uses it of clothes, of translations, of buildings and of behaviour, and the complaint is always that something has been assembled out of parts that do not belong together.
description_tr: Neither in the proper relation (不倫) nor of the proper kind (不類). 倫 is the word used for the cardinal human relationships, so both halves are about category — the thing has no place in any recognised order. English reaches for neither fish nor fowl, which matches the sense but understates the disapproval. Chinese uses it of clothes, of translations, of buildings and of behaviour, and the complaint is always that something has been assembled out of parts that do not belong together.
chineseExample_tr: 他的寫作風格不倫不類，無法歸入任何特定的類型。

example: The region was once fertile, but now it has become a wasteland.
chineseExample: 这个地区曾经肥沃，但现在已变成不毛之地。
description: 毛 is the hair of an animal and, by extension, the vegetable covering of the ground. Land (地) without (不) that covering (毛) is bare in a specific way — not merely poor but unable to grow anything. In the Gongyang commentary a defeated Duke of Zheng begs his conqueror to pity him and 锡之不毛之地, grant him some barren ground where he can withdraw with a few old retainers, which is the flavour the phrase keeps: the land nobody else wants. Modern Chinese applies it to deserts and wasteland, and figuratively to fields of study or markets in which nothing has yet grown.
description_tr: 毛 is the hair of an animal and, by extension, the vegetable covering of the ground. Land (地) without (不) that covering (毛) is bare in a specific way — not merely poor but unable to grow anything. In the Gongyang commentary a defeated Duke of Zheng begs his conqueror to pity him and 錫之不毛之地, grant him some barren ground where he can withdraw with a few old retainers, which is the flavour the phrase keeps: the land nobody else wants. Modern Chinese applies it to deserts and wasteland, and figuratively to fields of study or markets in which nothing has yet grown.
chineseExample_tr: 這個地區曾經肥沃，但現在已變成不毛之地。

example: He spends all his time on hobbies instead of focusing on his job.
chineseExample: 他不务正业，整天沉迷于自己的爱好。
description: Not attending to (不务) the proper (正) occupation (业). What makes the phrase sting in Chinese is 正: there is a right thing for a person in their position to be doing, and everything else is by definition a distraction. It is what parents say about a child's hobby that has begun to take up time, and it is applied to companies straying from their core business. Younger speakers now use it affectionately and ironically of their own enthusiasms.
description_tr: Not attending to (不務) the proper (正) occupation (業). What makes the phrase sting in Chinese is 正: there is a right thing for a person in their position to be doing, and everything else is by definition a distraction. It is what parents say about a child's hobby that has begun to take up time, and it is applied to companies straying from their core business. Younger speakers now use it affectionately and ironically of their own enthusiasms.
chineseExample_tr: 他不務正業，整天沉迷於自己的愛好。

example: The news of his sudden success spread like wildfire, as if it had taken flight on its own.
chineseExample: 他的成功消息不翼而飞，迅速传遍了整个城市。
description: The Guanzi observes that what has no wings and yet flies is sound — meaning that words travel without any visible means of doing so. That is the original sense, and it survives in describing how fast news gets around. The commoner modern use is the other one: an object that flies off (飞) without (不) wings (翼), which is the standard Chinese way of reporting that something has gone missing in circumstances that do not suggest an accident.
description_tr: The Guanzi observes that what has no wings and yet flies is sound — meaning that words travel without any visible means of doing so. That is the original sense, and it survives in describing how fast news gets around. The commoner modern use is the other one: an object that flies off (飛) without (不) wings (翼), which is the standard Chinese way of reporting that something has gone missing in circumstances that do not suggest an accident.
chineseExample_tr: 他的成功消息不翼而飛，迅速傳遍了整個城市。

example: Despite his efforts, he often felt inadequate compared to his more knowledgeable peers.
chineseExample: 尽管他努力学习，但总觉得才疏学浅，无法与同伴相比。
description: Talent (才) sparse (疏) and learning (学) shallow (浅). The formula is old: the Book of Han has Gu Yong opening a memorial with 材朽学浅，不通政事 — my abilities rotten, my learning shallow, no grasp of government — and then telling an emperor how to attend to the state. That is exactly how the phrase works: it buys the standing to say something by disclaiming the standing to say it. Learners should note that it is used only in the first person. Applied to somebody else it is not modesty but a direct insult, and Chinese speakers deploy it about themselves in prefaces, speeches and the opening of any awkward request.
description_tr: Talent (才) sparse (疏) and learning (學) shallow (淺). The formula is old: the Book of Han has Gu Yong opening a memorial with 材朽學淺，不通政事 — my abilities rotten, my learning shallow, no grasp of government — and then telling an emperor how to attend to the state. That is exactly how the phrase works: it buys the standing to say something by disclaiming the standing to say it. Learners should note that it is used only in the first person. Applied to somebody else it is not modesty but a direct insult, and Chinese speakers deploy it about themselves in prefaces, speeches and the opening of any awkward request.
chineseExample_tr: 儘管他努力學習，但總覺得才疏學淺，無法與同伴相比。

example: As spring arrives, the landscape transforms, bringing new life and joy.
chineseExample: 春天来了，草长莺飞，万物复苏。
description: Qiu Chi, writing to persuade a defector to come home, gave him the south in three clauses: in late spring, the grass of Jiangnan grows (草长), flowers come out on the trees, and the orioles fly (莺飞) in flocks. It was an argument, not a description — he was reminding the man what he had left. The phrase kept the picture and lost the letter. It now simply names the moment when spring is fully underway, and it is a set phrase in Chinese writing about that season.
description_tr: Qiu Chi, writing to persuade a defector to come home, gave him the south in three clauses: in late spring, the grass of Jiangnan grows (草長), flowers come out on the trees, and the orioles fly (鶯飛) in flocks. It was an argument, not a description — he was reminding the man what he had left. The phrase kept the picture and lost the letter. It now simply names the moment when spring is fully underway, and it is a set phrase in Chinese writing about that season.
chineseExample_tr: 春天來了，草長鶯飛，萬物復甦。

example: Her charm and grace allowed her to navigate the corporate world with ease.
chineseExample: 她的魅力和优雅使她在商界长袖善舞。
description: Han Feizi's pairing is blunter than the idiom that came out of it: long sleeves (长袖) make for good dancing (善舞), plenty of money makes for good trading. His point was about advantage, not skill — the dancer looks better because of the costume. Modern usage has quietly shifted the credit to the person, and 长袖善舞 now describes someone adept at working a room, an institution or a political system. It is rarely quite a compliment, and the original observation about resources is worth keeping in mind.
description_tr: Han Feizi's pairing is blunter than the idiom that came out of it: long sleeves (長袖) make for good dancing (善舞), plenty of money makes for good trading. His point was about advantage, not skill — the dancer looks better because of the costume. Modern usage has quietly shifted the credit to the person, and 長袖善舞 now describes someone adept at working a room, an institution or a political system. It is rarely quite a compliment, and the original observation about resources is worth keeping in mind.
chineseExample_tr: 她的魅力和優雅使她在商界長袖善舞。

meaning: Carriages like water, horses like dragons
example: The bustling city streets were filled with a constant flow of traffic.
chineseExample: 繁华的街道上车水马龙，热闹非凡。
description: Empress Ma of the Later Han, declining to have her relatives ennobled, described the traffic she had seen at their gates: the carriages (车) like flowing water (水), the horses (马) like a moving dragon (龙). She meant it as evidence against them. The phrase is now purely descriptive and entirely positive, the standard Chinese image of a prosperous street, and the empress's disapproval has vanished from it completely.
description_tr: Empress Ma of the Later Han, declining to have her relatives ennobled, described the traffic she had seen at their gates: the carriages (車) like flowing water (水), the horses (馬) like a moving dragon (龍). She meant it as evidence against them. The phrase is now purely descriptive and entirely positive, the standard Chinese image of a prosperous street, and the empress's disapproval has vanished from it completely.
chineseExample_tr: 繁華的街道上車水馬龍，熱鬧非凡。

example: In the competitive market, many companies strive to claim kingship and dominance over their rivals.
chineseExample: 在竞争激烈的市场中，许多公司都想称王称霸。
description: To style oneself (称) king (王) and style oneself hegemon (霸). The two titles are not synonyms and the distinction is old: the 王 rules by legitimate mandate, the 霸 by force and the ability to hold others in line. Claiming both is claiming everything. The phrase is always hostile, and its most common use is domestic rather than political — the person who has decided that some small territory, a department or a neighbourhood, is theirs to run.
description_tr: To style oneself (稱) king (王) and style oneself hegemon (霸). The two titles are not synonyms and the distinction is old: the 王 rules by legitimate mandate, the 霸 by force and the ability to hold others in line. Claiming both is claiming everything. The phrase is always hostile, and its most common use is domestic rather than political — the person who has decided that some small territory, a department or a neighbourhood, is theirs to run.
chineseExample_tr: 在競爭激烈的市場中，許多公司都想稱王稱霸。

example: The treaty was signed under pressure, leading to a fragile peace.
chineseExample: 在压力下签署的城下之盟导致了脆弱的和平。
description: In 700 BCE Chu besieged the small state of Jiao, drew its soldiers outside the walls with a decoy of unescorted woodcutters, and destroyed them. The Zuo Zhuan records that Jiao was then made to swear a covenant (盟) beneath (下) its own walls (城). That is the specific meaning: not a treaty that is merely unfavourable, but one signed with the enemy already at the gate and no alternative available. Chinese says it of any settlement accepted under that kind of pressure, and it always implies humiliation.
description_tr: In 700 BCE Chu besieged the small state of Jiao, drew its soldiers outside the walls with a decoy of unescorted woodcutters, and destroyed them. The Zuo Zhuan records that Jiao was then made to swear a covenant (盟) beneath (下) its own walls (城). That is the specific meaning: not a treaty that is merely unfavourable, but one signed with the enemy already at the gate and no alternative available. Chinese uses it of any settlement accepted under that kind of pressure, and it always implies humiliation.
chineseExample_tr: 在壓力下簽署的城下之盟導致了脆弱的和平。

example: His grand plans for success are just a fool's dream.
chineseExample: 他对成功的宏伟计划不过是痴人说梦。
description: A Song collection tells of the monk Sengqie, asked what his surname was and where he came from, who answered 何 to both — a pun, since 何 means 'what'. A later writer took the answers at face value and recorded on the monument that his surname was He and he came from the country of He. The compiler's comment is the idiom: this is what comes of explaining (说) a dream (梦) to a fool (痴人). The original blames the listener, and Chinese now uses it of the speaker, for talk with no contact with reality.
description_tr: A Song collection tells of the monk Sengqie, asked what his surname was and where he came from, who answered 何 to both — a pun, since 何 means 'what'. A later writer took the answers at face value and recorded on the monument that his surname was He and he came from the country of He. The compiler's comment is the idiom: this is what comes of explaining (說) a dream (夢) to a fool (癡人). The original blames the listener, and Chinese now uses it of the speaker, for talk with no contact with reality.
chineseExample_tr: 他對成功的宏偉計劃不過是癡人說夢。

example: Her eloquence allows her to articulate complex ideas effortlessly.
chineseExample: 她的口才使得出口成章，表达复杂的思想毫不费力。
description: The Book of Songs praises the people of the capital for speech that has pattern in it — 出言有章 — and the idiom sharpens this: what leaves (出) the mouth (口) arrives already composed (成章). 章 is a section of a written work, so the claim is that the person speaks in finished prose without drafting. It is high praise and slightly formal, and It is said of orators and of the rare colleague whose first attempt at a sentence does not need repairing.
description_tr: The Book of Songs praises the people of the capital for speech that has pattern in it — 出言有章 — and the idiom sharpens this: what leaves (出) the mouth (口) arrives already composed (成章). 章 is a section of a written work, so the claim is that the person speaks in finished prose without drafting. It is high praise and slightly formal, and Chinese uses it of orators and of the rare colleague whose first attempt at a sentence does not need repairing.
chineseExample_tr: 她的口才使得出口成章，表達複雜的思想毫不費力。

example: With her innovative ideas, she truly stands out from the crowd.
chineseExample: 凭借她的创新想法，她出人头地。
description: Ouyang Xiu, then the most powerful literary figure in the empire, wrote to a friend about a young examination candidate: I should get out of this man's way and let him stand a head (头) above (出) other men (人) in the world (地). The candidate was Su Shi, and Ouyang Xiu turned out to be right. The phrase describes rising clearly above one's peers, and it carries a faint trace of the original generosity — someone senior stepping aside is the setting in which it was coined.
description_tr: Ouyang Xiu, then the most powerful literary figure in the empire, wrote to a friend about a young examination candidate: I should get out of this man's way and let him stand a head (頭) above (出) other men (人) in the world (地). The candidate was Su Shi, and Ouyang Xiu turned out to be right. The phrase describes rising clearly above one's peers, and it carries a faint trace of the original generosity — someone senior stepping aside is the setting in which it was coined.
chineseExample_tr: 憑藉她的創新想法，她出人頭地。

example: The promotion seemed like a prize just waiting to be claimed.
chineseExample: 这个晋升机会唾手可得。
description: 唾手 is spitting on the palms, the gesture a labourer makes before taking hold of a handle — so the phrase is not about spit but about the moment just before gripping. What can be had (可得) at that point takes no more effort than closing the hand. The Later Han histories put it in the mouth of an over-confident commander. It carries that flavour still: Chinese often uses it of something described as easy by the person who has not yet had to do it.

What can be had (可得) at that point takes no more effort than closing the hand. The Later Han histories put it in the mouth of an over-confident commander. It carries that flavour still: Chinese often uses it of something described as easy by the person who has not yet had to do it.
chineseExample_tr: 這個晉升機會唾手可得。

example: The manager approached the project with a bold and decisive strategy.
chineseExample: 经理以大刀阔斧的策略推进项目。
description: Big knives (大刀) and broad axes (阔斧) — the heavy weapons of vernacular fiction, swung rather than aimed. Applied to action the phrase means sweeping and unsubtle, and Chinese uses it above all of reform: restructurings, budget cuts, redesigns done in large strokes rather than by adjustment. It is genuinely neutral about whether this is wise. The same phrase praises decisiveness and describes the destruction of something that needed finer handling.
description_tr: Big knives (大刀) and broad axes (闊斧) — the heavy weapons of vernacular fiction, swung rather than aimed. Applied to action the phrase means sweeping and unsubtle, and Chinese uses it above all of reform: restructurings, budget cuts, redesigns done in large strokes rather than by adjustment. It is genuinely neutral about whether this is wise. The same phrase praises decisiveness and describes the destruction of something that needed finer handling.
chineseExample_tr: 經理以大刀闊斧的策略推進項目。

example: The news of the team's victory brought great joy to the fans.
chineseExample: 球队获胜的消息让球迷们大快人心。
description: Greatly (大) gladdening (快) the hearts (心) of people (人). The phrase is specific to a public rather than a private satisfaction, and more specifically still to the pleasure of seeing a wrong put right. It is not used of ordinary good news. Its natural subjects are the conviction of a corrupt official, the collapse of a bully's position, a verdict that went the way people thought it should — and it names the collective relief rather than any individual's joy.
description_tr: Greatly (大) gladdening (快) the hearts (心) of people (人). The phrase is specific to a public rather than a private satisfaction, and more specifically still to the pleasure of seeing a wrong put right. It is not used of ordinary good news. Its natural subjects are the conviction of a corrupt official, the collapse of a bully's position, a verdict that went the way people thought it should — and it names the collective relief rather than any individual's joy.
chineseExample_tr: 球隊獲勝的消息讓球迷們大快人心。

example: Winning the award was a joy that exceeded all my expectations.
chineseExample: 获奖的喜悦大喜过望。
description: Ying Bu defected from Xiang Yu to Liu Bang and was received, on arrival, by a Liu Bang who did not get up, sat having his feet washed, and barely acknowledged him. Ying Bu went back to his quarters intending to kill himself, found lodgings, attendants and provisions laid on at the same scale as Liu Bang's own — and was delighted (大喜) beyond (过) what he had hoped for (望). The Records of the Grand Historian tells it as a piece of deliberate stagecraft, which is worth knowing about a phrase now used for any happy surprise.
description_tr: Ying Bu defected from Xiang Yu to Liu Bang and was received, on arrival, by a Liu Bang who did not get up, sat having his feet washed, and barely acknowledged him. Ying Bu went back to his quarters intending to kill himself, found lodgings, attendants and provisions laid on at the same scale as Liu Bang's own — and was delighted (大喜) beyond (過) what he had hoped for (望). The Records of the Grand Historian tells it as a piece of deliberate stagecraft, which is worth knowing about a phrase now used for any happy surprise.
chineseExample_tr: 獲獎的喜悅大喜過望。

example: He tackled the challenge alone, demonstrating remarkable perseverance.
chineseExample: 他单枪匹马地迎接挑战，展现了非凡的毅力。
description: A single (单) spear (枪) and one (匹) horse (马). The phrase describes a specific military image — the rider who goes forward without the formation behind him — and Chinese has kept both the admiration and the anxiety in it. Used of someone it means they took the thing on entirely alone, and whether that reads as courage or as a failure to ask for help depends on the outcome. It is very common in modern speech about work done without a team.
description_tr: A single (單) spear (槍) and one (匹) horse (馬). The phrase describes a specific military image — the rider who goes forward without the formation behind him — and Chinese has kept both the admiration and the anxiety in it. Used of someone it means they took the thing on entirely alone, and whether that reads as courage or as a failure to ask for help depends on the outcome. It is very common in modern speech about work done without a team.
chineseExample_tr: 他單槍匹馬地迎接挑戰，展現了非凡的毅力。

example: The thought of the upcoming exam made her heart tremble with fear.
chineseExample: 想到即将到来的考试，她胆战心惊。
description: 胆 is the gallbladder, which Chinese physiology treats as the seat of courage — the organ that fails first when nerve goes. So the phrase describes courage (胆) trembling (战) and the heart (心) startled (惊), naming two internal organs that have both given way. It is stronger than English 'nervous' and belongs with physical dread rather than worry: heights, examinations with real consequences, the wait outside a room where something is being decided.
description_tr: 膽 is the gallbladder, which Chinese physiology treats as the seat of courage — the organ that fails first when nerve goes. So the phrase describes courage (膽) trembling (戰) and the heart (心) startled (驚), naming two internal organs that have both given way. It is stronger than English 'nervous' and belongs with physical dread rather than worry: heights, examinations with real consequences, the wait outside a room where something is being decided.
chineseExample_tr: 想到即將到來的考試，她膽戰心驚。

example: His reckless decisions led to chaos in the organization.
chineseExample: 他的鲁莽决定导致了组织的混乱。
description: Wu Zixu, whose father and brother King Ping of Chu had executed, returned with a foreign army, found the king already dead, and had the corpse taken from its tomb and whipped. Reproached for it by an old friend, he answered in the words the Records of the Grand Historian preserves: my day is late and my road is long, and so I go against the way (倒行) and act against the order of things (逆施). It is a confession, not a defence. The phrase is used for conduct that inverts every accepted norm, and it is severe.
description_tr: Wu Zixu, whose father and brother King Ping of Chu had executed, returned with a foreign army, found the king already dead, and had the corpse taken from its tomb and whipped. Reproached for it by an old friend, he answered in the words the Records of the Grand Historian preserves: my day is late and my road is long, and so I go against the way (倒行) and act against the order of things (逆施).
