chineseExample_tr: 他的魯莽決定導致了組織的混亂。

example: She was admired not only for her skills but also for her integrity.
chineseExample: 她不仅因技能而受到赞赏，也因品德而受到尊敬。
description: Virtue (德) and ability (才), both (兼) possessed (备). The phrase matters in Chinese less as literature than as policy: it is the standard formula for personnel selection, and it is normally quoted with its second clause, 以德为先 — both, with virtue first. That ordering is the whole argument, and Chinese discussions of appointments return to it constantly, because the interesting cases are the ones where a candidate plainly has one and not the other.
description_tr: Virtue (德) and ability (才), both (兼) possessed (備). The phrase matters in Chinese less as literature than as policy: it is the standard formula for personnel selection, and it is normally quoted with its second clause, 以德為先 — both, with virtue first. That ordering is the whole argument, and Chinese discussions of appointments return to it constantly, because the interesting cases are the ones where a candidate plainly has one and not the other.
chineseExample_tr: 她不僅因技能而受到讚賞，也因品德而受到尊敬。

example: His innovative ideas transformed the struggling company into a market leader.
chineseExample: 他的创新想法把这家挣扎中的公司变成了市场领头羊。
description: Daoist legend credits certain adepts with the power to touch (点) a stone (石) and make it gold (成金), and the phrase began as straightforward alchemy. Its most interesting life is literary: Song critics borrowed it for the editor's art, the single altered character that turns a flat line into a good one. That is still its best use. Chinese applies it to teachers, editors and consultants — anyone whose contribution is small in volume and transforms the value of what was already there.
description_tr: Daoist legend credits certain adepts with the power to touch (點) a stone (石) and make it gold (成金), and the phrase began as straightforward alchemy. Its most interesting life is literary: Song critics borrowed it for the editor's art, the single altered character that turns a flat line into a good one. That is still its best use. Chinese applies it to teachers, editors and consultants — anyone whose contribution is small in volume and transforms the value of what was already there.
chineseExample_tr: 他的創新想法把這家掙扎中的公司變成了市場領頭羊。

example: His expertise in trivial matters does not impress the seasoned professionals.
chineseExample: 他在琐碎事务上的专长并未让经验丰富的专业人士感到印象深刻。
description: 雕虫 refers to carving in the insect script, and 小技 calls it a small (小) skill (技), one of the ornamental seal hands that a young scholar practised — fiddly, decorative work. Yang Xiong used it to dismiss the elaborate rhapsodies of his own youth, saying a grown man does not do such things. Li Bai later applied it to his own poetry in a letter seeking patronage. Both were being modest about work that was in fact very good, and the phrase has kept that job: it is used of one's own skills, and using it of someone else's is an insult.
description_tr: 雕蟲 refers to carving in the insect script, and 小技 calls it a small (小) skill (技), one of the ornamental seal hands that a young scholar practised — fiddly, decorative work. Yang Xiong used it to dismiss the elaborate rhapsodies of his own youth, saying a grown man does not do such things. Li Bai later applied it to his own poetry in a letter seeking patronage. Both were being modest about work that was in fact very good, and the phrase has kept that job: it is used of one's own skills, and using it of someone else's is an insult.
chineseExample_tr: 他在瑣碎事務上的專長並未讓經驗豐富的專業人士感到印象深刻。

example: The secret plans were exposed due to careless mistakes.
chineseExample: 秘密计划因粗心大意而暴露。
description: Qin Hui, chancellor of the Southern Song, is said to have plotted beneath the east window (东窗) with his wife to destroy the general Yue Fei, who was duly executed on a fabricated charge. After Qin Hui's death a medium reported meeting him among the punished dead, with a message for his wife: the business under the east window has come out (事发). Yue Fei remains a national hero and Qin Hui a national byword. The phrase is used when a concealed scheme surfaces, and it carries the implication of deserved exposure.
description_tr: Qin Hui, chancellor of the Southern Song, is said to have plotted beneath the east window (東窗) with his wife to destroy the general Yue Fei, who was duly executed on a fabricated charge. After Qin Hui's death a medium reported meeting him among the punished dead, with a message for his wife: the business under the east window has come out (事發). Yue Fei remains a national hero and Qin Hui a national byword. The phrase is used when a concealed scheme surfaces, and it carries the implication of deserved exposure.
chineseExample_tr: 秘密計劃因粗心大意而暴露。

example: In times of crisis, relying solely on one person can lead to failure.
chineseExample: 在危机时刻，单靠一个人是难以支撑的。
description: A single (独) timber (木) cannot easily (难) prop up (支) a building, and the phrase is usually given in full with the thing it is failing to hold: 大厦将倾，独木难支 — the great hall is coming down and one beam will not stop it. The image is structural rather than moral. It is not about weakness but about load distribution, and Chinese uses it to describe a competent person in a failing institution, where the point is that no individual effort is the right size for the problem.
description_tr: A single (獨) timber (木) cannot easily (難) prop up (支) a building, and the phrase is usually given in full with the thing it is failing to hold: 大廈將傾，獨木難支 — the great hall is coming down and one beam will not stop it. The image is structural rather than moral. It is not about weakness but about load distribution, and Chinese uses it to describe a competent person in a failing institution, where the point is that no individual effort is the right size for the problem.
chineseExample_tr: 在危機時刻，單靠一個人是難以支撐的。

example: He misinterpreted her words, taking them out of context to support his argument.
chineseExample: 他误解了她的话，断章取义地支持自己的论点。
description: In Spring and Autumn China, educated men quoted the Odes at each other, and the etiquette allowed cutting a stanza (断章) loose from its poem and taking (取) whatever sense (义) you needed. The Zuo Zhuan phrase is 赋诗断章，余取所求焉 — in reciting an ode one cuts the stanza out, and I take from it what I want — said by Lupu Gui, who was using the poetry habit as an analogy to excuse marrying a woman of his own clan. It was courtesy rather than dishonesty, because everyone knew the whole poem. The phrase has since reversed completely. It is now the standard Chinese accusation of quoting out of context, and it assumes the audience does not know the rest.
description_tr: In Spring and Autumn China, educated men quoted the Odes at each other, and the etiquette allowed cutting a stanza (斷章) loose from its poem and taking (取) whatever sense (義) you needed. The Zuo Zhuan phrase is 賦詩斷章，餘取所求焉 — in reciting an ode one cuts the stanza out, and I take from it what I want — said by Lupu Gui, who was using the poetry habit as an analogy to excuse marrying a woman of his own clan. It was courtesy rather than dishonesty, because everyone knew the whole poem. The phrase has since reversed completely. It is now the standard Chinese accusation of quoting out of context, and it assumes the audience does not know the rest.
chineseExample_tr: 他誤解了她的話，斷章取義地支持自己的論點。

example: To solve the problem effectively, we need to address the root cause.
chineseExample: 要有效解决问题，我们需要对症下药。
description: This insightful idiom originates from the story of the renowned physician Hua Tuo (华佗) during the late Eastern Han dynasty. In a time of widespread illness, Hua Tuo was known for his exceptional medical skills. The story tells of two officials, Ni Xun (倪寻) and Li Yan (李延), who both suffered from similar symptoms of headache and fever. However, Hua Tuo prescribed different treatments for each, explaining that Ni Xun's condition was due to dietary issues (requiring purgatives), while Li Yan's was due to cold exposure (requiring sweating). This idiom (对症下药) literally means 'apply medicine according to the symptoms,' emphasizing the importance of tailoring solutions to specific problems. In modern usage, it suggests taking targeted actions based on careful diagnosis of a situation.
description_tr: This insightful idiom originates from the story of the renowned physician Hua Tuo (華佗) during the late Eastern Han dynasty. In a time of widespread illness, Hua Tuo was known for his exceptional medical skills. The story tells of two officials, Ni Xun (倪尋) and Li Yan (李延), who both suffered from similar symptoms of headache and fever. However, Hua Tuo prescribed different treatments for each, explaining that Ni Xun's condition was due to dietary issues (requiring purgatives), while Li Yan's was due to cold exposure (requiring sweating). This idiom (對症下藥) literally means 'apply medicine according to the symptoms,' emphasizing the importance of tailoring solutions to specific problems. In modern usage, it suggests taking targeted actions based on careful diagnosis of a situation.
chineseExample_tr: 要有效解決問題，我們需要對症下藥。

example: Adding more features to the software was just an unnecessary action that complicated things.
chineseExample: 给软件添加更多功能只是多此一举。
description: One (一) action (举) too many (多此). Chinese has a family of expressions for this and it is worth hearing the differences: 画蛇添足 is adding something that spoils the thing, while 多此一举 is milder and merely wasteful — the step that changed nothing either way. It is very often used of oneself, in the mild self-mockery of having gone back to check a door that was already locked, and it is among the most common phrases in ordinary speech.
description_tr: One (一) action (舉) too many (多此). Chinese has a family of expressions for this and it is worth hearing the differences: 畫蛇添足 is adding something that spoils the thing, while 多此一舉 is milder and merely wasteful — the step that changed nothing either way. It is very often used of oneself, in the mild self-mockery of having gone back to check a door that was already locked, and it is among the most common phrases in ordinary speech.
chineseExample_tr: 給軟件添加更多功能只是多此一舉。

example: In the world of politics, it often feels like everyone is engaged in mutual deception.
chineseExample: 在政治界，尔虞我诈的现象屡见不鲜。
description: The Zuo Zhuan records the terms agreed when Chu's siege of Song was lifted: 我无尔诈，尔无我虞 — I will not deceive you, you will not deceive me. The idiom is built out of that pledge with the negatives stripped away, so a promise of mutual honesty has become the name for mutual bad faith. Chinese uses it of commercial and political relations conducted entirely in suspicion, and the origin is worth knowing, since the phrase began as the exact opposite of what it now means.
description_tr: The Zuo Zhuan records the terms agreed when Chu's siege of Song was lifted: 我無爾詐，爾無我虞 — I will not deceive you, you will not deceive me. The idiom is built out of that pledge with the negatives stripped away, so a promise of mutual honesty has become the name for mutual bad faith. Chinese uses it of commercial and political relations conducted entirely in suspicion, and the origin is worth knowing, since the phrase began as the exact opposite of what it now means.
chineseExample_tr: 在政治界，爾虞我詐的現象屢見不鮮。

example: The new policy transformed the entire industry overnight.
chineseExample: 这项新政策翻天覆地地改变了整个行业。
description: Sky (天) overturned (翻), earth (地) upended (覆) — the same four characters as 天翻地覆 in a different order, and the two are used interchangeably. If there is a distinction in practice it is one of emphasis: this ordering puts the verbs first and reads as slightly more active, which suits deliberate transformation, while the other reads more like a description of the resulting chaos. Both are used for revolutions, redevelopments and any change that leaves nothing recognisable.
description_tr: Sky (天) overturned (翻), earth (地) upended (覆) — the same four characters as 天翻地覆 in a different order, and the two are used interchangeably. If there is a distinction in practice it is one of emphasis: this ordering puts the verbs first and reads as slightly more active, which suits deliberate transformation, while the other reads more like a description of the resulting chaos. Both are used for revolutions, redevelopments and any change that leaves nothing recognisable.
chineseExample_tr: 這項新政策翻天覆地地改變了整個行業。

example: His decisions are often erratic, leaving everyone confused.
chineseExample: 他的决定反复无常，让大家感到困惑。
description: Turning back and forth (反复) without (无) constancy (常). What distinguishes it from ordinary changeability is that 反复 implies reversal rather than variety — the same ground covered in opposite directions, a decision made and unmade. It is always a criticism, and a serious one about a person: it says not that they are flexible but that their commitments do not hold, which is why Chinese uses it about allies and negotiating partners as readily as about moods.
description_tr: Turning back and forth (反覆) without (無) constancy (常). What distinguishes it from ordinary changeability is that 反覆 implies reversal rather than variety — the same ground covered in opposite directions, a decision made and unmade. It is always a criticism, and a serious one about a person: it says not that they are flexible but that their commitments do not hold, which is why Chinese uses it about allies and negotiating partners as readily as about moods.
chineseExample_tr: 他的決定反復無常，讓大家感到困惑。

meaning: Release a tiger back to the mountain
example: By letting him go, she unleashed a dangerous rival.
chineseExample: 放虎归山后，她释放了一个危险的对手。
description: Liu Zhang, governor of Yi province, invited Liu Bei in to help against a common enemy. His adviser Liu Ba warned him that admitting the man was releasing (放) a tiger (虎) back (归) into the hills (山), where it would recover and no longer be catchable. Liu Zhang went ahead; Liu Bei took Chengdu and the province with it. The phrase is used of any decision to let a neutralised threat regain its freedom of movement, and it always implies the mistake was foreseeable.
description_tr: Liu Zhang, governor of Yi province, invited Liu Bei in to help against a common enemy. His adviser Liu Ba warned him that admitting the man was releasing (放) a tiger (虎) back (歸) into the hills (山), where it would recover and no longer be catchable. Liu Zhang went ahead; Liu Bei took Chengdu and the province with it. The phrase is used of any decision to let a neutralised threat regain its freedom of movement, and it always implies the mistake was foreseeable.
chineseExample_tr: 放虎歸山後，她釋放了一個危險的對手。

example: Their innovative ideas have the potential to reshape the future.
chineseExample: 他们的创新理念有能力改天换地。
description: To change (改) the heavens (天) and exchange (换) the earth (地). Unlike most of its neighbours this is a modern phrase, and it belongs to the vocabulary of twentieth-century Chinese politics, where it described the remaking of land and society by collective effort. That history gives it a heroic register that 翻天覆地 does not have: this one implies intention and agency, a transformation carried out rather than merely undergone, and it is still most at home in official language.
description_tr: To change (改) the heavens (天) and exchange (換) the earth (地). Unlike most of its neighbours this is a modern phrase, and it belongs to the vocabulary of twentieth-century Chinese politics, where it described the remaking of land and society by collective effort. That history gives it a heroic register that 翻天覆地 does not have: this one implies intention and agency, a transformation carried out rather than merely undergone, and it is still most at home in official language.
chineseExample_tr: 他們的創新理念有能力改天換地。

example: The news of her departure left him heartbroken.
chineseExample: 她的离去让他肝肠寸断。
description: A New Account of Tales of the World records an army passing through the gorges, where a soldier took a gibbon's infant aboard. The mother followed along the bank for a hundred li, crying, until she leapt onto the boat and died there. They cut her open and found 肠皆寸寸断 — the intestines (肠) severed (断) into inch (寸) lengths. The commander heard of it and dismissed the man. The four-character form adds the liver (肝), which the story does not mention, because 肝肠 is the ordinary Chinese pairing for the seat of feeling. The phrase describes grief as an internal injury, and Chinese reserves it for the real thing — bereavement, not disappointment.
description_tr: A New Account of Tales of the World records an army passing through the gorges, where a soldier took a gibbon's infant aboard. The mother followed along the bank for a hundred li, crying, until she leapt onto the boat and died there. They cut her open and found 腸皆寸寸斷 — the intestines (腸) severed (斷) into inch (寸) lengths. The commander heard of it and dismissed the man. The four-character form adds the liver (肝), which the story does not mention, because 肝腸 is the ordinary Chinese pairing for the seat of feeling. The phrase describes grief as an internal injury, and Chinese reserves it for the real thing — bereavement, not disappointment.
chineseExample_tr: 她的離去讓他肝腸寸斷。

example: At the conference, he engaged in lofty discussions about philosophy and ethics.
chineseExample: 在会议上，他高谈阔论关于哲学和伦理的问题。
description: Lofty (高) talk (谈) and expansive (阔) discussion (论). The two halves both describe scale — the altitude of the subject and the breadth of the sweep — and neither mentions substance, which is the joke. The phrase can occasionally be neutral, but in practice it is almost always dismissive: it describes the person who addresses the largest available questions at length, generally in a setting where a smaller and more answerable one was on the table.
description_tr: Lofty (高) talk (談) and expansive (闊) discussion (論). The two halves both describe scale — the altitude of the subject and the breadth of the sweep — and neither mentions substance, which is the joke. The phrase can occasionally be neutral, but in practice it is almost always dismissive: it describes the person who addresses the largest available questions at length, generally in a setting where a smaller and more answerable one was on the table.
chineseExample_tr: 在會議上，他高談闊論關於哲學和倫理的問題。

example: Be careful what you say; walls have ears in this office.
chineseExample: 在这个办公室里，你要小心说话，隔墙有耳。
description: Across (隔) the wall (墙) there are (有) ears (耳). Early statecraft texts carry the warning in the barer form 墙有耳, and Chinese and English arrived at almost the same image independently, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing. The phrase functions as an interruption rather than an observation: it is what one person says to another mid-conversation, and it means stop talking about this here, rather than commenting on anyone in particular.
description_tr: Across (隔) the wall (牆) there are (有) ears (耳). Early statecraft texts carry the warning in the barer form 牆有耳, and Chinese and English arrived at almost the same image independently, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing. The phrase functions as an interruption rather than an observation: it is what one person says to another mid-conversation, and it means stop talking about this here, rather than commenting on anyone in particular.
chineseExample_tr: 在這個辦公室裡，你要小心說話，隔牆有耳。

example: In the heat of competition, they decided to strike when their opponent was unprepared.
chineseExample: 在竞争的激烈中，他们决定攻其不备。
description: Sun Tzu's first chapter ends with a pair: 攻其无备，出其不意 — attack (攻) where they (其) are unprepared (备), appear where you are not expected. The common modern form writes 不备 for his 无备; both negate preparation and the sense is unchanged. The two clauses are one instruction seen from either side. What the phrase adds to the ordinary idea of surprise is a target — it directs attention to the specific gap in the opponent's preparation, which has to be found before it can be struck. It is used freely in Chinese business and sport, and it survives translation better than most of Sun Tzu.
description_tr: Sun Tzu's first chapter ends with a pair: 攻其無備，出其不意 — attack (攻) where they (其) are unprepared (備), appear where you are not expected. The common modern form writes 不備 for his 無備; both negate preparation and the sense is unchanged. The two clauses are one instruction seen from either side. What the phrase adds to the ordinary idea of surprise is a target — it directs attention to the specific gap in the opponent's preparation, which has to be found before it can be struck. It is used freely in Chinese business and sport, and it survives translation better than most of Sun Tzu.
chineseExample_tr: 在競爭的激烈中，他們決定攻其不備。

example: After months of illness, he looked so frail, with bones thin as firewood.
chineseExample: 经过几个月的疾病，他看起来非常虚弱，骨瘦如柴。
description: Bones (骨) thin (瘦) as (如) kindling (柴). 柴 is firewood, specifically the dry brushwood gathered for burning, so the comparison carries dryness and brittleness as well as thinness. The phrase is not a comment on physique but a description of a body that has been depleted, and Chinese uses it about illness, famine and grief. It is blunt and rather pitying, and it would not be used about someone who was merely slim.
description_tr: Bones (骨) thin (瘦) as (如) kindling (柴). 柴 is firewood, specifically the dry brushwood gathered for burning, so the comparison carries dryness and brittleness as well as thinness. The phrase is not a comment on physique but a description of a body that has been depleted, and Chinese uses it about illness, famine and grief. It is blunt and rather pitying, and it would not be used about someone who was merely slim.
chineseExample_tr: 經過幾個月的疾病，他看起來非常虛弱，骨瘦如柴。

example: He had to scrape bones to cure the poison of his past mistakes.
chineseExample: 他不得不刮骨疗毒，以治愈过去错误的毒害。
description: The Records of the Three Kingdoms says that Guan Yu, hit by a poisoned arrow, was told the poison had reached the bone and that the arm must be opened and the bone scraped (刮骨) to cure (疗) the poison (毒). He held out his arm and went on eating and drinking with his officers while the surgeon worked, with the blood filling the dish beneath. The history does not name the doctor — Hua Tuo is the novel's addition. The phrase means treating a problem at its source, accepting that the cure will be worse than living with it.
description_tr: The Records of the Three Kingdoms says that Guan Yu, hit by a poisoned arrow, was told the poison had reached the bone and that the arm must be opened and the bone scraped (刮骨) to cure (療) the poison (毒). He held out his arm and went on eating and drinking with his officers while the surgeon worked, with the blood filling the dish beneath. The history does not name the doctor — Hua Tuo is the novel's addition. The phrase means treating a problem at its source, accepting that the cure will be worse than living with it.
chineseExample_tr: 他不得不刮骨療毒，以治癒過去錯誤的毒害。

example: He achieved great success, making his family proud and honored.
chineseExample: 他取得了巨大的成功，让家族光宗耀祖。
description: To bring light (光) to the clan (宗) and make the ancestors (祖) shine (耀). The direction is what matters: achievement is not the individual's to keep but flows backwards up the line, and in a system of ancestral rites the dead have a real stake in it. That is why examination success was a family event. The phrase is still used in earnest and also, increasingly, ironically by younger Chinese speakers describing the weight of expectation that comes attached to it.
description_tr: To bring light (光) to the clan (宗) and make the ancestors (祖) shine (耀). The direction is what matters: achievement is not the individual's to keep but flows backwards up the line, and in a system of ancestral rites the dead have a real stake in it. That is why examination success was a family event. The phrase is still used in earnest and also, increasingly, ironically by younger Chinese speakers describing the weight of expectation that comes attached to it.
chineseExample_tr: 他取得了巨大的成功，讓家族光宗耀祖。

example: The artist's work was so exquisite that it seemed crafted by supernatural hands.
chineseExample: 这位艺术家的作品鬼斧神工，令人叹为观止。
description: The Zhuangzi tells of the woodworker Qing, whose bell-stand was so fine that people said no human hand had made it. Asked his secret, he described fasting: after three days he no longer thought about reward or rank, after five about praise or blame, after seven he had forgotten he had a body and a court to serve. Only then did he go into the forest, look at the trees as they were, and see the finished stand standing in one of them; then he set his hand to it. Ghost (鬼) axe (斧) and spirit (神) work (工) is what the onlookers concluded. Chinese uses it for craftsmanship and for natural formations that look designed.
description_tr: The Zhuangzi tells of the woodworker Qing, whose bell-stand was so fine that people said no human hand had made it. Asked his secret, he described fasting: after three days he no longer thought about reward or rank, after five about praise or blame, after seven he had forgotten he had a body and a court to serve. Only then did he go into the forest, look at the trees as they were, and see the finished stand standing in one of them; then he set his hand to it. Ghost (鬼) axe (斧) and spirit (神) work (工) is what the onlookers concluded. Chinese uses it for craftsmanship and for natural formations that look designed.
chineseExample_tr: 這位藝術家的作品鬼斧神工，令人嘆為觀止。

example: With endless possibilities ahead, she felt free to pursue her dreams.
chineseExample: 前方的道路海阔天空，她可以自由追求自己的梦想。
description: Sea (海) wide (阔) and sky (天) empty (空), from the couplet about the fish leaping where the sea allows and the bird flying where the sky permits. The phrase has two quite different uses. Of circumstances it means unbounded scope, the situation with no walls in it. Of conversation it means something closer to rambling — 聊得海阔天空 is talk that has gone everywhere and settled nowhere — and that second sense is at least as common in speech.
description_tr: Sea (海) wide (闊) and sky (天) empty (空), from the couplet about the fish leaping where the sea allows and the bird flying where the sky permits. The phrase has two quite different uses. Of circumstances it means unbounded scope, the situation with no walls in it. Of conversation it means something closer to rambling — 聊得海闊天空 is talk that has gone everywhere and settled nowhere — and that second sense is at least as common in speech.
chineseExample_tr: 前方的道路海闊天空，她可以自由追求自己的夢想。

example: She faced numerous challenges before finally achieving her dream job.
chineseExample: 她在实现梦想的过程中，好事多磨，经历了无数挑战。
description: Good things (好事) meet much (多) grinding (磨). 磨 is the millstone, and the abrasion is the point: the phrase does not say good things are delayed but that they are worn against something on the way. Its natural home is romance and marriage, where Chinese uses it almost as a superstition — the courtship that keeps hitting obstacles is being tested rather than warned off. It is offered as consolation, and it implies the good thing is still coming.
description_tr: Good things (好事) meet much (多) grinding (磨). 磨 is the millstone, and the abrasion is the point: the phrase does not say good things are delayed but that they are worn against something on the way. Its natural home is romance and marriage, where Chinese uses it almost as a superstition — the courtship that keeps hitting obstacles is being tested rather than warned off. It is offered as consolation, and it implies the good thing is still coming.
chineseExample_tr: 她在實現夢想的過程中，好事多磨，經歷了無數挑戰。

example: His arrogant attitude made him many enemies in the workplace.
chineseExample: 他的横行霸道让他在职场上结下了许多敌人。
description: 横行 is moving (行) sideways or unrestrained (横), and 霸道 is rule by force as opposed to rule by right. So the phrase is someone moving through the world crosswise and governing by 霸 rather than 王 — trampling laterally over whatever is in the way. Chinese says it of local strongmen, of bullying officials and, very commonly, of children. It is a strong condemnation and specifically about the exercise of power over people who cannot answer back.
description_tr: 橫行 is moving (行) sideways or unrestrained (橫), and 霸道 is rule by force as opposed to rule by right. So the phrase is someone moving through the world crosswise and governing by 霸 rather than 王 — trampling laterally over whatever is in the way. Chinese uses it of local strongmen, of bullying officials and, very commonly, of children. It is a strong condemnation and specifically about the exercise of power over people who cannot answer back.
chineseExample_tr: 他的橫行霸道讓他在職場上結下了許多敵人。

example: The new students impressed everyone with their innovative ideas and fresh perspectives
chineseExample: 新生们以他们的创新想法和新鲜视角让大家刮目相看
description: Confucius said that those born later (后生) are to be held in awe (可畏) — how do we know that the ones coming will not equal the present? The second half of the passage is usually left out and is worth having: if a man reaches forty or fifty and has still not been heard of, then he is not worth fearing after all. So the phrase is not simply warm encouragement. 畏 is fear, and what Confucius describes is the proper unease of the established on meeting someone young and good.
description_tr: Confucius said that those born later (後生) are to be held in awe (可畏) — how do we know that the ones coming will not equal the present? The second half of the passage is usually left out and is worth having: if a man reaches forty or fifty and has still not been heard of, then he is not worth fearing after all. So the phrase is not simply warm encouragement. 畏 is fear, and what Confucius describes is the proper unease of the established on meeting someone young and good.
chineseExample_tr: 新生們以他們的創新想法和新鮮視角讓大家刮目相看

example: His robust physique and strong presence make him an imposing figure in any room
chineseExample: 他健壮的体格和强大的气场让他在任何场合都显得威风凛凛
description: A tiger's (虎) back (背) and a bear's (熊) waist (腰). The phrase specifies build rather than height — breadth through the shoulders and thickness through the middle — and it is straightforwardly admiring in a way that English has no neat equivalent for. It comes out of Yuan drama, where it describes warriors, and it is still applied almost exclusively to men. It suggests usable physical power rather than athleticism or good looks.
description_tr: A tiger's (虎) back (背) and a bear's (熊) waist (腰). The phrase specifies build rather than height — breadth through the shoulders and thickness through the middle — and it is straightforwardly admiring in a way that English has no neat equivalent for. It comes out of Yuan drama, where it describes warriors, and it is still applied almost exclusively to men. It suggests usable physical power rather than athleticism or good looks.
chineseExample_tr: 他健壯的體格和強大的氣場讓他在任何場合都顯得威風凜凜

example: The artist's work transcends mere visuals, evoking deep emotions and thoughts
chineseExample: 这位艺术家的作品超越了单纯的视觉，唤起了深刻的情感和思考
description: Su Shi wrote a matched pair about Wang Wei, who was both a major poet and a major painter: 味摩诘之诗，诗中有画；观摩诘之画，画中有诗 — taste his poems and there is painting in the poems; look at his paintings and there is poetry in the painting. The two halves are normally quoted together and the second became the idiom on its own. It describes art carrying more than its medium seems able to hold, and it has been the standard compliment for Chinese landscape painting ever since.
description_tr: Su Shi wrote a matched pair about Wang Wei, who was both a major poet and a major painter: 味摩詰之詩，詩中有畫；觀摩詰之畫，畫中有詩 — taste his poems and there is painting in the poems; look at his paintings and there is poetry in the painting. The two halves are normally quoted together and the second became the idiom on its own. It describes art carrying more than its medium seems able to hold, and it has been the standard compliment for Chinese landscape painting ever since.
chineseExample_tr: 這位藝術家的作品超越了單純的視覺，喚起了深刻的情感和思考

example: His aspirations were ultimately just a fleeting fantasy that never materialized
chineseExample: 他的抱负最终不过是一个转瞬即逝的幻想
description: A Tang tale has a discontented young man at an inn in Handan complaining of his prospects to a Daoist, who lends him a pillow. He dreams an entire life — a good marriage, high office, disgrace, exile, recall, wealth, grandchildren, and death at eighty. He wakes. The innkeeper's yellow millet (黄粱), which had been put on to steam before he lay down, is still not cooked. A single (一) dream (梦) over a pot of millet, and the phrase is used of ambition that turns out to be illusory, and of any grand prospect that evaporates.
description_tr: A Tang tale has a discontented young man at an inn in Handan complaining of his prospects to a Daoist, who lends him a pillow. He dreams an entire life — a good marriage, high office, disgrace, exile, recall, wealth, grandchildren, and death at eighty. He wakes. The innkeeper's yellow millet (黃粱), which had been put on to steam before he lay down, is still not cooked. A single (一) dream (夢) over a pot of millet, and the phrase is used of ambition that turns out to be illusory, and of any grand prospect that evaporates.
chineseExample_tr: 他的抱負最終不過是一個轉瞬即逝的幻想

example: The flavors of the dish lingered long after the meal was over, leaving everyone satisfied
chineseExample: 这道菜的味道在用餐后仍然萦绕在舌尖，让每个人都感到满足
description: 回味 is the aftertaste, the flavour that comes back after swallowing, and Chinese food writing takes it seriously as a separate quality from the taste itself. Applied to experience, 回味无穷 describes something whose returns keep arriving — the book that keeps opening, the conversation still being thought about weeks later. It is a strong compliment and a specific one: it says nothing about the immediate impression, only that the thing did not finish when it ended.
description_tr: 回味 is the aftertaste, the flavour that comes back after swallowing, and Chinese food writing takes it seriously as a separate quality from the taste itself. Applied to experience, 回味無窮 describes something whose returns keep arriving — the book that keeps opening, the conversation still being thought about weeks later. It is a strong compliment and a specific one: it says nothing about the immediate impression, only that the thing did not finish when it ended.
chineseExample_tr: 這道菜的味道在用餐後仍然縈繞在舌尖，讓每個人都感到滿足

meaning: Muddy the water, grope for fish
example: In the midst of the chaos, he took advantage of the situation to profit.
chineseExample: 在混乱中，他趁机获利。
description: The twentieth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. Fish in clear water see the hand coming; stir the water (混水) and the fish (鱼) can be taken (摸) by feel. The stratagem's own emphasis is on the first half — the confusion is manufactured by the person who then profits from it — which is stronger than the English 'fish in troubled waters', where the trouble may simply have been found. It is said of profiteering in a crisis and of people who prosper wherever procedure has broken down.
description_tr: The twentieth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. Fish in clear water see the hand coming; stir the water (混水) and the fish (魚) can be taken (摸) by feel. The stratagem's own emphasis is on the first half — the confusion is manufactured by the person who then profits from it — which is stronger than the English 'fish in troubled waters', where the trouble may simply have been found. Chinese uses it of profiteering in a crisis and of people who prosper wherever procedure has broken down.
chineseExample_tr: 在混亂中，他趁機獲利。

example: He always finds a way to benefit while others do the hard work.
chineseExample: 他总是能在别人辛苦时捞到好处。
description: This one is not Chinese in origin. It comes from La Fontaine's fable of the monkey who flatters the cat into pulling (取) roasting chestnuts (栗) out of the fire (火中), eating each one as it arrives while the cat burns its paw for nothing. The story entered Chinese through translation and settled into four characters. The phrase always describes the cat, not the monkey: it is used of someone taking the risk and the injury in an operation whose benefit goes to somebody else.
description_tr: This one is not Chinese in origin. It comes from La Fontaine's fable of the monkey who flatters the cat into pulling (取) roasting chestnuts (慄) out of the fire (火中), eating each one as it arrives while the cat burns its paw for nothing. The story entered Chinese through translation and settled into four characters. The phrase always describes the cat, not the monkey: it is used of someone taking the risk and the injury in an operation whose benefit goes to somebody else.
chineseExample_tr: 他總是能在別人辛苦時撈到好處。

example: Once bad habits are formed, they are hard to change.
chineseExample: 一旦形成坏习惯，就很难改回来了。
description: What has accumulated (积) becomes heavy (重) and is hard (难) to turn back (返). The image is of momentum rather than mere habit — something that gathered gradually, unopposed at every individual step, until reversing it would require more force than anyone now has. That is what makes it a phrase about institutions more than about people. In practice it is used of entrenched corruption, of bloated bureaucracy and of practices everyone agrees are wrong and nobody can stop.
description_tr: What has accumulated (積) becomes heavy (重) and is hard (難) to turn back (返). The image is of momentum rather than mere habit — something that gathered gradually, unopposed at every individual step, until reversing it would require more force than anyone now has. That is what makes it a phrase about institutions more than about people. Chinese uses it of entrenched corruption, of bloated bureaucracy and of practices everyone agrees are wrong and nobody can stop.
chineseExample_tr: 一旦形成壞習慣，就很難改回來了。

example: Tensions were high as both sides prepared for a confrontation.
chineseExample: 双方都准备好迎接对抗，气氛紧张。
description: It began as art criticism. A Liang-dynasty appraisal of calligraphy described one master's brushwork as having swords drawn (剑拔) and crossbows spanned (弩张) — taut, armed, about to release. The metaphor was about energy held in tension on the page. It has migrated entirely into the description of situations, and now names the moment when both sides are prepared and nothing has happened yet. Chinese uses it constantly in diplomatic reporting.

chineseExample_tr: 雙方都準備好迎接對抗，氣氛緊張。

example: He turned the tables on his opponent by using their own strategy against them.
chineseExample: 他用对手的策略反击了他们。
description: To take (将) the plan (计) and proceed by (就) that plan (计). The construction is deliberately circular, and the tactic it names is more specific than a counter-strategy: you do not block the opponent's scheme, you let it run and arrange for its success to be your success. That requires knowing the plan and concealing that you know it. It belongs to vernacular fiction and drama, where it is the standard move of the cleverer party, and Chinese uses it freely in business and politics.

chineseExample_tr: 他用對手的策略反擊了他們。

example: In negotiations, it's essential to empathize with the other party's feelings.
chineseExample: 在谈判中，理解对方的感受是至关重要的。
description: To take (将) one's own heart (心) and measure (比) another's (心). Zhu Xi uses it, and the mechanism is worth noticing: the standard proposed is not imagination but comparison — you already know what it is like to be treated a certain way, so the information required is available without any special sympathy. That makes it a more practical instruction than most words for empathy. It is commonly said as a request, meaning put yourself where I am for a moment.

example: When faced with adversity, we must unite and take action.
chineseExample: 面对逆境时，我们必须团结一致，行动起来。
description: Jia Yi's essay on the failings of Qin describes the rising of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang: they cut wood for weapons and raised (揭) bamboo poles (竿) for banners, and so (而) rose (起), and the empire answered like a shadow. The detail is the whole point — the rebellion that toppled the first empire began with farm labourers who had no arms at all. The phrase is used of uprisings that start from nothing and from below, and it retains a distinctly approving tone in modern Chinese.

meaning: Drain the pond to catch fish
example: If we exploit resources without care, we risk depleting them entirely.
chineseExample: 如果我们不加节制地开发资源，就会面临枯竭的风险。
description: Before the battle of Chengpu, Duke Wen of Jin asked two advisers how to face a stronger enemy. One recommended deception. The other, Yong Ji, answered that draining (竭) the marsh (泽) to fish (渔) will certainly get you fish, and next year there will be none; burning the woods to hunt will certainly get you game, and next year there will be none. The Lüshi Chunqiu records that the duke used the deception and honoured Yong Ji first. The phrase is now central to Chinese environmental and economic argument.

The Lüshi Chunqiu records that the duke used the deception and honoured Yong Ji first. The phrase is now central to Chinese environmental and economic argument.

example: The palace was adorned with golden decorations, reflecting its grandeur.
chineseExample: 宫殿装饰着金色的装饰，反映出它的宏伟。
description: 金碧 names two specific pigments — gold leaf and malachite green — used together in a style of Tang and Song landscape painting that was deliberately opulent. With 辉煌, blazing (辉) and radiant (煌), the phrase begins as a technical description of a palette, not a general word for splendour. That origin still shapes it: it is used of interiors, temples and palaces, of surfaces rather than of achievements, and it can carry a faint suggestion that the effect was expensive rather than beautiful.
description_tr: 金碧 names two specific pigments — gold leaf and malachite green — used together in a style of Tang and Song landscape painting that was deliberately opulent. chineseExample_tr: 宮殿裝飾著金色的裝飾，反映出它的宏偉。

example: The strategist presented a brilliant plan that turned the tide of the battle.
chineseExample: 这位战略家提出了一个巧妙的计划，扭转了战局。
description: In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Zhuge Liang sends Zhao Yun to escort Liu Bei into enemy territory with three brocade pouches (锦囊), each holding a plan (妙计) and instructions on exactly when to open it. Each is opened at the appointed crisis and each works. The phrase describes a solution prepared in advance for a problem that has not yet arrived, and Chinese uses it lightly — offering someone your 锦囊妙计 is offering a trick you have been saving.

chineseExample_tr: 這位戰略家提出了一個巧妙的計劃，扭轉了戰局。

example: The breathtaking performance left the audience in awe, feeling as if their hearts had been shaken.
chineseExample: 那场令人惊心动魄的表演让观众惊叹不已，仿佛心灵被震撼。
description: Zhong Rong, grading poets in the sixth century, wrote of Lu Ji's fourteen imitations of the old anonymous poems that they startle (惊) the heart (心) and move (动) the soul (魄), and that nearly every character in them is worth a thousand in gold. 魄 is the earthbound half of the soul in Chinese belief, the part tied to the body, so the phrase claims an effect reaching past the emotions and into the physical. It is used of thrillers and of genuinely dangerous experiences alike, and it is praise in the first case and complaint in the second.

chineseExample_tr: 那場令人驚心動魄的表演讓觀眾驚嘆不已，彷彿心靈被震撼。

example: He was so unsure about his next step in the project that he kept hesitating, unable to make a decision.
chineseExample: 他对项目的下一步举棋不定，始终无法做出决定。
description: The Zuo Zhuan reports a warning about a minister wavering over whether to restore an exiled ruler: a man who lifts (举) the chess piece (棋) without having settled (不定) on his move will not beat his opponent, and how much more so when the piece is a lord. The image assumes the reader knows the game — the hand is already committed and the mind is not. Chinese uses it for hesitation at exactly that point, after acting and before choosing, which is the worst available moment.

Chinese uses it for hesitation at exactly that point, after acting and before choosing, which is the worst available moment.

example: At the turn of the year the family wished each other a fortunate new beginning.
chineseExample: 新年伊始，祝您三阳开泰，万象更新。
description: This is the single most important New Year phrase of a Goat year, and it comes from the Book of Changes (《周易》). In the hexagram cycle, the eleventh month is 复 with one yang line born beneath, the twelfth is 临 with two, and the first month of the new year is 泰 with three — the point at which yin recedes and yang grows, and everything begins again. The phrase appears in 《易·泰》 as 'the small departs, the great arrives' and in the 《宋史·乐志》 as 三阳交泰. In Goat years it is deliberately written 三羊开泰, substituting sheep for yang: the two are homophones, and 羊 served in antiquity as a loan character for 祥, auspiciousness.
description_tr: This is the single most important New Year phrase of a Goat year, and it comes from the Book of Changes (《周易》). In the hexagram cycle, the eleventh month is 復 with one yang line born beneath, the twelfth is 臨 with two, and the first month of the new year is 泰 with three — the point at which yin recedes and yang grows, and everything begins again. The phrase appears in 《易·泰》 as 'the small departs, the great arrives' and in the 《宋史·樂志》 as 三陽交泰. In Goat years it is deliberately written 三羊開泰, substituting sheep for yang: the two are homophones, and 羊 served in antiquity as a loan character for 祥, auspiciousness.
chineseExample_tr: 新年伊始，祝您三陽開泰，萬象更新。

example: The whole courtyard was radiant with celebration on the first morning of the year.
chineseExample: 过年时家里张灯结彩，喜气洋洋。
description: The phrase descends from Fan Zhongyan's 《岳阳楼记》, where a visitor climbing the tower feels his spirit widen until honour and disgrace fall away and he is simply 喜洋洋 — his spirits (气) brimming over, joyous without reserve. 洋 originally suggests vastness, the spreading of water; doubled, it turns a private happiness into an atmosphere that fills a room. It became a fixture of New Year writing because of a second, quieter reason: 洋 is a homophone for 羊, so in Goat years the phrase carries the zodiac inside it without ever naming the animal. It is the most natural thing to write on a red envelope or a doorway couplet.

chineseExample_tr: 過年時家裡張燈結綵，喜氣洋洋。

example: The card carried the plainest and best of wishes: good fortune, and everything as you hope.
chineseExample: 祝您新春吉祥如意，阖家安康。
description: The commonest of all Chinese New Year wishes hides a sheep in plain sight. 祥, auspiciousness, is built on the 羊 radical, and in Han-dynasty bronze inscriptions the compound 吉祥 was regularly written 吉羊 — the sheep and the blessing were the same word. Ancient writers treated the animal as the emblem of everything mild, well-fed and safe, which is why the oracle-bone form of 美, beauty, is a human figure crowned with a ram's horns. Saying 吉祥如意 in a Goat year is therefore not a pun laid on top of the greeting; it is the greeting returning to its own root.

meaning: The antelope hangs by its horns
example: Her best writing leaves no visible technique behind — you cannot find the seams.
chineseExample: 他的诗如羚羊挂角，无迹可求。
description: Chan Buddhist texts describe an antelope (羚羊) that sleeps by hanging (挂) its horns (角) over a branch so that its feet leave no scent on the ground and no hunter can track it. Yan Yu borrowed the image in 《沧浪诗话》 to describe the poetry he admired most: work so complete that the labour behind it has vanished, leaving 无迹可求 — nothing to trace. It became the standard Chinese term for mastery that hides its own method, and it remains the highest compliment available to a piece of writing, a performance, or a piece of craft: not that it is skilful, but that you cannot see where the skill was applied.
description_tr: Chan Buddhist texts describe an antelope (羚羊) that sleeps by hanging (掛) its horns (角) over a branch so that its feet leave no scent on the ground and no hunter can track it. chineseExample_tr: 他的詩如羚羊掛角，無跡可求。

meaning: The sheep lost among the forking roads
example: With six competing strategies on the table, the team lost the thing it was chasing.
chineseExample: 方向太多，反而歧路亡羊。
description: In 《列子·说符》 a neighbour of Yang Zhu loses (亡) a sheep (羊) and sets out with a crowd to find it. They return empty-handed: the road (路) forked (歧), and forked again, and beyond each fork lay more forks than they could follow. Yang Zhu goes quiet for a long while and does not smile for the rest of the day. The story is not about a sheep. It is about how a search dissolves when the paths multiply faster than attention can divide, and it is one of the sharpest things classical Chinese thought has to say about scattered effort — an argument that too many directions is functionally the same as no direction at all.

chineseExample_tr: 方向太多，反而歧路亡羊。

meaning: Lose a sheep, gain an ox
example: Losing the small account freed the team for the one that mattered.
chineseExample: 这次调整看似损失，其实亡羊得牛。
description: From 《淮南子·说山训》: to lose (亡) a sheep (羊) and gain (得) an ox (牛) is a loss no one would refuse. The phrase is the optimistic twin of the far better-known 亡羊补牢, and it makes a different argument — not that damage can be repaired, but that a loss can be the price of something larger, and that the accounting only makes sense once you can see both sides of it. It is a useful thing to say to someone still grieving the sheep, and a dangerous thing to say too early, before the ox has actually arrived.
metaphoric_meaning: A small loss that yields a greater gain
description_tr: From 《淮南子·說山訓》: to lose (亡) a sheep (羊) and gain (得) an ox (牛) is a loss no one would refuse. It is a useful thing to say to someone still grieving the sheep, and a dangerous thing to say too early, before the ox has actually arrived.
chineseExample_tr: 這次調整看似損失，其實亡羊得牛。

meaning: A sheep's substance in a tiger's hide
example: The title was impressive; the authority behind it was not.
chineseExample: 他不过羊质虎皮，遇事就露怯。
description: Yang Xiong's 《法言·吾子》 supplies the whole image in one line: a sheep (羊) wearing a tiger's (虎) hide (皮) is delighted when it sees grass and trembles when it sees a jackal — because the hide changed, and nothing else did. The phrase is the Chinese answer to every borrowed uniform and inherited title, and its precision is in the word 质, substance: it does not accuse anyone of pretending, only of being unchanged underneath. What exposes the sheep is never the disguise itself. It is the first moment that requires the thing the disguise was standing in for.

chineseExample_tr: 他不過羊質虎皮，遇事就露怯。

meaning: A tiger loose in the flock
example: One experienced striker against that defence was never going to be a contest.
chineseExample: 他冲进对方阵中，如虎入羊群。
description: The picture needs no explanation, which is why the phrase survived: a tiger (虎) loose among (入) a flock (群) of sheep (羊) — overwhelming force meeting no resistance worth the name. It appears in Yuan drama and in the vernacular novels, usually to describe a single fighter breaking a line, and it carries a faint edge of judgement — the tiger is not admired so much as the flock is pitied. Modern use runs to sport, markets and any contest where the mismatch was obvious before it began. The useful nuance is that it describes a situation rather than a person: the same tiger in a different field is simply a tiger.

chineseExample_tr: 他衝進對方陣中，如虎入羊群。

meaning: A path like a sheep's gut
example: The route up the mountain narrowed until it was barely a track.
chineseExample: 山间只有一条羊肠小道。
description: Chinese has no gentler way of saying that a road is bad. The image is anatomical and exact — the winding, doubling coil of a sheep's (羊) intestine (肠), giving a small (小) road (道) — and it was applied first to real mountain tracks in the north, where the passes turn back on themselves so often that distance stops meaning anything. Writers extended it early to any course that is technically passable and practically punishing, and it still carries that double sense: not blocked, merely narrow, slow, and shaped so that you cannot see far enough ahead to know how much of it is left.
description_tr: Chinese has no gentler way of saying that a road is bad. The image is anatomical and exact — the winding, doubling coil of a sheep's (羊) intestine (腸), giving a small (小) road (道) — and it was applied first to real mountain tracks in the north, where the passes turn back on themselves so often that distance stops meaning anything. Writers extended it early to any course that is technically passable and practically punishing, and it still carries that double sense: not blocked, merely narrow, slow, and shaped so that you cannot see far enough ahead to know how much of it is left.
chineseExample_tr: 山間只有一條羊腸小道。

meaning: Fake yu player fills the count
example: He never spoke up in a single meeting yet shared fully in the team's bonus
chineseExample: 他在会上从未发过言，却照样分到了团队的奖金
description: Han Feizi records that King Xuan of Qi loved to hear the yu (竽), a reed mouth organ, played by an ensemble of three hundred at once. A man known as Mr. Nanguo, who could not play a note, asked to join and drew the same generous salary as everyone else, his silence covered by the sound around him. When King Xuan died, his son King Min preferred to hear the players one at a time, and Nanguo fled before his turn came. The idiom names the fraud rather than the instrument: 滥 is to pass something off, 竽 is the pipe, and 充数 is to make up the required number. It is used of anyone occupying a place they cannot fill, and self-deprecatingly by people who feel out of their depth in accomplished company.

example: The new office cut their rent and put them closer to their customers
chineseExample: 新办公室既降低了租金，又让他们更靠近客户
description: The History of the Northern Dynasties preserves this in the biography of Zhangsun Sheng, sent by the Northern Zhou court as deputy envoy escorting Princess Qianjin to the Turkic leader Shetu. His archery so impressed Shetu that the two rode out hunting together for a year. Seeing two eagles (雕) in the air fighting over a piece of meat, Shetu handed him a pair of arrows and asked him to bring them down; Zhangsun rode out and ran both (双) birds through with a single shot (一箭). He later served the Sui and spent decades dividing the Turks by diplomacy. The phrase long ago detached itself from the hunt and now means securing two results from one well-aimed action. It maps closely onto the English 'kill two birds with one stone', which makes it one of the rare idioms a learner can use correctly the first time they meet it.

example: Fixed on outbidding a rival, the firm never noticed its own debts mounting
chineseExample: 一心想压过对手，公司没察觉自己的债务正在累积
description: In Liu Xiang's Garden of Persuasions, the King of Wu resolved to attack Chu and warned that anyone who argued against it would die. A young attendant spent three mornings walking the palace garden with a slingshot, soaking his clothes in dew, until the king asked what he was doing. He pointed out a cicada (蝉) drinking dew and singing, unaware of the mantis (螳螂) poised behind it to seize (捕) it; the mantis, intent on its catch, unaware of the oriole beside it; and the oriole unaware of the slingshot below. All three, he said, were fixed on the gain in front of them and blind to the harm behind. The king called off the campaign. The saying is usually completed by 黄雀在后, 'the oriole is behind', and describes anyone so absorbed in a target that they miss the larger threat closing on them. A parallel version appears in the Zhuangzi.

A young attendant spent three mornings walking the palace garden with a slingshot, soaking his clothes in dew, until the king asked what he was doing. He pointed out a cicada (蟬) drinking dew and singing, unaware of the mantis (螳螂) poised behind it to seize (捕) it; the mantis, intent on its catch, unaware of the oriole beside it; and the oriole unaware of the slingshot below. All three, he said, were fixed on the gain in front of them and blind to the harm behind. The king called off the campaign. The saying is usually completed by 黃雀在後, 'the oriole is behind', and describes anyone so absorbed in a target that they miss the larger threat closing on them. A parallel version appears in the Zhuangzi.
chineseExample_tr: 一心想壓過對手，公司沒察覺自己的債務正在累積

example: The safety rules had been spelled out at every briefing before the accident
chineseExample: 事故发生前，安全规程在每次简报上都被反复强调
description: The Records of the Grand Historian anchors this phrase in Sun Wu's audition for the King of Wu, who asked whether the theorist could really drill troops and gave him a hundred and eighty palace women to try it on. Sun Wu formed them into two companies under the king's two favourite concubines, set out the drum signals, and went over the orders repeatedly (三令五申) before beginning. The women only laughed. He said that when orders are unclear the fault is the general's, but when they are clear and still disobeyed the fault is the officers' — and had the two favourites executed over the king's protest. The rest drilled in perfect silence afterwards. The phrase now describes rules laid down so often that nobody can claim not to have heard them, and it usually carries the implication that they were broken anyway.

example: They changed neighbourhoods twice to put their daughter near a better school
chineseExample: 为了让女儿就近上更好的学校，他们搬了两次家
description: Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women tells how the mother (母) of Meng Ke (孟) — Mencius — moved house three (三) times (迁) for her son's sake. They lived first beside a graveyard, and the boy took to imitating funeral processions and mourners' wailing. She moved to a house by the market, and he began playing at hawking wares and haggling over prices. Only when she settled beside a school did he copy the ritual, courtesy and study he saw around him, and she said this at last was a place fit to raise a son. The story made Mencius's mother the standard figure of maternal devotion in Chinese culture. The idiom is still used of parents who uproot the household for a child's education, sometimes admiringly and sometimes with a light edge.

example: His copy of the textbook had lost its spine from constant rereading
chineseExample: 他那本教科书翻得书脊都散了
description: Books in Confucius's day were bamboo slips strung together with leather (韦) thongs. The Records of the Grand Historian says that in his later years he so loved the Book of Changes that the thongs binding (编) his copy wore through and snapped (绝) three (三) separate times, and that he remarked he would master the book if granted a few more years. The image is precise about what devotion looked like before paper: not a note in a margin but a volume physically destroyed by rereading. It is reserved for study pursued to that depth, and stays closer to high praise than to an everyday compliment.

meaning: So happy, no thought of Shu
example: Three years into the posting abroad, he had stopped talking about moving back
chineseExample: 外派三年后，他已不再提起回国的事
description: When the kingdom of Shu fell in 263, its last ruler Liu Shan was resettled in Luoyang and given a comfortable title. The Han Jin Chunqiu, quoted in the commentary to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, describes a banquet at which his conqueror Sima Zhao had Shu music and dancing performed. Shu's former officials wept; Liu Shan enjoyed himself. Asked whether he missed his homeland, he said 此间乐，不思蜀 — 'it is pleasant here, I do not think of Shu.' An old minister coached him to answer next time that his father's graves lay west and he grieved for them daily. When Sima Zhao asked again and Liu Shan recited it, Sima Zhao said it sounded remarkably like the minister's words, and Liu Shan agreed that it was. The idiom is used of anyone so comfortable in new surroundings that home, duty or origin quietly stops mattering.
metaphoric_meaning: Too content to think of home

example: The redesign was announced with fanfare and then simply stopped being mentioned
chineseExample: 改版计划大张旗鼓地宣布，之后就再没人提起
description: Four characters that describe exactly what they name: 有 (have) 头 (head) 无 (lack) 尾 (tail). The picture is of a thing that begins and then simply stops — no ending arrives, not even a poor one. That is what separates it from its close cousin 虎头蛇尾, 'tiger head, snake tail', where a finish does arrive but arrives feeble; here there is no finish at all. It is the flat opposite of 有始有终, and the two are used as a matched pair of judgements about a person's character rather than about any one abandoned task. The phrase travelled well beyond Mandarin: Hokkien speakers say it as ū thâu bô bué, and a learner is as likely to meet it in Taiwan, Fujian or Singapore as in Beijing.

example: The winning general was thanked and then destroyed
chineseExample: 大功告成之后，那位功臣反而被清算了
description: Fan Li, having helped Goujian of Yue destroy Wu, left at once and wrote to his colleague Wen Zhong telling him to do the same: 飞鸟尽，良弓藏；狡兔死，走狗烹 — when the birds are gone the good bow is put away, when the cunning hares are dead the running hounds are cooked. Goujian, he warned, was a man to share hardship with but not ease. Wen Zhong stayed and was ordered to kill himself. Han Xin quoted the same lines at his own arrest centuries later. The other half, 鸟尽弓藏, is used interchangeably.
metaphoric_meaning: Discard allies once they are useless

meaning: Bend the chimney, move the firewood
example: The engineer who warned about the fault was not invited to the review
chineseExample: 当初提出隐患的工程师，事后并没有被请去参加复盘
description: A guest noticed that his host's chimney ran straight up beside a stack of firewood, and advised him to bend (曲) the flue (突) and move (徙) the wood (薪). The host said nothing. The house burned; the neighbours who scorched themselves putting it out were feasted in order of injury, and the man who had given the advice was not invited. The Book of Han draws the moral in a line usually quoted with the idiom: 曲突徙薪亡恩泽，焦头烂额为上客 — bending the flue and shifting the wood earns no gratitude, while the scorched and blistered are seated as honoured guests.

meaning: Speak of the tiger, face changes
example: Anyone who lived through that crash still changes colour at the word
chineseExample: 经历过那场崩盘的人，至今一提起就变了脸色
description: The Cheng brothers' recorded conversations distinguish knowing about a thing from having met it. Everyone knows tigers are dangerous, they observed, but the man whose face changes (色变) when a tiger (虎) is merely mentioned (谈) is the farmer who was mauled by one. The point is epistemological: his knowledge and yours use the same words and are not the same knowledge. The phrase is used of a fear that is disproportionate on paper and entirely earned in fact.

example: One committee vote against a decision already taken elsewhere
chineseExample: 在早已定案的事情上投一张反对票
description: In the Zhuangzi, Qu Boyu advises Yan He, who has just been appointed tutor to the violent heir of Duke Ling of Wei: 汝不知夫螳蜋乎？怒其臂以当车辙，不知其不胜任也 — do you not know the mantis, which raises its arms (螳臂) against (当) an oncoming cart (车) without knowing it cannot stop it? That is the excellence of its nature, and it is what will kill it. The image is not simply of futility — the mantis is brave and correct about the threat, and wrong only about the arithmetic. Chinese uses it of hopeless opposition, and it keeps a trace of respect for the insect.

description: Using (以) an egg (卵) to strike (击) a stone (石). The comparison appears across the Warring States philosophers and its point is that the outcome does not depend on force, effort or resolve — the mismatch is in the materials, and no amount of determination changes what an egg is. That distinguishes it from ordinary long odds. Chinese uses it for confrontations that are settled before they begin, usually to argue that the weaker party should choose different ground.

meaning: Cut the foot to fit the shoe
example: They kept the deadline and cut the parts of the product that made it worth having
chineseExample: 为了赶上原定的期限，他们砍掉了产品真正有价值的部分
description: The Huainanzi asks what kind of person, finding the shoe too small, would pare (削) the foot (足) to fit (适) it (履), or cut off the head to suit the hat. The absurdity is the argument. What the phrase names is the specific inversion in which the standard, the plan or the schedule is treated as fixed and the actual thing is trimmed to match — and Chinese uses it constantly about targets, quotas and processes that have outlived the purpose they were built for.
metaphoric_meaning: Distort the substance to fit the form

example: He spent his life on a proof nobody expected anyone to finish
chineseExample: 他把一生都投在一个没人指望能完成的证明上
description: The Classic of Mountains and Seas tells of the giant Kuafu (夸父), who set himself to race (逐) the sun (日). He caught up with it at the place where it sets, was seized by thirst, drank the Yellow River and the Wei dry, set off north for the great lakes and died on the road. His staff, thrown down, became a forest of peach trees. Chinese readers have argued for two thousand years about whether the story admires him or not, and the phrase carries both readings — overreach, and the grandeur of it.

example: Twenty minutes a day for a year is more practice than most people ever get
chineseExample: 每天二十分钟，一年下来比大多数人一辈子练的都多
description: Accumulate (积) the few (少) and it becomes (成) many (多). Dong Zhongshu argues the principle in a memorial recorded in the Book of Han, though in different characters — 众少成多，积小致钜, many small things make much, and accumulating the little reaches the enormous. Chinese pairs the modern form freely with related images: 聚沙成塔, sand into a pagoda, and 集腋成裘, armpit-fur into a fur coat, both of which are in this collection. What distinguishes this one is its plainness — no metaphor at all, just the arithmetic. It is the phrase used about savings, vocabulary and daily practice.

example: He never forgot who had lent him the deposit, and it showed twenty years later
chineseExample: 当年借他押金的人，二十年后他依然记得
description: Han Xin, starving and unemployed, was fed for weeks by an old washerwoman at the riverside. When he offered to repay her some day she was unimpressed, saying she had fed him because he was hungry and wanted nothing. Years later, made King of Chu, he had her found and sent her a thousand in gold (千金) for those meals (一饭). The Records of the Grand Historian sets the gift beside his other repayments: the village head who had turned him out got a hundred coins and a lecture on doing good by halves, and the youth who once made him crawl between his legs was given a post. Each sum is a verdict. The phrase means returning a kindness out of all proportion to it.
